docs.title: Conference Vaults
docs.text:
Per-conference vaults for biomedical, bioinformatics, and AI/ML meetings. Every page is sourced, cross-linked, and structured for re-use: tool entries with "How it works" deep-dives, trial dossiers with subgroup analyses, launch dossiers with vendor-PR vs. independent-benchmark labels.

Successor to conference-corpus. The FM → Virtual Cells talk-prep and knowledge-base content lives in fm-to-virtual-cells (password-gated). This site keeps the per-conference vault content.

docs.title: At a glance
docs.text:
• 37 conferences scaffolded across 2025–2026
  • ~109 deep dossiers built (tools / trials / launches / talks / keynotes)
  • 36-row Gantt timeline with a 4-criterion scoring rubric — see 2026 Timeline
  • 13 vaults content-complete · 24 scaffolded for live coverage at each meeting window

docs.title: Built vaults
docs.text:
Anchor — cancer research umbrella:

  • AACR 2026 — ~26 sessions, ~2,300 posters across 5 topics (agentic AI, single-cell & spatial omics, virtual cells, bioinfo / comp bio / AI methods, clinical trials). 6 tool dossiers (CHIEF, Prov-GigaPath, UNI, scGPT, Geneformer, Cell2Location).

Industry — financial / strategic:

  • JPM 2026 — J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference. Day-by-day digests + cross-day themes.

Bioinformatics / methods (full per-tool corpus):

  • Nextflow Summit 2026 — 3 session transcripts, day digests, themes.
  • EuroBioC 2025 — 26 tool dossiers + 6 keynotes + 3 day digests + themes. Every tool entry has a "How it works" methodology section.
  • GBCC 2025 — 32 tool dossiers (Bioconductor + Galaxy + integration) + 3 keynotes + 3 day digests + themes.

Sequencing platforms — public coverage:

  • AGBT 2026 — 23 platform launch dossiers (Roche Axelios 1, Element VITARI, Ultima UG200, Complete DNBSEQ-T7+, PacBio CiFi, Illumina TruPath, 10x Atera, etc.).

Cancer-clinical — retrospective trial dossiers:

  • ASCO GI 2026 — 6 trials (HERIZON-GEA-01, BREAKWATER cohort 3, daraxonrasib/zoldonrasib PDAC, REFOCUS, KEYNOTE-937, MSS-CRC synthesis).
  • ASCO GU 2026 — 6 trials (KEYNOTE-B15/EV-304, LITESPARK-022, PEACE-3, PSMAaddition, CAPItello-281, IMvigor011).
  • AACR Brain Tumors 2026 — 8 talks (CAR-T architectures, GD2 DIPG, vorasidenib combos, IDH vaccine, cell-state framework).
  • SGO 2026 — 8 trials (ROSELLA, RUBY 4-yr OS, BLUESTAR, MIRV maintenance, REJOICE-Ovarian01, etc.).
  • ACMG 2026 — 7 talks (NBS expansion, LLM ACMG/AMP classification, CHIP/mosaicism, NIFS, SF v3.3, hereditary cancer).

AI/ML — filtered light builds:

  • ISBI 2026 — 8 tool dossiers (Mahmood pathology FM keynote, Golland VoxelMorph, RIVA challenge, WBCBench2026, FAIBI workshop, segmentation FMs).
  • ICLR 2026 — 8 tool dossiers (sc-Arena, MedAgentGym, Generative Virtual Cells, Proteina Complexa, sc-FM Perturbation Adapter, MMedAgent-RL, Genomic ICL in Evo2, TEA).

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
1. Start at the 2026 Timeline for the year-at-a-glance Gantt plus a scoring matrix of every conference.
  2. Pick a vault from the top nav — each conference has its own tab with overview + program-notes + per-tool / trial / talk pages.
  3. Within a built vault — per-tool entries include a methodology "How it works" deep-dive; trial dossiers include design + subgroup analyses + FDA implications; launch dossiers cite source-per-spec with vendor-PR flags.
  4. Search — top-right search indexes session transcripts and page content site-wide.

See extraction notes and caveats for sourcing details.

docs.title: Rubric
docs.text:
We score each conference 0–2 on four criteria.

Criterion 2 1 0 Axis fit — extends ≥1 of the AACR axes (agentic AI, single-cell/spatial, virtual cells, bioinfo/AI methods, clinical trials) multiple axes one axis none Source accessibility — public material to extract from full abstracts / transcripts public coverage only closed Signal density — selectivity / SNR tight, high per-talk relevance broad, with relevant sub-tracks high noise Adds new vantage — covers a stage or domain we don't already have yes, distinct partial overlap duplicates existing

Build decision: Total ≥6 → full vault · 4–5 → light scaffold + selected dossiers · ≤3 → skip.

docs.title: What we're skipping (and why)
docs.text:
Nothing yet — all 12 cleared the bar at 4+. Two scored "light" rather than "full":

  • ESMO 2026 (5) — partial overlap with ASCO. We'll pull abstracts but lean on a single landscape page rather than full topic decomposition.
  • NeurIPS 2026 (4) — methods-relevant but huge and noisy. Filter to ML4Health, Foundation Models for Science, and AI-for-Drug-Discovery workshops only.

Conferences considered but not added (would score below 4 against this rubric):

  • HIMSS — health IT / business, low axis fit
  • AHA Scientific Sessions — cardiology, low axis overlap
  • AAAI / CVPR / ICML — methods-relevant but signal-density problem similar to NeurIPS; would duplicate that filter

If the rubric weights ever change (e.g., we start caring about cardio-onc, or open a "platform/biz" axis), this list flips fast.

docs.title: How to use this site
docs.text:
1. Browse by topic — each topic tab has a filterable, sortable poster table and a session list. Click any poster row to expand its full abstract in place.
  2. Search — the top-right search indexes session transcripts and page content. Poster abstracts are in the embedded tables (use the per-table search box for those).
  3. Read a session transcript — open the "Session Transcripts" tab for the full list, or click through from any topic page.

Cross-topic symlinks

Sessions often belong to multiple topics (e.g., Bo Wang's talk is both "agentic-ai" and "virtual-cells"). Each transcript has exactly one canonical page here; a topic page may list the same transcript cross-referenced from elsewhere.

docs.title: Corpus notes
docs.text:
• All session captions are Vimeo AI-generated English. Expect misheard names ("Bunne" → "Bonner", "Foersch" → "Firsch") and acronyms ("scGPT" → "SC-GPT"). See Caveats.
  • Poster abstracts are HTML-decoded and tag-stripped from the AACR Abstracts Online JSON; original HTML entities preserved.
  • Clinical-trial session transcripts were deferred — minisymposium content is largely a serial read of the posters. See the Clinical Trials page for the list of session IDs extractable on demand.

Source data lives in the transcripts/ and raw/ directories of the aacr-2026 GitHub repo (private).

docs.title: 2026-04-17-decoding-tumor-evolution-human-tumor-atlas-network
docs.text:
Date: 2026-04-17 Primary topic: single-cell-spatial-omics Cross-referenced from: single-cell-spatial-omics Word count: ~12,795

Auto-generated captions

This transcript is Vimeo auto-generated English. Expect misheard names and technical terms. Use the ripgrep/search approach for exact quotes.

All right. It is on the hour, so I will go ahead and kick off this session. For me, this is not just kicking off the session, but it's also kicking off the entire meeting. This is probably true for many of you. So today's session is entitled Decoding Tumor Evolution through the Human Tumor Atlas Network. We have one introductory talk from a program officer at the National Cancer Institute who will start out by telling you a little bit about the Human Tumor Atlas Network, and then we have three scientific talks representing three of the 10 atlases in HTAN. There's no time for questions after the first introduction, but there will be time after each one of the scientific talks. So without further ado, I'll introduce our first speaker, Dr. Indu Kohar, a program officer at the National Cancer Institute, who will tell you a little bit about the Human Tumor Atlas Network. Thank you, Hunter. A very good afternoon to all, and I thank the chair and the organizing committee for giving an opportunity to present and introduce our NCI's Human Tumor Atlas Network program. It's not moving. Okay. I have no financial relationships to disclose, and I'm here representing the entire NCI HTAN team. Members span across the various divisions of NCI as well as within the NIH. We know that traditional hallmarks are the basic guiding principles for malignant transformation of cancer from pre-cancer to advanced disease. But these relationships between these hallmarks are evolving, and the HTAN program is addressing such evolving relationship between the cancer hallmarks, starting from pre-cancer to late-stage disease. Again, the deep understanding of the biology of the carcinogenesis cannot be done without the advancement in the spatial omics technologies, and I'm here listing some of the recent technologies which include spatial transcriptomics, spatial proteomics, spatial metabolomics, spatial multi-omics, and 3D/4D spatial profiling. The NCI's Human Tumor Atlas Network program is a collaborative initiative to map the tumor evolution at a single-cell resolution. It aims to build highly dynamic three-dimensional atlases of pre-cancer and tumor. The main goals include the integration of molecular, cellular, and tumor tissue composition and architecture involving the tumor microenvironment and immune milieu, describe the transition across the cancer spectrum, premalignant lesions to malignancy, locally invasive to metastatic cancer, responsive to resistant cancer type, with the ultimate goal of enabling predictive modeling to refine detection and therapeutic choices. HTAN program was funded under two cycles, under Phase I, which was from 2018 to 2024. It encompasses various tumor types. Six of them are listed here: lung, pancreas, colon, breast, skin, and pediatric. The highlights from the HTAN Phase I is published in a collection in a "Nature" journal. It is a publicly available set of spatially resolved tumor maps describing transitions in cancer for use by the cancer research community. Some of the important discoveries include one study which examined the interaction among cancer as well as the non-cancer cells in six different tumor types. The study identified distinct substructures, which are called microregions, within the tumors, which have been associated with different activities and interactions, as indicated by a specific metabolic state or a T cell profile. Several studies also focused on colorectal cancer, including two that defined early molecular events that drive the transformation of precancerous lesions in colon to cancer. Two studies focused on breast cancer. One used single-cell sequencing, RNA sequencing to profile metastatic cancer from 60 individuals, while the other described the underlying genetic networks that define the breast cancer subtypes. Some of the common themes that came across these tumor types and analysis include the recurring pattern of cellular spatial patterns that is indicative of co-evolution of tumor and stroma, which are emerging drivers as progression of progression and resistance. Additionally, discovery of rare transitional dedifferentiated or plastic tumor cell types often conserved across tumor subtypes and correlated with the poor outcome. In addition, the study addressed the deep exploration of stroma immune and immune cell interactions. So far, HTAN has led to more than 200 publications and preprints, with 20-plus primary atlas publications and 50-plus new analytical and experimental tools. So the findings of the HTAN Phase I drives the implementation of HTAN Phase II, which was initiated in 2024 and is still ongoing. It is complementary to HTAN Phase I with respect to the diversity of the tumor types. It includes PCA as well as HTA center. PCA is the Pre-Cancer Atlas centers, which include skin, pancreas, brain, gastric, and myeloma, whereas the HTA centers include prostate, colon, ovary, lymphoma, and pediatric solid tumors.This is the general structure of the NCI Human Tumor Atlas Network, comprising of five BCA centers, five Human Tumor Atlas centers, the HTAN Data Coordinating Center, which manages the data, as well as the HTAN Steering Committee, which governs the program. In addition, there are several subcommittees and working group, including Precancer Atlas Subcommittee, Advisory Committee for Data Coordination, Methods Working Group, Visualization Working Group, Translational Working Group, and Outreach Working Group. HTAN is built on four core principles. One is the community resource, complement approaches, open communication, and data and resource sharing. Here, I'm showing how the HTAN data sharing and community engagement takes place. All these atlases, along with certain cross-network projects, generate huge amount of data. This data is then ingested by the Data Coordinating Center that uses their data platform and provides standards, validation, management, and governance. The data sharing is facilitated by HTAN portal, Cancer Data Service, ISP's Cancer Gateway, and Seven Bridges. Further, the DCC, the Data Coordinating Center, facilitates the community engagement through user supports, manuals, workshop, working groups, and data jamboree. This is a snapshot of HTAN data portal. Here is the QR code, which you can scan if you want to get more information on the various data and resources and tools available in the HTAN portal. As you see, there are 14 atlases now, spanning across 20 organ types with 2,400 cases and approximately 10,000 biospecimens. HTAN is not alone. It is part of a broader atlasing ecosystem. It is collaborating actively with the Human Protein Atlas, Chan Zuckerberg Initiative, Human Cell Atlas, HuBMAP in various ways, through a working group, workshops, cross-consortium metadata, as well as spatial biology meeting. How can you be part of HTAN? So HTAN basically offers researchers which are not currently funded by HTAN the opportunity to apply to join the program as non-voting associate members. If you want to be associate member, you please contact the HTAN Data Coordinating Center, email is listed here. And that way you will be able to engage in HTAN consortium activities through working groups, annual meetings, and developing collaborations. Overall, in summary, the NCI's HTAN program is addressing tumor evolution to accelerate cancer discovery. It is built for scale and collaboration. It's a NCI-funded network comprising of tumor atlas as well as precancer atlas centers, built by multidisciplinary teams, unified standards via Data Coordinating Center. It answers the questions beyond the scope of single study, addresses tumor heterogeneity and microenvironment at single-cell resolution, builds multidimensional atlas from precancer through metastasis, help identify biomarkers of detection, prognosis, and treatment response, additionally generates new biological insights and hypothesis. It also provides open data to the community, which they can use today through HTAN data portal. With that, I'll end my presentation here. Thank you so much. Thank you, Indu. And as I said, we did not build in time after Indu's talk, but if you do have questions, you can come up and introduce yourself afterwards. So my name is Hunter Shane, and I am one of the co-PIs of one of the phase two atlases, the precancer atlas of skin cancer. And I'm thrilled to also chair this session and kick off the scientific talks for today's session. So I will walk you through the journey from a normal type of skin cell known as a keratinocyte, to a common form of skin cancer known as cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma. These are my disclosures. And if you want to understand the evolution of cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, you need to first start by understanding what are the somatic alterations in normal skin cells. And I'll pose the thought experiment to the audience, and that's how might you do that. Your reflexive reaction is probably to just sequence normal skin, and this is not a bad idea. But the problem with this approach is that it gives you an average signal from the complex mixture of cells that are there. Now, to be sure, this has been used to great success in the past. You can go all the way back to 1994 when Doug Brash's group used this approach to show that there are p53 mutant patches of keratinocytes in normal human skin. And then, of course, Inigo Martin-Carrena and colleagues really turbocharged this approach in 2015 in a landmark paper, to show more generally the mutational landscape of clonally related patches of keratinocytes in human skin. But I would argue the ideal resolution to do this would be at single-cell resolution. In my opinion, single-cell DNA sequencing technologies have come a long way, but they still suffer from low levels of sensitivity and specificity in their mutation calls. And so to get around this challenge, our laboratory developed the following workflow, where we start out by extracting a bulk population of skin cells, and then we single-cell sort them so that there is now one cell per well in a 96-well plate. We clonally expand these cells as much as possible. These are cells from normal tissue, so they have a limited replicative ability. But it is easier to genotype from a starting point of, let's say, 100 cells than one cell. But to finish the job, we would lyse these small colonies of cells, releasing their genomic DNA and mRNA, and then further amplify these nucleic acid populations in vitro.And between the combination of ex vivo clonal expansion, in vitro nucleic acid amplification, and a heavy dose of bioinformatics that I'm not going to go into, we are able to call somatic alterations in individual skin cells at nearly 100% sensitivity and specificity. I think the value of this data is best exemplified with an example. And shown here is a skin biopsy that measures three millimeters in diameter. I hope you can appreciate that for all intents and purposes, this is physiologically normal human skin. It came from the back of a 75-year-old woman. She did have a previous history of skin cancer, as well as self-reported high levels of cumulative UV exposure. But this is normal skin from which we genotype 10 individual keratinocytes. And the first thing I want to point out to you is that many of these so-called normal keratinocytes actually have mutations known to drive keratinocyte carcinogenesis. This trio of cells has a biallelic loss of function NOTCH1 mutations, as well as loss of function mutations affecting p53, FAT1, PBRM1, NOTCH2. And then two of these cells further acquired yet another NOTCH1 mutation. And then one of these cells acquired yet another NOTCH2 mutation. And so if you're keeping count, these cells have up to eight pathogenic mutations in the same cell. Now, if you had done bulk cell sequencing, you might have gotten lucky and detected some of these mutations, but you would have never recognized that they were co-occurring within the same cell. Cancer is thought to arise after the accumulation of four to five pathogenic mutations, and so we were somewhat surprised that these cells can tolerate up to eight driver mutations, and yet that is insufficient to form a discernible neoplasm. Now, the second thing I want to point out is that many of these cells are clonally related. I cannot say with any degree of certainty how these clonally related cells are spatially organized, but we have drawn a schematic here of how they may have theoretically been organized. And this is drawn to scale if you assume that the size of each clonally related patch of keratinocytes is proportional to the number of cells within it. A couple things to point out here. It's perhaps not surprising that the cells with pathogenic mutations have formed a patch, but you'll see that there are also these two patches of keratinocytes without any apparent pathogenic mutations. And not only that, they are of a similar size, and I'll circle back to that point in a couple of slides. Now, the last thing I want to point out to you is the extraordinary range of mutation burdens of these cells. And you might not have initially recognized this because I had to introduce a break in the y-axis in order to plot all this data on the same graph. But these three cells with pathogenic mutations have 40 times as many mutations as their neighboring cells without pathogenic mutations. So what's going on here? What's shown here is more generally the landscape of somatic alterations from individual keratinocytes. And exactly as I showed you in the previous slide, somewhat paradoxically, most keratinocytes actually have somewhat low mutation burdens with relatively low proportions of UV radiation-induced DNA damage. But there's this tail of keratinocytes with extraordinarily high mutation burdens. And when you ask what's notable about them, every single one of these has an underlying pathogenic mutation, typically in the p53 or Notch signaling pathway. So this is another example where had you done bulk sequencing, you would have correctly deduced that the average mutation burden per cell is around five mutations per megabase, but you would have missed the fact that this is actually a mixture of cells with one mutation per megabase and some with up to 50 mutations per megabase. Now, this is a classic example of a mutator phenotype, meaning that these p53 and Notch pathway mutations are causing those cells to accumulate mutations more rapidly than their neighboring cells. But are they doing something else, such as inducing a proliferative advantage? And I'm not so sure that they are. So shown here is the inferred surface area of each clonally related patch of keratinocytes that we could detect in the study. I'd like to thank, of course, AACR for this wonderful time and, above all, NCI and H10, because this has been really a wonderful collaboration between all of the H10 members, and we've been learning a lot from all of the different cancers. So I'll take you through our multiple myeloma atlas and really understanding the transition from precancerous MGUS and smoldering myeloma to overt myeloma and how we can prevent it. These are my conflicts of interest. So if you think about multiple myeloma, it has two well-known transitions of precursor conditions. One is called MGUS, monoclonal gammopathy of undetermined significance, and the other one is smoldering myeloma. And they're very different because MGUS is very common in the general population. Anyone over the age of 50, it's about 3% to 5% of us walking around with it, and it increases more and more as we get older. Smoldering myeloma, which is defined by having 10% plasma cells or cancer cells in your bone marrow, is the next transition of that. And in these patients, their chance of progression to overt myeloma to end organ damage is much higher. So instead of being only 1% per year, now it's 10% per year, so 10 times higher. And in some of those patients, when we see them, they have something called high-risk smoldering myeloma, meaning that they will go on to develop end organ damage or overt myeloma, 50% chance in two years. So when I sit down with a patient and I see them and I tell them, "You have high-risk smoldering myeloma," I'm basically telling them, "You have a 50/50 chance of getting fractures in your bones, kidney failure, anemia in the next two years." And yet we do nothing about it. So we had a question, and part of the H10 was this: Can we be more precise in our definition of who is high risk in the population, and who are those patients who we should be treating early, while others who may never progress in their lifetime, we should leave them alone? And currently, the markers that we use are basically very clinical markers. How much tumor burden you have, how many plasma cells you have in your bone marrow, are they 20%? How much M spike you have, which is the protein we secrete in the blood or light chains. And these are really only tumor burden markers. They don't tell you anything about the biology. They don't tell you anything about the immune system or genomic alterations. So we asked the question, should we really intervene in those patients early? And we're trying to look basically like the solid tumor people, like breast cancer. In breast cancer, we screen early and we use mammography or colonoscopy in colon cancer. Yet I can tell you in multiple myeloma, a blood disease, we can use a very simple blood test called serum protein electrophoresis, and it's much easier to screen by a blood test than doing mammography or colonoscopy. And even when we find those patients with high-risk smoldering myeloma, which is very much like a malignancy, like a Stage 1 or Stage 2 breast cancer, we tell our patients, "Watch and wait. Do nothing until you have metastasis everywhere, basically." Just like metastatic breast cancer. Wait until you have fractures, bone disease, or kidney failure, and then I treat you. And that's a problem. That's basically saying to a patient with multiple myeloma, "Wait until you have advanced disease, and then I treat you." So the way we were thinking of this is can we diagnose those patients early and potentially treat them early and shift the way of thinking into an early interception?To do that, you need to be more precise in your risk stratification. So I'll show you some of the work that we've been doing with our H10 collaboration here. And the first one was trying to understand the genomic alterations that can be predictive of progression in our patients. So here we took 218 patients with MGUS and smoldering myeloma and compared it to patients who have already gone to overt multiple myeloma, and we did whole genome sequencing. And this is hard to do from peripheral blood or bone marrow cells, especially when you have very small numbers of cells. But we were able to find those alterations, and then we put them on a scale. We wanted to make this something that's clinically relevant for our patients, so I can tomorrow go to the clinic and tell them, "Here is your genomic score." And we call that the MM-like score. And it's a simple score of how many you have that are more MGUS-like, which is only 14, 16, or 14, 20, and how many are myeloma-like, which, as you see here, NRAS, KRAS, 1q amplification, MYC alterations, and so on. And you balance them, and if you have more of the one, then you're more myeloma-like, and if you have more of the MGUS-like, then you're actually MGUS-like, even if you have a high tumor burden. And that's a critical one that we can now use in the clinic. But we said, "Well, that's not really using single-cell level information, and that's also not looking at the transcriptional changes that occur in the patients." We know that many patients may have a 14, 16, or a 1q amplification, and yet they don't progress to multiple myeloma. There is something more beyond the genomic alterations of those patients. So we decided to do single-cell sequencing with BCR sequencing so that we can truly look at the malignant plasma cells versus the normal plasma cells. And here we looked at 1.7 million cells from 226 patients. And this was a collaboration with Gary Guss at the Broad Institute, where we tried to ask the question transcriptionally, what's happening in those patients? But because those are the same patients, we also did whole-genome sequencing. Another question was, what can you define beyond the DNA level and beyond genomic alterations? Now, this was a hard thing to do because we're now comparing tumor to tumor, but also bone marrow plasma cells versus peripheral blood circulating tumor cells, and we're also looking at normal cells versus normal cells. And you can ask a lot of the questions here. The first one we wanted to do is, can we look at those transcriptional changes that occur during transition from a normal plasma cell to an MGUS cell to a more malignant transformed smoldering myeloma or myeloma cell. And you can see that we found 16 transcriptional signatures that were defined in those populations, including cell cycle regulation, as you probably expect, MHC Class II, checkpoint regulation, and so on, circulatory capacity. But then we took those and went and tried to see which ones truly predict for you progression to multiple myeloma. And we found that six of those signatures were very critical for that progression from MGUS to smoldering myeloma to overt myeloma. And this is very critical, especially beta-2M, which is in the MHC Class I. And you can tell that this is critical because we use beta-2M as one of our predictors of progression in our patients, and the ISS classification of multiple myeloma. Now, we further validated that in the COMPASS data. This is a larger data set that has overt multiple myeloma from MMRF, and we indeed found that in the same signatures were found even if you have overt multiple myeloma. So this is not just the precursor conditions, but can also be applied in patients with overt myeloma, even when they receive therapy. Now, the next question we said is, well, that's good enough to have signatures, but let's try to find a classifier that can predict for me, if I take a patient with smoldering myeloma and I looked at their cells, I can tell where they are in their transition from normal to MGUS to smoldering to myeloma because the way that we classify our patients clinically may actually be wrong. I may be classifying some patients who have MGUS that truly have more smoldering myeloma in their transcriptional biological changes and vice versa. A patient with 10% plasma cells, so I call them smoldering myeloma, but they will never progress. They're behaving more like MGUS. So can I take your cell and by single-cell signatures, tell you where you stand in that transition period, and can I put it in the axis of progression? So here what we did is we tried to do a malignancy score and a disease score. Malignancy score just tells me, are you normal or a malignant plasma cell? And with 100% accuracy, we can tell at the single-cell level if this is a normal plasma cell or a malignant plasma cell. Then the next question is, what is the malignancy score as a disease progression from MGUS to smoldering to myeloma? And here we actually classified it from the MGUS and myeloma samples and then came back and looked at it in the smoldering samples. And we indeed found that you can create a score, we called it the MST score, that can predict for you progression, and it correlates, of course, with disease burden, with the light chain, with the M spike, but it can actually predict for you progression, not only in the MGUS and smoldering myeloma and myeloma patients, but also again in the COMPASS database, which is the overt myeloma patients. And that classifier is critical for us because again, beyond the DNA data, we can use it now in the clinic as a classifier to tell us at the transcriptional level what's happening to the patient. Now, the next question we asked is, can it add anything more beyond the DNA level? I already know that my patients have genomic signatures, which is the MM-like score. Should I add on it the RNA data, or is just reflecting what happened at the DNA level? And here what we did is we actually removed the DNA information because we found very weak correlation between RNA and DNA from the same patients, and we went back and said, "What is the transcriptional change that is occurring above and beyond what you have at the genomic level from the DNA mutations?" And you can find that the circulatory capacity, the ability of the cells to circulate in the peripheral blood, as well as histone chaperone proteins and genes, were critical for that transition, which tells you that there is a lot of work to be done beyond the DNA level to really tell us why those cells become more malignant, even in the early MGUS stages in our patients.Because circulatory capacity and because the CTCs, or circulating tumor cells, are so prognostic in our patients, and we know that by flow cytometry, we went back and said, "Then let's do a larger cohort of single-cell sequencing in the peripheral blood so that we can really define what's happening in the bone marrow, but only in the peripheral blood." Can I just use a blood sample from you and tell you if you have the genomic alterations that are in the bone marrow? And potentially, we can also stop doing bone marrow biopsies in our patients because they're very hard to do, and patients don't like to do it. So here, this is work that we did from 74 patients and 29 healthy control, where we looked at both the bone marrow biopsy and the peripheral blood over time, again, from healthy MGUS, smoldering, and myeloma. And what we did is, again, with 1.2 million cells, looking at single-cell BCR sequencing and transcriptional changes, looked at the tumor versus normal and peripheral blood versus bone marrow. But we asked a different question here. We said, "Can I predict what happens in the bone marrow on the FISH or whole genome sequencing data in a peripheral blood sample?" And here you can see with this confusion matrix, we were able to predict everything that you see in a bone marrow biopsy by FISH or whole genome sequencing in a peripheral blood sample, even in some of those samples that had some alterations that are not detected in the bone marrow. It was because they had a couple of clones that were different in the peripheral blood. And in fact, you can do that with only 10 cells. And that was the SwiftSeq method that we developed to try and predict progression in our patients, but also to give you value in a blood sample with 10 cells in the peripheral blood. Now, it's critical for us to think, as you always do, that tumor cells don't live alone, and they have an ecosystem of immune cells, non-immune cells, and the whole microenvironment. So we asked the question, can we look at the immune cell signatures, again, across time from MGUS to smoldering to myeloma, and what happens with an early myeloma cell interaction with immune cells, and can we harness that in the future for developing therapeutics, especially immune therapeutics, for our patients with smoldering myeloma? So here we took 877 tumor samples as well as immune cells and tried to do a large atlas, again, of immune cell signatures across the spectrum, healthy, MGUS, smoldering, myeloma. But because we also have the single-cell sequencing of the tumor cells, now we can look at the interaction between both of those types of cells. So we don't have time to go over all the data, but I'll show you some of the compositional and transcriptional changes. And over time, you can see that there is a lot of compositional changes that occur, including CD4 naive T cells, central memory T cells, including Tregs increasing over time as you go to myeloma, CD16 monocytes, and you have less plasmacytoid dendritic cells and CD14 monocytes. But what was interesting, because we have the tumor cells, we found a strong correlation between the cycling of the tumor cells and the granzyme B CD8 TEMs. And that was showing us that indeed, patients who are progressing from smoldering myeloma to overt myeloma are the ones who have more of those granzyme B CD8 TEMs, sort of trying to respond to the tumor cells and trying to respond to them in a way that is basically exhausted despite being effector cells. If you look at the immune programs in those and actually try to look not only at the compositional changes but at the signatures across all of the immune cells, you find that interferon signaling was present not only in the tumor cells but across many of the immune cells, T cells, myeloid cells, and so on, as well as other signatures that were correlating with myeloid suppressive cells. And the other thing that we did was T cell receptor clonality, and we tried to look at the TCRs in those patients. And what we found is that as you progress to overt myeloma, you have less and less diversity because you have very specific sub-clones of T cells that are responding potentially to those tumor cells. And we're now trying to look at all of those TCR clones that are expanding and responding to the tumor cells. Now, what else are we doing with the spatial question with the H10? Here we're trying to take all of this information and take it at the spatial transcriptomic and proteomic level. And to understand that, as we know very well, the bone marrow biopsies that we do in our patients are very hard to actually look at them because we do decalcification, which actually messes up all of your DNA and RNA, and then we put them in paraffin-embedded, and then we try to say, "Let's try to do what the solid tumor people do." But it's very hard to do that in bone marrow biopsies. But bone marrow biopsies are very critical because all of the data I showed you in bone marrow aspirates, which is what we pull first from the first pull of our patients, does not reflect everything that's happening. It's not just the spatial localization of the cells and how they interact with each other. You're also missing a lot of the stromal cells, adipocytes, as we talked about, endothelial cells, and so many other architectural changes that occur in the bone marrow. So we spent a lot of time trying to develop a spatial proteomic method, and here we used IMC, which is imaging mass cytometry, and we developed 36 antibodies that would work on IMC that we validated by immunohistochemistry and immunofluorescence to make sure indeed they work on a decalcified bone marrow biopsy. And you can see here that we have CD3 and CD138, then you can classify it as T cells and myeloma and so on, and finally have enough signatures of all of your tumor cells and immune cells to ask those questions. So when you look at all of this data, we started seeing that adipocytes, actually, because you lose them a lot when you're doing all of those cuts and decalcification in your bone marrow, we couldn't even call the adipocytes, and we couldn't call megakaryocytes because they're too big. So we had to develop a new package, which is available, called the AdipoFinder, where you can actually recapitulate the data of the adipocytes, and now look at all the cell-to-cell interactions in those patients. And we decided to look in a study of 98 samples of CAR-T, either cell or silta cell, so patients with multiple myeloma who received the cellular therapy, CAR-T. If I take their sample before going on the CAR-T therapy, can I predict whether they will respond to therapy or not? And can I predict their toxicity? These are very critical questions for us clinically.So the first thing we did is we started to look at those cellular neighborhoods, cell-to-cell interaction between myeloma cells, immune cells, and others. And it's very important to show that indeed it's not just any change that occurs in the bone marrow. The cells actually do sit in very specific cellular neighborhoods, and it's very similar to what we see in solid tumors. So when we look at those cellular neighborhoods and put them together, we start seeing indeed that some of those neighborhoods are actually predicting not only a progression-free survival to CAR T, but also overall survival in our patients. And many of those signatures were not just about tumor burden, which is in red here, the plasma cells or the tumor cells, they were also about the mixture between the tumor cells and the immune cells. So here is an example of how a tumor and immune cell interaction occurs, and sometimes it gives you a very bad prognosis, and sometimes it gives you a very good prognosis, which are very different depending on the types of myeloid cells or tumors to immune cell interaction that are sitting in that cellular neighborhood. And finally, we said it's not just about response to therapy, but also the cytokine release syndrome and the prolonged cytopenias that we see with our patients. Many of them may not recover their counts for a long time. Can we look at that inflammation that occurs in the microenvironment, and can we predict with accuracy that those patients will have potentially that inflammation, CRS, or prolonged neutropenia because we can potentially prevent it? And indeed, you can find that specific interactions between myeloid cells, and dendritic cells can predict for us prolonged neutropenias in our patients. So finally, why do we do all of this? We do this because we want to treat our patients. And I can tell you finally, we have the first FDA-approved drug for smoldering myeloma, which is daratumumab. But that's the beginning, not the end. And in fact, we want to actually improve things by using immunotherapy in our patients with smoldering myeloma. And to do that, we've done two clinical trials as a proof of concept that indeed you can make a difference by treating early and by harnessing the immune system with cellular therapy or bispecific antibodies. So here with a bispecific antibody called teclistamab versus LenDex, which is our traditional way of treating smoldering myeloma, we compared those patients and treated them to see if truly our hypothesis is true that your immune system is better in the earlier stages, that your tumor burden and your clonal evolution is not as extensive as it is in overt myeloma, then you should probably have an amazing response if you use your best therapy, immunotherapy, as early as possible. So with that, we showed the first data of the first 12 patients, but the study is completed, so hopefully we will show the rest of the data soon. But this shows you the first proof of concept that a bispecific antibody, a T-cell engager, showed us 100% response rate, 100% MRD negative disease, which means there's no evidence of tumor cells in the first 12 patients, and with less infections and less cytokine release syndrome compared to the overt multiple myeloma. And here is one of our patients. This was patient number two, and you can see his light chains were significantly high. And after just receiving the first few doses of teclistamab, you can see complete resolution of his lambda light chain, and it's still in an MRD negative disease three and a half years later. And he sent me this picture when he was bungee jumping in New Zealand, so I'm using this as the best quality of life measure for patients who are on a bispecific antibody. Now, the other study, which was also the hardest thing to do, was can we convince the FDA and pharmaceutical companies to give us cellular therapy, CAR T therapy, not in the relapse refractory setting, not in the newly diagnosed, but in smoldering, in asymptomatic patients. And I can tell you this will be a plenary session Monday morning, so please come and visit and hear us talking about it, of 20 patients who Omar Nadeem will be presenting with CAR T. But we showed the first six patients a couple of years ago, or actually last year in the American Society of Hematology. And this is a teaser for what you're going to see Monday. But again, 100% MRD negative disease with one and done cellular therapy, which tells you again that the proof of concept matters if you use your best therapy or immunotherapy and you use your T-cell engagers early on. So with that, I hope I took you through a journey of precursor multiple myeloma. Can we diagnose them early? Can we risk stratify them with genomic, with immune, with single-cell sequencing, and spatial transcriptomics and proteomics to really define those patients who will benefit from therapy? And then can we apply our best therapeutics, especially immunotherapy, in those patients to potentially intercept and cure our patients with myeloma? With that, I'd love to thank, of course, our lab members, clinical members, all our funders, Gaddy Getz, who all our work we do it in collaboration with him. And above all, our patients. Thank you. Yeah, thank you for the talk. It was super nice. Well, you said that you had BCR data for the single-cell analysis, and as far as I know, this premalignant condition can be kind of oligoclonal from the BCR level. Have you looked at it? Do you observe this oligoclonality? And if you do so, do you see differences in these scores from progressing to myeloma? Yeah, great question. So yes, all of our samples have BCR sequencing. And in fact, the more you go towards malignancy, the more there is a major BCR clone. And this is true also when we do VDG sequencing for adaptive. You may have other subclones, smaller subclones, but most of the time it's a major one clone. But you're right. And we have other studies that I didn't show here called MGAP, which is the very early event of a change of monoclonality, and you do see those oligoclonal cells, and they compete with each other until one of them actually becomes the major clone. This was not a journey, this was a rollercoaster. It was incredible. I know that multiple myeloma is also classified by significant hypomethylation. So we heard about transcriptomics and DNA. What is methylation play a role in the characterization and outcome for multiple myeloma? Yeah, great question. I think we are deficient in a lot of the epigenetic regulation, methylation, and so on, and we do definitely need to do more. There has been many studies, but not enough and not at the single-cell level. So absolutely, we need to do that. Okay. If there are no more questions, I want to thank the speakers for keeping us on time and for these great talks, and thank you, audience, for all of your questions. If you have any questions that you were too shy to ask, you can feel free to come up and introduce yourself afterwards. That closes today's session. Thank you.

Good afternoon. So just before I start, the QR code here is to submit online questions. So if you want to scan it briefly now and then you don't want to stand up to ask your question in public, you can do so via the QR code. So good afternoon and welcome to session ED03. I'm Charlotte Bonner. I'm an assistant professor at EPFL. I'm affiliated with Computer Science and Life Science, the AI Center and the Cancer Research Institute, and I'm super excited to share this session on foundation models and multimodal AI for cancer research. So cancer is inherently multimodal, so no single data type, let it be pathology or any other type of imaging, genomics or patient records really tells the full story on its own. And the promise of multimodal foundation models are really that they may finally let us aggregate everything that we can collect of a patient, and at the scale and in particular, the biological resolution that we need in order to understand the disease. So the question this session takes up is how do we build such multimodal foundation models? How do we connect them to agentic systems? And then how do we basically design them in a reliably enough way so that they can be used for cancer research and eventually patient care? So in the next 90 minutes, we will have three complementary talks that walk through the question of virtual patient representations with those multimodal foundation models. We talk about models that reason over disease dynamics and scientific knowledge. And last but not least, agentic systems that can plan and in particular, verify their own reasoning. Each talk is followed by a discussion window, so if you have questions or questions here will be dedicated to those minutes. So let's get started. I will actually give the very first talk. I will speak on virtual patients with multimodal foundation models and agents. So I will go to the next slide. As I just mentioned, cancer biology is multimodal. So we have not only multimodality, but often patient data that is really on a resolution of sometimes month, otherwise decades. And we can look at health records that are usually in natural language. We can look at genomic information. We have sometimes, especially for beyond standard of care patient, drug screening information. And then we have multiple ways of looking at tissue from the routine histopathology to, at this point, spatial omics, spatial proteomics, that give us really a molecular insight into a patient's tissue. And so the data collection I just screened here on the lab on the screen is not just an invented multimodal profile that we might have. In fact, it's the data corpus that is now sitting on the Swiss supercomputer that is from the Swiss Tumor Profiler study that looked at multimodal patient profiles to understand what do we need in order to best understand a patient biology and find the most accurate treatment. So how do we incorporate everything into some representation that we can grasp, something that we decode or call a virtual patient? We need to be able to look at all those modalities, combine the information that we have, and in particular, we need to deal with the fact that most of the time we will have only a subset of those modalities, and we need to complement some modalities with others. How do we do this across the scales of biology, where we have information on the molecular, on the cellular, on the tissue, and on the organ level? How do we integrate on the one hand, but how do we use those representations to now forecast in silico or simulate the what if? What if I would give this patient treatment A or treatment option B? And then ultimately, we need to incorporate everything to have some profile that lets us basically retrieve similar patient profiles. A patient that is very similar to a past case that I've seen where treatment A worked very well, or to find the best options or inclusion criteria for clinical trials. And this is a tremendous effort and really something that requires innovation on AI itself. So that's exactly what my lab is focusing on, building AI systems that allow us to build those virtual patient profiles. And what we think it needs is, on the one hand, multimodal foundation models about which we will talk today. It requires generative AI. That's something we will particularly cover in the second talk of this session. Can we now forecast the what if and simulate what would happen? Or even generate one modality from the other? And then last but not least, nothing is worthwhile if we have no systems to read all this information. We, at this point, actually know that those multimodal foundation models capture more than we think, but we have no way of extracting it. And we might use agentic system, or I will show you some initial generation of systems that decode us or give us AI-derived biomarkers that can be used for clinical decision-making. So a virtual patient is not built overnight. So we will start with a virtual tissue platform. How can we build those multimodal foundation models for tissue biology where we have so many different modalities that measure complementary but very different aspects of tissue? The goal again is to integrate all those different modalities that we have, use it to enable in silico forecasting. Is this the best foundation we have to now simulate the effect of a treatment? And then also extract novel biomarkers, and I will show youThose systems will enable us to actually guide what needs to be collected of a patient. Do we always need a spatial proteomics screen? No. Right? Many decisions can be simply made from routine pathology. But sometimes it's interesting to look at the molecular readout of protein A or protein B. Which is the most optimal panel? And so on and so forth. Many questions that AI can actually help us design. Let's look at classical methods that have found quite a success recently that are built on histopathology. So a generation of histopathology foundation model, what is special about histopathology, it's an RGB image, so an image that consists of three channels, red, green, blue. So something in AI we are very familiar with. We have vision transformers, in particular, those developed by Meta that are incredibly powerful and turns out we can use the same architectures for histopathology. So we are looking at histopathology in a way that we have a massive data corpus, many different cancer types, many different hospitals, thousands and hundred of thousands of slides. And now we are tiling those images in small patches and learn internal representations that are informative enough that we can use very small linear regression or linear probing to ask questions such as cancer subtyping, cancer grading, and so on and so forth. But the moment we use a different modality, if we want to get a molecular insight into a tissue and we move to a data type that is not just an H&E, we struggle. Why? Spatial proteomics, for example, is not an RGB image. It's an image where every assay looks at a set of proteins, and it might in clinical study A look at protein ABC, and then the next clinical study actually looks at protein DEF. And we actually have a lot of those proteins, so we have not three RGB, but actually sometimes 40, 80, 150 plex protein panels. So here it already starts. How do we build foundation models for those type of data modalities? And then right here I showed you just an initial cohort. We are at this point at 30 clinical studies where we train our foundation models. Here you see an initial set of 15. There's not a single study that has the same set of proteins. So we really need to step back and think, what is an AI architecture that is able to digest this complexity of data? And then in particular, histopathology records very different information from spatial proteomics. How can I use methods or how can I build multimodal foundation models that meaningfully integrate information from both that I can probe with either histopathology or spatial proteomics? So that's the very first part, and we already see that for integration, we need to think about new AI architectures. Thinking about those principles led us to write a perspective. You see many authors, many ideas. How do we build multiscale multimodal foundation models for cell biology, ultimately for cancer biology? And many of the ideas that we laid out in this perspective published in Cell are now in the architectures that I will present to you. So here's a multimodal foundation model, the very first foundation model that is truly multimodal. So it's not just learning a representation of one modality, a representation of another modality, but actually a joint representation that can be queried from either modality. And you see here that this is not any more a vision transformer developed by Meta for RGB data, but it's actually a transformer developed for biological samples. So from the level of tokenization, how do we define a unit that these transformers process until the loss function that defines the learning signal, this is all designed to be tailored for biological tissues. We need to decode the protein identity because the model has to process more than just this is channel red, this is channel green, this is channel blue. We are able to process here in the same way histopathology, but also the complexity of any random input of a set of protein markers measured in a spatial proteomics experiment. So this is an example of a multimodal foundation model, and I will show you in the next second what it enables us to do. How is it trained, right? For this, we need to collect datasets that are of a certain scale, and you can see here why those histopathology models are trained on hundreds of thousands of data. We have very, very few patients for which we have multimodal data. We've collected here the largest open source dataset that has, I think up to now, it's actually 5,003. The one that will be published is 4,605 patients for which we have spatial proteomics and histopathology. It requires also actually compute of quite a scale. So those models are actually trained and much larger than standard vision transformers because the data that it has to process is just simply much more complex. And we see that the more data we have, the more parameters those models need. How do we do this? Right? My lab is very small. We are working on Switzerland supercomputer, so national infrastructure that is built for cancer biology or that benefits cancer biology because those models get more and more demanding. It's one model with many capabilities, right? So this is the beauty of foundation models. We have a representation that is general enough to now ask many questions. We can look at simple classifier questions like what is the outcome? What is the cancer type? What is a certain mutation? But we can also look at the-- like do a tissue analysis. In particular, we can segment as well as cell type all in one shot.We can look at virtual staining. We might have only an H&E and want to decode what has been measured. And our model I will show you is actually better than models that have been only solely trained on this task. But we can also decode all the other proteome of the proteome that has not been measured. So we measure five of the minimum protein panel, and we actually just virtually stain the rest. But what I'm most excited about is that this type of model can actually guide experimental design. What is the most optimal protein panel? When is a histopathology enough? When is a spatial proteomics experiment needed? So, I'm really interested in the CellFlux MM. I'm wondering how does it fill the somatic gap between the visual morphological changes and the transcriptomic signature or molecular signature? Yeah. So, I think the idea here is that there's both complementary information from these different modalities. And so, I think one direction is that when you try to work on modeling them jointly together, you can try to leverage a data you have from both. I think a very interesting direction is taking small amounts of data where you have in those data sets both modalities, but also very large unimodal data sets. So there's much more data that's unimodal and trying to pull all of these together to try to achieve the improved models. And then the other direction is also trying to go from one modality to the other. So, for example, you may have cheaper imaging data and you want to also try to then predict what the transcriptomics may look like. And so I think ultimately, at the core of good performance of these models in general is having strong representations, and those strong representations that allow both joint modeling, but potentially also decoding between them. Okay. And another quick question about the flow matching. I know that the flow matching will provide a continuous and a very smooth trajectories, but how do you model some discrete transitions, like the apoptosis, and other biological process? Yeah. So I think this is a good question, and I think it is a challenge. I think that both we have to understand better what kinds of trajectories are being learned. So first of all, we are modeling these in the latent representation and to try to then understand what's being learned here. But I think also there is then also opportunity to look at these at multiple layers, like hierarchical modeling. So right now we may be looking at particular single cell transformations, but maybe you can look at what happens over also populations of cells and how those may evolve. And then I think there's also additional methods that will be needed to come in to properly model all these things. Thank you. Sure. Thanks. Hi. Great talk. You partially answered my question. I was also interested in the CellFlux MM. So it sounds like for the imaging and transcriptomics data, you have a small set of matched data and then a much larger set of non-matched data. So where you have the matched data, how are you ensuring that you have enough power to actually get a foundation model out of it? And then where it's not matched, so much of your talk talked about doing these distributions across different batch effects and things like that, so how are you handling that where you have unmatched transcriptomics and imaging data? Excuse me. So, I think you're right. I don't think the matched data pair data is enough to train... I mean, we don't have the data to train as large scale foundation models as we want. So I think the goal will be to take-To learn a single model, but that learns from matched data where that exists and learns from unimodal data where you have that. But you can bridge across them because you have each modality across both of these types of setups. Awesome. Thank you. Okay. Take a- First of all, thank you very much for this interesting talk. I just want to check the time because I can't see the time. Last one. Okay. I have this question. So I'm interested in training a vision language model, but my medical data consists of several images, but with one caption. The caption mentions some of the important findings from a few images. And do you think, is there a standard way to train vision language model in this case? So you're saying you're having multiple images- Mm-hmm. ... with a single caption? Yes. So yeah. So I think that the naive thing is, well, each image is associated with this caption. Or you have one big image, if this was a multi-panel image with a caption. But obviously, it will create noise. You may have signal overall. You may still get some model if this is a part of your data. But I think actually one promising route is caption rewriting. So are you able to, through some knowledge, you know something about how these images are different, but to be able to refine those captions to better fit each image individually. And so one possibility is using, in fact, you can use LLM sometimes to help with this or some agentic system where you're injecting some knowledge. But ultimately, if you want to say that these images correspond to different semantic concepts, then you will probably want to refine your captions to embody that. That makes sense. Thank you very much. And also, I want to mention that when I started studying deep learning, I saw separate videos of you from YouTube, and it's good to see you here. Thank you. This is a Stanford class on deep learning, so thank you. Thank you very much. Thanks so much, Serena. So we will have a final speaker, Michael Moore. He's an assistant professor of medical AI at ETH Zurich. So his work focus really on the development of agentic systems for medicine, and in particular on agents that can plan, evaluate, and verify their own reasoning. And that's exactly the capabilities that we will need before any of those systems will be deployed alongside physicians. So Michael's flight got canceled. The airline is on strike, so he's joining us remotely as a recorded talk. Let's see if this works. Welcome to my talk about reliable medical AI: agents that plan, evaluate, and verify. First of all, I'm very sorry I cannot make it in person. I assure you I have not been uploaded, but my flight had been canceled short notice. AI is permeating our everyday lives, if we want it or not. But there is a positive side. It will and should change healthcare as we know it to the better. It will help us better integrate multimodal data that might be spread across different systems and different formats, and will allow us to diagnose patients more comprehensively and earlier and help us also target therapies. But there are also some big obstacles in AI in medicine field. For instance, we have been working with models that require a very fixed type of data modality input, solve a very narrow problem, and are of limited explainability. I believe we need to work towards AI systems that are more flexible, that can ingest and produce different modalities interleaved, that can adapt and learn from context, and that are able to reason explicitly with biomedical knowledge and clinical intuition. This vision we first presented three years ago in a perspective, where we presented a new paradigm for how foundation models can unlock generalist medical AI. Meanwhile, there has been new challenges arising, especially around confabulated and unverified outputs, and here we really need to develop new methods, new strategies to ground and verify outputs of AI systems. The fundamental problem is that, despite recent advances of AI systems in the medical domain, many systems typically rely on language models, and they are just estimating a distribution over the most likely next word. And they are not necessarily grounded in the world. But this is a problem, because if a patient presents with a specific symptom, there might be an entire myriad of different differential diagnoses that might be rare hiding behind this patient. And to unravel this case, we need to actively seek information and collect various types of tests that might be different from case to case. So it is not enough to just learn about all the disciplines and all the diseases, et cetera, in a book, but we actually need to interact with environments.And this behavior is actually much harder for language models than previously assumed. We showed that already two years ago, that if you provide a language model, you confront it in some type of agent clinic where a doctor and patient are all played by language models, and you provide different tools to the doctor. It will be much harder for such a doctor agent to come up with the right diagnosis if the case has to be interactively worked up as compared to those case profiles where you have these exam-style benchmarks, where all the information is being presented on a silver platter. So here you see one by one how many models drop drastically in performance if they have to actually do the workup on their own. This brings us to where my research lab comes in. So we want to develop and evaluate flexible medical foundation models as well as AI agents that are grounded in multimodal biomedical knowledge. This covers different branches of topics, which we will go into more details next. To briefly tell you who I am or what I have done so far, I actually started out with medicine, pivoted then into a machine learning PhD at ETH Zurich, and then got completely lost to the machine learning and AI field at Stanford, where I did my postdoc for working on medical foundation models. And now since fall 2024, I have the pleasure to lead the medical AI lab at ETH Zurich. Okay. Now back to business. So how do we really unlock medical AI agents? What do we even mean with agents? We have heard this term a lot recently. And another question we want to also tackle here is how can we make them reliable? Because we don't want our AI agents to go delete our entire email inbox. So the first step is we need to make sure that our AI agents have access to some high-quality external knowledge sources, so they have to be grounded. But how do we do that? Conventionally, a language model would just take in a question, for instance, some instruction, and produce an answer. And in a more agentic environment, language agents would actually have some kind of environment at disposal where it can use different types of tools, query against databases, use calculator, and so on, to then come back with a more grounded or well-informed answer. And it also can take actions in this environment. So let's zoom in a little bit on how an agent should retrieve information. How did language models do that previously before we were talking so much about language agents? So a very classic paradigm is that we take a query provided to a language model, and then that language model is able to search some database of documents. This could, for instance, be your guideline documents that you care about. And then we retrieve some documents that are most relevant and then prepend that to the input to the same language model, and that will then produce an answer that has access to these very specific relevant guideline documents. This sounds all nice in theory, but the problem is that currently we use just a massive amount of text chunks that are completely unstructured. So retrieving from this is actually quite hard and quite leaky and noisy. What we would like to have is a more organized representation of the data, where there's a neat hierarchy, and we know exactly how to navigate the space to retrieve the needle from the haystack. I think this is also relevant in oncology, where it's really hard for an AI system to retrieve the exact single case study or paper that was relevant in a molecular tumor board. So to address this in a general medical domain, we propose this Myriad dataset and also approach. What we have been doing here is we basically try to get away from this unstructured approach of surfacing information to language models and structuring knowledge at scale into query-response pairs. This then enabled us to build a large-scale atlas of roughly six million medical question-answer pairs, each pair being grounded directly from a passage in the peer-reviewed medical literature. We actually find that Myriad on its own, just as a knowledge corpus, can be swapped in, and it can improve standard basic RAG applications. We see that it also has improvements in agentic RAG, hallucination detection. It can change how we do literature analysis and train retrievers. In this example here on a more challenging benchmark, MedExpertQA, we see that compared to standard RAG, we can improve quite a bit by just changing the representation of the same knowledge. This is not changing the content of the knowledge. It's just changing the representation in this Myriad format. AndI think it's also important to augment not only language models, but also to augment humans. So we also have some demo where we show this atlas and where humans can navigate this, explore, look up the QA pairs, click on the original sources to then provide feedback. So we now learn that we can improve language models and language agents by grounding them and by improving the methods of how we ground them. But how do we really make them more reliable? For this question, I would like to pivot over to a related project that we published last year at a leading natural language processing venue as an oral presentation. Which is now instead of connecting a language model to a neatly organized corpus of information, we're actually trying to take it a step further and say, well, it's not enough to just give a language model access to a neatly organized corpus of knowledge. We actually want to check individual reasoning steps that a language model produces. So previously, we just had this setup where a language model would make any sort of statement and on its own would have to go and check in the literature. Now, we try to disentangle those two tasks and have some kind of policing language model, which we in the field would call a process reward model, that would analyze each individual statement or reasoning step that the base language model does on the left. It has the ability to check the literature and guideline, et cetera, to then come back to the language model and say, "This step is correct. This step is wrong." And just by training such a verifier or such a process reward model, we can actually improve many different language model by just hook plugging it in at inference time. And this was quite interesting because in the general, like math or code domain, we don't see this generalizability. We're also following this work up with endowing this critique or this reward model with more capabilities. And this we then call a process reward agent, where you can see on the left, language model might perform an entire tree search over different hypotheses and reasoning steps, whereas now online in real-time, this process reward agent can interfere and steer this reasoning process by checking individual steps against guidelines. So to move to the last part, I would like to quickly tease with some other exciting applications of AI agents that we have been working on very briefly. I'm sure that Charlotte will also talk about it, so I will not only highlight it here briefly. We are quite interested in actually advancing the benchmarking of agents for molecular tumor boards. We already had some first work at NeurIPS last year, and we're also very interested in advancing also agents in the multimodal radiology space, which I think also has some great applications for oncology. In this work that's very old, it just appeared on archive today if everything went well. So in this work, we built an agent that would analyze step-by-step 3D imagery. So here, chest CT. And we find some very encouraging results because this agent has the ability to faithfully represent what happened in the reasoning trace or in the entire agent loop, so to speak. Great. With that, I would like to come to my final summary slide. So I'm convinced that the medical domain is still very hard for AI, even for foundation models. So we cannot just assume we can purely scale away all the problems, just throw more data at bigger models. So we really need research. We need new methods to really increase reliability and trustworthiness of those systems. External tools can really augment language agents and make them more reliable. We can use that just as a test time. We can use it during training. There's many different ways how those external tools can be introduced to improve multimodal reasoning. I hope I could also convince you that it really matters how we represent knowledge that our agents ingest and how we really surface it to them. And I hope I also could get you excited about new avenues, how we can really carefully check individual reasoning steps such that the future of language models and language agents is not just one where we care about the final accuracy, but where we really have this defensible trace of reasoning steps that on their own really make sense and build up to a conclusion that is defensible. Great. With that, I would like to thank you so much for your attention. I'm sorry once again that I could not present in person, and I'm also very grateful for all our great collaborators, and on the left you see our very small and growing team. So unfortunately, thanks so much, Michael. Unfortunately, it's 3:00 a.m. for him. He didn't stay up to take your questions. I don't dare to answer yours. So we will close the session just very briefly. So thanks so much to both Serena and Michael, and in particular, your questions that kind of completed and well-rounded the session. We covered foundation models, how they tackle multimodality. We tackled generative models and agentic systems, and I think you very much see that in the end, it needs a combination of those, and we are very much in active research of building up the benchmarks, building up the models, building up the problems. So I hope you enjoy the rest of ACR. There will be an AI panel where you see my face again on Tuesday. And otherwise, thanks so much for attending.
