Good afternoon. A very warm welcome to our session here. I'm not Jakob Kata. I wish I were, but I'm not. Jakob could not make it today with some of the logistic challenges coming from Germany to here. So we are very fortunate, however, that he was able to send his recorded talk. So we'll get there in a second. I'm George Visilo. I'm the Chief AI for Science Innovation at AstraZeneca, and I'm going to pass here to my impromptu co-chair. Hi. Very nice to meet all of you. T. Rubihani from Recursion Pharmaceuticals, VP of Translational Strategy. So it's an immense pleasure to have all of you here during lunchtime today because we are witnessing a new era of translational research, clinical development across academia and biopharm. It is happening. It's a reality, and I think here we will have the opportunity of discussing how the research is evolving today, how the future looks like, and what it is that we need to do to get to the future that we're all talking about. Because AI is no longer the future, it's happening today. So without any further ado, let's move to the first talk, that's by Professor Jakob Kata. He is the Chair of Clinical AI at University of Dresden in Germany, and he also has a laboratory at University of Heidelberg in Germany as well. He has been a leader in terms of the development of AI-driven biomarkers in oncology, and he has also developed a number of frontier solutions in the agentic space, actually helping us reimagine tumor boards from first principles through the lens of AI, not with AI. It's extremely exciting. So, I'm going to ask our technical team here to play the video now. Let's hope it works. Fingers crossed. Hello and welcome. My name is Jakob Kata. I'm Professor of Clinical Artificial Intelligence in Dresden and Heidelberg in Germany. My flight was canceled. I'm late to the conference, so I have to pre-record this. Very sorry, but I will be there for the Sunday sessions and Monday sessions. Please get in touch. And now I want to share my slides and share with you my talk about multimodal and agentic AI in biomarker discovery. Here are my disclosures. Let's look at how the field of AI developed in the last 20 years. It all started with what we now call classical machine learning methods, where you train machine learning models to, for example, work with tabular data or with pre-extracted features from images to solve tasks such as prediction, prognostication, classification, et cetera. But, of course, as we all know, these methods were not sufficient for the complexity of data we face in cancer research, specifically image data, for example, histopathology images. So the field was completely changed in the 2010s when deep learning came along, and we were able to train deep learning models on large image datasets or other complex datasets for tasks such as classification, object segmentation, many others. In the 2020s, in the last couple of years, the field has been changed again by the advent of foundation models. These are big models that you train once with self-supervised learning on a large heterogeneous image cohort or dataset, and then you can use them and fine-tune them or apply them to additional downstream tasks. And typically, if you do this two-step approach, then you don't need as much data for the downstream tasks, and you can solve them much better. Another type of foundation models is, of course, large language models. These are just big foundation models that have been trained on natural language, so they can be used in natural language processing, but they have also obtained a generalist world knowledge and of course, are the basis for all the chatbots, ChatGPT, and everything that everybody's using. I think the most interesting part of these large language models is that they have enabled the technology of AI agents, where you take a large language model and you connect it to other tools so that it can solve complex tasks. Here, I'm going to show you a few examples how all of this comes together, how we can use deep learning to develop multimodal or unimodal biomarkers, and how we can then use AI agents to develop them much faster. First of all, let's speak about the biomarkers. And I want to just share this terminology that we have developed in our professional society, ESMO, European Society of Medical Oncology last year, and this has been published as a guideline. We've looked at the entire field of AI in cancer research and oncology, looked at the publications, looked at the products that are out there. And there's three classes of AI-based biomarkers, where AI is being used to derive properties of tumors that help us make better treatment decisions. Class A is using AI for biomarker quantification, and this is very simple because here what you're doing is you're just recapitulating the human workflow. Okay? So imagine a PD-L1 stained immunohistochemistryslide in lung cancer. Normally, a human would read this and would score the PD-L1 staining intensity. Now you can train AI systems to do the same thing, obviously with potentially much better reproducibility and also faster turnaround, et cetera. And many of these Class A biomarkers are already on the market. Class B would be the use of AI to indirectly measure existing biomarkers. For example, using pathology slides to make inferences about genetic alterations. There's now a lot of research available and also commercially approved products whereby you can predict microsatellite instability in colorectal cancer from pathology slides, EGFR mutations in lung cancer, gene fusions, many other mutations, tumor mutational burden, and many of these can be inferred just from the pathology images. This is a Class B biomarker. There's also other works that have shown that you can predict IDH mutational status from brain imaging in glioma patients. So there's a lot of work here. These biomarkers are typically not perfect, but good enough to be useful as pre-screening tests. Class C biomarkers are entirely new biomarkers where we train, for example, on radiology images, pathology images, genomic data, one of these, or all of these, or any combinations of these to predict treatment outcomes directly. For example, you can train an AI model to predict resist response based on these baseline images, or you can train an AI model to predict survival and/or adjuvant treatment efficacy, et cetera. You can predict clinical endpoints directly, and this would be a Class C biomarker. If you're interested, if you're working in this field, this has been published last year in "Annual of Oncology" and we think that this could be a scaffold to talk about these AI biomarkers. Now, what does it have to do with agents? I've already mentioned initially that large language models, of course, everybody knows large language models that can be used as chatbots. They can also be enriched with additional context. For example, medical guidelines or your personal documents that the chatbot can access. But if you generalize this more, what you get is an agent. Agents are large language models that can interact with any other software or any other tool to perform additional actions that they cannot perform natively. For example, to interact with a web browser or a command line interface. And then you can build them also in a way that they iterate and perform multi-step problem-solving. Let me introduce some terminology here. The AI model itself, the large language model, has weights. It's just a bunch of weights with the architecture, and this is the actual model. It has been trained once and then you use it. You can place this in harness, which would allow for example, computer use, browser use, terminal use, et cetera, and then you can package this harness in apps that people use. There's just some examples here. This is of course, already a bit outdated, but I think it's important to get this terminology right. And how does this apply to drug development, biomarker development? Well, it applies because a lot of what we do in biomarker development, drug development is just a human using a computer, right? In a very simplified way, it's a human researcher looking at experimental data, making a hypothesis, writing code, running code, debugging code, making presentations, et cetera. All of these steps can be performed in principle by an AI agent. Now, probably today's agents are not ready to do this completely autonomously, right? But again, what we are seeing right now is that the LLM-based AI agents that are available right now already automate part of this pipeline. And ultimately, I think it's safe to say that anything a human does with a computer can ultimately be automated. Let me show you some examples. We've built these agents in our research group mainly for clinical applications. So these are very relevant, of course also for biomarker development and biomarker application. One example is this work where we built a tumor board agent. You have a large language model. You give it access to a patient case, all the radiology, all the pathology images, all the genomic data that the patient has, access to a database of clinicaltrials.gov, et cetera, and then the agent does stepwise reasoning and uses tools to analyze all these data and comes up with a recommendation. We validated this obviously against human experts and found a very good performance. We've also developed autonomous agents, and this is unpublished, should come out soon, where we have agents that can look at patient cases and then not just piece all the diagnostic information together, but also take actions in that they, for example, can request additional imaging, request procedures, request laboratory tests, and then you can basically, we again benchmark this against human doctors, so you can basically automate the entire treatment journey in this scenario.So how does this relate not just to biomarker application, but also to the development of biomarkers? Well, as I said, anything a human developer does with a computer can ultimately be done with an agent. Right now, there's different components of this that can be done with agents. Many people are using this. In my lab everybody's using this. In many other labs, in industry, everybody's using agents, specifically coding agents, software development agents such as Claude Code or Codex are, of course, very powerful. And they are generalist agents, general purpose agents that are also very good at bioinformatics tasks and research tasks and biomarker development tasks. And in fact, many people are using them for this purpose. This is just an example, asking Claude Code to do a QC on genetic data. It's probably not perfect, but it can be done. Of course, I have no conflict of interest here, but there is many companies out there that are developing this, basically domain specific agents. And now the question is, and I think that's an unresolved question, what is really the secret sauce? What makes a drug development agent, what makes a biomarker development agent unique, right? Can you just use Claude Code or do you need more specific scaffolding? I think the answer is evolving, right? For as many cases, generalist agents are very good. For other cases, you might need specific agents. Another example where I don't have any conflict of interest, right? One of the trailblazers in this field, one of the pioneers was, of course, Jure Leskovec and his group's paper, Bi omni, and their agentic applications in biomedicine. Some of these you can reproduce nowadays with Claude Code. Some of these you cannot because they require specific tooling that is embedded. So the field is evolving super fast. What I think is one of the most important scientific questions is how to evaluate agents. I really like and highly recommend this Pokemon evaluation of agents where you can basically take large language models and give them a harness that lets them play Pokemon Red in this case. And then you can see how these agents solve the problems, how they basically succeed in solving tasks iteratively, how they advance through the game, through the different milestones in the game. This example is of course highly outdated, but you can see that each of these lines is one large language model in an agent harness playing Pokemon. And you can see that there's differences in how they advance through the game. And this is a benchmark. This is a classical agent benchmark where you test the capabilities of these agents for multi-step problem solving. And I think these are the types of benchmarks that we need. We cannot just like previously in AI, have one system that produces one output. We compare it with the gold standard, and then we have our performance. No, we have to look at the procedures that the tool calls benchmarking is now-- Benchmarking of agents is now becoming very complex, and we still need to develop the conceptual frameworks for this. And I think if we can formulate biomedical research, biomarker development as we can formulate games such as Pokemon Red, then we will make advancements in providing good benchmarks for agents. I want to close with one warning slide. Agents are of course-- any AI systems and agents in particular are of course susceptible to many pitfalls. There's of course hallucinations, many other potential problems. We are very interested in attacks on agents, attacks on AI systems, for example, prompt injection attacks whereby a user that interacts with an agent can hide prompts in the input data, even in images, even like invisible texts and images. And of course, there are many efforts ongoing to harden large language models and other AI systems and agentic systems against these attacks. But there is no universal cure here, and it's still possible deliberately or accidentally to perform prompt injections. For example, when pathologists write with a pen on a slide, PT3, then a lazy agent will typically just look at the text and not the image and become confused, right? We've done these two studies. Dr. Fersch who led this study on the right-hand side, he's also going to give a talk here in another session. So if you're interested, please reach out to him. And with that, I want to say thank you for your attention. I hope that this was interesting. Please reach out. Here's my email address. Again, I will arrive a bit later and there's a session tomorrow. There's a plenary session on Monday at 8:00 a.m. Thank you very much. Thank you very much to the other speakers and see you there. One of the benefits of technology. And actually, before we move to the questions here in the room- Hello and welcome. Just because I praise technology, we have a glitch. Anyhow, so there was a question online already that what are The AUCs, the sensitivity and specificity values associated with Class 3 biomarkers. And I had the opportunity of actually asking Jacob as he flies here. So his answer was that this is an excellent question and not an easy one. That there's no universal cutoff. Actually, in this context of the Class 3 biomarkers or Class C here, what's imperative is that there is clinical utility and that validation in adequate data sets is performed. One important point, in particular, when we move to these biomarkers for which there is no gold standard that we can perform directly an analytical validation, is that we may not need full explainability of the model. What we need is validation in multiple data sets that are fit for purpose. Imagine the levels of evidence that we require for clinical utility being also applied to this framework of biomarkers driven by AI. Just because we are using really cutting-edge technology does not give us poetic license to bypass the levels of evidence that are required and sufficient for us to deliver something in the clinic that is transformational. Do we have any questions in the room? Tiru and I will try to fill them in the absence of Jacob. One, two, three. So thank you so much. So we move to the next talk ahead of schedule. Can you believe it? Efficiency. Let's do it. So I have an immense pleasure here to invite Tirup Behanie, my impromptu co-chair today. She's the VP for Translational Strategy at Recursion, and it's a company that actually is doing drug discovery and clinical development through AI first principles. Tirup, it's such a pleasure to have you with us today. I look forward to your talk. Thank you very much. Good afternoon, everyone. Thank you for being here, and thank you to the ACR organizers for inviting Recursion to be a part of this very important discussion. As my co-chair has said, it's very topical for our industry, and I'm excited to be a part of it. Today what I was hoping to do is to walk through a couple of examples of our clinical stage programs that really highlight how Recursion is using AI in practice to inform everyday decisions across the R&D continuum. So from biology through to chemistry through to the clinic. So first, a quick introduction on Recursion Pharmaceuticals. We are a novel medicines company. We are aiming to produce better molecules, more differentiated molecules, for more meaningful outcomes for patients. And we're using AI, as I mentioned, across the R&D continuum to help us get there. We have proprietary multimodal data at industrial scale. We've designed purpose-built models with the ability to answer key biological, chemical, and clinical questions. And importantly, we've built bilingual teams, so both scientists that are fluent in AI, as well as AI engineers that are fluent in science. And together, these teams can create biological insights that we can translate then into clinical strategies and eventually execution, and hopefully we can show meaningful outcomes for patients. But the real differentiation for Recursion is how it all comes together. Because we believe that we're one of the few AI-native companies that has end-to-end operations, so really applying AI, again, across the R&D continuum. And we believe that's because it's important not only to improve the decisions that we make in one area of R&D, but really across the entire value chain. So here I'm introducing our Recursion platform, the Recursion OS. And it really is sort of broken up into three distinct pieces. But the reason to bring these models is that the insights that we generate are to address four main tasks that we have as a pharma company. First, to reimagine patient selection through a multimodal biomarker space. But here we are not trying to do this, the most complex biomarker that you'll find, a small population that respond. No, we are developing this on the basis of maximum parsimony.So what is the smallest set of parameters that would be required and sufficient for us to identify the largest population that would objectively benefit from one of our therapeutic agents alone or in combination? Second, we are using this approach to de-risk the transition from our Phase 1, Phase 2 studies to Phase 3 studies. Why? Because these models are able to generalize from smaller sample sizes. So the idea here is, okay, we don't want to be sitting with 40 patients' worth of data after Phase 1 and render that critical decision to move to a Phase 3, having that level of uncertainty. If we can bring the insights from these models, we can make better decisions. That's why I was asking the question about the pursuit in that domain here. The third, how can we improve the probability of success of our Phase 3 studies? And here, it's using another property of the foundation models as well. That's to generalize from sparser data. When we have a Phase 3 study, we don't have the depth of translational data that we have from a Phase 1 or Phase 2. So can we use those models to help us actually render better decisions there as well? And all of this, to be honest, is just to address our fourth point. We'd like to develop the next generation of combination treatments that will be transformational for patients. I think it's a shared goal that all of us have to move the response rates to a much higher level through the combination of therapies, and I think we'll get there together. At the end of the day, the ultimate goal is to transform patients' lives and actually to advance our bold ambition in oncology. That's to eliminate cancer as a cause of death. I think it's a shared goal that all of us have here. We realize that that approach with the multi-modal foundation models coming from a clinical perspective is one of the scales that we need to be aware of. We also understand now that for us to get to the point that I'm articulating here, we'll need to have the different scales for the development of these domain-specific models, from an atomic level to the cellular level. And you hear a lot about virtual cells, and I'd like us to define exactly what you mean when we say a virtual cell being developed, and then from the patient level. What we are learning as well as these are developed is that if we take the embeddings from one scale and actually refine and fine-tune them with the others from another scale, we get even better insights. So it's likely going to be an ensemble of models that will allow us to get to the point where we need to be. Yes, to derive those insights that actually will be transformational for patients at the end of the day. But we needed to start somewhere. And I have to say that for us at AstraZeneca, AI is really not the future, it's our reality. We're doing this. We actually have been pursuing this for over a decade. And one of the spaces where AI has had already an impact is in computational pathology. That idea that we can apply artificial intelligence to computer vision of pathology images actually started over 10 years ago. First with deep learning, convolutional neural networks applied to pathology images. It was really exciting, but now we are getting to the point where we're seeing the maturity of those solutions. A great example is our quantitative continuous scoring system. That's basically a fully supervised method where we use handcrafted annotations to develop a model that can quantify the expression of targets at a subcellular level, membrane, cytoplasm, and nucleus, in a really quantitative way at the single-cell level. We actually applied this first to the development of our antibody-drug conjugates. The first was our antibody-drug conjugate that targets Trop2. In that space, immunochemical assay, semi-quantification by pathologists, people like me looking down a microscope, actually, we could not get to a predictive biomarker. With the use of the quantitative continuous scoring system, we have now demonstrated in the context of the tropionlongo one and tropionlongo two that actually you can quantify the expression of Trop2 on the cell surface in the cytoplasm, derive what we call the normalized membrane ratio. And that normalized membrane ratio is a surrogate for the internalization of Trop2 as a target. And that is a surrogate marker for the response to our Trop2 target in ADC. And actually, this is a great example of one of the types of biomarkers that Jacob Cutter articulated in his talk, the type C, yeah, where we don't have an equivalent by humans, and we are developing something new here, something that cannot be quantified trivially with our approaches. It's really hard then to develop and validate this. You need validation in multiple datasets. And actually, we're seeing the impact of this biomarker in the next few months, few years with some of the prospective clinical trials we're running at AstraZeneca in the space of non-small cell, non-squamous, non-AGE lung cancers. The reality, however, is that for us to develop the solution that received breakthrough device designationBy the FDA. The first ever to receive that designation in that context of therapeutic prediction. Actually, for us to develop that model, it took us... I will let you guess. Imagine. How many hours of pathologists handcrafting annotations to train the model were required? Do you have an idea? So I'll tell you, 40,000 hours of pathologists to develop one model for one indication, one tumor type. It's hard to scale, isn't it? So we asked a question last year. What if we brought a pathology foundation model, highly capable, to actually reduce or even replace the need for handcrafted annotations for the development of the model? Not the biomarker, the model to quantify a specific target. And what we have witnessed is that you can go from 40,000 to four and a half, even to zero. You just do the benchmarks and the validation extensively. It's quite incredible, isn't it? And it's extremely exciting because not only for us, it's for the whole community. This is a principle that if we have the most capable models, we can start pressure testing, as long as we have very clear evaluations and benchmarks. Those are absolutely essential. And I'm going to reiterate again, evaluations and benchmarks for everything that we do, and then extensive validation of the biomarker once the biomarker is developed. Where we're trying to get to now is to integrate not only pathology, but multimodal data to help inform patient selection strategies. And for us to do that, we need to be able to connect our data with the models to develop insights. And for that, we are developing a whole agentic framework to do just that. That circuitry that's required and sufficient to connect our data with the models in a way that we derive the embeddings from these models. We can actually use them to derive the new hypothesis and test them, and even generate new data to test the hypothesis. But for us to get there, I'm afraid to say that it's going to be really, really hard to do this as an island, and I would not suggest you to try this at home. Actually, rather, what we need to do is to build an ecosystem of partnerships whereby we can actually bring together domain experts on one hand with people with extremely deep technical expertise, the right orchestration on top, and then at the bottom, the right infrastructure. And when I say infrastructure here, it's your data infrastructure, your compute, all of the platforms that are required and sufficient to do that. If one can bring all of those components together, then we allow ourselves to ask the killer questions, the questions that actually really matter for our patients. So we have been building this ecosystem with hyperscalers on one hand, with the frontier AI companies, with specialized AI companies. And we have several declared partnerships with Tempus, with Pathos, with Modelo, with Immune AI, with Okin. This is all happening. And we also have partnerships with academics. And I have to say that I've joined AstraZeneca, and I have an incredible number of meetings with academics who are actually developing the next generation of solutions, seeing from around the corner, and we need to be there because the pace of technological development is unprecedented. And finally, that actually we started last year in September, we've brought into these ecosystem partnerships patient advocacy groups. Because developing the AI solutions without having the voice of the patients is really, really hard. We need to understand what their needs are. Not that they will constrain everything that we're doing, but having that information help us define what the path should look like. Another point that I would like to discuss with you is that we also approach AI from a three-level perspective. As I mentioned to you, in clinical development, if you think about the first layer, the model layer, the data of incredible volumes in adequate diversity with the edge cases being adequately represented is essential to develop the most capable models. And I subscribe to the notion that we first need the most capable models, then we can distill them down to find, let's say, the smallest model possible that would provide the answers to us, but we need to develop the most capable to begin with. So we are actually there developing these models through partnerships. Where we actually are actively engaged internally is in developing the solutions, the second layer, utilizing those models to address specific questions. For that, we are also building a really complete stack of evaluations and benchmarks, task-specific and end-to-end, to test how performant these models are. With those solutions, then we have to develop the third layer, that's the applications. What will touch the patients? What will actually get to the point of informing decisions? And we build this in-house using our datasets, but we actually partner then with diagnostic companies, tech bio companies, biotech companies, to get this to the patients. We're not a diagnostic company. Our primary purpose here is to develop the transformational treatments to our patients.So we are focused on our primary purpose, and we do this through partnerships. And I'm certain that by bringing all of this together, this ecosystem of partnerships, and understanding the roles that we'll be playing, we can get to the next wave of innovation. One final point, one final thought that I'd like to share with you, that I've come to realize through experience and exposure, first and foremost. I had not thought about it when I first started, that AI in a pharma company of the size that we are is not a technological challenge, it's a challenge of people, process, and culture. And we need to help and enable our team members to upskill and to transform themselves. And we have to reimagine processes, first principles, to deliver the solutions that actually will be transformational for our patients and will allow us to take many steps forward towards our bold ambition in oncology. That is, to eliminate cancer as a cause of death. With that, I'd like to thank you so much for your attention, and I'd happily take any questions you might have. Thank you. Thank you very much. Kiro, I'm afraid that we are the only thing between them and lunch. So let's just be aware of that. Sounds good. While people are making their way to the microphone, I'll give you a question that came up online. Have you used BCMA and CD33 also as an ADC AI-induced biomarker? I'm not in a position of commenting on specific solutions here today, but we are investigating all of the different potential strategies for patient selection, not only in solid tumors, but in heme as well. So watch this space. Sounds good. We'll take a question from the right-hand side. Hi, George. Thank you for the very inspiring talk. I embrace your enthusiasm, okay, but here is a question. You mentioned a lot-- Sorry, Andrea Sotteriva, Computational Biology, Human Technopole Milan. You know me. You mentioned a lot foundation models, multimodal foundation models. Now, in language and images, they work very well because their information is very dense, okay? And we have three, four orders of magnitude more data, okay, for free from the internet. Now in biology, information is sparse and data is scarce. And I understand you propose, as you said, to build up this data infrastructure. But realistically, if you take off your AstraZeneca hat and you keep your research hat, as a scientist, as humanity, how do we generate enough of this multimodal data in biomedicine to really build models that are predictive? Andrea, that's such a great question, and thank you so much for asking. I think here, if you think about petabytes in biology and clinical development, a lot of it lies in the imaging space. A lot of petabytes of data from radiology, from pathology images. What we've learnt over the last few years is that if apply self-supervision to pathology images and radiology images, if we solve feature extraction really well, we can derive new insights. Really new insights. And we are putting this to test, and actually, there is a delta between just doing this with traditional approaches, and if you use the embeddings to derive the new insights. So this is one modality. Then when you combine pathology images with pathology reports into a vision language model, you derive even more insights. And actually, you can use then those models to help you understand the mechanistic basis of some of the predictions made. So it's building that stack. We are also seeing in parallel many companies developing extremely sophisticated strategies to develop the data sets required for the training of these models. So we are getting to that point where the data is going to be sufficient for us to develop the first generation. What is really important here is that it's not been solved yet. Two problems have not been solved yet. The development of the semantic layer across data modalities in a truly multimodal way, and the second is that the utilization of time as a first dimension in the multimodal embeddings. These are two problems that we hope to help solve over the next year. Does that make sense? Yeah. We can talk a bit more later, maybe, but thank you very much. Thank you. We'll take a question from my left. Hi, George. Thank you for the amazing talk. My name is Arshad Ahmed. I'm with OneCell AI, and I'm a little biased here, so just bear with me one second. A lot of the discussion centered around, we hear Tempus a lot, in terms of the data and basically the foundation of the data. If that's not solid, then everything else falls apart. Right? So I see three big limitations, and I would love to hear your thoughts on those. One is these are done in archival samples, right? These are not fresh biopsies. They're done in bulk. These are not done in single-cell level. And these are not done in longitudinal samples, right? So these are done at the baseline, but it's hard to get biopsies longitudinally unless you do a ctDNA, but it's not single cells.What's your view on the next generation of the Tempest database that'll drive the next generation of foundation models, which will be fresh, longitudinal, and single-cell level data, which also have perturbations in it? Is anyone working on that, or is that a white space? Is there even a need for it? What's your view on that? Thank you so much for the question. I had that slide with the atomic, cellular, and patient level. The patient level is what we could do today. And actually, one important point is that those longitudinal samples are like gold dust, because if you can include them in the pre-training, it becomes really more powerful. Second, we need to bring the time dimension to that, and one can start deriving that dimension through the de-identified clinical notes. Because there are so many time points, we may not have the samples, but we can start understanding chronology and temporality. Now, your final question, do we need to generate the single-cell data with perturbations, let's say, where we understand exactly which parameters we changed, and quantify before and after? Absolutely. And I believe that many in this ecosystem are directly involved in the generation of those data sets. And they will actually bring the next generation of the models. We'll take another question from online. What is your perspective on the black box nature of these AI tools and their use in a regulatory-heavy environment? That's such a great question, actually. I'm not sure if that word black box is applicable anymore. Because actually, the level of system introspection that these models can perform today is quite incredible. The regulators are actually evolving with us. Before, mechanistic and explainability was a condition that was sine qua non, was mandatory. And as you could see in the ESMO guidelines, the EBHI, and also in discussions with several regulatory agencies, the main requirement now is multiple validation of the solutions derived. If we have explainability, even better. But what's essential is that we demonstrate the performance of the particular AI solution in terms of clinical utility, very clearly, with adequately powered data sets, and done in a way that's scientifically rigorous. That's what I would submit. But the partnership with the regulatory agencies now is super exciting because they're prepared to iterate with us and to think about the next wave of innovation. I think we can have time for just one more question. We'll go to the right of me. Hi. Thank you so much for the great talk. My name is John Wu Kong from UC San Diego. I had a really similar question from the question actually asked by the online audience, which is model interpretability. And my two questions, one question is how much validation would be needed? For example, how many cohorts or how many number of samples in addition to the training data set and the validation and benchmarking data set, can we be sure that the model is we think is going to be generalizable? Generalizability is the question. Absolutely. And the second question is, once you go beyond unimodal foundation models and building a multimodal foundation models, I would think that the interpretation will be much more harder because you now have to investigate not only the unimodal model features, but you have to really understand how these multimodal features interact with each other, which raises another layer of complexity in terms of interpreting the model. So I'm wondering, what's your thought on that? So let's begin with the second question first. Mm-hmm. Let's imagine a narrowly fusion model where most of the additional information derived is in the form of nonlinear correlations in the latent space. How do you explain this, yeah? And that's why the regulators are saying you need extensive validation, because that we may not be able to semantically translate into words. But for us to get there, because then we are getting into the territory of open-endedness, aren't we? We don't know the answer to the question. We're trying to derive a new question because our traditional train of thought cannot get us there. Is that correct? Yeah. If so, then we need evaluations and benchmarks for all the sub-tasks and tasks as we progress. And then we need validation in multiple data sets. The magic number, I do not know. It's going to be context-dependent and solution-dependent, and we'll need interactions with the regulators so that they can articulate what would be required and sufficient for us to satisfy the principle of safety for the patients, and that the AI is actually performant enough and robust enough to be shipped clinically. Got it. Thank you so much. I think we're all set, and I think we're going to have to move out of this room. So we have to vacate the room. First, I'd like to thank you so much for your attention. I'd like to thank you so much for asking the provocative questions and for pressure testing us, and for sitting through this session that despite the logistic disruptions that we faced, Lufthansa did not help. We actually got the message across here, and I would like to thank you again for spending this Saturday with us. Thank you.

Good morning, everyone. I think we'll go ahead and get started. Thanks for grabbing your coffees and getting here early for this 8:00 AM session. We appreciate it. This is Educational Session Two, Senescence in Cancer. I'll be your chair. I'm Marcus Versetti, coming from UMass Chan Medical School. Just to go over some logistics, this is a 90-minute session broken into 30-minute increments. Each speaker will have 20 minutes presentation, 10 minutes for question. And we encourage a lot of discussion, so please either come up to the mics for the question, or you can scan this QR code or use the app and we can read your questions online as well. So we encourage you to have a great discussion with us. One little hiccup, so unfortunately, Jennifer, who was our first speaker, had an issue with her flight, so she can't make it in person, but luckily, she was able to record her talk. So you'll see her recorded talk. And Drew Pardal, one of her colleagues, will be answering questions for her. So we really appreciate Drew stepping in. And I'm also joined by my colleague, Clement Smith, as well. Just a quick intro to senescence. We know the field has really changed dramatically over the last 20 years. First described as a cell cycle arrest pathway, we know it to be a potent tissue remodeler, immune remodeler with both pro and anti-tumorigenic effects in cancer. The development of single-cell and spatial technologies now, and also senescence reporter mice, have really allowed us to dive in to this heterogeneity where we can find basically any cell in the body can undergo senescence from stresses we get every day or stresses that accumulate over a lifetime, and they can impact cancer therapies as well. So our hope is that dissecting the mechanisms by which senescent cells contribute to progression or clearance, we can design rational therapies you might have heard of called senolytics or senomorphics to target senescence to make it more tumor suppressive. As you'll see from the speakers today, I think it also takes a lot of multidisciplinary approaches from different cancer spaces to really tackle this complex question of senescence in cancer. So we will get started with our first talk today from Dr. Jennifer Elisseeff, who is Professor of Biomedical Engineering at John Hopkins University. Her talk will be a great intro to our session on defining senescence and implications for cancer. Good morning. I'm sorry I'm not there in person. I had some flight challenges on the last flights heading from East Coast. So, unfortunately, I'm recording, not there in person, but I did plant a collaborator in the audience to answer any questions that may come up. But I'm really happy to be able to share our work today in the field of senescence. Here are my current conflicts and previous conflicts, partially related to the presentation. So I'd like to present a little bit of background first, our approaches in tissue engineering, because they really influence how we approach senescence. And then talk about our work in senescence in articular trauma and arthritis and fibrosis. And from that experience, how it led us to look at ways we can better define what is a senescent cell and the concept of senotypes. And finally, I'll discuss senescence and what we've learned in those other models and the potential implications in cancer. So I come from the tissue engineering field, as I mentioned, and we spent many years looking at biomaterials that could serve as scaffolds for things like stem cells, and that we could integrate biological signals into these materials. And I mention particular stem cells because that really has guided a lot our concept of cell states and proliferation versus differentiation. A cell that's proliferating usually doesn't differentiate, and when we think of a senescent cell that's secreting actively lots of factors, it's really in a differentiated state. So we translated technologies in the area of cartilage and soft tissue fillers, and these experiences in the clinic really guided us to the immune system and the concept of regenerative immunotherapies. So today, we think of tissue engineering as manipulating immune stromal networks that are sensing and regulating tissue structure, and you'll see that senescence plays a role here, and we think it's an interesting node and a hub for these interactions. So we first started characterizing what is a natural immune response after tissue injury, and what does it look like in a healing wound versus a non-healing wound characterized by fibrosis and inflammation, and can we use this information to redirect that non-healing wound to a healing environment? And this has applications in cartilage and fibrosis, and we recognize that the tumor was described many years ago as a non-healing wound. In a healing wound, we can look at things like muscle and pro-regenerative therapies that are stimulating repair, but then work has shown that tumors that are responsive to therapies such as immune checkpoint blockade have a phenotype of wound healing and wound resolution. So if we look at wound healing and kinetics, the wound-healing process has been well-characterized in the context of the immune system, stem cell mobilization, wound closure. But senescence is also a part of the wound-healing process. So in a healing wound, you'll have senescence initially increase and then decrease. But in a non-healing wound or a wound characterized by chronic inflammation, senescence or markers of senescence remain high.So senescence in hard-to-repair tissues. As I mentioned, we started in cartilage repair for a tissue engineering application, but we recognized even if we had a perfect therapy to rebuild tissues, if there was inflammation, such as interleukin-1 beta, it would not repair very well. The tissue engineering wouldn't work. At the same time, collaborators Nat David had recognized that senescent cells could be an interesting therapeutic target for a number of applications, in particular osteoarthritis, where senescent cells had been seen in cartilage explants being taken from patients undergoing knee or hip replacement. So what is a senescent cell? Well, the history of the field has really looked at senescence in vitro. So first looking at the Hayflick limit and replicative senescence. So after cells have been cultured for a long time, they stop proliferating, as is connected with decrease in telomeres. It was also recognized there was stress-induced senescence that could be stimulated by oxidative stress, genotoxic, and oncogenic stress, and the proliferative stress being another mechanism. But much of this has been studied in vitro. So these cells were characterized with a number of markers. So beta-gal, for example, HMGB1, movement from the nucleus to the cytoplasm, and p16, cell cycle related gene, was seen to be upregulated in some cells, although well recognized to be an imperfect marker. But many of the tools are built around p16. So these cells are in growth arrest, but they are secreting a senescence-associated secretary phenotype. This SASP is what is implicated in the function of these cells to increase tumor production or related to the diseases associated with aging, such as heart disease, diabetes, and arthritis, as I mentioned. However, these cells are also recognized to be an important part of embryological development and tissue repair. So how are these cells both good and bad? Well, research has shown that senescent cells are a part of wound healing, and that is through secretion of PDGF, platelet-derived growth factor. And then our work on senescence as an example where the accumulation of senescence is associated with disease in the joint and arthritis. So from the arthritis perspective, we looked at an injury, anterior cruciate ligament transection, where the cartilage lining the surface of the joints degenerates after that injury. It's a chronic wound. Senescent cells, as I mentioned, were recognized to be a part of the arthritis process. And when we did senolysis or removal of senescent cells, either through molecules or through transgenic animals, we could restore the cartilage. And we observed reduction of SASP factors, reduction of pain, and we were very surprised, we also saw an increase in tissue repair when those senescent cells were removed. Now, luckily, I had an immunology collaborator who recognized some of these SASP markers, IL-6 and IL-1 beta, and told us, "Well, these molecules are connected to T cell differentiation." So we looked in that same model and saw increases in IL-17, both in the joint and in the draining lymph nodes, increasing with injury and disease. And when senolytics were added in both young and aged animals, a decrease in IL-17. So there seemed to be a connection between senescence and IL-17. So to further explore this, we induced senescence artificially in vitro and cultured these cells next to naive T cells. And in the presence of TGF-beta, we see a significant increase in IL-17 production by these T cells. We also took Th17 cells that we skewed in vitro and cultured them next to healthy fibroblasts and saw an increase in p16 and SASP factors, including IL-6. And we phenotyped these cells a little bit more and have a signature of an inflammatory-induced senescence from this in vitro model. So we can use inflammation as an additional mechanism for induction of senescence that may be more physiologically relevant than some of the others that I listed before. So again, when we think of tissue structure, this communication between the immune system and the stroma that's regulating the matrix and vascularity, senescent cells are playing a big role in that interaction. Now, continuing on the matrix discussion of tissue structure, senescence is associated with fibrosis in murine models and in human tissues. These are markers for p16 and p21, so associated with fibrotic diseases in these tissues. And we can see in other fibrosis models, this is a fibrosis around breast implant, and p16 is in pink here, and we can see p16 cells stretched out with a fibroblastic morphology. We also see p16 cells around the vasculature that is adjacent to this fibrosis. So we're interested in this network and understanding what a senescent cell is, and we're a part of the SenNet program at NIH that's looking to define what a senescent cell is in vivo in tissues, in both mouse and human tissues.So we first used the biomaterial model to study fibrosis, and this is a nice reproducible model where we can get consistent fibrosis. We have the same inflammation and abnormal vascularity. And you can see here that we have red p16 positive cells sort of adjacent to macrophages associated with the fibrosis stretched out again like a myofibroblast. But then we also see some associated with vascular structures, and you'll see that this is a common theme. So, yes, single cell, of course, is popular, and sometimes you can see p16 expression in single cell, particularly with the newer techniques. But in general, it can be hard to find p16, and again, as I mentioned, it's not a completely accurate model of marker for senescence. So in these fibrosis models, we can look at the cell types there. But in order to really capture p16 cells, we used a genetic model developed by Jan van Deursen and Darren Baker, p16 Cre. And with our biomaterial model, we could see that, number one, as it's recognized in the field, a small number of senescent cells are present. And when we look further at which cell types are senescent, we see a lot of stromal cells that are senescent, CD45 negative and CD29 positive and CD31 negative. There are also some I'll show you later in the tumor model that are CD31 positive. So when we pull out and sort just that subset of senescence, CD29 positive, we can perform bulk sequencing and get a signature which we call senescence signature. And when we look at what's there, we saw a lot of markers, enrichment in vascular-associated genes, but also chondrocyte differentiation genes. And while we worked on cartilage before, this is not a cartilage environment. When we look at how we can capture and identify senescence in single cell, we use transfer learning to then look at that signature, and in each cell, is that cell similar or different to that signature? So we can see senesc positive cells. This is the fibroblast population here, both activated and myofibroblasts. And then we see pericytes, a smooth muscle cell population that's also senescent. If we look at markers of these cells, in particular SAS factors in these subtypes, we can start getting phenotypic information of the activated fibroblasts versus the myofibroblasts. There's also an inflammatory fibroblast and a perivascular senescent cell or pericyte, which each senescent cell is expressing different markers. But single cell and the clustering is a way to bin cells into a certain phenotype, but it doesn't tell us much about patterns. So working with Ilana Furtak, we used her CO-GAPS program using non-negative matrix factorization to instead look for patterns of gene expression that can cross these cell identification clustering. And so we see patterns of gene expression within those senescent cell types, and we can connect that with spatial data to start seeing these niches where the senescent cells are and which cells are around there. So we have a fibrotic niche, a vascular niche, and an immune niche. And the cartilage niche is in the fibrosis, but it's expressing markers that are typically associated with cartilage and tendon tissue, which is avascular, similar to fibrosis. So just to give a summary, and this will be a preprint soon, we can look at transcription factors, cell surface markers that might be unique to these different subtypes of senescent cells, and SAS factors that can be associated with extracellular matrix, matrix degradation, immune factors, and growth factors of these different senescent cells or senotypes. Now we're very interested in how these cells are communicating. So senescent cells are a particular node in the network of cell communication. So we use a program that we developed called Domino Signal, which looks at transcription factor activation associated with receptors, and then connecting that with ligand expression. So a little bit moving backwards compared to some other standard receptor ligand programs. Now if we look at this in a muscle repair model, so good repair in a young animal versus poor repair in an old model. If we look in a young animal at communication, here's our senescent subtypes down here, we can see communication through a number of cell types, the immune cells, vascular cells. But in the old animal, it's really taken over by T cells, and this cartilage-like are really highly fibrotic cell types. So the senescent cell type and its communication is important. Now finally, interest here with tumors, the tumor microenvironment being characterized as a non-healing wound. Matt Wolf has done work looking at, for example, the lung tumor biopsy where we can see p16 positive cells in the stroma where there's fibrosis, so the pink cells here. And these are different than, of course, the tumor-associated senescence, which has been studied.And here's a close-up of these fibroblasts. But we still see these vascular-associated cells. And in the tumor model, we do see some senescent endothelial cells and pericytes. But I'm going to talk about something a little bit different. We see senescence also in fibroids, where we, again, have the fibroblast, vascular-associated in combination. So it's important when we talk about senescence in the tumor environment, that there are multiple senotypes. And the matrix these cells produce is important for enhancing tissue mechanics. All right. And we're looking forward to your talk. Thanks. All right. Thanks very much. Let me start off by thanking the ACR, the organizers, for selecting a presentation from my lab for this highly informative educational session on cellular senescence. So here are my disclosures. And I can only thank the previous speakers for so well introducing the topic that there's not much to add, but a little bit. In the clinic, we often don't know whether we look at a wound or cancer. So as obviously as we learned from the previous presentations, an intimate relationship between derailed wound healing and cancer. So senescent cells, as we all know, are an intrinsic component of the multicellularity of cancer as an organ. But I like to make the point, although it was pointed out by my previous colleagues, that in an acute fashion, senescent cells in wound healing are an essential component for proper wound healing. I'd like to make a point which, in my view, is obvious but is not really deeply discussed. Senescence is not a binary state. It's not in or out of senescence. And actually, it may matter over time how long, how strong, and in what kind of trigger this trigger is applying to cause maybe initial senescence, light senescence, actual senescence, and perhaps something like super senescence. I would not claim senescence is reversible. I believe it's neither reversible nor irreversible, but there is a state beyond senescence. I like to share that with you. We have data why we believe this is not philosophical, so that if senescence is reversible, it was not senescence. This has to be permanently reestablished. So this is complicated. But if we look at the more specialized senescence markers, we would have type-specific senescence vulnerabilities as compared to targeting the core machinery in terms of a shared senescence vulnerability. So the more uniform program is good and bad senescence throughout the body, while the more diverse or multiple types of senescence may give you specific senescence functions and you may argue, I understand that from a clinical perspective, you want to target the bad ones and want to leave the good ones intact. Whether that's achievable, that's a different question. I'm not making an argument for either point, but I like to go for the second half of the talk through an intense analytic approach where I share with you the addressing of a rather uniform aspect of cellular senescence and what the consequences of this might be. In the chronic detrimental senescence, that's obviously the space in which we like to eliminate senescent cells in order to see anti-aging effects, fibrolytic effects, and anti-cancer effects. So if I could choose, I would try to optimize dose scheduling in order to leave senescence beneficial in the first place and apply senolysis in a scenario where I can eliminate those which dictate unwanted disease pathologies. So that's what we aim for, to control cancer, actually even prevent cancer, and attenuate aging by pan-senolytic approach. And I'd like to share with you how we harness the redox imbalance in senescent cells for senolysis and what the clinical effects in preclinical models might be. For this, we teamed up with a medicinal chemist from the Free University in Berlin, Jörg Rademann, and colleagues, and set up a redox-based drug screen because we came across metabolic imbalances in senescent cells driven by NADH as a background, which could allow us to screen for an oxidative activation of candidate drugs in order to produce further oxidative stress to selectively eliminate senescent cells. So get a dual selectivity of an agent, which is now called Senlytic, for the elimination of senescent cells. So this agent we retrieved from the drug screen, Senlytic, is indeed activated by NADH. You see the higher the NADH we provide, the higher thePeroxide H2O2 output is, and this is countered by GSH. So in conclusion, high NADH, low GSH levels would activate this agent. Here you look at a number of senescent scenarios, therapy-induced, oncogene-induced, oncogene inhibition-induced senescence. And the common feature of all these senescent types is this altered NADH/GSH ratio across the cell types. Notice that senescent cells have an elevated pool of labile iron, and this LIP can be measured by Ferro-Orange. And you see that across different senescence inductions, we see this elevated pool. But senescent cells are protected from ferroptosis. We are coming to this in a second. If we provide a chelator here, Desferrioxamine, we can reduce these lipid iron pools. So this concludes that Senlyt helps to utilize iron in the so-called Fenton reaction to produce OH radicals and to kill. But I like to mention that another arm of killing by Senlyt is via classic apoptosis, as blockable here by cVAD-fmk. But in conclusion, we use two modes of cell death, ferroptosis and apoptosis, and even strongly apoptotically compromised tumor cells can still be killed via the ferroptotic pathway. Senlyt has high senescent selectivity. You look at four scenarios, non-malignant settings or tumor settings in the mouse or in the human species. And you can see from all these graphs that there is a huge senolytic index and great advantage to selectively kill senescent cells as compared to proliferating cells. That's reiterated here. It's difficult to read curve, sorry about this, but what it tells us is that Senlyt is at least as good or better, obviously, than other established senolytics in killing at low concentration senescent cells, but with limited toxicity to their proliferating counterparts. And there's a genetic senescence dependency if we test p53-proficient versus p53-deficient cells. It's the proficient and senescence-capable, but not the senescence-incapable cells we can kill by this agent. Just to go through a few more vignettes, this is replicative senescence in a setting where we have cells arresting after a certain number of divisions as compared to HTERT positive cells. It's only the RS cells which can be killed. We look at virus-induced senescence. Some cells can undergo virus-induced senescence. You see that on the left. Others don't, and only those which undergo this are susceptible to Senlyt. Again, to remind you, there is equally an altered GSH/NADH ratio in these aged lungs. And if we apply Senlyt to those aged animals, we not only remove the senescent cells, which is nice to see inside you, we also reduce the collagen cuffs, which is interesting because apparently you can eliminate senescent cells, and by the endogenous fibrolytic activity of the body, you even reduce collagen cuffs. So that's a demonstration of in vivo clearance of senescent cells. Senlyt is of very limited toxicity, to say the least. We don't see differences in body weight. We don't see differences across major cardinal lab or cell blood cell parameters. We can use Senlyt as an augmentative or consolidative agent upon chemotherapy. You look here at chemotherapy or TIS in a lymphoma model where only p53-proficient lymphoma cells with an apoptotic block underwent cellular senescence.And if we take those cells, apply senlytic, we kill the senescent, but not the equally treated p53-deficient cells. And we can test that in vivo. We administer lymphoma cells, lymphomas grow in recipient fully immune competent mice, and then we first apply chemotherapy and second senlytic. And it's senlytic which in senescent lymphomas, extends survival of the mice in virtually all settings. But if we use p53 null lymphomas, the addition of a second drug here, senlytic, is ineffective. We can look at oncogene-induced senescence, first in vitro. We take MEFs from LSL, MEFs and activate their BRAF. Then they turn senescent, and we can eliminate them by senlytic. We can do this in vivo in these very same mice, in which we activate BRAF by provision of hydroxy tamoxifen, CRE is activated, BRAF is on, we get nevus cell nevi pigmented skin lesions. You see that in the middle. And if we provide senlytic, we can reduce these p16-positive lesions. That is particularly nice to look at the ears of these mice, you see these dark spots in the ear, and if you provide senlytic, they disappear again. So another example for in vivo clearance of senescent cells. We can drive this a step further, and that's a pretty interesting model. Based on tamoxifen, we can turn on BRAF. But we can use tamoxifen in addition in this compound mouse containing two p53 ER alleles to restore functional wild-type similar p53 levels. In this setting, we get the same result as you just saw, but we have the opportunity to remove tamoxifen at some point in time, which means that there are BRAF-positive lesions now no longer with active p53, therefore on their way to form melanomas. And that's indeed what's happening in this model. You see the lesion at the back of the mouse. You see the skin tumor, and you can even see metastasis to inguinal lymph nodes in the lung. But if we now in this window of opportunity where we have only OIS nevus lesions provide senlytic, the result is the following. We see delayed and reduced melanoma genesis in this model due to senlytic. We can also target RAS senescent cells. This is simply retroviral provision of oncogenic RAS. And you see on the left, we can provide senlytic and eliminate those cells. If we do RAS activation in p53-deficient cells, there is no effect of senlytic. The interesting point is now using an old-fashioned chemical cancerogene, NMU, N-methyl-N-nitrosourea, because that causes RAS mutations from endogenous alleles. The result is same. We see senescence in response to NMU, and this senescence can be eliminated by senlytic only in p53 proficient cells. Now we took this to the next level and did this in vivo. So we treated mice, normal C57 black 6 mice with NMU. We get, among other things, RAS activating mutations. And all these mice will succumb to T-cell lymphomas in a limited period of time, as you can see. If you use a background here, Suva minus mice, which can no longer establish this H3K9 trimethylation mark. So they get instantly with no tumor blocking senescence, these T-cell lymphomas. If you do this in wild-type mice, it's much less impressive. About half of the mice will get over time T-cell lymphomas because there's a senescence barrier. But if you now provide senlytic after NMU provision to these mice, you virtually prevent tumor formation from incipient RAS lesions in this animal. So with this, let me conclude that we look at senlytic as a novel compound class that is activated by and kills via senescence-associated oxidative stress. It has senolytic activity across virtually all types of senescence with no obvious systemic toxicity. It extends lifespan, I didn't show that, and attenuates age-related pathologies. Prolonged survival after debulking chemotherapy, limits the progression of BRAF positive nevi to full-blown melanoma, eliminates OIS restored melanoma. I didn't show that, but you see the bullet point here. And it prevents RAS-driven tumor formation by eliminating incipient OIS lesions. So in summary, what does it mean for senolysis and pre-cancer? We can target an universal core feature of senescent cells here, and metabolic imbalance by an pan-senolytic that's feasible and effective. And using a short pulse dose schedule achieves clearance of senescent cells in vivo, whose proof is in clinical routine, certainly not trivial. Pan-senolysis covers multiple detrimental features of senescence, and I'm not seeing an advantage of a more selective senolytic approach, and that's of course open to a controversial discussion. Cancer preventive and aging attenuation treatments may require repetitive applications, and I can't tell you today, but I expect that in the range of every 6 to 12 months to be needed. No overt toxicity was observed, but long-term effects need to be monitored, especially upon repeated applications. With this, I think I have mentioned in particular the colleagues who contribute to this work, and like to finish my presentation to this double-edged session that it's maybe not so double-edged if we just eliminate in tight windows senescent cells once in a while. Thanks for your attention. Thanks, Clemens, for the very thought-provoking talk. The senlyt is super exciting. I guess I'll ask the first question. You've proven that it can eradicate senescent cells in so many scenarios. If you took it into the clinic, what indication would you first try, and why? So we are at the level where we try to push this agent through pharmacokinetics and different species, and are close to consider early testing in cancer settings. I'm grateful for the question since we are at the AACR, and heard about osteoarthritis. There are many diseases, age-related pathologies, where senolysis or SAS modulation may be very important. But we also talk about to bring those candidate agents actually at the bedside, bring it to clinical registration. And I believe as an oncologist hematologist, that probably the cancer space is the fastest way to demonstrate efficacy and bring these agents to the clinic, and then potentially into non-cancer settings. I will take a question here. Can I? Hi, wonderful talk. Thank you. Thank you. My question is maybe a naive question, but what about in cancer heterogeneity, the probability to select the most proliferative cells by using a senolytic drug? This possibility is given since we will be targeting obviously the senescent cells. But if I may say so from changing the perspective, one of the most critical problems in cancer is therapy surviving persister cells, and these persisters are typically low to non-proliferating cells, dormant cancer cells with overlapping features to cellular senescence. If we would get a handle on those cells by a senolytic approach, we would probably make a major achievement. And I'm certainly not arguing that this is all what it takes to eliminate potentially relapse-promoting cells. You might be very right, but I think the therapy surviving slow to no proliferating persisters are a central problem to target. Thank you.
