Okay. It's 10 on the dot. So good morning, everyone. It really warms my heart to see so many people in the room talking about cancer neuroscience. A few years back, we had to convince people that nerves exist in cancer. So that's a great thing to see, at least for me personally. My name is Maron. I'm a head and neck surgeon at MD Anderson. I'm also studying the intersection between nerves and cancer. I'm really honored to have Dr. Will Wang and Dr. Logan Walsh here with me. I have no financial disclosure. Just having you here means that you all believe that there are nerves in cancer. So this is the first documentation of nerves in cancer over 100 years ago. I used to say that not a lot has been done since, but in the last five years, we really see a booming of a lot of papers and data that keeps flowing that talks about the role of nerves in cancer and, not less importantly, how nerves actually regulate the anti-tumor immunity. When we're talking about nerves, it's important to remember that nerves come in different forms and flavors. For those of you who don't remember from medical school or physiology class, we have the central nervous system, brain, spine. We have the peripheral nervous system, where about 95% of the human tumors arise. And it splits into the somatosensory system, sensation, motor movement, and also the autonomic nervous system that controls everything in the background, our heart rate, our perspiration. And they have different functions, and they have different modus operandi. Some of them have more electrical activity, some less, and they're using different neurotransmitters. This is a small study that we did at MD Anderson, looking at patients with oropharyngeal cancer, stratifying and trying to identify the different types of nerves that exist in the tumor microenvironment. And we've seen that it's not just that their nerves are important, but the different types are important in order to understand the clinical outcome, the pathological features like invasion, progression. But today, we're going to focus our discussion on the crosstalk between nerves and cancer in the context of immunity. We know that nerves and cancer actually interact in order to support tumor growth and support blood vessels to the tumor, but it also regulates the anti-tumor immune response. So, we're going to hear now from Dr. Walsh about how we're going to analyze those interactions in the tumor microenvironment on the protein level, and then from Dr. Wang on the RNA level. And then we're going to have a QA and going to look how we can also look at clinical databases and bulk approaches in order to validate our findings. So Dr. Walsh. There you go. Thank you. Well, thanks very much. Good morning, everyone. Thank you very much, Dr. Amit, for the invitation to speak at this session, and for this cool title that I didn't provide, but it's a pretty cool title, so I'm very happy with it. I have nothing financial to disclose except for the fact that it kills me to say that I actually don't study nerves and cancer. I know it warms your heart that it's so important. I've recently sort of embarked on the field, thanks to these guys and collaboration through Sebastian Talbot. But I do study spatial biology, and so since this is one of the educational sections, we thought it'd be kind of important to talk a little bit about spatial omics. Really, in the last five years, we've accelerated into this spatial omics era, and everyone seems to be talking about spatial transcriptomics, spatial proteomics, metabolomics, et cetera. And there's a lot of commercial solutions that are available out there, but I think a lot of people dive right in because they're commercially available. But there's a lot of bottlenecks and things that I think people need to consider. So as this is an educational session, we thought it was kind of important to build up this concept of how you're going to look spatially at the tumor immune microenvironment, and then how we can then layer in the nerve part of that for studying anti-tumor immunity. And so this is a review that I wrote a couple of years ago now, which is slightly outdated, but even a few years ago, it highlights just the breadth of commercial tools that are available now to study spatially at the transcriptomic level, the proteomic level, the epigenetics, and metabolomics. And what's kind of cool about these technologies, or some of these technologies, is they're actually non-destructive. In the past, when you wanted to study a tumor, you'd take a section, and then you had to take a next section for the next tool, and the next, and the next. In this context, what you can do is you can actually use these non-destructive technologies, and on the same piece of tissue, you can run spatial transcriptomics, then you can run metabolomics, and then you can run proteomics on the same tumor tissue, which we think is really cool, and we think it adds a lot of value for doing multi-omic profiling. The big bottleneck, as I mentioned, in the field, has been on the analysis side. So these references, a couple of years old, are already completely outdated, I feel. I think what's great is with theincrease in the use of bioRxiv. We have every single week a new bioRxiv paper, it's really hard to actually keep up with, by various groups who are solving a lot of the problems that I'm going to sort of highlight in the next 15 or 20 minutes. And so people are doing amazing work to solve some of the basic challenges with spatial biology. And so I think if you are looking for tools and the latest and greatest, I think you should also consider a lot of the work that's on bioRxiv, and I'll reference a few of those studies as we go forward. And so for the purposes of my talk, just because of the most sort of advanced, and I think it's the broadest category which most people work on, I'm going to focus on looking at spatial transcriptomics and the proteomic side of things. And both of these methods were named Method of the Year for Nature Methods. It's been about five years since spatial transcriptomics was Method of the Year, and then just a little over a year ago, Nature Methods named spatial proteomics. This cover's actually an image from my group. And there's so many different types and instruments and companies, and everyone's pushing you, telling you that it's the best, and you should do this panel, and you should do that panel, and 200 genes and 500 genes and 5,000, five million and five billion. And everyone's just getting worked all the time from every different company about what's the biggest and the best, and what's the difference. And people always ask me, what's the difference in the different things? So I want to just go sort of into broad categories. You have on the spatial transcriptomics side of things, we have these imaging-based or optical in situ transcriptomics, where you're directly visualizing RNA in place, and some examples of those are your MERFISH, your seqFISH, your Xenium, CosMX, et cetera. So you have on one side, you have this sort of direct measurement, and on the flip side, you have a sequencing-based or NGS type of approach, where you have some barcodes, and from those barcodes, you'll then sort of mash up your tissue with those barcodes. You have them fixed in some sort of spatial orientation that you can co-register to them later on, and I'll give you a couple of examples of that later. Examples of that are Visium, Visium HD, Stereo-seq, Slide-seq, et cetera. On the proteomic side of things, again, we sort of have two broad categories. The first one is, again, an optical-based approach where you have either DNA barcodes or fluorophores that are visualized, usually cyclically. So you stain with a few, you wash them off, you stain with a few more, you visualize, you wash them off, and examples of this are your CODEX, PhenoImager Opal, IBEX. And then you have your sort of mass spectrometry-based imaging. So in this case, what you do is your antibodies are labeled with various metal isotopes of a different weight. You stain your tissue with all your antibodies, and then you either excite them or you ablate them, and you measure the amount of antibody using mass spectrometry. So those are the broad categories. So you usually have optical or direct, and examples are IMC and maybe TOF. Okay, so we get these beautiful pictures. So here's just a few pictures that have come out of my group looking at spatial omics in a variety of different settings from different tumor models. You can see on the bottom left corner, we have actually a DRG with a number of different nerves, which I hope warms your heart a little bit. And so we have been working on this, and I think one of the big travesties, though, is that I've seen a number of publications that people have these beautiful clinical cohorts, and you could tell that they ran these commercial technologies, but they just didn't really know what to do with them. And so they put these really sort of sexy pictures in their papers as just sort of an add-on bit, when the reality is, is there's so much rich, amazing information here, and we just need more tools and technology to be able to sort of unlock what's available within these sections. And so in order to do the neuroimmune characterization, we first need to go and consider all the things that are dealing with immune characterization inside of these datasets. And so the workflow is really quite simple, and when I made this slide, I thought, "This is way too stupid for me to put into a presentation here." But the reality is, every single dataset that we have in my lab, and we've done hundreds of them, we first, and the most important thing, is to identify where the cells are, so cell segmentation. You need to know where the cells are and where the boundaries of the cells are in order to then go on to the next step, which is what are the cells or doing immune phenotyping. And this is so important, and I think this is where a lot of groups actually get it wrong, and it affects all of the downstream interpretations. You can have the best clinical cohort you want, but if you don't accurately identify where the cells are and what the cells are, it's going to mess up everything that you infer afterwards. And so think about a piece of tissue. Okay? So tissues are complex. They're very compact. They're dense. And we're often cutting these tissues in just a small two-dimensional slice. Now, when you have some sort of normal piece of tissue, like skin, for example, here, and you can sort of slice it in an orientation that you know, and you have, here's the epidermis, the dermis, the muscle, the fat. You can have some sort of orientation, but in tumors, typically, you're just sort of getting a random disoriented bunch of cells and you're cutting through it. Okay? So you don't really have an orientation, an up, a down. You're just sort of cutting directly a small section through the tumor. So if you're trying to track nerves in that tumor, it's not so simple. Now, imagine that you have a single cell, so this is just sort of to represent a nucleus that exists within any piece of tissue. Depending on where you cut that nucleus, you're going to get a different size or a different piece that could be represented across different scales.And we all know that nuclei aren't also just round circles, right? I'll give you two sides of the argument, so I'll probably just argue against myself and shoot myself in the foot right now. But the reality is, on one side, we constantly go in, we take a random biopsy from a patient, just of one region of a tumor often. We send that off clinically, and that's how we make clinical decisions right now off of some random piece of tissue. So, there's that side of the coin. On the flip side, we often include multiple cores from various regions within our data sets to try and account for heterogeneity. The fact is that these technologies are so expensive, and Will alluded to the fact that we really need to decrease the cost of these so we can start doing them on whole sections to be able to encapsulate that. My group's actually shifted away from doing a lot of these for predictive and clinical values and moved to whole sections on H&E's just for that region or for the reason of the heterogeneity. But I will say that we published this a couple of years ago, that we developed deep learning models using these spatial multiomics to predict clinical outcomes within patients. And when we take vastly different regions of a tumor that are actually quite unique with the heterogeneity and the composition, these models are capable of predicting clinical outcome with these different samples from different regions of the tumors with high accuracy in the mid-90s. So there is differences, but there's something unique about tumors overall and their architecture that can be picked out with some deep learning models. So those are just my unfiltered thoughts. It's not going away, but this is what we're limited to given the cost of these. So we got this question from multiple people in different kinds of variation. How do you guys tackle the heterogeneity issues in your lab from sample to sample, from slide to slide? Yeah. I echo everything that Dr. Walsh said. I think this is the ever challenge for everybody. I think there's other techniques you can do. So you can try to certainly minimize heterogeneity that's ateriogenically introduced by reducing batch effects. A lot of times, if we're comparing things directly, we'll try to get them onto the same experiment, onto the same slide. So at least you're not introducing other forms of, I guess, you could consider heterogeneity. I think powering these studies, knowing what your question is, and what power really means in that context. I think with all the omics, spatial included, thinking about multiple testing correction is just, I think, honestly not even where the field is at, but there's a lot of potential for spurious results, and heterogeneity can contribute to that, especially if you don't think about the question and how best to power the question and how you're selecting specimens and the number of specimens and things like that. And then I think the other thing is trying to, before you really believe in a result enough to then do the functional validation and then eventually, hopefully, get to clinical translation, trying to, with these more descriptive approaches, look at it from as many different angles as possible. Yeah. And if things converge on the same thing, regardless of which technique you're using, which specimens you're using, then you're very likely-- Maybe you miss some more subtle biology- Yeah ... but you're more likely to hit on real biology. I think functional validation is key here. Yeah. Yeah. Yeah. Thank you. Sorry. No worries. Go ahead. Sorry. I asked that question about improve the statistical sound. I got lots of inspirations from all the talks, and I'm wondering, is it possible to improve the statistical sound by comparing certain workflow, like start from the bulk transcriptomics, like from the last talk, and at least we can focus on the certain target. We already know what target we want to be targeting from the bulk sequencing, and then from the spatial, we can maybe focus on the imaging-based and just that few proteins. And then, if we cannot get what we want, we can slice deeper and get more slides until we really visualize every protein and the cell-cell interactions. So yeah. Is there any certain workflow can help us to improve the understanding of the heterogeneity? I would say that ironically, we're talking about all the nuances of these technologies, but I review a ton of spatial papers, and the main reason why I think some of these papers don't make it is not in the rigor of the analysis or not because they're accounting for heterogeneity. I think it's actually the clinical cohorts that they choose. So sort of echoing what Will just said, it's super important that you're powered, and you're powered with apples-to-apples comparators. If you're looking at response to therapy, or you're looking at survival, it's probably the most common thing people use. They often have a mixed bag of cohort of what they can get from the clinic, and they're taking these samples, and they're doing all these amazing, cool profiling things that are very statistically strong. But you're enriching with some outcome with a late-stage versus an earlier-stage patient or some other super compounding variable. So in my opinion, what I see is to really focus on the clinical question and make sure that your cohorts, if you're looking for to compare some sort of outcome, response to therapy, et cetera, are significantly powered in an apples-to-apples way so that you're looking at these things directly and not comparing something that really shouldn't necessarily be comparable. Thanks. That's cool. Thank you all for three incredible talks. I want to ask a question about some of the biology. The techniques are awesome, but we know that in lung cancer, palliative care improves results. We know that this neuroinflammatory signaling is bi-directional. So the inflammation makes certain nerve signaling worse. Nerve signaling makes this inflammation. It can change the inflammatory state. So I guess my question for you is, is palliative care, where we're using a lot of things that modulate nerve signaling, is that also oncology care? But just speculating, if you don't mind. There's a lot of activity in this field looking at things like sodium channel blockers, like lidocaine, whether or not they're affecting the tumor progression. What's the role of opioids, right? What's the role of beta blockers? All of those things are matters of ongoing investigations in different groups. We know that anxiolytics like benzodiazepines, now the group from Guido Kramer showed that they are associated with worse patient survival. So there are a lot of confounders to those things, and it's very muddy. But this is an excellent question and an active matter of investigation by many groups around the world. Thank you. It's great talks. I was wanting to zoom in on the perineural invasion talk about most of the data that you showed was that in primary versus metastatic tumors, and thinking about site-specific metastases and how perineural invasion could be different and be contributing to the unique metastatic niche versus primary disease. You can comment on that. Yeah, thank you. So the data I showed was in primary disease. I think that's a really important question. We are starting to look at that. And I know there's other groups interested. I'd say it is a little bit tricky in pancreas cancer to certainly have matched samples because we often don't resect metastases, right? And usually, the patients, their functional status doesn't usually help them. But for certain diseases, like other GI cancers where we do that, like colorectal, there's maybe an opportunity to be able to study matched analyses in primary met of neural environments. We're very interested in also, as you said, organ tropism for metastases, but also looking at neuronal subtypes, right? We didn't really talk about it very much, but it's clear that it's not one size fits all for these different nerve bundles. They're usually mixed, right? If you look at these larger fibers, right? There's going to be mixed between the different neuronal subtypes, parasympathetic, sympathetic, sensory, and then even finer categories beyond that. So I think all those things will likely have nuanced roles. We don't generally see as much perineural invasion in, say, liver mets as we do in the pancreatic primary in the cases where we have seen it. But the innervation patterns are very different, right? So how much of, if you hold the cancer cell state as constant as possible, you just change it to a different microenvironment, or vice versa, right? You take two different cancer cells in terms of very different phenotypes and then put them in the same neural microenvironment and see. Those are the types of experiments I think we need to do to really get at your question. Okay. Thank you. Thank you for a very impressive talk. I have a question in terms of you look at most gene expressions abroad could just follow up with just said that's the perineal invasion there, but mostly just total. Do you have sample you can dissection out the efferent sensory nerve, sympathetic nerve, parasympathetic nerve? What is the nerve type that's most likely to be invaded via the tumor cells? This first question, maybe ask first question. So most likely nerve subtypes to be invaded? Yeah. So most of the evidence is pointing towards sensory and sympathetic subtypes. So because you only have small amount of transcription because there's no nuclear, so you're saying nerve fibers, from limited amount of message RNA, you can get this data from the- So that's mostly at the protein level. Oh, it's look at the protein. Protein level. Okay, got it. There is also support by Nishida Silver Group in University of Michigan. She published this in Clinical Cancer Research and follow-up paper that looked exactly on that. And she showed that sensory and sympathetic, like we just heard, she used a bunch of markers for sympathetic. But, yeah, those are the most common nerves. Yeah. My second question that because nerve injury is first initiation of the nerves in regeneration and infiltration, and these are major because of Schwann cells or it's because of direct damage to nerve fiber bundles? Both. Both? Yeah. So if we develop therapeutic agents, do you think a more effective target to Schwann cells or target to both Schwann cells and nerve fibers? Again, probably both, but we currently don't have those means to mitigate directly the perineural invasion. Yeah. Okay. Thank you. Sure. Mm-hmm. Have you looked at nerve growth factor in terms of is it a positive thing for the immune circus or negative? I mean- Yeah ... it's developed neuropathy. There's a lot of work in the perineural invasion around different types of nerve growth factor. It's a family of actually four ligands, NGGF, BDNF, NTF3, and GDNF. And they all have been linked to more rapid tumor progression and perineural invasion, not necessarily neuropathy, that's a whole different question. But this family of ligands have been associated with tumor progression, yes. Thank you. Sure. Thank you everyone for staying with us. Have a great meeting.

Auto-generated captions

This transcript is Vimeo auto-generated English. Expect misheard names and technical terms. Use the ripgrep/search approach for exact quotes.

Okay, everyone. Thank you very much for coming to this educational session on 3D cell imaging and cancer. We've located our second speaker, but I'm sorry to tell you that our third speaker, Carolyn Larabell, who was going to talk about quantitative 3D views of whole cells using soft X-ray tomography, is not going to be here today, and we've not managed to secure a video, I'm afraid. So what we're going to do is Ashley and I are just going to extend a little bit our talks, and then we're going to do what we're supposed to do in these sessions anyway, which is to have a more extended Q&A and panel discussion. So as we go to that last piece, I'll welcome anybody who's interested in that to come forward, and it'll make it easier for us to use the preset microphones. So before we start, let me just say, and some of this was written up in the introduction, which I had made. Just a moment. Ashley. Ashley. Okay, thanks so much. I got lost. Yeah. No. Do you want to sit up here or you want to sit down there? We'll get everything working. You have 25 minutes. We were just checking that she wasn't going to talk 2D. It is going to be 3D, so I think we're safe. So I wanted to just say an introductory remark before I start on my own session, and it was in the comments that I'd written as an introduction. I think it's important as we talk about 3D imaging today, to acknowledge a few things. First, that 3D imaging is intrinsic to everything that we think about in radiology, so it's all tomographic. So that has to be there. Secondly, as I mentioned, pathologists have traditionally had a kind of 3D mindset, and it manifests itself in the fact that diagnostic pathology on a tissue level will look at many sections before coming up with a summary view, and also will typically focus up and down on a single section, particularly using what's called high powered field, and the high powered field then allows you to get a 3D view. And I think what's different in what you're going to hear about today is taking the same fundamental concepts but trying to make them more systematic and a little bit more quantitative. And you're going to see in the two talks, and then hopefully in our follow-up discussion, a sense both of where we are and where we're going, and how this inevitably relates to what's going to be a much broader range of two-dimensional methods. So, with that, let me start in on my presentation, which is going to be about highplex 3D microscopy. I want to start off a little bit with a problem statement here, talk a little bit about spatial profiling, and 3D imaging. Then I'm going to tell you about three biological applications, necessarily fairly quickly, identifying cytotoxic tumor cell interactions, looking at pathways of tertiary lymphoid assembly, and then neuroimmune interactions. And the logic connecting these is really going from the tightest spatial scales to the largest scale. Let me also mention here that if anybody's interested, all the papers related to this, some of them are just being posted to bioRxiv this weekend, can be accessed via this QR code, and I'll pop it back up at the end of my talk. So just to set the stage for this, the motivation that we've had in the group to try to think about this kind of spatial profiling technology is not simply to get deeply into individual cell types, which we obviously recognize is important to understand in the immune system, what type of cell, its activity state, but also to get access to location. And here's a tracing that I made of a primary melanoma, as it turns out, with just some of the kind of features that you encounter here. Does it matter whether the T cell is infiltrated or is in the surrounding stroma? What is T cell exclusion look like when you have tumor domains of different sizes? What about the role of the vasculature, for example? And then clinically about these clustered assemblies, tertiary lymphoid structures, or SILTs, for example, in the colon, in which a lot of T cell programming happens, T and B cell programming happens outside of the primary lymphoid organs. The other thing, of course, on a much smaller spatial scale, sort of imagined here on the right, and we'll see some images of this, is trying to get access to true anti-tumor reactivity, and we're going to look at this in today's talk, surrounding T cells. And of course, in a human setting, there's no way that we can use tetramers. We don't typically know what the antigen is, and it may in fact be quite diverse. And so actually working out which subset of T cells might be reactive in the tumor environment is a challenging problem. So the methods that I'm going to talk about today are of a family of methods. This is an open source version that we built, but it's the typical method that's used here. And they're these cyclic accumulation technologies, and so you end up building a high-dimensional image. They can be as high as 100 or 150 dimensional. Some vendors claim yet more. And they're typically built up by sequentially collecting lower dimensional images. And the individual cycles can be anywhere from, say, three colors up to 20 or more, but the idea is to use a microscope optimally to get at molecular information that allows you to subtype individual cells. And then what I'll show you today in a paper that we just published at the end of last year is that you can take all of that and now move it into various forms of three dimensions. And I'll tell you a little bit about why you might want to do that. This is on a 35-micron section of a primary melanoma. And in this case, we have a 54-plex image, which allows you to go fairly deeply into individual cell types, and activities.And so if we look across sort of the range of applications, and I think both Ashley and I will discuss this, is you have different ways of trying to get access to the third dimension. Serial section, in some ways, is the simplest, but it's also fairly time-consuming and difficult. I'll show you some of that data. Light sheet microscopy is used almost universally in model organisms and has only just come into the fore now in humans, and I'll show you that. And then various forms of high-resolution confocal microscopy. And you might ask, why would I need a range of techniques? All of which, by the way, are happily in the facilities we already have in our institutions, is because you're trying to scale all the way from intact tissues on a millimeter scale down to the functional properties of cells at the levels of their organelles. So a couple of quick basics here. If you just imagine in any 3D imaging, typically these are mounted to microscopes, inverted microscope here, so the x, y axis, the z axis is typically the most difficult one, and it's what we mean by 3D as opposed to 2D. But it's important that you also think about the size of the specimen as well. Diagnostic histopathology requires whole-slide imaging, which is going to be a couple of centimeters of tissue if the specimen is that large. Anything on sort of TMA size is not going to work at all to look at things of the size you're going to see about today. There are various ways to get access to that third dimension, and those of you who are microscopists know there are many more than I'm showing today. The two I'm going to mention are optical sectioning microscopy, so using the capacity of a microscope to focus on a fairly thin slice of tissue. I'm going to show you images where we take 250 sequential optical sections, and you can then build a three-dimensional image. And those microscopes are in routine use in pre-clinical studies around the country, but again, not much applied in the areas we're interested in of human histopathology. And the other one, which is our set of volumetric methods, very diverse in terms of instrumentation, use light-sheet imaging, and those are directly volumetric. So they can collect large volumes of tissue down to cellular resolution, and by far their widest application is in studying the mouse brain and similar neuroanatomy. The other thing that most of you, I think, will be aware of is that the numerical aperture, which essentially is how fat is your lens, and the fatter your lens, the more expensive it costs, so anywhere from 4,000 to 20,000 for the big fat lens here. The numerical aperture ultimately determines resolution. And so the point of showing you this is that 3D imaging is identical to high-resolution imaging. Because as you get a higher resolution in x/y plane, you get a higher resolution in z, and you therefore need to collect the third dimension information. And you can see that simply here. So this is lenses going from $1,000 to $20,000. Here's sort of the imagined object here, so sort of delta function. And you can see that you get a narrower and narrower sort of reimage of this point spread function. And this is what you would see in x and in z. So the third dimension, the one along the optical axis, is always the hardest to sample. And you could say, well, what does looking at a dot have to mean? Well, here's ECAD actually on a melanocyte, an invasive melanocyte, and you can see, you could imagine that the ECAD is simply made up of an appropriately distributed set of point spread functions, the so-called convolutional aspect of optical microscopes. And so that's sort of what it looks like. So if you're going to cut a thick section of tissue, this is about 30 microns, and we'll see why you're going to do that, stained just for two colors. You can see on the left, with just standard microscope, wide field microscope, it's a pretty fuzzy thing. On the right, you're going to see the confocal optical sectioning, one focal plane shown here. So the 3D equals resolution. Resolution equals the ability to see deeply into individual cells. So what we're going to look at now is sort of the first set of results we got out of this a couple of years ago now. And the goal here is to try to find that morphology in a T cell which is associated with active killing. And what we realized, if you go to a standard five-micron histological section, they can sometimes be 10 if you go to the vendor show, but five is the norm in diagnostic histopathology. These are cut from FFPE tissue, so everything I'm showing you today is designed to work with standard histopathology workflows. And what you'll find is essentially no nuclei and no cells, almost without exception, are intact in a five-micron section. If you go to around 35 to 40 microns, you could say, why not go much thicker? Well, one thing is we're trying to preserve clinical specimens in many cases. But that thickness is suitable that about 70% of cells in a typical epithelial cancer will now be intact. And so we'll ask ourselves whether that's important, and you'll see, I think, pretty clearly how it is. And this is the work of Clarence, Alex, and Daniel, and so I'll try to credit the people who did this as I go along. So let's now go into one of these three-dimensional images, 130 optical planes here. You're going to see a video of this in a moment. We pulled out just one dendritic cell and two T cells. We got 50 channels on this, so we have a sense of phenotyping, and we're going to ask ourselves the question, did it matter whether I chop the cell in half or not? And so what I'm going to do is take this complete image, and this is side on, by the way. And here it is again. I'm going to chop it up as though this were sectioned like a standard five-micron tissue section. And then I'm going to create a virtual 2D image. This is actually much sharper than you would normally have seen, but nonetheless, it serves the purpose. And if you do that, you're going to find is that you get a very high rate of misidentification of critical immune cell lineages. And the reason for that, of course, is that-These are highly polarized markers. So if you chop a cell into many slices, you're going to miss the vast majority of the LAG-3, for example. In many other cases, you'll find that signals are actually on top of each other because cells lie on top of each other in tissue, and so you perceive what was in the upper cell to lie in the lower cell, and you're going to end up with, for those of you who use these methods, our favorite cell, which is the epithelioid T cell, the T cell that carries E-Cad, for example. And in Xenium images, for example, that can be up to 40% of T cells, and it's probably because of this lying on top of each other. And then finally, of people who are developing reagents, you're often going to find that you have the schmutz that you can't get rid of. And we now realize that the schmutz you can't get rid of is often just part of a process of a cell whose nucleus you're missing and you don't recognize it as such. So what really has come out of this thick section imaging is two things then, the capacity to exploit resolution to get at function, and critical, because remember, in the human tissue, we sometimes go pre-treatment, post-treatment, but we don't typically have a time dimension. We don't have a CRISPR knockout in there, so morphology is what's reporting on function for us. And here, it just gives you an example, and again, pulled out of one of these images, of a neutrophil on the left and a fairly round-looking T cell on the right, and you can see individual organelles. And those actually can be informative, as we'll see, for activity, particularly the cytolytic granules. So the idea behind now looking for active T cell killing is we have a somewhat bewildering number of markers. And depending on when and where you wish to publish, you will choose the appropriate subset. Currently, obviously a lot of interest in the early lineage determinations. But there are a whole bunch of other classic features, like the fact that you have granzyme B-containing granulysin or perforin-containing granules. Those are going to be oriented relative to the microtubule organizing center. You would expect in this type of imaging to see a separation of around 20 nanometers between the T cell and its target, and eventually, for at least a subset of cells, you'd hope to catch the actual cytolytic interaction underway. So the question is, could you do this with this type of imaging? And so here now let me show you what that dataset that we collected looks like, and there are a whole bunch of them, but I'm just showing you one. We're going to peel back some of the layers so we can see what's going on. Using the channels I'm not showing you, we can actually go through and determine the likely function of each of these cells. We have a memory T cell, a helper T cell here, an effector T cell, a dendritic cell, and a tumor cell. And one of the things we've learned in doing this imaging, by the way, is the average T cell in a tissue is making between five and 10 functional contacts with its neighbors. And so here what you're looking at actually is that T cell with LAG-3, so checkpoint marker up. It nonetheless actually is highly cytotoxic, so it actually contains those oriented green cytotoxic granules. They're trying to kill, as we interpreted here, that Mart1-positive tumor cell. We're rotating so you can see different sides of this. But nonetheless, even though this is a cytotoxic interaction, there is this strong PD-1, PD-L1 inhibitory reaction going on in the exact same cell, in this case mediated by a dendritic cell. So to the first approximation then, we can actually pull these types of interactions out, and I've just given you a few of them here. And morphologically, we can determine whether they have cytolytic granules in the right place. Interestingly, in these tissues, we can't really image the cytoskeleton satisfactorily. But using super-resolution imaging, again, a standard feature on these types of instruments, we can look at membrane contact distance down to 30 to 50 nanometers. And so we believe that there we're capturing a functional immune synapse. And by going back and forth, work underway, back and forth between organoid experiments and what I'm showing you here, we hope to functionalize these kind of critical morphologies. Interestingly, the average T cell, and we looked at this in colorectal, and ovarian, and melanoma cancers, has a distance to its immediate neighbors of around one micron. So typical membrane-membrane distance is in these tissues around a micron. When a T cell's invading into an epithelial surface, its interaction distance will be about 400 nanometers. And then we think when it makes a functional synapse, that goes down and stabilized over about five square microns, and it gets down to about 30 nanometers, which is consistent given the resolution of these instruments with what we know from electron microscopy. There are a lot of shape differences you can also capture, and these are difficult in what is standard tissue profiling out on the vendor show there because the resolution is insufficient, but also because you aren't capturing whole cells. So this is just to show you what a T cell actually looks like in tissue. It's relatively rare to see them round. Here we're actually imaging them based on CD8. They often have this extended structure here, which pathologists tell me they often call squiggles. But in highly activated regions where they're interferon positive, you can see they form these very distinctive spike-like protrusions. And that's the kind of information that, to be frank with you, we don't really know how to interpret. It's universal in what we do in tissue culture. Morphology is how we look at all these things, and so we now need to, beyond marker space, functionalize contacts and functionalize morphology. And that's the state of the art of this type of imaging. So let's look at a slightly larger spatial scale. And this is a project that we've been doing in lung tissues, two wounds that do not heal, a lung adenocarcinoma and, of all things, tuberculosis. And I'm actually going to show you some TB pictures here, but bear with me, because there's a fundamental similarity in both. And what we're trying to look at are tertiary lymphoid structures. And I think-- So this is going to be now both T cells and B cells in big lumps. We know TLSs are very important in the action of immunotherapy, but also in natural tumor surveillance. And they're typically organized in a developmental series, excuse me, that goes from a kind of early TLS, where you'll see an aggregate of B cells, but you don't have the formation of a germinal center, to the beginnings of a germinal center, and then finally a complete germinal center, where you have follicular dendritic cells and other characteristic features.And if you just go through and you start to section happily through, and you go ahead and just image this, you'll find that a single follicle or a single, in this case, TLS, can actually be called any one of the three different developmental stages, depending on where you slice it. And of course, there's no mystery in this. The thing looks like an olive, and so whether you hit the pit or not depends on where you cut it, and also just how big the pit is. And so, the degree of error varies to some extent with the tissue section. So, Emmanuel, Jerry, Zoltan, Sohail, and Brigitte in my lab went through, and we've actually been doing large-scale serial reconstruction here. So you could ask why serial reconstruction, and it's because we want to span up to a couple of millimeters of tissue. And I'll show you in the end how we can do that without a serial reconstruction. But this allows us to do a multi-omic approach. And the tissue here is a couple of square centimeters, so we're looking at around 60 million cells. And we have sufficient antibodies that you can begin to subtype these cells. And so this is sort of what that kind of reconstruction looks like. And one of the immediate things-- By the way, if you're interested in this, if you flash the QR code later, you can get to the bio archive paper. So this is actually what a typical TLS looks like, both in LUAD and in this case, in the infected lung. And that it's an extended structure that's not individual balls, but actually they've all sort of grown together. They look like a Jerusalem artichoke actually to some extent. And they can contain multiple germinal centers at different developmental stages. This is not something that we had expected to see. But we've now built up 470 of these individual structures, and here you can get sort of a picture of what that looks like, and we know what cells are in them, et cetera. And then that we can ask ourselves, could we put these cells in any kind of a logical developmental series? And so the method that we've used is called optimal transport. So I think many of you are familiar with trajectory-based methods that are used in transcriptional profiling, and the idea is you have a high-dimensional transcript profile, and you try to find the next profile in a series, different cell, for example, that would be closest to it. Here, we're actually doing what optimal transport was initially developed for, which was building forts in the 19th century. And the thing we're minimizing is called the Earth mover's distance, and it's in fact still called the Earth mover's distance. And in this particular case, we're saying if we have two structures, we want to find those that are closest to each other if we allow only cell birth, cell death, or cell movement. And birth in this case can also be delivery from the vasculature. And so that kind of mechanical and sort of physical idea allows you now to build up a trajectory series. And this is what that trajectory looks like ultimately. So you start down here with a very, very small, and I'll show you a picture of this, a very small, kind of partially formed aggregate. They then go-- And you'll see they're actually sort of two kinds of attractors. And we know that these ones are actually around the vasculature, and in this case, these are around necrotic domains in the tissue. So we actually see a distinction. But the critical take home, I think, for this is that all of what we have in two dimensions been concentrating on early, primary, secondary, vast literature on that is in fact squished in one little corner. And because we can't correctly perceive the larger architect, we've missed all the variance in green, if that makes sense. That third category is in fact far more variable than the other categories are from themselves. We can get some confidence in these cases of this type of trajectory just by looking at physical properties. So along one of these trajectories, the things get bigger. We can see they get more compact. So we can look in the core of the TLS and say whether the cells are getting more compact, and that kind of compaction is a known feature of maturation. And then we can look at particular cell types, like here, the interactions of T cells or B cells with follicular dendritic cells and their maturity. So in terms of those features, we sort of built the kind of plausible developmental trajectory. And then you can ask yourself, "Well, what's different between these things?" And it turns out that actually what's fundamentally different, and we're looking here at how many B cells do you have, how many immature follicular cells, and how many mature follicular cells over time. And you can see that one set of these structures matures very early. Those are the ones deeply embedded in vasculature. And the other set, the one that's proximal to necrosis, develops substantially later. And so this would be the beginning of saying that this kind of TLS reconstruction can give us a view of the maturation state of these, and obviously you'd now like to look at this, for example, in the presence of an absence of an ICI therapeutic intervention. What AI is allowing us to do is to help us quantify, to visualize, and to combine multi-omics in new ways, and to link that to clinically meaningful data. And as we continue to use AI, I think we'll be able to go beyond individual planes and think about how to combine these modalities. Thank you. Yeah. If anyone has any questions, please come up to the mics. Hello. Two excellent talks that just blows you away. Very practical problem when you're working with clinical material. In this case, we focus a lot on prostate needle biopsies. The pre-analytic variables that you can't control the way you can if it's a mouse model, how do you handle things like the time between the recut and whatever molecular or immunohistochemical or immunofluorescence analysis that you're doing? Do you have sort of boundaries, or do you have storage conditions? What do you find is the most practical way to deal with that issue? Yeah. It's a good question. I do think it's one of the biggest challenges with analyzing clinical tissue is you often don't know. You don't know how quickly was this tissue fixed. You don't know, was it left in the sun? A lot of the guides you see online of applying, say, Visium, they estimate how old of tissue you can analyze. But I've seen applications that we take 1990s tissue, and the quality is beautiful. And we have some tissue collected a month ago that we don't know why, but it's- Awful ... unusable. It's awful. I think so much of it has to do with the pieces of the pipeline that we can't see. And it's difficult to solve, to be honest, unless you had the whole pipeline kind of monopolized. So what do you do on a day-to-day basis? You've asked for blocks. You've asked for recuts. Do you want just to move into whatever your analytical method is within days, within weeks? What do you find to be something that you can do routinely? Yeah, I would say with my own applications, we often focus on uncommon diseases. So it's impossible to say, "Okay, this tissue's no good. Let's wait till the next one comes." Because we maybe need to analyze the 20 patients that have been seen since 2000 with this disease. So it's not so much about how can we change the way we collect tissue now to make it all as good as possible, though that is also something that needs to be done, but also how can we salvage these unique and invaluable samples that have been sitting since the '90s, the '80s, and what can we still get out of those today? Okay. Well, thank you. Hey, Andy. Yeah. Imagining us going into this general discussion session. You got a question? Thank you very much. I was going to-- Totally agreeing with you. I don't think we have the solution to the pre-analytical variables. What I would say, and it would be interesting to see if Ashley says this, one of the beauties of the H&E reconstruction or even the synthetic is it's actually pretty robust. So we too go back- H&E is tough. Sorry? H&E is very robust. It is. And we also find that protein imaging, we've done-- Some of the sections that I showed there are 15 years old, right? That we have to face the block to get off the oxidation. But proteins are robust. The biggest difficulty is in transcriptomic profiling. And typically, less than two weeks from sectioning is a requirement. So I think it's why this sort of emphasis that everything will become transcriptomics is sort of unrealistic. What we found, and it's interesting, here's the same, we found about a third of specimens in a cohort that we collect within a surgical nurse setting, so it's a little fancier. A third of them have pre-analytical variables that we still haven't managed to fully understand. And so in those cases, we do have methods to try to get at least minimal information. We've published some of those, too. Well, thank you. Well, thank you so much for a wonderful talk, Dr. Creamer. So I have a question that comes from a problem that I'm facing and the project that I'm currently working on. So even I work on pancreatic cancer, and so we know that there is a lot of heterogeneity in the morphology of PDAC. There are well-differentiated glands, and then there are diffusely infiltrating tumor cells. And it is only plausible for us to imagine that these two morphologic features have very distinct biologies. So I was wondering if you do have a solution to segment these two units in the time of image processing even though they have a similar biomarker profile. For instance, I would expect to see pan cytokeratin in these diffusely infiltrating tumor cells as well as the well-differentiated glands. So even when they express the same profile of biomarkers, how do you morphologically segment them based on AI? Yeah, that's a good question. I would love to talk to you at the end about this, too. We actually have an ongoing study looking at some of the same questions, and how we've been distinguishing them is by size and continuity. Okay. That we think of these big tongues of invading glands as kind of collective epithelial-like invasion. But then we can also distinguish this mesenchymal-like invasion when you have just a few clumps of cells invading by themselves. And in H&E, they honestly look almost nothing alike. Even cytologically, the nuclei don't look that alike. But the biggest, cleanest way that we can distinguish them is just by connectivity and size. How many cells is in this collected unit? Got it. Thank you so much. One-- Ashley, if I could. Why don't you sit at the- We can do the joint questions. We can go to the joint question session, if that's good. We have quite a while. So anyone, if you also have ideas, please feel free to speak up. We have-- Because we-- No, it didn't come. Yes, we don't have the video. So we have 20 minutes to engage in a broader discussion. I was going to say, one thing that-- I showed a picture of a bunch of T cells of different shapes, and they sort of seemed to be sitting in some landscape. That actually was similar to what Ashley described. It was actually an UNI model embedding. And what's interesting is these things are just visually totally different. These machine learning AI models can neatly discriminate them. A human can discriminate them, but none of the morphometric features that we've used in the pre-machine learning era are any good. Like, is it prolate? Is it ellipsoid? How long is it? How fat is it? And so to some extent, there's been in your history there, 30 years of tissue morphometrics that have been very disappointing. And I think what's sort of exciting now in these quantitative analyses coming out of machine learning is they're able to-- They're incredibly intuitive, if you've ever tried them. They're able to recapitulate classifications that you would visually agree with and then extend beyond that. And so I think that's a very big step forward. And one setting that I've seen is in melanoma diagnosis. I'm a PhD, not a diagnostician, but if you look at the AGC7 to 8 manual, we lost three molecular features. So the number of lymphocytes is no longer a diagnostic feature, and the number of proliferating cells is no longer a diagnostic feature. And the speculation is not that those are not important for cancer, but it's just extremely difficult for histopathologists moving quickly to quantify those types of features. And so that would be a case where the model acting like a pathologist would really be supportive. And of course, that's how we do Pap smears. So we know in a sense that it will work. So I think you have the right problem to bring up. Yeah. Thank you so much. Nice talk, Peter and Ashley. I was thinking that, have you ever tested a real-world case where the pathologist may have a disagreement or it's very subjective interpretation, and see how your AI tools can help make it more accurate? Is this mic on? Yes. Okay. Yeah. I think I have a good application that we've done just that, and it's not so much a question of beating the pathologist. It's not testing, saying a pathologist is not good. I think pathologists have shown a shocking ability to link what they can see visually in a slide to patient outcome. But we have one ongoing study that we wanted to ask, how difficult is it to identify some things pathologically? So we took thick blocks of human tissue and cut about 50 sections each, and specifically found blocks with something called vessel invasion. So it's the beginning of metastasis when cells invade into a blood vessel. And diagnostically, it can be used in staging. If pathologists see cells inside the vessel, it means the patient may have metastatic disease, even if it wasn't found on imaging. And what we found is if we isolate a vessel invasion in a block of tissue and we collect all the images below that moment following the blood vessel, only about half the time can a pathologist definitively call this a vessel invasion. Because in so many instances, it just doesn't have all the diagnostic qualities to call in the clinic, even though we know it exists because we can follow it continuously. And I think it shows not that pathologists should be able to identify this because, say, if the endothelium of the vessel is missing, it's impossible in that slide. You couldn't do anything about it. But can we now use AI to identify something else holistic in that slide that a pathologist could use as a cue? Yeah. No, I agree with you that sometimes the diagnostic features could be missing, but sometimes they also could be extraordinarily difficult to make a call. We've had an example recently where we were looking for a structure called multinucleated giant cells in the lung that show up as they're a fusion event for macrophages and epithelioid histocytes. And it's tricky to call because it's a three-dimensional structure. By the way, all the tissue profiling technologies throw it out because it's a cell with many nuclei. And what was interesting, we had three pathologists annotating for us so we could get an inter-rater reproducibility, and then we had a foundation model scoring, actually learning from them iteratively. Very much as Ashley said, I think it was difficult to score in many cases, but what was really interesting was the model and the humans, the three humans on actually three different countries, came to a much better understanding in the end by working with the machine. So that was actually really interesting. We ended up in that group with a pretty good consensus view that neither the machine initially had achieved because it has hallucinations, et cetera, or the individual humans had done by annotation. So I also think there's going to be a way in which this will help as a kind of teaching tool, because as it exists now, as you probably know, is you get 10 negative slides and 10 positive slides, and you train on that. This, I think, will be a much more interactive way to do it and actually be very exciting. Yeah. Thanks, Peter. Thank you. That was a very good presentation. I'm Bob Edwards, Pittsburgh. I'm a surgical oncologist who has a lab that takes out a lot of tumors and fallopian tubes and infiltrating lesions looking for CD8 infiltration. And what I've been struck by is there's three major dilemmas that we have. The lack of correlation of the STIC lesion with the development and bulk of ovarian cancer, the inability to characterize CD8s in tumors that have involuted, and then the presence of TLSs and whether or not they're prognostic for a given cancer. So I know these are big, broad questions, but when I was looking at the AI reconstructions, I was thinking maybe the way we're choosing to do our sectioning now reflects our inability to understand the three-dimensional relationship. And are there-- This is a little off what you were talking about, but it was inferred. Maybe the approach to processing the tissue needs to be changed to look more carefully at what it is we're actually sectioning. Rather than doing serial sections, maybe we need to do targeted sectioning. I don't know. I wonder what you thought about that. Yeah. No, I think it's a good question. Especially as I think in the tissue atlasing community, both within fallopian tube and any place in the body, in the skin, in the GI system, people have been thinking about these lesions that we all get as we age. And as we've now been pushing so much money into the field, I think we find that all of us develop so much as we age that just stays benign. If we exhaustively looked at a fallopian tube, we find STICs even in-- One of those women was 25 and we found two STIC lesions. I think it shows that what pathologists see in the clinic with techniques like CFIM is the lesions big enough to be caught by that kind of even sampling. And it's not to say that the small lesions need to be found. Maybe they don't if it's likely to stay indolent. But does some technology exist that might not be pathology, like tubal washing, something else that could be done that could know if you have a STIC lesion, but maybe you don't need to know the location? Because we now know we all have these, so how do we identify the active ones? Yeah, no, that's great. I think probably both of us would be happy to work with you on some of those surgical specimens. We too are looking at STICs.The other thing to say on that is, so we have noticed actually in the example I gave of TLSs, is they're actually, if you got a single section that didn't go, for example, through the germinal center, and you were going to ask yourself, could you determine that that was a true TLS as opposed to a loose aggregate? And the answer with some precision is yes. So there are features that we don't currently evaluate in 2D sections that are sort of like Plato's shadow there, sort of informative. And I think that's the sense that this kind of 3D data sets will help us become a ground truth. Another example is we noticed in the paper that actually Ashley showed, Lin et al., we actually looked at the siculation that's seen often at the leading edge of a colorectal cancer, the budding it's called. And these have been interpreted as little spheres of cells that are part of the metastatic process, but that's not correct actually, they're the ends of fingers. And so, again, as with the colon, that view and that view have been interpreted as totally different structures, but they're simply the two orthogonal views. So I think all of those things are going to help us interpret the 2D data. One other thing we haven't talked about very much, by the way, is cost. So, one of the things that we've been doing in 2D 20-plex imaging is trying to push the cost down to $500 per section or lower, and I think that's going to happen. The H&E methods are really quite inexpensive. And so I think the moment you want to scale or apply in your setting, they're going to have to be inexpensive costs. I think doing $15,000, $18,000 per slide, exciting though it is, is really very limiting. So, the cost aspect of this is a big deal, because it really limits the science and medicine that can be done. And I think that also shows the value of these synthetic staining methods, that if you can do the highplex labeling and the H&E on the same slide, if you can build, say, an H&E to a multiplex model, now you can go back to all those clinical H&Es that have been banked, scan them all, and then do one of these multi-omic studies at scale. I think it's the only way, is no one's going to have half a million to stain a thousand patients' tissue, but can we use AI to scale up these methods? I wonder if in the future, the biggest barrier we're going to face is, beyond the cost of doing it, is going to be a kind of ethical barrier, right? Our hospitals are all holding onto these images now, both because they see profit, but I think they're concerned that big for-profit companies are going to exploit them in ways. So I think we're going to have to think carefully about how we can ethically, as we have done with the Human Genome Project, share this type of data. Yes. Hello, Andreas Boser from Milton here. So we have recently outlined and published a method how you can do the clearing of a material, and then afterwards sectioning it, and then do a multi-omics approach, let's say, with hundreds of antibodies on the same section from this part. But due to the procedure of the clearing and afterwards the rehydration, we still obviously have distortion of the tissue. And now we are still struggling with the part, how can we best superimpose the optical sections with the physical sections after the maximal analysis, let's say. Is there a good method, software, which you would suggest how you can best get rid of this morphological distortions to better superimpose both? Yeah. It's a good question. I can give you my best attempt at a solution that we've been employing. I've been helping link quantitative phase imaging to H&E, that it's the same issue, that you have the H&E doesn't exactly line up at the whole slide level to the phase imaging. Excuse me. And so what we've done, if you think of a lot of the synthetic stain models, they don't need the whole slide to be flawlessly aligned, they need high-quality tiles. So the solution we have, as inelegant as it is, is a tile-based alignment, is let me take this piece of the H&E and align it to the image, and the next piece of the H&E and align it. And as long as you do that kind of systematically one by one, I have found that it's one of those times that a manual step gives a lot of value at the end, is having a student look back at 10,000 matched H&E and IHC images and tossing out the bad ones, it adds so much quality to the model. Even if it's a diffusion model, a GAN, anything, the quality in is quality out. There's obviously also Ashley's CODA method. For lung reconstruction, we've actually found we've had to do more non-rigid alignment as you do, and we've even been using the ANTS setup. So that's actually used for tomography in CT imaging, and it's got a great toolbox for doing nonlinear sort of morphing. The trick there is you got to segment everything first, because once you morph everything, at the single-cell level gets a little screwy. But the tools we have, we'd be happy to share with you. But they were inspired by the tools you built, so. The methods we were using is called ANTS, A-N-T-S. You wouldn't have heard of it, but it's universal in CT imaging, in experimental C. So there's a whole series of tomographic alignment tools for 3D. If you write to us, I can show you what we've done. Thank you very much. Christoph Cooper from Aachen, Germany. Also, really, I'd enjoyed the two talks. I have two very different question. The first one is more related to the sectioning. So sectioning of 35 micrometer FFPE tissues, I think is quite tricky. I would really love to learn how you do it, and particularly if there are any artifacts in the 3D tissue that you induced by this type of sectioning, if you've controlled for that. Another question is related to the 3D data that you presented and deanalysis. So most of the time what I saw is that you mainly use2D data analysis types, and then, the Uni2 model is trained on 2D sections. So obviously, of course, a foundation model in 3D doesn't exist yet maybe, but particularly because you mentioned connectivity, what would be other approaches maybe to analyze the 3D structures that you described? Why don't you take 3D and I'll do 35 microns? Yeah, it's a good question. And to be honest, we typically have been applying foundation models 2D image by 2D image. I think the CT space is a good place to look to see what might change moving ahead. That as opposed to taking individual 2D tile inputs, they go cube by cube, so you have that Z context in mind. I think it would be amazing if somebody could develop a foundation model that could do the same. But you can imagine the imaging they would need as an input isn't something that a lot of teams have. No, I think one thing there is it would-- unfortunately, with all the disruption that's happened, is there is no good repository for these data. So like you, we put it on S3 and we let people download, but that's expensive. Neither in Europe, which frankly is far ahead of the US in a lot of these imaging things, but nothing at the NIH has been sustained actually enough to make it possible. Because I think if you had all these data sets, it would inspire groups to come in and build that. Let me briefly describe-- Happy did the protocol for 35, we can show you. It's interesting, you cut it, it curls a little bit as you would imagine, depends on the wax. We lightly relax it with a little bit of heat, and we float it in superglue. So in fact, we superglue all these things down, which seem completely insane, but was invented-- or not invented, was developed by a student in my lab. And so actually there are glues to hold it down. And you can actually do all sorts of tricks, it turns out, with glue and histology. So, UHU might be the glue you would use in Aachen. Thank you very much. Yeah. Again, the protocols are online, but happy to give you more. Peter, I was interested in the light sheet microscopy that you were looking at, and you just mentioned that it can go as deep as a millimeter in thickness. How deep do you think in the future you could go? Because examples like melanoma invasion is commonly more than a millimeter in Breslow's depth. Do you think it could go deeper than a millimeter? So it already does, right? So there were two issues there. One is there are many types of light sheet microscopes, right? And the deeper you go, even with very good clearing, the less likely you are to be a true single-cell resolution. But the real issue for us is we were trying to preserve immune cells, as you would be interested as well, I think. And so we don't do delipidation. So clearing typically uses strong delipidation and then refractive index matching. And that's how in a mouse brain you can go a full centimeter or more depending on the instrument. So we found with non-delipidation-- So delipidation, there is the occasional CD marker, immune marker that will survive, but most don't. So we've gotten about 20 of them to work with a non-delipitating clearing method, and that practically is limited to about two millimeters. So it's all in the chemistry. So there's every reason to think that it can be extended. There is the additional issue there that we're doing cyclic imaging, so we are trying to push the five-color limit that Ashley mentioned. We've gotten up to 20 colors, and that brings in these distortions, et cetera. But it's all engineering. Those things are just engineering solutions. I think fundamentally, the tissue is capable. Fundamentally, the technology is there. So, I think it's completely solvable to get the entirety of an invasive stage 2B melanoma. Is that what you're looking for? And another question, unrelated. Where does the pathologist fit into this equation? Because they're used to looking in two-dimensional space. Is it to do with education of what the tissue now looks like in three dimensions to then educate the pathologist to maybe use this for future diagnosis? Yeah, I think it depends on the specific study. We do have some studies in pathology education. The vessel invasion one that I mentioned that we want to build an atlas of vessel invasions and make them all public so that pathologists can see easy cases that I could teach you in two minutes what a vessel invasion looks like. It looks like this. All the way down to the challenging cases that maybe none of the pathologists that we tested them on could identify, but we know based on continuity that it is. I think that's an instance when ideally this type of data could be fed back into the medical education system to educate pathologists. A second case is, like you mentioned, linking pathologists to the AI and seeing can the AI model teach pathologists something that they could use in the clinic. So in the 2D foundational model application that I showed today, we've been taking text inputs and image embedding inputs and seeing how well does a text-only model do when it's looking at extensive pathologist notes. So how well do pathologists do today? And then next to that, we have an image embedding model that does this beat the text model? And if it does, can we make back what they call attention heat maps so the model can tell us what location in the slide did it look. And if we can see something consistent about what the model is looking at, can we give that back to pathologists and say, "Okay, tell me now, what was the model looking at? And is that something that you could begin to make note of in the clinic?" And in fact, in this application, we find what pathologists call the leading edge, and depending on the shape of that leading edge, it's indicative of the outcome. Which is something pathologists kind of subjectively know, but they don't make note of it today in the clinic.So this is a place that we can have that feedback loop. Fantastic. Thank you. Yeah, let me just add to that. I think, first, you're not a pathologist, and I'm not. So in my lab, this is known as path-splaining. It's a bit like mansplaining. It's non-pathologists explaining pathology. But our pathologists, everything we do engages them as it does at Hopkins. But that's not the norm, right? I think out on the floor, if I could be a little controversial, it is seen as all a branch of genomics, right? Because of the spatial transcriptomics. So I think really figuring out how to engage them. One difficulty is that pathology departments-- So we work with the Brigham and Women's pathology department, which was among the most storied in the United States. And in modern American medicine, it's becoming a service center rather than a research center. It's all about revenue value units. And so I think re-engaging that community in research should be an incredibly high priority from a kind of national funding priority, because you're just not going to understand what we've shown today without people, without surgeons, without oncologists, and they're not in the room. It's bewildering to me. Absolutely. You need pathologists on your side to get this. Agree. Yeah. And the radiologists and the surgeons, right? But it's not how our funding in this country is currently constructed. So maybe we'll take one final comment or question, because we should wrap up. Just fantastic tools and fantastic pictures and looking at biology and everything, but I keep getting back, maybe it's from too many years of tumor boards, of false negatives, false positives, sampling errors, and gold standards , particularly for imputing data and that sort of thing. And I'm kind of fuzzy where this is all really going from that standpoint. Let me just say that it's a fantastic thing to bring up, right? I think there is quite a bit of trying to develop analytical accuracy in this. It's coming along more slowly. This isn't as well-developed as laboratory medicine from that perspective. One thing we have actually, in our own work, been much criticized for is sort of looking at the kind of questions you showed, which are really diagnostically difficult. Like what is the transition from abnormal morphology in the skin to the first melanocytic lesion? Where would you make that call? Where in a breast cancer have you got the first DCIS? I don't think either of us imagine that we're answering those questions yet. What we're trying to do is put not just a bunch of tools together, but put together the conceptual foundation of addressing those tools reliably. So if imagine right now exome sequencing is a clinically practical tool that is used universally, there was a lot that had to come along, discovering all the driving oncogenes, developing the methods, and I think we're sort of in that early phase, developing the methods. I do believe, as Ashley has alluded to, that bringing a more quantitative analytical framework that's still human or physician in the loop, is going to be incredibly powerful in this field. Because AI is nowhere is it more powerful than in dealing with images. So see this as a clinical application coming along. Having said that, very simple things, we can now count mitotic indices with AI very quickly. We can fully quantify tumor infiltration using these tools. So there are some simple things that are ready to go, but all the issues you brought up, as with the question of pre-analytical variables, they haven't gone away. Yeah, I listened to an excellent talk a while back by Elliot Fishman on AI and CT imaging, and how he put it was, and we can make the analogy to pathology, but the goal of these AI tools, it's not, can we eliminate the pathologist and can we do what they can do so we don't need them? Especially at academic hospitals, you can find a specialist in anything who's going to today absolutely beat any AI that we can develop. But as an example, my family lives in Wisconsin in a township. It has a population less than 1,000. So when they go to a hospital, they see a GP who's not a specialist in anything they have. And if my dad has, say, a skin lesion, can we get a Johns Hopkins pathologist's mind and embed that in the AI and give those tools to these small-town hospitals that so many people go to? And it's not going to make the diagnosis, but can it flag his case and say, "You should look at this a second time. You should maybe suggest this patient go to Mayo Clinic," and help take the academic hospitals down to these small towns? It's interesting. I was buttonholed by a bunch of pathologists who are now all retiring, and have studied leprosy and these rare tropical diseases, and those diseases, when they were more prevalent in the Western world, everybody went to the London School of Tropical Medicine to be trained. Nobody's being trained to diagnose them anymore. And so in fact, we're behind where we were in the 1950s. I think those are things that could also probably be embedded. Yeah. Well, thank you everyone. Thank you, Ashley, for a fantastic talk.
