This transcript is Vimeo auto-generated English. Expect misheard names and technical terms. Use the ripgrep/search approach for exact quotes.

All right. Welcome to our educational session on fibroblast dynamics, how heterogeneity shapes the tumor microenvironment. I'm going to be talking a lot about fibroblasts. And you have this QR code up, so this is how you can go online and type in questions. We also have two microphones. You are more than welcome to come up and ask questions at the microphone. But if you'd like to type your question online, that's the QR code, and then it will pop up on the computer here so we can read out your question. All right. Great. All right. Do you want to come up? No. Okay. All right. My name is Stephanie Duggan. I'm an associate professor at Dana-Farber Cancer Institute and Harvard Medical School, and we'll be talking to you today about fibroblasts and anti-tumor immunity. These are my disclosures. All right. So when we think about fibroblasts, this is one of the most fundamental cell types. It's part of every normal healthy tissue. These are the cells that are making your connective tissue, performing lots of structural functions, and although this session is about fibroblasts and cancer, I do want to iterate that these are normal cells that are very important for homeostasis. And they're not just one kind. And so if you look in various tissues, the fibroblasts are poised for separate functions in those tissues. All of them make extracellular matrix, some more than others. But they also have a lot of metabolic functions. They can secrete a lot of proteins. These are cells that are really good at protein biosynthesis that's important for making extracellular matrix, for remodeling extracellular matrix. But they can also do things like secrete growth factors and cytokines that can call in immune cells as needed or restrain them as needed. And so this is a picture form, but it actually comes from a lot of transcriptional profiling. This is a really nice study from Shannon Turley's group, where they looked at healthy tissues, and you can see the tissues here. And a lot of them were public data sets where they subsetted out fibroblasts and just asked, "What does the fibroblasts look like in lung, in bone, in intestine?" And they're slightly different. And so you see that there's some heterogeneity. They're all capable of making extracellular matrix, but they have slightly different gene transcriptions that make the normal functions that are needed in those tissues. A huge function, of course, is to produce the extracellular matrix. We think of this in terms of collagens, but there's also a lot of proteoglycans in there. Huge amount of ECM components. This is an incredibly diverse set of proteins that can be cross-linked in long fibers, that can be cross-linked in a more chaotic way. And a lot of the remodeling of the extracellular matrix is also performed by fibroblasts. Macrophages can contribute, too. But in terms of both building and breaking down collagen, making matrix metalloproteases to make sure that the extracellular matrix is appropriately remodeled. This is a cartoon, but also some really nice work. This study was led by Richard Hynes' lab, asking what proteins are there? And I think proteomics has really led the way in this, where you can take the extracellular matrix from a tissue, you can decellularize it, and ask, "Well, what is left?" And it's a surprisingly rich set of proteins, some of which are the core matrisome that are detected across tissues, but some of them are also more tissue-dependent. And asking what does a tissue need in its extracellular matrix can be very revealing about the function of the fibroblasts that secreted it in the first place, and that tissue in particular. And so we talked a bit about healthy homeostasis, but of course, tissues can become inflamed. And one of the huge important roles of the fibroblasts is to sense tissue damage and to help mediate the wound healing and remodeling of the extracellular matrix. Is it really truly imprinted in what's going to happen with the travelers? Yeah. So, and again, that's a good question. So, I think a lot of it is hardwired. So if we take the fibroblasts out and culture them in vitro, we see that the response to these cues are really hardwired into the fibroblasts. Sure. Right? And so that would indicate that even if they travel with the tumor cells to a site of metastasis, that the way they would respond at that metastatic site might be similar to what they would respond to in the primary tumor. I think where we still don't know enough is how many of the fibroblasts we're finding, either in a primary tumor or metastatic site, are from the tissue of origin versus the ones that have actually either traveled with the tumor cells or being recruited from the bone marrow, such as fibrocytes, et cetera. Right. And one of the challenges is really having robust markers that do not change over time depending on the tissue that they're in. So how can we track this with epigenetic markers, for example? Right. So once we track them, then we need to study their reciprocity because now they're going to be companions. Yeah. Absolutely. I think really picking apart the sort of underlying mechanisms of those interactions, I think is going to be critical. And I think we haven't really discussed this in much detail here, but in particular, the structure in and around the ECM as well, I think is just going to be so important in terms of how those interactions drive the tumor phenotype and immune phenotype ultimately. Yeah, I made you said that. All right. Oh, you have your question? Yeah. So maybe this is for the whole panel. So, given that all of these CAF targeting approaches work great in mice and then they fail in the clinic or make it even worse, should we start thinking about other animal models in looking at these therapies? Or should we be comparing the human setting with the mouse setting a little bit more to figure out what are the exact differences that account for these phenotypical differences we see with the different species? Yeah. So I think that's a very important-- If I may start. Yeah. So I think that's a very important question. So I would be very careful with discarding the mouse model, right? Actually, I think some of the fundamental challenges we've had in terms of translating from mouse into human, I think some of it is just because we don't understand the underlying biology well enough. And I think that some trials have probably been started too early, right? Where we really haven't understood what we're looking for in the biomarker. I think it's worthwhile really thinking about having other models. I think the best model to study this sort of thing is ultimately the human patient, right? And so actually having access to tissue from clinical trials, even if it's not a stromal targeting agent, but for any other agent, right? Would really help us understand the interaction network and how they respond under those conditions. I think that the sort of fundamental biology is really where we're lacking, if you ask me. Yeah. I'll maybe bluntly say what Claus is too humble to say, that I think his approach really is such a critical way forward to, yes, use mouse models that incorporate lymphatic vasculature and inter-organ crosstalk and things that we really need in vivo models for. But to really have as a critical intermediate step, these sort of the brilliant engineering platform that you've developed or other kind of patient-derived models to complement those and at least understand whether some of the paracrine signaling mechanisms we've seen in mice hold true in patient-derived models, whatever we choose to make them before moving forward and translating. It does seem like a critical intermediate that hopefully will be incorporated more kind of across the field. Great. Okay, with that, we will close our session. So thank you. Thank you. Awesome talks, guys. Yeah.

Date: 2026-04-18 Primary topic: single-cell-spatial-omics Cross-referenced from: single-cell-spatial-omics Word count: ~16,020

Auto-generated captions

This transcript is Vimeo auto-generated English. Expect misheard names and technical terms. Use the ripgrep/search approach for exact quotes.

Well, welcome everybody. This is the Macrophages as Therapeutic Gatekeepers from Biology to Clinical Application session. I'm Jennifer Guerrero. I'm from Brigham and Women's Hospital, and I'm joined by Dr. Tyler Miller from Case Western Reserve University School of Medicine, and Dr. Tom Marron from the Tisch Cancer Institute. We designed this session to highlight emerging translational strategies to reprogram, constrain, or selectively eliminate immunosuppressive myeloid states to improve clinical outcomes. Together, these talks, we hope to demonstrate, will emphasize how disease-specific biology can inform scalable, clinically actionable myeloid targeting strategies. So I'm the first talk. Great. Thank you very much. And, I'm going to be talking about lipid-associated macrophages, their role in tumor progression, and novel strategies that we've developed to target these cells. And so a lot of this data will be unpublished, so I want to acknowledge those who contribute to it up front. My lab has spent an extensive amount of time trying to understand the different types of myeloid cells, specifically macrophages in breast tumors. But what we're finding is that a lot of these, the diversity and heterogeneity is applicable beyond just breast cancer. We have specifically focused on lipid-associated macrophages. So I'll tell you about one of the projects where we have identified lipid macrophages are responsible for therapy resistance, and we've identified strategies to target them clinically. And then in the last bit of my talk, I'll share, really for one of the first times publicly, a novel strategy that we've developed in which we're using CAR monocytes to eliminate these lipid-associated macrophages. So we know that macrophages are abundant across solid tumors. And I always like to start with this immunohistochemistry because I think that the visual representation is quite striking. So here on the left, this is normal breast tissue, on the right is a breast tumor. The dark brown staining indicates CD68 positive macrophages, of which about 50% of the tumor are composed of these macrophages. We also know that patients who have higher numbers of macrophages, shown here in the green, have worse relapse-free survival, as well as overall survival. So why is that? Well, I always think about the homeostatic function of monocytes and macrophages. Monocytes go to sites of damage, of infection, and they facilitate repair and protective programs. They do the same thing in tumors. So cancer cells secrete factors that recruit these monocytes to the tumor. And when the monocytes get to the tumor, they differentiate to a macrophage, and they sense that there's low oxygen, poor nutrients, and so they become the type of cell that helps repair the tumor or repair these damaged cells, and in doing so, helps the cancer cells survive. These macrophages also secrete factors that lead to angiogenesis, metastasis. They themselves are impaired in their ability to present antigen. They recruit suppressive T regulatory cells. And importantly, they inhibit the recruitment and function of cytotoxic T lymphocytes. So given the abundance of macrophages and their role across solid tumors, there's been a huge interest in developing strategies to either inhibit these cells, deplete these cells, or to inhibit the things that they do, the suppressive factors that they make. And so, despite that I've spent more than a decade here, many of the things on this slide were, I was responsible for putting them on this slide, or my lab was. I am the first to admit it's not a home run. We're not curing cancer yet by targeting tumor-associated macrophages. And I think it's because we don't know how these drugs are really working. We don't know what subsets of macrophages these therapies are working on, and we don't know who is best going to benefit in what setting. And so, I think that this diversity and complexity of these cells is actually, if we could better understand it, we'll have better strategies to target them. And so this is an example of some of the diversity, where this is immunofluorescence on the same breast tumor, and five commonly used macrophage markers are shown here. You can see in this Venn diagram that there's very little overlap. So if you're talking about a CD163 positive macrophage, and I'm talking about a CD68 positive macrophage, we might not be talking about the same cell. In addition, where they're located in the tumor is important. Their metabolic programming is important. Also, their tissue specificity may be important. Every tissue in your body is 5% to 20% tissue-resident macrophages, and they have really important functions. The macrophages in your brain, they're involved in synaptic pruning, whereas macrophages in your liver or spleen are involved with clearing debris and other things. Macrophages in different tissues have different transcriptional, epigenetic programming. And so potentially, as infiltrating monocytes get to solid tumors, they may have different roles among the different tissues, and it may be something we need to consider when targeting them in different tissues. Okay. So we set forward to try to understand, in breast tumors, the diversity, the heterogeneity of macrophages, like many other groups have done across other solid tumors. And we had two approaches. One was to use publicly available data sets, and the other one is, we used an in-house cohort of primary tumors that we obtained from the Dana-Farber Brigham and Women's Cancer CenterAll of these samples had single-cell RNA sequencing, and then our cohort had a matched paraffin-embedded tissue that we could use for imaging and spatial analysis. And so to make this huge effort into just two short summary slides, we performed all the RNA sequencing, or we reanalyzed the RNA sequencing, and we identified multiple subsets of macrophages. We subclustered out the macrophages. We then used a number of strategies to try to understand what each subset was doing. So we used differential expression of the genes. We correlated different subsets of macrophages with T regulatory cells and cytotoxic T cells to try to understand that relationship between the different subsets of macrophages. We used gene set variation analysis. We used spatial analysis, as well as ex vivo functional studies. And so this is the summary of our findings, where we identified, again, these multiple subsets. We have common, the highly expressed genes are shown here on the top, and then we have these predicted functional characterizations. And so we're going to focus on two of these subsets, the GPNMB TAMs and this darker black box, and these SFP1 TAMs down here. These are really the ones that emerged as being highly suppressive, both having signatures of lipid metabolism. And so they also were the two most abundant macrophage populations out of all the macrophage subsets that we could characterize across these breast tumors. And when we looked more closely, for example, at their hallmark pathway enrichment, we see that the GPNMB TAMs have evidence of lipid metabolism, fatty acid metabolism, and these SPP1 TAMs, in addition to lipid metabolism, they also were involved in hypoxia. And so you might have noticed I didn't use M1 or M2 at all. This is my favorite slide. These states don't exist. M1 is a LPS interferon gamma-stimulated macrophage ex vivo. Fine. You can say that. But in a biological setting, this is not a state that exists. And so I urge you to characterize your macrophages by the genes that they express, by the cytokines they secrete, by the predicted functional signatures or confirmed signatures. So what are these lipid-associated macrophages? Lipid macrophages, you can actually see lipid droplets inside of them. They're well described across solid tumors. They express TREM2, CD36, SFP1, APOE, both at the translational level and then also at the protein level. In normal breast tissue, I'm not sure how well this is projecting, but CD68 macrophages are here in red, which you can see throughout the normal breast tissue. Over here in the breast cancer, you can see this yellow, which indicates uptake of these green lipid droplets. So these, again, the lipid-associated macrophages, are well described across solid tumors, and they are considered highly suppressive. We had identified them in our single-cell analysis as having relationships to suppressive T cells. And so others have also characterized lipid-associated macrophages as inhibiting phagocytosis, suppressing T cells, and involved with migration and invasion. We actually had previously identified lipid-associated macrophages as a main driver of therapy resistance in BRCA-associated triple-negative breast cancer. So we had previously published that olaparib, which is a PARP inhibitor used to treat BRCA-deficient breast cancer, in mice induced the recruitment of highly suppressive lipid macrophages. We had this BRCA 53-deficient model of triple-negative breast cancer. When we treat the mice for five days, you can see that there's an increase in macrophages. These macrophages express CSF1R and PD-L1. When we use olaparib on healthy human donor CD14 positive monocytes to understand how PARP inhibitors may be inducing macrophage phenotype, we then find that as a direct effect of the PARP inhibitor, PD-L1 increases, but more significantly, CSF1R increases. Again, this is just a PARP inhibitor on a differentiating monocyte ex vivo. And what was striking is that we had performed both proteomics and transcriptomics, and overwhelmingly, the signatures that emerged to be most significantly different in these PARP inhibitor-treated monocytes was lipid metabolism-related signatures. And indeed, we identified that CD36, which is a lipid uptake receptor, is activated to be expressed after PARP inhibitor treatment. So we're using bone marrow cells from mice. We're differentiating to macrophages with or without olaparib. And the flow cytometry here, the vehicle-treated murine bone marrow is here on the left, and then the olaparib treated is on the right. You see the expression of CD36 on the x-axis, so you're getting a major increase in CD36 lipid receptor expression. They also have high levels of PD-L1 and CSF1R, so really bad macrophages. And indeed, when we went back to our mouse model, we could identify more characteristics of these lipid macrophages. So this is this P53 BRCA-deficient breast cancer model. Again, these are immunocompetent mice. You treat the mice with olaparib for five days. You have a bit of a decrease in tumor volume. When you look just at the macrophages, these macrophages after olaparib treatment express PD-L1, the lipid uptake receptor CD36, CSF1R, TREM2, and other markers suggesting suppressive phenotype.So, at the same time we were identifying these really suppressive macrophages, we were making another discovery, along with several others at that time, which are cited here, that actually PARP inhibitors were inducing DNA damage in the cancer cell, which is part of its mechanism, but it was activating the cGAS-STING pathway, which leads to secretion of type I interferons. This type I interferon results in T cell recruitment. These T cells become activated, and they're required for PARP inhibitor monotherapy efficacy. We also saw increase in PD-L1. And so, this really suggested that potentially we could enhance PARP inhibitor responses by adding a T cell activating agent, such as some sort of immune checkpoint blockade. However, there's been more than a dozen trials at this point that have tested PARP inhibitors plus immune checkpoint blockade, and so far, those trials have failed to show that the combination is better than PARP monotherapy. This is a trial from our colleagues at Yale that tested the PARP inhibitor olaparib plus atezolizumab. And you can see here that the progression-free survival and overall survival is the same. And so we asked, "How could this be possible that if you're getting interferon responses to the PARP inhibitor, you're getting more T cells. Why isn't the immune checkpoint blockade working to enhance PARP inhibitor responses?" Well, you know the punchline. We hypothesized it was the lipid-associated macrophages that we had already identified to be present, at least in the murine tumors. And then we actually have some new mechanism of why PARP plus immunotherapy might not be working. Dr. Kenichi Shimada from my lab will present that on Monday, so go see his poster. So we had identified these lipid-associated macrophages increased in T cells in the murine models. We had identified that cGAS-STING is increased after PARP inhibitor responses. But we wondered, does this happen in the human setting? And so we worked with Dr. Philippa Lynch and Claudian Isaacs, who were the PIs of TALAFE, which is talazaparib, followed by the combination talazaparib plus avelumab in advanced breast cancer. And we have pre-treatment biopsies after one month of PARP monotherapy and then after PARP plus avelumab. For the purposes of today, I just want to show you the pre-treatment biopsies in Biopsy 2 to understand what PARP inhibitors do in the human setting. This is the amazing correlative analysis team that I get to work with. And so we have worked very hard to understand the correlatives from this trial, led again by Kenichi Shimada. So indeed, PARP inhibitor increases this immune response. You see the transcriptional regulation and increase in PD-L1, NK cells, T cells. You see that activated T cells emerge after PARP inhibitor responses, but you also get these suppressive macrophages, CD163, CSF1R positive macrophages. This is what the tumors look like. So this is a baseline sample, and then this is after talazaparib. You can see the green and the red macrophages throughout the tumor, so more macrophages. We then performed digital spatial profiling to understand if there was induction of these lipid-associated macrophages, so we can find areas high in macrophages and then perform whole transcriptome sequencing. And indeed, after PARP inhibitor therapy, there was an increase in lipid signaling, specifically in the macrophages. So this was very cool, right? The clinical data was similar to what we saw in the murine setting. So we went forward to see how can we target these lipid-associated macrophages. One of the most clear phenotypes that we had observed initially was the emergence of CSF1R positivity among these macrophages treated by PARP inhibitor. So CSF1R is expressed by mature macrophages. It's a receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor, the signaling pathway, and its ligands are CSF1 and IL34. If you follow the CSF1R field, you know it's been tested across many solid tumors without a ton of success. However, there are two FDA approvals. One is for tenosynovial giant cell tumor, in which the patients have a translocation of CSF1. So it's just they're highly infiltrated by CSF1R positive macrophages, which is shown here, and eliminated with the anti-CSF1R therapy. And these patients derive benefit from this strategy. More recently, CSF1R axetilimab was approved for chronic GVHD. And so in our mouse model, we tested would anti-CSF1R enhance PARP inhibitor responses. And so here is our BRCA1 P53 deficient model of breast cancer. The monotherapy and vehicle-treated animals succumb quite quickly to the disease. Olaparib induces a median overall survival of about 100 days, which can be doubled out to 200 days with the addition of anti-CSF1R. Both the PARP monotherapy and the combination therapy was dependent on T cells, because when you deplete T cells, you significantly reduce the efficacy. I just want to show you that we also had the PARP plus PD-L1 arm in here. And I wanted to highlight that actually, so here in brown is PARP plus PD-L1. It looks just like PARP monotherapy. So this model might have predicted the lack of clinical responses that we saw.And so when you have the combination of PARP plus anti-CSF1R, you have increased T cells, interferon signaling, STING activation, really good anti-tumor responses with less suppressive macrophages. You reduce tumor growth and metastasis. So we've moved forward to the clinic. This is the AXLAP phase 1b trial of axcitilimab plus olaparib. It's in metastatic HER2-negative breast cancer with BRCA1 or PALB2 mutations. Patients receive 14 days of olaparib, followed by the combination of PARP plus axcitilimab. It's led by the very talented Philippa Lynch and Dr. Shapiro, and I serve as a translational PI. We're more than half enrolled. It's very exciting. All the tissue and blood are in my lab, so we'll have the opportunity to understand what's going on in these tumors. So I presented this part of the story, where the PARP inhibitor induces DNA damage of the tumor. This leads to activation of cGAS/STING, secretion of type I, recruitment of CD8 T cells. But at the same time, this response activates tumor-associated macrophages that become lipid-associated, increase lipids, CD36 expression, CSF1R, and TREM2. And so we thought, "How else might we target lipid-associated macrophages more broadly and not in the context of a PARP inhibitor?" And when we go back and look at our single-cell sequencing, we see that these two populations of lipid-associated macrophages have high expression of TREM2. Now, TREM2 is a receptor, specifically on macrophages, myeloid cells, that mediates homeostasis in tissues, really by eating up all of these different things. It's involved in phagocytosis. It's a regulator of inflammation. And so we know that TREM2, from work from others, is an unfavorable prognostic biomarker across many solid tumors. We have shown in breast cancer that high expression of TREM2 is associated with worse clinical outcome. And really importantly, TREM2's actually only expressed on tumor-associated macrophages, so these are all different tumors, and the brown staining is TREM2, but not in normal tissue. So the tissue-resident macrophages have very low expression of TREM2. Preclinically, there's been work to show that antibodies against TREM2 have demonstrated some efficacy. This is a sarcoma model from Marco Colonna's lab, where the TREM2 antibody delays tumor progression compared to the control. Anti-PD-1 makes that a little better. This is a study from Miriam Merad's lab, where they showed that anti-TREM2 results in decreased lung tumor burden. And another example from breast cancer, where anti-TREM2 delayed tumor progression. Really interesting and excitingly, in the last couple of months, two big papers came out from "Cancer Cell." One was from the Merad Brown lab at Sinai, where they used CAR T cells to get rid of full R2 macrophages, and separately, another CAR T product against TREM2 macrophages. So these CAR T cells, if you just look here, these CAR T cells against anti-TREM2 could reduce tumor burden and extend survival. In the same issue of "Cancer Cell," Ito Amit's lab also demonstrated that CAR T cells against TREM2 was effective in reducing colorectal and fibrosarcoma. So this is really good proof of principle that targeting TREM2 is important. It can reduce tumor burden. But we also know that CAR T cells have not been effective across solid tumors. There are seven FDA approvals for CAR T cells, but these are all in heme malignancies. So far, there's no approvals for solid tumors. And so both antibodies and CAR T cells have a hard time penetrating solid tumors. The CAR T cells are inhibited by macrophages in the tumor, and they're generally not pan-cancer. And so here, in the last couple of minutes, I want to propose a new strategy called macrophage replacement, where we're using monocytes, which I hope I emphasized in my first couple of slides, actively as part of their homeostatic function. They go to tumors, right? That's just what they do. And so the monocytes rapidly infiltrate the tumor that express this TREM2 CAR. Once they get to the tumor, they become CAR macrophages that express TREM2. They destroy TREM2-positive macrophages and then become the type, these CAR macrophages secrete cytokines and activate T cells and kill cancer cells. So some proof of principle, we generated human CAR monocytes. This is work led by a very talented post-doc of my lab, Dr. Dan Michaud. So we generated the effector cells. These are U937 cells that express the TREM2 CAR. No expression of TREM2. And our target cells are THP1, which have some expression of TREM2. And what we find is that the THP1, these are red. The U97 are green. And so when you put them together and see the red and green on the same plot here, indicating that there has been a phagocytosis event. However, this has not happened when the effector cells have a mesothelin CAR, an irrelevant CAR. We also know that these TREM2 CAR monocytes, upon ligand engagement, they secrete TNF alpha. And we can demonstrate additional phagocytosis using Incucyte assays, which is a better reader of actual phagocytosis and not just binding.In the murine system, we've used this really cool tool. It's the HoxB8 monocyte system, which is a progenitor self-renewal monocyte system that's under the control of estrogen. So when you remove the estrogen, the cells differentiate out into macrophages. And so we use these as our effector cells in the murine system to target these Ros264.7 Trem2 expressing cells. And indeed, you can see that there's a nice phagocytic events that occur when you put these cells together. Now, in the mouse models, we have shown that we had to pick a mouse model where we at least knew there were some Trem2 positive macrophages. So you see here the E0771 breast tumor line has Trem2 macrophages. So we started here. We IV inject about five million Trem2 CAR monocytes into the mice and then look to see what happens. So at day 10, we see that the untreated mice have this many CD8 T cells. Untransduced monocytes that we infuse in have same number of T cells. But when we use the Trem2 CAR monocytes, we see an increase in CD8 T cells. That translates to about a 50% reduction in tumor burden. And we can further enhance that by adding anti-PD-1. So we think that this approach is superior from prior cell therapy because the monocytes have superior homing, penetration relative to CAR T cell. There's a superior remodeling that happens with the Trem2 CAR monocytes as opposed to the Trem2 antibody. Importantly, Trem2 is expressed by all tumor macrophages and not tissue-resident macrophages. And so as we move forward to the clinic with this, we'll probably follow the footsteps from Charisma Therapeutics, who put both CAR monocytes and macrophages into patients. And so, we'll continue to work on this strategy by enhancing the product, by changing intracellular signaling domains, adding cytokines, and then thinking about how this will go to the clinic, either with CD14 monocytes or HSC type of approach. So I hope that I convinced you that intentional analysis of macrophage subsets is important to understand in a different specific context what types of macrophages need to be targeted for anti-cancer therapy. We identified these really suppressive macrophages that were associated with lipid metabolism. And so we think this represents a new strategy to eliminate really your choice of tumor macrophages, but we think that Trem2 is a really attractive target. So I just want to thank my lab who has done this work, our funding agencies, all of our collaborators, and I'm happy to take a few questions with the three minutes I have remaining. So if you can just come to the microphone so that the online audience can hear. Very nice work. A little bit fast, but really nice. A lot of data. So I just have two curious questions. Is this lipid macrophage terminally differentiated, or if you treat with some cytokines, they can change phenotype? And do you need to treat the CAR monocytes with something to make them go to the tumor better? Or just like- Yeah. So they are terminally differentiated macrophages, but whether we can switch them to a different direction, I actually suspect you might be able to play a little bit with their plasticity there. We haven't done that exact experiment. No, I don't think we need to treat the monocytes with anything. All right. Thank you. Congratulations. This microphone. Yeah. Great talk. My first question is about the lipid-associated macrophage. I'm kind of curious, so for the primary resected tumor, so you saw this population. How about in the breast cancer metastasis- Yeah. Great question ... this drug also have similar effect? Yeah. So Ito Amit, I believe, a couple of years ago, published a really nice paper on Trem2 macrophages in lung metastases from breast tumors, and those tumors were surrounded by Trem2 macrophages. So that data exists. We are really interested in what happens in liver metastases from breast tumors, and we see these lipid-associated macrophages actually in higher numbers. This is a project led by Gabriella Antonellis, who should be here somewhere. So we see them there, and we think it'll be effective in the metastatic setting. Great. Just kind of a follow-up question about, so if you want to target the macrophage, target the lipid-associated macrophage and the normal other type of macrophage, yeah, the strategy the same or different? Sorry, just say the last part. If you want to target the lipid-associated macrophage, will the strategy be the same as the other type of macrophages? If you want to block the macrophage tumor immunosuppressor effect, something like that. Yeah. It's similar. We can chat later. Okay. Okay. Yeah, go ahead. Thank you. So you showed a subpopulation of these locally proliferating tumor macrophages, and that's been shown before, but not really been explored. Have you guys investigated the tumor-modulating roles of these and how your therapies may impact that population? I don't know why I can't hear. What's the first part of your question? Oh, that's much better. The locally proliferating tumor macrophages that you showed- Yeah ... at the beginning, there's a lot of evidence of those out there, but nobody's really explored the tumor-modulating properties of those. So have you guys? Yeah. No, I don't think so. I mean, theBone marrow-derived macrophages are not likely to be super proliferative. It'll be the tissue-resident macrophages that are proliferating. And so where those go into which subsets, I think that they can become any of the subsets. That's really interesting question and work that's underway. Yeah. Great talk. Two quick questions. Why do you think these methods would be superior compared to an antibody that would deplete by ADCC? Yeah, great question. I think that there's several reasons. One is that antibodies have a difficult time penetrating into especially these really macrophage-rich, suppressive, hypoxic areas, without blood vessels, for example. So monocytes will get there. They're already there. So that's one advantage. Got you. Yeah. And then a quick one. Do you envision that a therapy like this might be like what's happening now with CCR8, where there seems to be some promising data in combination with PD-1? Yeah. Do you think that this will differentiate and have single-agent activity or ultimately require checkpoint inhibition? Yeah. We are aiming for the absolute best monotherapy that we can get. I think it will require cytokine delivery and some sort of T cell activation, but that might be as a single product and not require immune checkpoint blockade, for example. I see. Thanks. Yeah. Thank you. Just maybe one last quick one. Hi. Yeah. Have you seen, do your CAR monocytes express TREM2 at all? Yeah, great question. So in the mouse system, we use a TREM2 knockout bone marrow, and then in the human system, for the clinical product we're working on, it would be a knockdown strategy. And have you looked at the CAR mon to macrophage after tumor killing and stuff? Do they get reprogrammed by the microenvironment? Yeah. It's a great question, too. We're still evaluating that. In the early time points in the mice, no, it looks great. Depending on the cytokine it's loaded with, we hope that that's enough to activate a durable anti-tumor T cell response, and also we have strategies to have suppressive cytokines enforce a anti-tumor phenotype in macrophages. So, there's so many things we can do here, but it's a really important consideration. Yeah. Thank you. Okay. So now we are going to turn it over to Tyler Miller for the second presentation. Perfect. All right. Thanks, Jen. Thanks for the invitation. Thanks to the organizers for putting this session together. It's clearly a very popular one. Great to go second because Jen gave a fantastic overview of tumor-associated myeloid cells. I'm going to talk about redefining these myeloid cells and spend time on that, and then targeting these in solid tumors using brain cancer as a model system. But I think everything that we do here is probably really applicable to other tumors. I don't have any relevant disclosures. So immunotherapy has really revolutionized care for certain cancers, and I'm convinced that active immunotherapy is our best shot at curing gliomas. Unfortunately, it hasn't worked so far, and we've tried. I think there's lots of reasons for this, but the most important hurdle we have to overcome is the immunosuppressive environment that's imposed by these myeloid cells. And I love showing this picture. Here in brown is microglia in the normal cortex, and then you get a higher grade glioma. You get activation of these microglia and then proliferation of them. And in glioblastoma, you get this chock-full of immunosuppressive macrophages. They can make up to 50% of all cells in the glioma. And so the question that my lab tries to answer is: How do we overcome that myeloid suppression to create effective immunotherapies for glioma patients? And we've taken this long view approach where we have to create both a platform for discovery and translation, and that's built on two pillars. One is we have to understand the problem better to create the foundational data sets to understand these myeloid cells, and we use single cell RNA sequencing, spatial transcriptomics, and increasingly spatial proteomic data sets to understand them better. And the second really important arm is we have to have a functional model system where we can test human myeloid cells in matched human cancer cells. And I was really lucky during my postdoc that Penn came out with this GBO model. And this is where you take tumor directly from the OR, you chop it into small pieces. You don't dissociate to single cell. You keep it intact piece, like one millimeter pieces. You grow it in an orbital shaker, and that allows you two to eight weeks of time where you have the whole intact tumor microenvironment, including the myeloid cells, T cells, stromal cells, and you can perturb these during that time, and you can understand how that perturbation impacts all the different cell types in that system. After a couple of months, you lose the vast majority of the tumor microenvironment cells, except for the malignant cells. But you have the malignant cells in their own extracellular matrix. You can add back on human monocytes, T cells, CAR T cells. They will infiltrate in and start to express many of the same programs they do in the primary tumor. Okay. So I'm going to talk a little bit about our mental model here. And our view is that immunosuppressive myeloid cells are a top target to make immunotherapies more effective for our brain tumor patients and solid tumor patients. That single cell genomics combined with patient tumor organoids are a really powerful platform for both therapy discovery and translation. And I'm going to spend some time on this, that we should move beyond Louvain and Lighting clustering, which is typically projected on a UMAP, to understand our single cell RNA sequencing data. This is a receptor on macrophages that binds to phosphatidylserine, which is seen on dying cancer cells that are either dying because of a therapeutic response or also just rapid turnover in the tumor immune microenvironment. And when macrophages take up these cells through this mechanism, it actually induces a very tolerogenic phenotype. And so potentially we could block this. And there's been many attempts to block this. Unfortunately, we haven't seen much success. I would say the most promising was this drug citrovatinib. So this was not AXL specific, but this bound to AXL and a few other. Many of these tyrosine kinase inhibitors are very dirty. In this second-line study in lung cancer, I was nearly certain this was going to be a positive study. We were comparing it to docetaxel, which should be a relatively low bar. A combination of PD-1 blockade and this AXL inhibitor did not reach statistical significance as far as improving median overall survival. It is a bit of a dirtier AXL inhibitor, but there are some more specific AXL inhibitors like bemsetinib, which has been tested and looked somewhat promising in very difficult-to-treat lung cancers, such as those who have SDK11 mutations. But unfortunately, those studies have also been stopped due to a lack of ability to show a significant improvement. So I do think that this is an interesting space. I think we just need to better understand the pathway and probably the most optimal combinatorial approaches. So I could talk for about 18 hours about all the drugs that are being developed to target macrophages, but thankfully, two of our trainees just published this review in "Cancer Cell" a few weeks ago, so I highly encourage you guys to check it out. They give a very nice postmortem as well as a status of many of the drugs that are in development that we're trying in the Phase 1 unit. So, our work in the lab and our work in our Phase 1 unit is really focused on understanding how we can disrupt this emergency myelopoiesis. So, as was described by my colleagues, there are a variety of tumor factors that are really hijacking your bone marrow. They're revving up the expansion of these monocyte progenitors, the granulocyte and monocyte progenitors. They then also imprint on them a very immunosuppressive phenotype. They then leave the bone marrow, and they traffic through a chemokine gradient into the tumor microenvironment, where they differentiate into these monocyte-derived macrophages. These then enable further tumor growth and metastasis, and there's a very vicious cycle here, and we need to figure out how we could potentially disrupt this. We've tried things like CCR2 inhibition to block this. That was not effective. And so one of the main focuses is understanding how, once these macrophages are already really being differentiated, how we might be able to reverse that. Or maybe this whole differentiation step here that's happening within the tumor, how could we potentially block that as well? So we've done extensive single-cell analysis on macrophages from both human lesions. These are untreated non-small cell lung cancer. We have similar data sets in colon cancer, in bladder cancer, and in liver cancer. And we see both in lung cancer and also in this preclinical model, when we're looking at their functional status, we see this very strong IL-4 signaling pathway that is induced. So this suggests that these cells, these monocyte-derived macrophages, have seen IL-4 and that IL-4 receptor-related signaling is really significantly activated in these cells and likely is doing something to drive their polarization. So we found this intriguing and IL-4 classically in medical school, we learn about this whole nice, once again, black and white thing, which is not real. But type one versus type two immunity. So type one immunity, these are the good guys, antiviral, antitumor responses. And type two immunity is thought to be this vestigial thing. So classically, we thought of it as important for antihelminth responses. We don't see a lot of helminths in New York because we use too much bleach and Purell. So we do have lots of atopy, though. So we cannot have bake sales in New York because everyone has horrible allergies, and these atopic conditions that are very strong in type two cytokines like IL-4, IL-5, IL-13, are also very pro-tumorigenic. This whole pathway is very pro-tumorigenic, and it overlaps with some of the functional phenotypes that we're seeing in these monocyte-derived macrophages. And this is not a new observation on our part. Lisa Coussens, who's a former president of AACR, her lab has been working on this for over a decade. They had this study that looked at blocking IL-4 and combining it with classic therapies for breast cancer, which is the model that she studies. And you can see here in combination with classic therapies like radiation or taxane therapy, you actually see synergy, which makes sense because the type two immune response is very much of a healing response. So if you are causing damage with radiation or chemotherapy, that's inducing this healing response, and that healing response is actually very pro-tumorigenic. So potentially by disrupting this, by taking out the IL-4, you might see some synergy.So we saw this data and we said, "Well, that's interesting. What is it going to do with PD-1?" Which is obviously how we're now treating triple negative breast cancer, lung cancer, and many other solid tumors. So using the KP model, which is exquisitely insensitive to PD-L1, it really doesn't do anything for those mice who are developing these metastatic lung cancers. If you block IL-4, here using a neutralizing IL-4 antibody, we actually see a significant decrease in the growth potential of these KP lung tumors. We have a slightly more responsive model, the KP1 model, where PD-L1 does do something. It does decrease the tumor growth potential. You can see that it's just as good as IL-4 blockade, and if you put them together, you actually appear to see some sort of immunologic synergy, really significantly reducing tumor burden. So I saw this data and I said, "That's super exciting. How can we put that into humans?" And what we're thinking is that we have this emergency myelopoiesis. It's a variety of these tumor-derived factors. And this is already published data, so you should take a look at this paper that shows that there's really a cocktail of cytokines and chemokines that are being secreted by the tumor. They're going systemically, they're hijacking your bone marrow. They're activating type II granulocytes, which are actually up to 5% of the cells in the bone marrow, which I didn't know until we did this study. You basically are activating these type II granulocytes. They're pumping out lots of IL-4. This is then imprinting the granulocyte monocyte progenitor. These then expand, and then these very immature immunosuppressive monocytes then traffic into the tumor microenvironment. And once again, we have this very vicious cycle. But nicely in preclinical models, if we use an IL-4 neutralizing antibody, you can really cut this off right here in the bone marrow. So the bone marrow is where all the IL-4 is being made, and using the systemic IL-4 blockade or IL-4 neutralizing antibody, you cut off this entire production of these monocytes and you see very nice antitumor immunity in many preclinical models. Thankfully, in humans, we have a drug that already has lots of safety that blocks IL-4. It blocks the IL-4 receptor alpha, so disrupting both IL-4 and IL-13 signaling. This has been studied in many atopic conditions, including one of my pediatric colleagues at Mount Sinai gave this to kids as young as one, so you know that it's a very safe drug when you're giving it to a one-year-old. So I said, "Why don't we try this in patients that have lung cancer who are progressing on PD-1 blockade?" So this is what I call a rescue study. So basically, I have patients that have relapsed refractory non-small cell lung cancer. These are patients that receive first-line immunotherapy with or without chemotherapy. Most of them do well initially, and then they're continued on maintenance PD-1 blockade, so typically pembrolizumab, or if they had stage III disease, durvalumab, and they're continued on that for up to two years. Unfortunately, most patients eventually start to progress. So all we do here is we just continue that immune therapy that stopped working, and we add on three injections of dupilumab, which binds to the IL-4 receptor alpha, so blocking that type II signature. We're not selecting for patients who have lots of type II immunity per se. And we did biopsies before and on treatment and collected a lot of blood to see how this drug was actually working in vivo in humans to see if it correlated with mice. Nicely, the fourth patient we put on this trial, this was a smoker who had received chemoradiation. He had a very nice response initially, and then he went on to immunotherapy consolidation. Very soon after starting immunotherapy, he had progression not only in the initial radiated tumor bed, but also in the retroperitoneum. He had a very painful lesion here in his back. All we did was continue immune therapy, and we added on three doses of dupilumab, and the patient went into remission. Basically, his pain regimen of morphine eight times a day went to zero within a few weeks, so we knew that the drug was actually working. And he then went on to receive two years of immunotherapy, and then he stopped, as is common practice. So we had some nice responses. We had these biopsies that showed that in a subset of patients, we actually were inducing a de novo antitumor response. We were seeing formation of tertiary lymphoid structures and nice changes. And we did see about a third of patients reachieve control of their disease. And so these were patients where their disease had been progressing, so they normally would just go on docetaxel, which is a mediocre and very toxic chemotherapy. And here, a third of the patients, after we gave them those three doses of dupilumab, could just continue their previous checkpoint blockade, and they achieved significant benefit. So we're in the process of really trying to figure out what is the biomarker that identifies this subset of patients that have some sort of type II signature mediated resistance, and then there's probably something else going on in the other two-thirds of patients. One way that we're doing that is we're exploring this in the neoadjuvant setting, and so we're giving a single dose of cemiplimab, which is a PD-1 antibody used in lung cancer, as well as a single dose of dupilumab. And then just two weeks later, we're taking them to the operating room so we can see exactly what's happening to those cells. We get biopsies, and we can compare the biopsies at baseline with the tissue. We're actually running this in collaboration with the SCHUM. It's supported by a CRI grant. So our working hypothesis of this emergency myelopoiesis is that there's these tumor-derived factors that are really hijacking your bone marrow, your type II granulocytes. They're pumping out IL-4. They're imprinting on your myeloid progenitors that are then effluxing from the marrow, trafficking to the tumor, and setting up this vicious cycle. You give some dupilumab, and in a subset of patients, that can disrupt this. However, like I said, two-thirds of patients are not benefiting, but we know that there's a variety of other potential targets here, and I told you there's a cocktail of about eight different cytokines and chemokines that are coming from the tumor and leading to this effect in the bone marrow.And one of the things that we saw that was part of that cocktail are interleukin-1 alpha and interleukin-1 beta, and we see a very strong interleukin-1 alpha and beta signature in monocyte-derived macrophages. So we've been studying lung cancer in old mice. They much better recapitulate the bone marrow of old humans and also the lung status of old humans. Nine-year-olds, thankfully, do not get lung cancer, so we shouldn't be studying lung cancer in seven-week-old mice. And one of the things that we did was we looked at IL-1 beta, as Tyler had said, we know that this inflammasome activation really drives an immunosuppressive phenotype. And anybody who hears about IL-1 beta lung cancer will run out of the room because we did huge Phase III trials of canakinumab once we saw a bit of a signal from a trial in cardiovascular disease called the CANTOS study, and those trials were all negative. The addition of IL-1 beta to standard immunotherapy did absolutely nothing. Here, when we use anti-IL-1 beta, the tumors grow just as poorly as they do in a control of, once again, 72-week-old mouse, which correlates somehow with a 65-year-old human. I'm not sure of the math equation there. And also we were interested in IL-1 alpha because we actually saw a stronger signature of IL-1 alpha that was specific to the monocyte-derived macrophages, but also IL-1 alpha blockade itself did nothing. But then when Matthew, who's a superstar MD PhD student in Miriam Merad's lab, she's my partner in crime, doing all these preclinical studies. If you add IL-1 alpha and IL-1 beta together, we all of a sudden saw this very nice signature. He had this data right around the time that we were grappling with the joys of COVID in New York City and basically throwing all spaghetti at the wall and seeing what stuck, and we had tried anakinra with some success in some of our patients. And so we threw anakinra in these mice, and we also saw a very nice anti-tumor effect. So we obviously didn't want to just look at one mouse model. That's always the best way not to publish something. So in, once again, our old mice, we had some orthotopic models of colorectal cancer with a cecal injection here or pancreatic cancer. And this is not a new finding that in old mice, tumors grow faster, and that's very well established. That's why old people get cancer, one of the reasons why old people get cancer. But interestingly, we see a lot more inflammatory inflammasome activation in the old mice versus the young. And indeed, when we give anakinra to these old mice in this colon cancer model and this pancreatic cancer model, we see a significant decrease in the growth potential. So we really think that we're disrupting this inflammation that occurs in the setting also of inflammaging, which is just the chronic inflammation that we have over time as we age, particularly living in cities like New York. And we really see that we're able to disrupt this inflammaging-related pro-tumorigenic milieu. So based on that, we're going back to our rescue model, and we're basically just adding IL-1 blockade to this. And so we're doing a trial right now where we give 28 days of anakinra. This is a daily injection, which is a bit of a pain for patients, but we're trying to see if we can see some synergy between IL-4 and IL-1 blockade. So finally, I just wanted to talk about some of the work that we're doing in a much more difficult setting. I'm not sure why this is blurry, but in colon cancer, microsatellite colon cancer, we know that these are patients that do not respond to immunotherapy, and this is particularly true for patients with colorectal mets. And so this is actually from one of our patients who had their primary colon cancer removed, as well as an oligo met from their liver. And you can see that in the primary tumor, there's lots of CD8 T cells. The colon cancer is where we actually developed the Immunoscore many decades ago, so we know that there's lots of T cells there. They're just not doing their job. But in liver mets, we really see a dearth of T cells, and we see a very stromal fibrotic lesion. And this is one of the many reasons why we think we really don't see any response in patients with liver mets. This is the study of botbal, this is a souped-up CTLA-4 given with a PD-1. And we've seen that in the patients with liver mets that we put on this combination, we really don't see any benefit. While we see a significant benefit in a subset of patients, particularly in some of the neoadjuvant studies that have been running, and we're going to be updating this study in the near future. So how can we overcome that very resistant milieu? So the signature, this monocyte-derived macrophage signature that I've been talking about and that Jen and Tyler have been talking about, we really see it across tumors. So we're so myopically focused oftentimes on let's develop a lung cancer therapy, and we don't realize that the immune system can only be hijacked in a finite number of ways. And we really think that this Type 2 signature is seen in every tumor type that we've ever looked at. So we initially said, "Well, let's try IL-4 blockade." And indeed, in this model of metastatic colon cancer to the liver, so this is an AKPS model where we inject cells into the spleen and they metastasize to the liver. It's extremely insensitive to PD-1 blockade. It might actually even cause some hyperprogression if you believe in that. But if you give IL-4 receptor alpha blockade to these mice, you actually see a significant decrease in the tumor growth, and you actually see synergy with PD-1 blockade, even though you didn't see any monotherapy activity here. It's an important thing for investors who are always insisting on monotherapy activity. Here you actually see the combination. And interestingly, when we look at tissue from these mice, you see that IL-4 receptor alpha blockade induces a bit of an influx of immune cells, but you really see lots of these CD8 T cells infiltrating when you give this cocktail of the two. So we have some nice preclinical rationale. And one of the interesting things was when we were looking in colon cancer in humans, we have a large single-cell data set that we're going to be publishing soon of human patients that had untreated colon cancer that was resected. And we noticed that unlike our lung cancer patients, where monocytes that we saw in the blood had already seen IL-4, had been imprinted in the bone marrow. We don't see that in colon cancer patients, and we don't see that in these mice that have colon cancer, either an orthotopic colon cancer in their cecum or metastatic to the liver. We didn't see them in the monocytes in the blood, but we see them in the monocyte-derived macrophages in the tumor. So it suggested maybe in this setting, the IL-4 is coming from somewhere else. And indeed, with an IL-4 reporter mouse, we saw that the eosinophils, there was lots of eosinophils in our colon cancer patients, but particularly in this preclinical model. And they were really making the vast majority of the IL-4, and we see an increase in the number of eosinophils in these lesions compared to a normal liver, and all those eosinophils are pumping out IL-4. And doing some receptor ligand interaction, what we realize is that that IL-4 probably is related to fibroblast production of IL-33. So IL-33 is an alarmin. There's been a few drugs recently that have shown some promise in COPD. Targeting IL-33, it's also a Type 2 cytokine of sorts. And what we see is that in tumors, particularly the fibroblasts, are making a lot of IL-33, and we know IL-33 is very good at maintaining the survival and activity of eosinophils. And when we look at the... This is, once again, the mouse model of the liver met. We see that within the tumor, there's lots of cells that are expressing IL-33, and we see that they're all these fibroblasts, these stromal cells surrounding the tumor cells. When we look at our human samples, we also see lots of IL-33 coming from the fibroblasts. And basically, our data is really showing that your tumor-derived, and particularly CAF-derived IL-33, is activating the eosinophils in the tumor immune microenvironment. They then make IL-4 that then polarizes the monocyte-derived macrophages. We can even block this whole upstream signaling by using an anti-IL-1 RAP. This docks out or blocks not only IL-1 alpha and beta, but also ST2, the IL-33 receptor.And so here, once again, in this model that doesn't respond to PD-1 blockade, if you add anti-IL-1RAP, it appears to have a very nice anti-tumor effect and synergize. And so we have these two different models where we block IL-4 downstream or upstream. Both seem very promising. So we have this trial, a platform study now ongoing, where two of the arms of the platform study are looking at these cocktails in patients with colon cancer that's metastasized to the liver. And we also have an oligometastasectomy trial looking at the use of PD-1 and IL-4 very briefly in patients that are having tumors resected from their liver. So with that, thanks first and foremost to the patients who are part of these studies, that spend way too much time with me and my colleagues. Miriam Murad is my partner in crime, and these sorts of studies literally take hundreds of people. So thank you. Happy to take questions. Hi. Great talk. So I was curious, this is the first I've seen eosinophils really brought into the mix of the tumor microenvironment. Do you expect that you would see eosinophils driving this IL-4 production in other tumors as well? Do you think this is specific to CRC, and do you think it's also specific to MSS CRC, or would you see a different immune signature in MSI where you have a lot more of the mutagenic proteins? So in lung cancer, we actually do not see local production of IL-4. We don't see a lot of eosinophils either. Eosinophilia in the blood is a very mixed bag. If you look at studies correlating response to immunotherapy with eosinophils, some papers say eosinophilia is a great marker for response, and others say it's very immunosuppressive. They're definitely a complicated cell. They're a difficult cell to study, and so that's probably why we don't know enough about them. Interestingly, when we look at different tumors in humans, but also in the models, we see IL-4 as part of all of their stories, but it's always coming from somewhere else. So in ovarian cancer, we're actually seeing IL-4 being produced by ovarian cancer cells themselves, and strangely, we actually see this not only in human samples, but also in pre-clinical models of ovarian cancer. And so I think that it's more complicated than we realize. I was just telling you, we have shared immune programs throughout. I think IL-4 is a shared immune program throughout. It's just where the IL-4 is coming from might be different from one tumor to another. It might also be different from one patient to another. Thank you. My question is, do you have quantified the result about how many myeloid cell the human body mobilized? You mean in the setting of cancer, how many are being mobilized? Yes. I think we all showed a picture that showed that sometimes the majority of immune cells in a tumor, so literally tens of billions of cells, are actually macrophages, and those are primarily monocyte-derived macrophages. So we see this emergency myelopoiesis, this expansion of granulocyte, monocyte progenitors, really across all the tumors, and you see a significant expansion compared to any sort of healthy control in the bone marrow and the blood, then obviously the tumor is chock-full of these cells. The half-life is a real big question. We don't know that in humans. We know that they're constantly being recruited and enabling tumor growth and metastasis, but we don't know how long they actually live in humans. Unfortunately, that's very difficult to track. So we don't know, are they turning over once a week, every 72 hours, or are they sticking around for a few months? So how great is that recruitment? And that's an important question if we're thinking about finding ways to block recruitment, for sure. Actually, my question, it also has a specific setting. It's the cancer patient after the treatment, after chemo or radiation treatment, and how much the bone marrow mobilize the myeloid immune cell get into the tumor. Do you have estimation? No. I don't have specific data on that. I think that we know that the tumor is releasing all these factors, so as you kill off tumor with radiation and chemotherapy, you could argue you're going to have fewer cancer cells and fewer stromal cells pumping out those cytokines and leading to expansion in the bone marrow. But also, as part of this healing response to those very toxic insults, that might actually do the opposite and really drive that expansion. So it's hard to really know. I bet it's going to be very different from one patient to another. Thank you. One more question. Yeah. Really nice data. My question is, does this IL-4 blockage change the PD-L1 expression in the tumor or in the macrophage that could also interfere with the association with PD-L1 treatment? That is a very interesting question, and I do not know. We're looking at the tissue right now, the pre- and on-treatment biopsies, and so we'll see if we see a difference. The issue is that in the responders, they're going to have more T cells pumping out interferon, and that's going to induce upregulation of PD-L1. So it's going to be hard to sort of isolate the effect of the IL-4 versus just the IL-4 is leading to better anti-tumor immunity, and then you have more PD-L1. Okay. Thank you, Tom. And before we conclude this session, I just want to acknowledge the involvement or engagement in this room. We had two full overflow rooms and hundreds of people online, so I think we won in terms of how many people attended our session. Sure. But I think it reflects the movement in the field. So, we know now that it's not if we should target macrophages, it's just that we need to target them and how to do that. So, thank you all for being part of this movement, and thank you to Dr. Marin and Dr. Miller

This transcript is Vimeo auto-generated English. Expect misheard names and technical terms. Use the ripgrep/search approach for exact quotes.

Okay, in an effort to keep us on time, I'm Louis Chodosh. I have the honor of chairing today's session, Advances in Understanding Disseminated Tumor Cells: An Emerging Opportunity to Prevent Lethal Breast Cancer? With a question mark and the emphasis, I suppose, on the question mark. I'm from the University of Pennsylvania. I will introduce our speakers momentarily. So by way of introduction, the focus of this session is on this problem, breast cancer recurrence. So we all know breast cancer is the most common cancer diagnosed amongst men or women. And fortunately, five-year survival is quite good, approaching 90%. And as a consequence, breast cancer is by far the most prevalent cancer in the world, with more than 12 million breast cancer survivors globally. The majority of women are in what we would call a no evidence of disease period, or the surveillance period, in which there is nothing. There is no disease evident on a scan. However, in following patients, up to 30% of women will ultimately recur following a variable latency period, and that recurrence, typically metastatic recurrence, is responsible for nearly all mortality from this disease. Now, breast cancer recurrence has the interesting property shared with prostate cancer in which recurrences can happen after many years. So in some cases, 25 years or more after definitive treatment of the primary tumor. And while these sorts of kinetics are typically associated with estrogen receptor positive breast cancers, it is also seen to some degree with estrogen receptor-negative tumors as well. And this very long stochastic latency period has brought up the question of whether these cancers may pass through a dormant phase. Now, arguably, the current clinical approach to breast cancer is front-end loaded. That is, there is definitive treatment of the primary tumor. Women enter the surveillance period, and there are really very few therapeutic interventions during that surveillance period to prevent recurrence other than anti-estrogen therapies and CDK4/6 inhibitors for ER positive breast cancers. Now, during this period, patients are observed. There's no active monitoring. There's no clinical test that will tell you whether a woman is part of the 30% who might ultimately recur. And this causes a lot of anxiety, understandably, and decreased quality of life for patients because they can never know whether they're cured or not. So I would argue that the failure to intervene during the surveillance period is a missed opportunity, that simply watchful waiting is not enough. So why do some breast cancers recur? Well, as one of our speakers, Christoph Klein, and others have shown, over the period of years in which a breast cancer grows to reach a clinically detectable size, there are cancer cells that make their way into the bloodstream, disseminate to distant organs, and can basically sit there as single cells or micro metastases as DTCs or minimal residual disease. And at some point, in some women, DTCs can reactivate growth and give rise to recurrent metastatic cancers. So DTCs are the reservoir from which recurrent tumors arise. And again, the fact that they can survive in their host for decades raises the question of whether they pass through a dormant phase. So if one looks at bone marrow aspirates in early-stage breast cancer patients, up to 40% will have detectable DTCs in their bone marrow, shown here by pancytokeratin immunohistochemistry. And that's important because the presence of DTCs in early-stage patients is strongly associated with an increased risk of recurrence and decreased overall survival, as you might expect for cells in this reservoir that gives rise to recurrence. So DTCs are really both a biomarker to identify early-stage patients who have an increased risk for recurrence, and we can also think of them as a potential therapeutic target, as we'll talk about in today's session. And I would say the main questions that we have to answer to get to that type of clinical approach is, first, what are the biological properties of DTCs? What are the mechanisms by which they persist and recur? And can we translate that information to prevent recurrence? And today, we have three speakers who will address each of those particular questions. So I will speak first about approaches to clinical translation targeting DTCs. Then we will have Dr. Amoya Sreekumar, who is one of the AACR NextGen Stars, who will talk about a particularly interesting mechanism by which dormancy is enforced in tumor cells. And then we will have Dr. Christoph Klein from the University of Regensburg in Germany, who will talk to us about the biology and molecular characteristics of patient-derived disseminated tumor cells. So with that, I will start my talk. These are my disclosures. Okay, so if really all breast cancer mortality or the vast majority is due to lethal recurrent breast cancers, the goal of preventing breast cancer mortality could presumably be achieved by preventing recurrence, if that's the lethal event. And the strategy that I'm going to talk about is depleting this reservoir of DTCs or at least preventing them from reactivating. And the approach, as I mentioned earlier, is really to say, look at DTCs as bothThe prognostic marker of risk and the target for therapy. And the steps are: understand the mechanisms of dormancy and reactivation in these cells, develop better methods to detect them and to characterize them at a molecular level, and then to use that information to develop clinical approaches to target these cells to prevent recurrence. So one of the approaches that my laboratory has taken over the years to understanding dormancy biology is developing genetically engineered mouse models for human breast cancer that make use of the doxycycline-inducible, mammary-specific expression of oncogenes of interest in the mammary epithelium. And as shown here, when mice are put on doxycycline in their drinking water, in this case, they turn on the HER2 oncogene, and that drives the development of hyperplasias, and then ultimately invasive mammary adenocarcinomas that will metastasize. And as an example of oncogene addiction, with these mice with extant primary tumors, if doxycycline is removed from the drinking water, HER2 is then turned off in a tumor which has multiple mutations. These tumors rapidly regress to a non-palpable state over the course of several weeks, essentially a genetic approximation of targeted therapy. But if you follow these animals over time off doxycycline, just as in patients, tumors will recur stochastically and via a variety of escape pathways, and they really do it after a variable latency period. If you look at the site of a regressed primary tumor and genetically marked tumor cells, you can see that there is a collection of residual tumor cells that persists in these animals, which enables us to isolate them, query their biology, and try to understand the mechanisms of survival and recurrence. One important element if one follows the proliferation of these tumor cells, within three to five days after instituting this genetic targeted therapy, the proliferation rates crash, cells exit the cell cycle, and remain in this persistent quiescent state for many weeks, as shown here as well by BrdU labeling of these dormant residual lesions. But if you put animals back on doxycycline, turn the oncogene back on in those residual tumor cells, they rapidly reestablish proliferation rates and reenter the cell cycle. So they are genuinely reversibly quiescent or serially dormant. If we isolate these dormant RTCs, what we find is that they exist in a distinct cellular state. So dormant residual tumor cells are in a state that is different, both from the primary tumor cells from which they arose and the recurrent tumor cells to which they give rise. And this is true in multiple different animal models for dormancy and recurrence. And interestingly, across these different models, dormant RTCs share a variety of gene expression alterations. So what makes us think that this reflects anything relevant about human disease? Well, Amalya Sreekumar, who's in my lab and here speaking today, did very interesting work where she developed a core mouse dormancy signature from in vitro and in vivo mouse models of dormancy, and then applied it to neoadjuvant therapy breast cancer patient data sets in which there were initial biopsies of primary tumors pretreatment, and then surgical excision of the remaining residual lesions. And what she found in the majority of data sets is that there is an enrichment across multiple patient cohorts of this mouse core dormancy signature in the post-treatment samples from patients. And interestingly, this was independent of therapy, so seen both for endocrine therapy or chemotherapy, short or long. And this argues that therapy-refractory residual tumor cells that persist in patients following neoadjuvant therapy exhibit changes in gene expression that are similar to those associated with cellular dormancy in mice, arguing for at least some relevance of these models to the clinic. So using models such as this, we ask the question: can we identify dormancy-specific responses to therapy that we could leverage? Well, the inverse of that is, of course, chemotherapy, which effectively kills proliferating tumor cells but has very little effect on dormant tumor cells. So can we find the inverse of that? I'll show you one example of this to begin with. So this is Notch activation, looking at the Notch intracellular domain in dormant residual lesions in mice, showing that Notch is activated in maybe 40% of residual tumor cells in these mice, and we know this is Notch activation because it's blocked by the gamma secretase inhibitor.
