From patient samples, you mean? Yeah, from patient samples. That's something we're actually in the process of doing. We have access to patient samples, and we're trying to see if we can identify, as predicted by the gene expression signatures, are we also able to look for these features there. Thank you. Hi there. Thanks for the great talk and very interesting work. I'm wondering if you know what the exact link is between loss of SOX5 and enhancement of proliferation. What part of the cell cycle machinery does loss of SOX5 ultimately drive? Mm-hmm. And then if there's time, I'll have a second question. Okay. That's a good question, actually. There are many parts of the study that require further elucidation mechanistically, including how SOX5 is being temporally regulated, that we don't have a good handle on. It's interesting you mention that. There are contexts in which SOX5 has been studied predominantly for its oncogenic functions. One that is more similar to what we see with quiescence is actually in the context of neurogenesis, where loss of SOX5 can promote a proliferative burst and deplete neural progenitor cells. Why that context matters and what it's actually doing to the cell cycle remains to be studied, but I think constitute important questions here. Thanks. I think I'll let the other person go. One last question, which will be the person behind you. Great talk. Thanks. So one question for the preclinical translation aspect is, beyond the genetic SOX5 knockdown or knockout, is there anything on market for the osteogenesis blocking at the residual state that you could do in vivo or preclinically? Yeah. So I think the proposal or the best approach would be the opposite. If we could try and actually enrich this program and maintain cells in a dormant state, that would be great. We don't know how to go about that yet, but actually, as I mentioned in the previous response, having a better handle on how SOX5 is being temporally activated would get us there. So that's future directions and things we're working on. And with that, we'll thank Dr. Srikumar for an excellent talk. Our next speaker, we're honored, came all the way from Germany, across the ocean for this. We are honored to have Dr. Christoph Klein, who will bring things home by telling us things that probably most of us here don't know about the molecular characteristics of human DTCs. Yeah. Thank you very much for this invitation here. You learned yesterday evening, MRD is a hot topic since three years. I was surprised to learn this, because actually the study of the seed of metastasis is actually much older. So in 1987, Gertrud Müller had a wonderful idea, which is still used today, to use cytokeratin and EpCAM as markers to detect disseminated tumor cells in bone marrow. And as it has been explained, and I will not go deeper in this, this is an opportunity, after surgery or local treatment, to prevent relapses that may arise from disseminated cancer cells. This research has gone forward. Many patients have been screened. Also, this data has been shown before. And what you can see here is, yes, disseminated tumor cells have an impact, but counting is certainly not enough to achieve the goals. And therefore, more than 20 years ago, we started to isolate these cells by micromanipulation because these cells are super rare. You find one or two cells in one million bone marrow cells, and we use two markers, cytokeratin to analyze cells for DNA analysis, and EpCAM for RNA. And for the rest of my talk, I will make a very important differentiation. I classify the cells by the clinical stage of the patient, where we isolated these cells. So if a patient has no metastasis, I will call the cellsM0 disseminated cancer cells for M0 stage, and if the patient has metastases, M1 disseminated cancer cells. I will summarize a few results very quickly. So what we learned in mice and men or women was that dissemination actually starts very early. So here you can see this is a spontaneous mouse model where we followed the growth of the primary tumor, and we asked when can we find cells in bone marrow or other organs in transgenic mice? And the surprising finding was long before we have a tumor. That is actually why I call the cells mostly disseminated cancer cells and not tumor cells, because we have no tumor when dissemination actually starts. Now, this is similar also in patients. Here you can see the sizes, the diameters of the primary tumors, and then from patients, many patients, and you can see there's not much change. In most cases, you have no disseminated cancer cells, and if you find them, it's basically independent of the size of the primary tumor. So seeding starts early, and there is no increase as the primary tumor grows. And you can plot the same data in a different way, where you determine the risk of de novo seeding at a given size, and you can see that at the diagnostic size, seeding risk has already tenfold decreased. So seeding is an early process, something that we do not really understand yet, but it goes with the molecular biology that we found or the genomic profiles. Here, for example, you can see a typical histogram of copy number alterations. You see the gains here on chromosome one or eight or 17 in primary tumors. You can find very similar patterns in the metastasis. But when you look before metastasis in disseminated tumor cells, cancer cells, there are certain genetic changes that are not present yet, which raises a question, what happens if we cut out this tumor, the source of cells that have this amplification? It probably means that evolution needs to reacquire these changes. And therefore, we started to address the phylogenetics of individual histories by going for a single cell analysis of the phylogeny of disseminated tumor cells. And we teamed up with the Weizmann Institute in Israel, with Udi Shapiro and Ofir Raz, and tried to isolate, generate the history of disseminated cancer cells. So what did we do? We isolated the cells. We did a whole genome amplification. We sequenced 12,000 microsatellite sites and therefore performed a huge paternity test, basically. The problem is you do not have parents; you have just the descendants of the cells. But we had a very simple question. We wanted to understand where does the disseminated cancer cell leave the primary tumor, at what stage? Now I'm showing only one patient in detail, but what you get when you do this with several patients is first you get a very nice separation here between the cancer cells and the normal cells in most of the cases. I'm showing you one breast cancer patient where we took single tumor cells. At surgery, bone marrow aspiration was performed. We isolated the cells from the bone marrow. We used control cells of different types. And the patient, seven years later, relapsed with metastasis, and at that time point, we could isolate circulating tumor cells from the bloodstream that bona fide were derived from the metastasis. And we had the simple question: Are the disseminated cancer cells derived from the most advanced clone of the primary tumor, or does it develop somehow in parallel? So this is the disease course of the patient. Primary tumor was taken 2009, and the bone marrow cells as well. Seven years later, we got the circulating tumor cells, and in between, the patient received all types of therapies. And one therapy I just want to point out here, it was tamoxifen, so anti-hormonal therapy. And this is the tree that we get. What you can see here is the primary tumor cells, the metastasis-derived circulating tumor cells, and the non-tumor cells. And you can see here these triangles. These are boot signals of significance in a way that the tree at this position is very stable. So these are in bootstrap experiments. Here is a clear separation. The arrow points to the head. So this area is completely different from this area. This area here is completely different from this area. And the first thing that you notice, the primary tumor and the met-derived CTCs, they are very different. They separated early on. Now, the disseminated cancer cells, seven years before, one is here, one is here, and then surprisingly, we find circulating tumor cells very well separated from all the rest of this area. And then you look for estrogen receptor mutations. Here in the primary tumor, not treated, all Y type. Here, treated, you find the mutations.Now here you've the disseminated cancer cells. They don't have the mutation, but one of the CTCs actually has it, surprisingly, completely unrelated to this cell here. So the clustering seems to show that the circulating tumor cells left very long time ago, and because some of them cluster closer to the normal cells, an early distant. The circulating tumor cells here on this side, clustering with the normal cells may have been dormant for quite some time because they did not evolve into the killing clone here. And also it may reflect that important mutations may actually acquired independently. So very briefly to summarize this, I set these points. So it became very clear we need phenotypic information on these disseminated cancer cells, and that's why we isolated the cells and performed whole transcriptome amplification and RNAseq of these cells. And I'm showing you now data that are derived from more than 1,000 patients where we search for these individual cells from different cancer types, breast cancer, prostate, lung, and esophageal cancer. Now EpCAM is not the best marker for cancer cells because it's not so specific as cytokeratin is, because you will find in normal healthy donors also EpCAM positive cells, which is a big problem. So we noted that cancer-derived cells are stronger stained. They're brighter. They're a little bit larger. It's no problem if the patient has metastasis to identify morphologically clear cancer cells in the bone marrow. They are very, very different. So these were our criteria. And so we isolated 1,000 cells, and the data were long time unclear until Huijin Kirkulu, our bioinformatician, brought some sense into it. So these are the cells that we isolated from the patient, and we quickly identified that by EpCAM staining, we had isolated different cell types, which expressed EpCAM, plasma cells, erythroid progenitor cells, some rare immune cells. But then we had a big cluster here with the M0 derived disseminated cancer cells and the metastasis derived cells. And when we projected these cells into the bone marrow atlas that had been published, we saw that the erythroblasts integrated here, the plasma cells integrated here into the bone marrow atlas. But we find two new continents in the bone marrow atlas, one for the M0 DCCs, and here the M1 DCCs clustering closely to the stromal cells of bone marrow, rare cells, similar to the fibroblastic cells here, the M1 DCCs. So that was strange that they clustered so far apart from each other, and we wondered what is the differences here. So we looked into the gene expression profiles with unsupervised clustering. And since we had different cancer types, we used the M1 DCCs and did unsupervised clustering. What you can see here, the algorithm can perfectly separate these cells. It's clear what is a breast cancer, what a prostate, what a lung cancer cell. When we did the same with the M0 DCCs, the surprise was big. We couldn't differentiate these cells. What looks like kind of a cluster here for breast cancer versus the others is nothing but the sex of the patient. If we remove the sex-associated genes, we will have a complete mix of these cells. It looked like the cells had completely forgotten where they are coming from. So we compared these two cells here, and we found for the M1 DCCs, we found expected terms like luminal epithelial cells, epithelial cells, epithelium mesenchymal translation. The surprise came when we looked into the M0 DCCs. You find here stem, stem, embryonic, placenta, pluripotent stem cells, terms related to complete differentiation loss of these cells. So we looked, we used algorithms for stemness and high potency scores and found that actually the M0 DCCs had very, very high stemness and potency scores, even higher than ERPs. And this is surprising because ERPs are actually the cells in the adult with the highest stemness and potency scores because they produce 2.5 million red blood cells a second. So here you can see this, and this is data from fetal cells versus adult cells, and the fetal cells always have the higher score except here for the erythroid progenitor cells. Now we use the data, the stemness scores, and applied it to the lung cancer patients where we had the survivals quickly. So we took from each patient where we had isolated a cell, the highest stemness score, and if the patient had a high stemness score, it was in this category, or it had a low stemness score. And what you can see, the cells with the highest stemness scores, the EpCAM positive cells with the highest stemness score, can perfectly separate the survival of the patients.So in this case here, that in about two or three, two and a half years, all patients were dead that had a single cell with such a high stemness score. Now, this was striking, so we moved forward, not relying on the bone marrow atlas, but taking an atlas of all human cells, and we projected the cells that we had isolated from the patients into the human atlas, which also contained embryonal and fetus-derived cells. And what you can see here, that the M0 DCCs actually cluster very closely to human embryonic stem cells. Now, this was really surprising, and we looked further when in embryonic development do we find the highest similarity. And we started with the zygote, the fertilized egg, and went on to the 16 cell stage. And we find in these cells incredibly high enrichment of genes that are linked to these very early stages. Whereas the standard classical metastatic cells that we can isolate does not enrich for these cells, because they undergo a later stage gastrulation, which comes later in embryology, and express these typical genes. So maybe we have a very early stage here of embryonic development somehow activated in disseminated cancer cells, and so this is our current focus in our research to elucidate this a little longer. But then was obviously the question for breast cancer, do we also find a correlation with this? And this is very early data that we just got two weeks ago, the follow-up of the breast cancer patients. And what you can see here, this is just the finding, the separation of group patients where we did not find EpCAM positive cells and patients where we find EpCAM positive cells. And you can already see that EpCAM is actually a good marker to find these cells, because most of the events occurred in the EpCAM positive breast cancer population. So most patients we will identify. And now we use this group here with the EpCAM positive cells and separated those into those that had these embryo-like cells and those that didn't. And this is very promising, I think, although it is not significant yet because very early stage here in follow-up analysis. But so far, all events occurred in the group with the embryo-like disseminated cancer cells. So there's one thing that I would like to point out, which I find striking. I mentioned that we could not separate the cells from breast, lung, and prostate cancer. But in lung cancer, when we find these embryo-like cells, most patients die here in an early time point. In breast cancer, most of the patients die later. So the cells are very similar, but the clinical course is very different in these two cancers. And this is very puzzling, and we started to look into this. And with the help of David Blumenthal, I learned that you can have similar gene expression profiles, but different gene regulatory networks underlying them. And here in this regard, you can see here the comparison between lung cancer and breast cancer are very different. So the gene regulatory networks that regulate the speed of regrowth, if this is linked to it, are very different here. So now we have this phenotype. The metastatic seed appears to be very different from manifest metastasis in primary tumors. The embryo-like DCCs form a subgroup that is associated with risk of metastasis. And although these embryo-like DCC phenotypes appear to be similar, there is some underlying differences that needs to be explored, and maybe these differences are linked to the dormancy periods that we see more frequently in breast cancer. So the last few minutes, I just want to point out the direction of the research that we are taking now, and I just want to introduce you an approach to get a little bit more ideas about the biology in patients. And here in the lab Ati Aliozin and Speaking of Cheech develop a new way to analyze the phospho proteome signaling pathways in single cells. I just want to mention this. This is a technology which has been used before. You label antibodies with a DNA tag. The specificity here for us is that we add as a tag exactly the same adapters that we use to amplify the genome of a single cell. So when we isolate a single cell, we cut the genome into pieces, link adapters, and do PCR. And now we have the same PCR primers here on the identifier that tells us which antibody has bound. So when we isolate the cell together with the antibody, we can sequence the antibodies bound and the genomic amplification... changes. So basically, the experiment looks like you detect the cells with cytokeratin and EpCAM, you add the DNA tagged antibodies, you isolate the cells, and you can read out the whole genome and the profile of the antibody. And you can do this also with patient samples. And the method is very quantitative, which I want to show you here. So we use different cell lines that express different levels of HER2, and then you have the antibody here. You detect it with a secondary antibody, so the tagged antibody is detected by a fluorescent antibody, and then you can correlate the PCR value with the intensity of the staining. And this is really quantitatively doable here for even single cells. So with that, we wanted to look as a proof of concept into the activation pathway here, HER2, phosphor-HER2, phosphor, phosphor-Akt, phosphor-Stat. We used this, and I just want to show you one patient because I found this interesting and a bit provocative. It's a neoadjuvant setting. We take bone marrow sample when the port is given to the patient, we get the first bone marrow sample, then the patient is treated, and three months later, surgery is performed, and the second bone marrow sample is taken. So here we had a HER2 amplified breast cancer patient. We isolated one cell, and the patient got treatment against HER2, and we could identify in this patient six cells after treatment and isolated these cells. And here is the result. You can see here, I apologize for the poor quality of the-- this is a Mac problem. So you have here the normal cells for the readout of the antibody, and you have the putative DCCs, and you have a positive control. And you can see that in all cells, these pathways are all activated. And one cell has a very high increase in HER2 staining, and it also has an amplification here of the locus. So it goes together, and it tells you that even after three months treatment with this antibody, you can detect resistant cells against this treatment in the bone marrow of a patient. So these are the questions that we are currently working on. So which pathways actually regulate this phenotype of the DCCs? Has this pathway maybe something to do with the therapy resistance? Is there a functional link? And then when there is such a specific phenotype, and I think probably we do not have a two cell embryo like cell normally in the body, this could hint that there are additional targets to be identified, which may be specific for these disseminated cancer cells. I showed the people who did the work with some pictures, but there are many more people involved who isolated these cells, who did various aspects in this work. I want to thank the patients that donated the bone marrow for these studies over many, many years. And if you are interested in the topic, I just want to use the opportunity to inform you that there will be a conference next year also on dormancy and minimal residual disease. Thank you very much for your attention. Questions for Dr. Klein? That was fascinating. Congratulations. I'm curious in your perspective about whether the founder, the truncal founder mutation for those M zero cells is in a pluripotent, more stem-like cell to begin with. And also, is there an earlier onset of disease? Actually, this is the weakest point in my story that you're asking. We were looking obviously also for truncal mutations so far, but we have done this with a panel sequencing, and we find mutations in these cells. And actually in lung cancer, we also find shared mutations between the primary tumor. But in breast cancer, it's very difficult. Breast cancer in general is not a typical cancer for mutations, that is driven by mutations. I can at least say so far we have not identified PI3 kinase mutations or P53 mutations shared between these cells and the primary tumor. So maybe the beginning of cancer and dissemination is something different than our canonical mutations. Thank you. Hi, Christoph. So the cell that you described, the embryonic-like disseminated cancer, sounds really like a cancer stem cell. So there's studies that show that that EMT embryo-like state is kind of like a cancer stem cell. I wonder then, can you actually find them now that you have a signature in the primary tumors? And I'm wondering if even if they are there, whether there's an acquired dormancy phenotype on top of that embryonic stem-like signatureDoes that make them actually different when they do get to the bone as they enter dormancy? So EMT is not the prevalent term that we call enriched in these disseminated cancer cells. So it seems to be before gastrulation. That was actually why we looked into this zygote two-cell early embryos, because we did not identify EMT as this characteristic. Mm-hmm. Do we find cells of this type in the primary tumor? So Huijun has looked in published data of lung cancer, and actually there is a few studies where lots of cancer cells were sequenced, and she finds a few cells resembling this phenotype, this gene expression pattern. This needs to be extended, the studies in the primary tumors that we looked in of our patients, we couldn't do this because all this tumor went into paraffin. Hi, Christoph. Patrick from Genentech. I just have a question related to the profiling of the M0, M1. Do you see the interleukin 6 trans signaling in those cells? Yeah. Sort of to ask if that embryo-like signature contains some of the interleukin 6 signaling based on what you've previously- Yes ... mentioned. Yes, absolutely. Yeah. So that is the- Yeah. IL6 signaling is activated, yeah. All right. In these cells. Thank you. There you go. Hi, thank you for your presentation. I really appreciate it. I have a question regarding the embryoid DCC population get resistant, and you show that we have the up-regulation of HER2 in associated with the perforation of ERK, AKT, and STAT3. So I just wonder, do you have any plan to target those kinase? Because you say that they have no specific drug or there are no therapies to target the embryonic stem cell right now. So do you have any plan to target those kinase based on your pre-data that you already found? I'm sorry. I had difficulties to understand your question. So you were asking about these pathways that we found activated in these four cells that we analyzed? Yes. So you show that embryoid DCC have the in screen expansion of the phosphor ERK, phosphor AKT, and phosphor STAT3. So I just question, did you have plan to try some targeting those kinase to figure out how we can prevent embryonic stem cell? Well, at the moment, this is just a proof of concept. So we were just establishing the method, and we just wondered whether-- I actually expected all these cells completely dormant, right? So no phosphor HER2, no phosphor AKT, no phosphor STAT. Maybe STAT, yeah, activated by some cytokine signals. How this goes further, we will probably focus on-- So basically you can use many antibodies. You can scale this up. It's just a matter of money, 20, 50, 100 proteins that you label your antibodies. But these cells are so rare, so you need to get as much information out of a single cell. This is always the problem, because this nightmare of thousand patients investigating it, it's ongoing thing since 15 years. It's really a lot of work. And so we will scale this up and look for activation pathways, embryonic genes, and candidate dormancy pathways that may be activated. Thank you so much. One last question. Okay. Thank you so much for your talk. I was just wondering, since you do see IL6 upregulation, you mentioned, and then also the phospho-ERK, phospho-AKT signaling, how are you differentiating these cells from senescent cells that are potentially having upregulation of these same pathways and then that's driving the SAS production? Yeah. So you're completely right. There's more questions than answers at the moment. And, no, I can't tell you exactly what these cells are, what the biology is at the moment. The activation of the IL6 pathway, we have seen before in the transcriptomic data. Mm-hmm. So I think they are not senescent cells at the moment, so by other points from these profiles. Okay. Thank you. Yeah. And with that, that brings this session to a close. Please join me in thanking our speakers.

Good afternoon. Welcome to this Advances in Organized Research sessions. So the session is about gastric and gastroesophageal cancer dynamics, including pre-cancer evolution, metastasis, microenvironment, and therapeutic breakthrough. This is my disclosure. So gastric and gastroesophageal and esophageal cancer are very important cancers because there are more than a million case newly diagnosed each year and associated with very high mortality. The TCGA has published a very nice paper about the molecular subtypes along the whole upper gastrointestinal tract, from the esophagus to the gastroesophageal junction, down to the stomach. And up in the esophagus is mostly esophageal squamous cell carcinoma, which is a kind of very different tumor, whereas down in the gastroesophageal junction, you begin to see the predominance of the CIN subtypes of adenocarcinoma. When we progressively move up into the upper gastric body and antrum, the diversity of the cancer become increased, where there are some very gastric-specific subtypes like the EBV-associated gastric cancer, the genomically stable, or with substantial overlap with the diffuse histology types of cancer, and the MSI cancers, coexist together with the CIN subtype. So previously, treatment of gastric cancer or gastroesophageal junction cancer has been really limited to chemotherapy, mostly based on 5-FU and platinum. But in the recent year, there has been increasingly molecular biomarker, like the MSI subtype, being respond to PD-1 inhibitions. The PRD1 high tumor can be treated by anti-PD-1 as well. And then the recent emergence of the claudin 18.2 as a marker for antibody against it. This is a lineage marker for stomach tight junction cells. And then there is very exciting breakthrough in the HER2-positive gastric cancer, especially those with PD-1 expression. And we are going to have speaker talking a lot about this, which is really exciting development. And there are second-line and third-line treatment, but the efficacy is really limited, and we still need a breakthrough in this area. In parallel, there are technological evolution, including organoid models, new animal models, and multiomic profiling, as well as the single-cell and spatial transcriptomic that allowed us to develop deep understanding, both in the pre-cancer evolution and also in the tumor microenvironment. And with this background, today, we are going to have three talks. Myself talking about the pre-cancer evolution of the upper gastrointestinal tract. We have Dr. Jaffa Ajani from MD Anderson Cancer Center talking about molecular heterogeneity and also advances in HER2-directed therapy. We also have Dr. Yelena Janjigian from Memorial Sloan Kettering to talk about resectable gastroesophageal cancer, time to rewrite the standard. So I'm going to start with the first talk, and we will have Q&A section after each of the talk, and also a general discussion for all three of the speaker. So you can either ask question right at the end or leave it to the end of the general discussion. So my laboratory is a molecular pathology laboratory, and we are interested in the pre-cancer evolution as well as the molecular classification of gastric cancer. More than 10 years ago, we have done a very comprehensive profiling of gastric cancer and identified these four molecular subtypes, each having their own driver mutation, in which now we are seeing emerging targeted therapy towards each of these molecular subgroups. So in parallel, we have built organoid model trying to understand all these molecular subtypes. And we have now a bank that represent virtually all the molecular subtype, including some of those that are previously underrepresented in cancer cell lines like the ALK fusion model, the RhoA mutation model, as well as the EBV and some diffuse gastric cancer models. In parallel, there is evolvement of many different modification to the original organoid cocktail that adapt to different organs in which you can actually grow organoid from cancers from these various organs, epithelial organ especially. And in parallel, the exciting development is now because of this, you can actually grow pre-cancer models covering all these different organs, and I'm going to mainly cover the intestinal metaplasia model in this talk. SoIntestinal metaplasia is the conversion of gastric cell into intestinalized cells, and it is usually a consequence of chronic inflammation, and it has a wide prevalence, especially in Asian population. Histologically, it has been classified into the complete and incomplete type, and the incomplete type is said to be associated with a higher risk of gastric cancer conversion. However, study of this is limited because there is no representative sensitive 2D cell line model, and the animal model, especially in mice, only partially resemble human metaplasia. And mice mainly displace the so-called spam instead of true intestinal metaplasia. In collaboration with Mike Stratton in Sanger Institute, we have done a deep whole genome sequencing by microdissecting individual crypts in individual gland in the stomach. And through study of more than 200 whole genome sequence of individual glands, we observe the number of SNVs increasing with age in both non-cancer and cancer patients. So this is probably the range of normal, what you would expect. By the age of 80, you will have around 2,000 SNV mutation in each of the gland in your stomach. But in some of the gastric cancer patient, we see outliers with elevated somatic mutation, and these correlate with chronic inflammation, denoted in red, and also intestinal metaplasia. And indeed, if you look at intestinal metaplasia, for the glands that has it, it has around two-fold elevation of the SNV and three-fold elevation of the indel rate. So this is example of what we have dissected, a cluster of intestinal metaplasia glands and then some gastric glands. And when you trace their evolutionary branch, you can see that all these metaplastic glands actually comes from a common ancestor, suggesting that there is actually clonal expansion from a common ancestor, and the asterisk all along in these trees would denote intestinal metaplasia. So this is another example of a bigger piece of mucosa in which you can see that each of this red gland denote a metaplastic gland. You can see families of it around it, but we only dissect one to represent them. You can see they are completely independent in terms of their lineage, showing the heterogeneity, and the field effect is dramatic. And if you imagine you are a gastroenterologist, you can biopsy this area in which you get this IM glands cluster, and this area is a totally different cluster. And only in this one cm area of mucosa, you already get, I would suppose tens or twenties of different metaplastic clones, each with their own different driver or different mutations. So it is a very complex disease because of the heterogeneity. So this phylogenetic tree shows each patient in which the glands that we have microdissected, and you can see the predominant mutation, this clock line mutation of SBS1 and 5. But you can see in the metaplastic glands denoted in asterisk, you can see the blue mutation signature coming off, which is the SBS18, suggest to be linked to ROS injury. And then interestingly, this is the indel signature again, in the metaplastic gland, you see a change in ratio between the ID2 and the ID1 signature. An ID2 signature is more enriched in tumor, especially MSI tumor. So you can see in the early metaplastic process, you already get this progressive shift in mutational signature towards a more like a cancer. So we have studied extensively the biobank of organoid that we have collected in which we grow the organoid. And then with the transcriptome, you can see this is the metaplastic organoid. This is the reference gastric and colon organoid, and we characterize them by the colon and the stomach signature score. And you can see that for the metaplastic organoids, some of them actually retain the gastric signature but begin to express the colon signature, whereas other progressively get lost in their stomach signature. So I think this spectrum probably represent the complete or incomplete transition in the metaplastic process. And this organoid model, you can see they, like the glands that we dissect, they have elevated somatic mutation rates, they have copy number alterations, and these are the key drivers that we found. They don't have the very advanced cancer driver like P53 mutation, but ERIT1A mutation is pretty common. And the most dramatic change is actually in the epigenetics. So we can see in the metaplastic organoid, hypermethylation and downregulated gene and demethylation and upregulated gene. When we map this to the genes that related to the gastric or intestinal signature, actually, we found that some of the gastric signature genes denoted in black balls here arehypermethylated and downregulated, whereas these red genes are denoting the colon signature are demethylated and hyperexpressed. So the whole process seems to be highly epigenetically related. So the interesting genes, claudin 18, there is intense interest because the claudin 18.2 is now a target therapy. You can see they are expressed in the membrane of the antrum or body organoid, but in the metaplastic organoid, you can see progressive reduction in its expression. And probably this could constitute one of the escape mechanism to the claudin 18.2 targeted therapy, where as you can see induction of the metaplastic, the intestinal signature gene. So we perform single-cell analysis on the organoid culture, and you can see if we plot these individual organoid in the x-y axis, the colon and stomach score, you can see the organoid with a hybrid colon and gastric stomach score are in many of the organoid models. And here there is a normal gastric cells contamination, which are the gastric cells that has the gastric score but very low colon score. But you can see the heterogeneity in the spectrum. Some cells has more advanced intestinal differentiation, but other cells are more hybrid, and the lighter color is denote the cells after Wnt withdrawal when we try to induce differentiation. So what worries me though is, of course, not the over-treatment, because that's important, but also the patients who are not responding, right? We talk about de-escalation, but what do we do for the majority of patients who will not be achieving complete response or major pathologic response? Who are those patients? How can we help them? Well, so we know that the big bad elephant in the room, and this is data we published from CheckMate 649, which was a large Phase 3 study, showing that majority of chromosomally unstable tumors, which is the cancers that we see in the West predominantly, don't benefit from immune checkpoint blockade in first-line setting. The hazard ratio is 0.92. The dogma is all to focus on PD-L1, and people will fight to death about what cutoff of CPS one to four or CPS less than 3.5 we should use. But really the elephant in the room is that it's something beyond PD-L1, and PD-L1 is just another sort of easy thing that we can assess. But chromosomal instability drives immune evasion in many of our patients that we're seeing in the clinic. So this is plug number one for one of the talented bioinformaticians and scientists that work with my lab. So Jerry Zhu is presenting this abstract today looking that, of course, everything is a spectrum. Nothing is as simple as just calling someone chromosomally unstable tumor. And we identified six reproducible CIN architecture features that define aneuploidy, focal amplification, and subclonal evolution. And really the purpose of this exercise was to use the facet analysis from close to 2,000 cases that we already did at MSK, but also the huge rich database of the CheckMate 649 whole exome data that BMS shared with our group to put in a framework, a unified clinical molecular framework to standardize how do we define CIN assessment to enable clinical patient stratification in the future, both in first line, second line, but also in early-stage tumors. The other important feature we saw is that in patients-- So we've been using chemoimmunotherapy in early stage disease well before the approval based on Matterhorn. So we amassed quite a group of patients mostly in standard practice who got chemoimmunotherapy. Now we're seeing some of the recurrences. So Dr. Chak and my group looked at genomic instability and predicted recurrence after perioperative immunotherapy in gastroesophageal cancer. So check out the poster. This small snippet of the data does not give it justice, but there is a story on, again, giving chemoimmunotherapy while the tumor is in place still, and even inducing a second immune response after recurrence, how CIN tumors affect that, and how the timing and duration of treatment may be important. So this is an important factor for us to consider, particularly since, of course, in the age of Matterhorn, we have to decide what to do with these patients when they recurSo what we're also seeing is that even if you induce-- So once you've been immune, sort of exposed, and if you're trying to induce a second response, sustained treatment induces increase in interferon gamma, but it does not-- So you're seeing what you would think would be adequate response, but it does not translate to clinical benefit. And this is from a phase two study that Sam Citrin in my group is running. Again, come check it out. This will be April 20th at 2:00 PM. So why is that? Well, what we're seeing, and I know Sam Baccom and Ashley Loughney gave a great talk yesterday, but chronic tumor cGAS associated with immunovasion and poor survival, and it's important, particularly in our cancers. This is data from breast cancer showing that if you have acute cGAS activation, it's potentially a good thing and can induce immune response. But what we often do, and what happens in the setting of CIN tumors, it burns out to chronic activation, which actually causes suppression of STING, and as a result, immunovasion. And this data from breast cancer patients showing that if you have, as you see here on the bottom red survival curve, cGAS high and low STING, it's a really bad thing for patient survival and outcomes. And now we're seeing the same in gastroesophageal cancer. Again, we see chronic cGAS high tumors, and we're seeing STING low. And what we're also seeing is there's a tumor stromal uncoupling between cGAS-STING axis, where we're seeing different expression. And I think what earlier discussion about heterogeneity and importance of tumor microenvironment in the stroma. In fact, again, going back to are we really looking at the right biomarkers, cGAS-STING activation appears to be, at least in our limited cohort that we looked at so far, a stronger predictor of poor prognosis in patients treated with immunotherapy than chromosomal instability itself. So considering it's potentially a druggable target, it's really important for us to continue to study this and characterize it. We're all together, sort of international group of researchers focused in the global engine for target discovery. MSK is just epicenter of it because we happen to both to have a big translational program, but also run phase three studies. And it's great to be able to collaborate with several industry partners who are then able to share with us raw data from some of these studies and use it for target discovery using newer AI tools within silica medicine, but also global collaborations. So we meet twice a year. It's both in person and virtual, and if you're interested, please feel free to ping me, and you'll be invited to the group. Our next retreat is coming up May 4th. And thanks to ACR and Stand Up to Cancer, many of these efforts are funded through various mechanisms, and these are some of the collaborators we pulled in over the years because this disease is definitely in the United States, a relatively orphan disease, where we don't have big foundations throwing millions of dollars at it. And so to have some key aspects of this funded through ACR and Stand Up to Cancer, Turkoos, Gemini, Debbie's Dream Foundation has been amazing. So in conclusion, what we're seeing here is a shift in paradigm where we're able to push the envelope and cure more patients. Because I think historically, this focus on palliation and just prolonging survival, this nihilistic approach has been centered in our disease. But now we're seeing even in metastatic, but certainly in early-stage disease, people are being cured. And what drives these cures is early immune priming, generating deep responses that will enable organ preservation. What we need to really understand is the tumor biology, including the spectrum of chromosomal instability, innate immune signaling, and that will shape immune response and interrogate all the biomarkers dynamically as we're really understanding how these tumors adjust and change while on treatment. And only working together in collaboration can we do this. We have an amazing team at MSK. I see patients in a day, 30 patients in a day. So really it takes a village to cure these patients. Really dedicated symptom management nursing care is a big part of this. And so thank you for attending the session, and I bought us four more minutes, so we have more time. So I have a few questions from the floor as well. Maybe I would like to invite Dr. Jenny to come up. We can have a group Q&A. So first, I have a question from the internet audience for Dr. Yelena. In view of current guidelines, do you offer to diffuse TPS less than one and or node negative? Yes. The answer is? Yes. Okay. So the second question. In view of the negative results for KN-525 and innovation studies, what would you assume make the pembro trastuzumab combo work? Well, KEYNOTE-585 used a doublet, and we are seeing combination therapies with FLOT-based regimen. I think if we wanted to talk about things why 585 was negative, we would need another 20 minutes. But in short, it's the combination of trastuzumab, pembrolizumab together with FLOT that is what's driving these responses because if you remember, our initial Phase 2 data of CAPOX, pembro/trast showed 100% disease control rate, and even in the large Phase 3 KEYNOTE-811 study, the complete response rate was 20%, so in the metastatic setting. So really, it's not a difference between, I think we need to be very clear. In this case, anti-PD-1 therapy, anti-PD-L1 therapy, these agents are equivalent. It's really not because of pembro versus durva, why Matterhorn was different. It's the change in the backbone, but also in a clinical trial design. It was much more simple, and I would say elegant design. So there's questions or- Christoffer has opinions about that . Yes. So I personally don't believe that addition of taxane would change the outcome like that in context of immunotherapy, because there are many trials from China now without a taxane showing benefit. So I think going forward, we will have to focus on what you mentioned, is the more underlying biomarkers in addition to a PD-L1. Philip Dennis from Novo North- I would just clarify that, of course, I think there's a different in biology. We're dealing with G junction tumors, and I think there may be some difference in that. But please go ahead. Philip Dennis from Novo Bridge. I have a question about claudin 18.2 expression. For Dr. Leong first, in your metaplastic organoids, claudin 18.2 was decreased. So is cell surface 18.2 really only evident when cells are fully transformed and when truly malignancy is present? So I think claudin 18 actually is a lineage marker. I don't think it's a neoplastic marker. So is that- Well, its subcellular localization changes, right? That's the dogma, that it's a tight junction- Mm-hmm ... protein that's accessible in the cell surface- Mm-hmm ... in pancreatic BTC and gastric cancers, right? Mm-hmm. But I'm curious when in the process of transformation that takes place. I didn't know if you have data to that question. Yeah, so my belief is because it's a gastric lineage marker and during the metaplastic process, what we are seeing is in some metaplasia when especially it become very advanced intestinal, the gastric lineage markers start to reduce. So this is what we're talking about in the metaplastic process. So I'm not sure whether in the cancer it could undergo the same types of... Because, a lot of gastric cancer actually has inherent probably metaplasia as the stem cells. So, it depends on the state. If it's a hybrid, it may still retain the claudin 18, but it may switch to more intestinal phenotype. I suppose that could be a form of resistance. Is locally advanced, resectable, is the prevalence of 18.2 the same as in metastatic? Has anyone looked at that? I think it depends on which antibody. I find that the claudin expression is really variable depending on who's looking at the, and what cutoffs you use. But in our experience so far, it's very similar. I had a question for you. Mm-hmm. So, as you know, the young onset is an epidemic for our disease as well. How do they develop? What type of metaplasia are you seeing in young patients with this disease? Have you looked at- You mean in gastric cancer? Yeah. I think it's the same metaplasia. Mm-hmm. And I also find it, the complete and incomplete classification, I think it's always a spectrum. And if you look at the heterogeneity we see in the microdissected individual gland, so if you look at it carefully, often you will see both complete and incomplete in the same patient. So it's really which one eventually gained enough driver mutation to get transformed. And it looks like based on our data, the one that are more hybrid, that probably are more likely to progress because of this plasticity and fetal reversion. Yeah. But they can, I think if you look at the clonal organoid, they show different spectrum, right? So I think to start with, the cell that turn neoplastic probably may have certain epigenetic point to start with. But whether they can still deviate afterwards, I'm not sure. Yeah. Well, a very nice presentation. I have three questions. First is, if you only observe a single tumor in a patient but you have so many mutations in the gastric mucosa, why is it that we see only one tumor? So what is the difference?The second question is, if we see so many heterogeneities, and metastases, and primary tumor, how do we handle that in diagnostics? Because all we have is the primary biopsy. The third question is, we do have sexual dimorphism. I haven't heard anything about how you treat women and men separately, how you incorporate this information about sexual dimorphism in treatment and diagnostics of gastric cancer. Thank you. So for the first question about the heterogeneity, I think it's kind of a few effect. So I think the difficulty is, if you look at the heterogeneity, basically, there are many, many glands, each acquiring their mutation, the chromosome change independently. But the chance of any one of them progress is pretty low. So that's why at the end of the day, you end up mainly with one dominant cancer. But I think in the early cancer evolution, you may have many different parallel evolution clones, but eventually, maybe one out-compete all the others. So that's the answer to point number one. So that's why by the time we see the gastric cancer, it usually originate from one clone. The sec- Fitness. It's fitness, right? Fitness. Yes. Yeah, exactly. Many mutation in the gastric mucosa, you say you have shown that. Yeah. One eventually will develop into cancer. Yeah. What happens to the remainder? I think it's not so easy to developing cancer, so they may remain as metaplasia, they may become dysplastic, but they may be still in the field in the adjacent area. Yeah. So how we cope with diagnostics? Maybe I can take that one. Yeah. I think what we really need to cope with is, and it's a circular argument, but right now the diagnostics are actually quite good, it's the therapeutics that are lacking. So the truth is, yes, there is some heterogeneity, but there's not that much of a difference between the primary and the met. The p53 mutation is the same. I would say 70% or 80% of genomic alterations, if you sequence both, are very similar. The difference comes in maybe some levels of expression of HER2 or PD-L1 and so forth, but they probably aren't that important to begin with, right? So I think what we need to catch up on is actual better therapeutics, and the diagnostics then will lead. Functional imaging, as Jeffrey said, and it's logical, you can't biopsy all the mets anyway. So I think what we've developed is functional imaging, so using radio tracers as a way to really just get a sense from the patient what level of the burden of the biomarker they have. And then you could prior strata... You think the tumor is HER2 positive, but then you go in and only 60% or 70% of the primary tumor in the met express, and we see that with HER2 PAT. 80% of patients have heterogeneity. We know that. But if you don't have an alternative to target, you will still use HER2. You'd need to develop other treatments before, and I think it's fine to do it in parallel, but the field of therapeutics has really lacked in this disease. Thank you very much. Yep. This side. Yes. Hi, my name is Chandra Gul. I'm a general surgery resident and a postdoc in surgery at Stanford. Thank you for an excellent talk. This is a question for Dr. Chen Zhijian. Hopefully, I'm saying your name right. Yes. You spoke about the neoadjuvant immuno-chemotherapy and how that's becoming the gold standard for gastric cancer. I wonder if you have any perspective on the extent of lymphadenectomy that we currently do as a surgeon. I know a lot of the Eastern perspective historically is doing pretty aggressive lymphadenectomy, and that's what used to be considered adequate. Now with immunotherapy, are we thinking about leaving some behind for adequate therapy or response? Curious to hear your thoughts. Yeah. So looking at the pancreas experience with Vinod Balachandran and the adjuvant vaccines, I think your point is well taken. Sometimes these lymph nodes are important. In fact, doing a splenectomy and taking out more lymph nodes was associated with less of immune response. For our disease, it's slightly different because we're doing everything neoadjuvantly, and I think where the field is moving forward to doing more and more while the tumor and the lymph nodes are in place, and using surgeries almost as a staging procedure where you have to take a lot of lymph nodes out, so you know sort of what it-- Because first of all, you're worried that there's residual disease, but also to adequately stage. So I don't see the field-- In fact, right now, I think that what I struggle most is as I'm selecting centers or designing the next phase three, is quality control. Because with the surgeons, it's just you and the patient, and maybe some nurses that report to you and would never tell you, "Well, your surgery was not good enough." Right? So, that's what we struggle with. And also the fact that if you do have a good immune response, sometimes it looks like the lymph nodes are growing, but in fact, they're all residual response of therapy. So we have not deescalated surgery. I think maybe that's going to be in the next phase. But I see it's either all or nothing. You either do the surgery or you don't. But right now, the D2 lymph node dissection is the same. It's a modified version where they leave the spleen behind. Thank you. I have a couple of questions, Dr. Judkins. The first one regarding you are showing the STING pathway, STING, cGAS pathway, the increase the STING pathway can associate the poor survival. But STING actually innate immune can increase the interferon gamma or actually anti-tumor. I don't know what's behind the rationale for this poorly differentiation association with this high STING pathway as a first pass. I know. I knew that it was going to be very controversial because you could approach it from two different factors. And I suspect that in each individual tumor type, but also within each even gastroesophageal cancer, depending on where in the trajectory of the CIN tumor you look, STING can be a good thing or a bad thing. So in our cohort now, what we're seeing is that we are seeing low STING expression. STING pathway through interferon gamma can up-regulation PD-1. I'm not sure in this patient you gave additional PD-1 or PD-L1 treatment. Do they have a better response or not? So the cohort we have are all IO-treated patients, so that's why we know what immunotherapy response or duration of treatment benefit was. And what we are seeing is these were pre-treatment samples. Okay. So these were not one sort of post-progression samples, post immunotherapy. Another question regarding to Dr. Johnny Bo, for you because you treat the patient. I'm wondering because diffuse type of intestinal have different etiology and molecular biology and the genetic difference, do you treat the patient different or similar? Based on what? So I think pure diffuse type of tumor patients, they do very badly generally. But we start with the biomarkers, the four biomarkers that Yelena showed, and then you can do NGS. But consistently, the diffuse type will do poorly. Maybe with claudin, they will do a little bit better. But we don't treat based on phenotype. We're treating based on biomarkers and other profiling. Okay. Another question also both to yours regarding the immune therapy. I know PD-1, PD-L1 mostly is tested in the clinical. However, do you ever treat a patient and use TIGIT? You mentioned the TIGIT plus PD-1. Are there other LAG-3 or other? Do you have any better clinical response than PD-1, PD-L1? Yeah. So the TIGIT story, unfortunately, is negative as many other tumor types. So there was a large Phase III study that will be presented at ESMO GI in Munich that was negative despite very promising Phase II study. And LAG-3 data is also negative, unfortunately. So the only hope is with PD-1 CTLA-4 because of this Catenilimab FC silent bispecific. But it's too soon to say because the Nivo/Ipi data, the CheckMate 649 data looked promising. But because there was no chemo, because of the toxicity concern, there was a crossover in the survival curves. So it's too soon. The new bispecifics are going to probably produce good results. So one anti-PD-1, anti-PD-L1, anti-VEGF, or EGFR HER3 with ADC, they are showing some good progress. But a lot of work needs to be done. Okay. Yeah. One question for Dr. Leung on the cancer evolution in this field. I'm curious if we can detect what's going on during the pre-cancer to cancer, the transition. Yes. Any genomic bottlenecks during the transition pre-cancer to cancer? You show the mutation cluster, you use the mutation and the epigenomic and the copy number, and do you have a chance to check the timing of this event? And the ultimate question is, can we detect, as you say, the diagnosis is good. Is it possible to detect cancer in pre-cancer stage if, say, we have the precursor? That's my question. Thank you. So I think there is an intense interest in predicting which metaplasia will progress to cancer, right? I think the problem is for the metaplasia, it's quite common, but only a small percent progress. So you need to find ways to predict the one that will progress. So based on our organoid model, we feel that those metaplasia with chromosome 20 gain is probably biologically, at least from our model, seems to have more neoplastic phenotype. So in parallel, I also cite some study, for example, from Singapore groups. So they actually have other risk progression marker like mutation count, even clonal hematopoiesis, and ARID1A mutation. So I think this is still work in progress. But I think with more data and more biology, I think for certain we should be able to find better markers. Thank you. Yes. The last question? Yeah. Yeah, I have one question. Thank you for the nice talking. The question for Dr. Elena. In new adjuvant in MSI-H patients, you showed your clinical trials that combined dual IO with chemotherapy, the effect is better. But have you ever compared single IO with chemotherapy and dual IO with chemotherapy in this kind of patients? Because in many clinical trials, single IO with chemotherapy has already pretty good effect. That's a great question, and I will cover some of this in the discussion. It's actually not my data, it's Alberto's data, Infinity, and Sara Leonardi is here too. So they're presenting the durva/tremi. But that's a very good question. I think because of the heterogeneity in MSI cancers, we know that anti PD-1, like dostorlimab data, right, in gastroesophageal cancer was not as good as it was in rectal. So at a minimum, chemoimmunotherapy is needed. But I think CTLA-4 is a very attractive option because we know from CheckMate 649, looking at, at least numerically, we never compared head to head, but FOLFOX nivo versus nivo ipi, it looked better in terms of, again, small numbers, hard to extrapolate. But we know that if you respond to ipi, you never progress, right? So we know that. And also FOLFOX is not easy. And in Alberto's study, doing one dose of tremi is enough. So instead of being on six months of FOLFOX nivo or a flott durva, certainly, it's very appealing. So I think the way that we approach it is that we usually start with dual immune checkpoint blockade, but we watch the patient very carefully, and if it looks like radiographically or clinically they're progressing or not responding, we then pivot to either flott durva or FOLFOX durva or something like that. Thank you. Mm-hmm. But come to the session on Tuesday. There'll be a lot more on that. Okay. So thank you very much for your attendance. And I also want to thank the speakers. Thank you. We should take a picture. Yeah. We should take a picture together. Thank you for the invitation. Yeah. Enjoyed it.

Good afternoon, and thank you for joining this particular session on neuroimmune crosstalk in cancer. These are my disclosures. So for many of us who are very interested in the tumor microenvironment, you can see all the usual suspects, the stromal cells, the cancers, the macrophage, the neutrophils, the T cells, and the B cells. However, something happened in Germany 175 years ago. Rudolf Wagner found that when he stimulated the nerve in a dog, the spleen moved. So he contacted his friend, Jacopo Andy, and he said, "Can you do an experiment for me with human data?" So his friend did the same thing with a decapitated human, something that I truly do not want any one of you to try. And then subsequently, a lot of people, including Paul, could start tracing these different nerves. So all of a sudden, for us who are cancer biologists, we start thinking about what if all that we've been doing, looking for the metabolic adaptation that would stimulate the immune system to improve immunotherapy or genomic instability, which would also be something that we really now know can stimulate the immune system against cancers. So this neuroimmune crosstalk in cancer becomes real because that stimulation of the nerves that the spleen moved, perhaps what we're doing is sending a message from nerves into the immune cells. And of course, there are the central nervous system and the peripheral nervous system, and mainly what we're going to be talking about is the peripheral immune system. We can have the autonomic nerves, which is splitting into the sympathetic, which makes norepinephrine, fight and flight, and then the parasympathetic make acetylcholine. But this is not really secretable, the acetylcholine from the T cells to other cells and in the neurons are mainly synapsis. So we will talk about today, the three of us, how these nerves actually play in, innovate, and crosstalk with the tumor microenvironment. Now, the field is slowly growing now. As of last year, 2,000 papers have been published on neuroimmune crosstalk. Out of that, about a quarter of them are now starting to ask questions with respect to what will be involved in the cancer setting. Today, we have three speakers who are all very seasoned in this field, and we have, as you can see here, written some reviews for those of you who want to get involved. I will give the first talk, Tumor Immune Microenvironment: Time to Chat. Professor Trumpp will talk about neuronal innervation of pancreatic cancer, and Professor Talbot will talk about nociceptor neurons impact on antitumor immunity. My journey came in 2008. I was at dinner at a metropolitan club in New York, and I met some neurosurgeons. They told me stories which made me so curious that we started working together as a group. The story was that although extrapolation from the German stimulating nerves, acetylcholine was indeed found about 100 years ago, and that if you actually stimulate the nerves, there would be more of this acetylcholine. But what was curious and mysterious was that up to todayIt has been very difficult to find cholinergic parasympathetic nerves within the spleen, the lymph node, thymus, and the liver. So the question then is, where is the acetylcholine coming from? As it turned out, that these autonomic nerves do usually hit a celiac ganglion. In the case of parasympathetic, they hit a celiac ganglion with acetylcholine, but then it comes out acetylcholine. But in some of these situations, like in the spleens and the liver, very likely, that the parasympathetic nerve comes in as the acetylcholine within the celiac ganglion made a switch. With time, you make norepinephrine. And these are the main organs where it had been very difficult to find fibers of acetylcholine. So what was easy to do- Several years ago, what was easy to do was to actually make a mouse with ChatGFP, not ChatGPT. And that, in a way, would be found that the CD4 cells and the CD8 cells were making a little bit of it. So to make a long story short, within the last 10, 15 years, we've been looking at the idea of how these T cells and these B cells make acetylcholine along the way. Norepinephrine can stimulate T and B cells to make acetylcholine, depending on the B cells and where they are. The T cells can be stimulated by norepinephrine, but T cell receptor, together with IL-21, is perhaps the main stimulus. So why? It's because when we have inflammation in certain part of the organ, the message has to go back to the brain, and the brain send back a message to exactly the same place where there is an inflammation or a cancer. And that way it gives the immune system an extra boost or an extra dampening signal so that we can control our physiology and pathophysiology. I just may give you an example. The two viruses many of you are familiar, they are called LCMV, and the Armstrong forms an acute infection where there are lots of short-lived CD8 effector cells. But the clone 13, which only differs by two amino acids and was originally found in the brain of a patient, has a persistent infection where there is exhaustion and CD4 cells get involved. So the number of CD4 cells that make acetylcholine in the normal mouse is about 2%, and CD8 cells is almost nothing. However, if you infect it with a lymphocytic choriomeningitis virus, about 50% of the T cells are pumping out acetylcholine. But what is interesting is the acute infections will jump from zero to very high and come straight back down to zero, whereas the protracted infection, the CD8 cells hang around to make sure it's clean, and the CD4 cells do the same thing, but they maintain a higher baseline. So we say, "What are these doing?" So Maureen Cox decided to delete acetylcholine transfer from the T cells only. So the whole mouse has every cell that makes acetylcholine the way it should be, but now the T cells cannot make acetylcholine. You can see definitely does this result reveal a genetic proof of function for Chat in T cells viral infection. What is the mechanism? It did look like that in absence of acetylcholine from the T cells, the blood vessels are smaller and fewer, and we suspect that the acetylcholine, in addition to chemokines and adhesion, will then interact with endothelium and then induce the muscles to dilate so that the T cells can go out. And it makes sense because only those T cells that had the T cell receptor amplified or stimulated should be going out. Now, just to kind of confirm this, Peder Olsson and us collaboratedTo show that in mice that have T cells making acetylcholine, the blood pressure is lower. And more recently, he was able to show that in patients with severe circulatory failure, those patients who do have acetylcholine do much better than those that do not. Perhaps have something to do with activation, dilation, hypoxia, whatever, we do not know. And in mice, when induced EAE, a form of MS, it is these T17 cells that parries the acetylcholine that causes the disease, and those that do not, actually do not. So it's become clear that T cells, and later I will show you the B cells, that this acetylcholine that is being conveyed to them allows them to basically function in a more proper way, amplifying or slowing down certain physiological functions. So I think this is really the beginning of an iceberg. So I am of the opinion that every single cell of your body needs these adrenergic and acetylcholine receptors at some point, at some time. You may not see them now, but something happens, they will come up or they will come down. The basic message is, somewhere something is happening pathophysiologically. The message goes to the brain, comes back, usually it's vagal nerve that hits a celiac ganglion, then express into a sympathetic nerve, and they will secrete norepinephrine to activate the T cells and the B cells together with the T cell receptors and the B cell toll receptors. They would then not secrete acetylcholine, but they will then basically make a synapse with almost every cell of your body at the right time, in the right place, for the right reason. Now, this is going to take a long time to solve. There are five muscarinic receptors, GPCRs. There are 16 nicotinic receptors, but some of them form heteropentamers, making the situation so complicated that I begin to believe there may be dozens, if not 100 of these receptors. And there are these nine adrenergic receptors, which are GPCRs. So Kai Qi in Beijing found that the alpha nine is actually required for the maturation of B cells into plasma cells. Shangfen Liu in our laboratory did a very interesting experiment. He found that the alpha nine is on double positive thymocytes. A message from a T cell within the thymus gives it an extra calcium signal, which would double the number of T cells in your body. So this is the way the brain is saying, as evolution progresses, we are exposed to more viruses, more bacterias, we need more T cells, and alpha nine provides that. Well, how do I think that? Because when he knocked it out, then there is less T cells repertoire, about half. And the T cell receptors composition and the repertoires are different. Such that, in fact, when given autoimmune diseases, it is less. Moving on to the germinal center, where T cells and B cells were given maybe three, four, five days to come up with not only the best cytotoxic T cells, but also the one with the highest affinity B cell antibodies to neutralize the pathogen. That race for time is completely controlled by acetylcholine from the T cell telling the B cells not to blow every single B cell, but only the ones with the highest affinity, so then they can become the even higher and higher and higher within the three, four, five days that you only have before the pathogen takes you away. At the same time, the B cell will tell the T cells what to do with another acetylcholine signal.The complications is so immense that multiple muscarinic receptors switch on to nicotinic receptors during that maturation in order that we actually do have exactly what we need.
