When they reach axonal branch point, those axon potential can actually travel back to the periphery, where they will lead to the local release of neuropeptide. Neuropeptide is the thing that they use to communicate with other neuron or other cells in the tissue. Classic neuropeptide are substance P and CGRP. So what happened is locally, this substance P and CGRP will act on capillaries. They will increase blood flow, increase vasodilation. They can increase the chemotaxis and adhesion of immune cells, and eventually they will loosen the tight junction of these blood vessel, and this will allow the immune cells actually to get out of the capillaries and come in the microenvironment. And the consequences of this is it will put in very close vicinity immune cells and sensory neurons. So this allow for this local crosstalk between the nerve and immune cells. So this local crosstalk has been shown to be super important, control immune responses at various barrier site. Classic barrier site are, for example, the skin. A lot of work has been done by the lab of Isaac Chiu in the context of bacterial infection. There's also interaction in the lung. A lot of data has been done in the context of asthma, including from my lab and also at the gut, again during bacterial infection. So neuroimmune interaction are important to regulate immune function. For example, during, as I mentioned, bacterial infection or viral infection or wound healing. But what happen in the context of cancer? So we decided to study this because it was not really known. So we chose melanoma as our working model. Why we chose melanoma? Because it's a great model of immunosurveillance, and we know that the skin is densely innervated by sensory neurons. We are also not expert in cancer, so we thought this would be easy enough to actually measure tumor growth. You can just use a caliper and looked at the growth on the skin. So what we normally do is classic model, for example, B16-F10, that we inject orthotopically in nociceptor intact in ablated mice, meaning that we have mice in which we can specifically eliminate subtype of neuron. Then we typically look at the presence of itch or pain, which are marker of sensory neuron activation. Eventually, we looked at the presence of nerve that will infiltrate the tumor. At endpoint, we harvest the tumor, and we immunophenotype those tumor, and we looked at immunity. So here is one of the first experiment that we did, is we give melanoma to our nociceptor intact and ablated mice. To eliminate nociceptor, in this case, we use a TRPV1 cre diphtheria toxin. So this mice actually, as I mentioned, will actually kill specifically pain transmitting neuron and mainly the neuron that produce neuropeptides. So what we found is that in absence of sensory neuron, we have smaller tumor growth, and we have longer survival. And when we immunophenotype those tumor, we found that there were more CD8 T cell per milligram of tumor. But most interestingly, we found that there were higher interferon gamma positive CD8 T cell, and it seems that those T cell were less exhausted. So lower level of PD-1, LAG-3, and TIM-3 positive CD8 T cells. So this suggests that perhaps the neuron control immune function. But we ask ourselves, can the cancer cell also impact the function of neuron? So to study this, we decided to use a co-culture approach in which we co-culture DRG neuron in the presence or absence of melanoma.We did that for 48 hours, and then we FACS purified each cell type and RNA-Seq them. And we found that when the neuron were co-culture with the cancer cell, they drastically overexpressed many different neuropeptide, including Calcitonin which encode for CGRP, so this classic neuropeptide. So as I mentioned, neuropeptide are the mediator by which neuron impact immunity. So we ask ourself, can this CGRP would be able to impact T cell function? So we looked at this in many different ways. I'm going to show you one which is the simplest one. We harvest basically naive splenocyte CD8 T cell, we make them to be cytotoxic, and we expose them to CGRP. And what we found is that CGRP seems, again, to drive the exhaustion of those T cell, meaning they express higher level of PD-1, LAG-3, and TIM-3, and lower level of interferon gamma. This effect was actually absent when we harvested a RAMP1 knockout CD8 T cell, RAMP1 being the receptor for CGRP. Not showing you all the data, but we eventually shows that if you put CGRP on OT-1 CD8 T cell, they were less able to eliminate B16-F10 ova. So we really think that CGRP is able to drive exhaustion of the T cells. But to confirm this in vivo, we decided to use a RAMP1 knockout mice. RAMP1, as you may know, have no B and no T cells. So what we did is we transplanted either a RAMP1 wild type or RAMP1 knockout CD8 T cells, so T cells that do not respond to CGRP. So in these mice, in which the T cell cannot respond to CGRP, we found that there's smaller tumor growth. In some of our mice, we co-transplanted both RAMP1 wild type and RAMP1 knockout CD8 T cell. And using CD45.1 and CD45.2, we could track each subset of T cell within the same tumor. And what we found, I think, is pretty interesting. Again, lower exhaustion in our RAMP1 knockout CD8 T cells. So less PD-1, LAG-3, TIM-3 positive CD8 T cell. But to really confirm that, we actually FACS purify and then RNA-Seq those T cell. And again, in the knockout CD8 T cell, there's lower expression of Tox, Eomes, and other markers, suggesting again that there's perhaps lower exhaustion of CD8 T cell. So is this relevant for patients? So if you looked at TCGA data, you see that high RAMP1 expression melanoma seems to be bad for the patient. But most interestingly is when you looked at single-cell RNA-Seq data. So Aviv Regev had two paper published from melanoma patient. So because it's single cell, you can parse T cell in different populations. So we parse them either expressing high level of RAMP1 or low level of RAMP1. So within melanoma patient, if you express high level of RAMP1, the T cell, again, seems to be more exhausted. So higher expression of PD-1, TIM-3, LAG-3, CTLA4. Not showing you all the data. The paper has been published now for a few years. But what we found is that melanoma is densely innervated by sensory neuron, that melanoma activates sensory neuron by the secretion of SLEEPY. The sensory neuron will locally release CGRP. It will act on RAMP1 positive CD8 T cell and drive their exhaustion. And what we eventually found is that if you block the sensory neurons using different drug, for example, QX314, or if you block the RAMP1 receptor using the IBN4096, you prevent or you reduce T cell exhaustion, which are then able to fight better the tumor, so we have smaller tumor growth. Now I'm showing you some data that we looked at neuron signature. As we all know, when we looked at TCGA data, we normally looked at only one marker. So Ben HK, actually created at University of Toronto, created that tool which he called predictio.ca, which you can access. It's freely accessible. It's pretty cool, where you can look at different expression of different marker. So we wanted to look at a neuron signature, in this case, classic marker of neuron, including Trpv1, Nav1.8, RAMP1, and we found that our signature seems to be very bad for patient survival. It seems to be even worse than T cell exclusion. So having this neuron signature within cancer excuse me, seems to be very bad for patient. Then again, if we looked at the signature and whether a patient would respond better or not to IO, we found that only for melanoma, again, having this neuron signature seems to be a predictor for bad responsiveness to immunotherapy. So I'm going to show you data that's been generated or led by my colleague Alex Birbrair at Wisconsin Medicine. And he ask itself what happened with melanoma when they metastasize to the lung. So all our data so far were in the primary site. What happened in lung mets? So to do this, he used, again, B16-F10, in which he injected intravenously to a nociceptor neuron reporter mice. In this case, it's a Nav1.8 Cre TD tomato. And what he found in comparison to normal lung, the lung that were actually bearing those metastasis, they were more innervated. So there's perineural or perimetastatic innervation, but there's also intrametastatic innervation. So there's presence of neuron in and around those lung mets. So what would happen if you eliminate those neurons? So if you use RTX, which is a drug to eliminate sensory neuron, he said there were less metastasis. So then he wanted to confirm that using genetic model. In this case, he used chemogenetics. To do this, he used a Nav1.8 Cre-HM4QDI, in which you can specifically, in this case, block sensory neuron via the injection of CNO. And he found that if you inject CNO in those mice, you're actually decreasing, again, lung metastasis. So what is happening in those lung met? What is the crosstalk between the nerve and the lung mets? So first of all, if you looked at TCGA data in patient that have lung metastasis, you can compare a live patient and patient that eventually pass. In patient that pass, he saw that there were higher expression of RAMP1. And then again, if you looked at survival data, it seems that in patient that express high level of RAMP1, they seems to survive less.But what was super interesting is when you actually compare primary melanoma to a melanoma that actually metastasized to the lung. So if you harvest these guys and profile them using qPCR, we see that the melanoma that actually met to the lung drastically overexpressed RAMP1. This is about 10 or 20-fold higher expression of RAMP1. So then he ask itself, what happen if we remove RAMP1 expression of these cancer cells? So he used CRISPR-Cas9 to knock out RAMP1 out of YUM 1.7. And he sees that in absence of RAMP1 expression on those cancer cell, there's also less lung metastasis. Another thing that he discover is that RAMP1 is not specifically only expressed on the cancer cell. They seem to be also expressed by PDGFR beta positive cell. PDGFR beta is our marker of pericytes. And again, if you compare a normal lung to a lung that actually is bearing lung mets, the pericyte drastically overexpress RAMP1. Here it's 100-fold overexpression. Another thing that he discover is that CGRP positive neuron are in very close proximity to those pericytes, suggesting that perhaps the neuron is able to control pericyte function. So to look into this, he decided, well, he use the Cre-Lox toolbox to actually flux out RAMP1 out of the pericyte. And what he discover is that in absence of RAMP1 on those pericyte, there's smaller tumor growth. Then one of the question of one of our reviewer was, is this relevant for patient? And he asked us a very tough question where he wanted us to do a clinical trial in metastatic melanoma in the lung, which as you may think, this would be pretty complicated. So we're trying to go around this question where Alex was able to access about 100 million patient data set. And he looked at whether those patient were actually having melanoma or not. And he found about 40,000 patient that had melanoma, and some of those patient were actually treated with RAMP1 antagonists. So now there's RAMP1 antagonists on the market, and they are used to treat migraines, for example. So the acceptance of this drug is pretty recent, but he was still able to find about 120 patient. But the cool part was that those patient that were actually treated with those RAMP1 antagonists seems to actually be doing better than the control patient. So of course, these data have a bit of caveat. We don't know when the treatment was started. We don't know when the indication of the treatment. But nevertheless, it seems that using RAMP1 antagonists potentially is helping patient with lung metastasis, or actually metastasis in general. This is not only lung. So again, not showing you all the data, but something really cool that he found is that primary melanoma, when they met to the lung, they start overexpressing RAMP1. They can then respond to CGRP produced by these nociceptor neuron. He found that this will drive tumor growth. He also found that pericyte will also overexpress RAMP1. They will receive signal from nociceptor neuron, and that will drive proliferation and angiogenesis of the tumor. So now I'm going to show you, over the last five minute, another story that's now published. Wanted to see how nociceptor neuron control tumor growth beyond CGRP, and this is work that's been carried out in collaboration with Moran Amit at MD Anderson. So what we decided to do, and it's very similar to what Andreas actually showed you, is how melanoma or whether melanoma are reprogram, or whether how melanoma reprogram tumor innervating neurons. So to do this, again, very similar to what Andreas did, we injected melanoma in the INPA of the mice. Why the INPA? Is because we can specifically trace these neuron to L3 to L5 DRGs, harvest those L3 to L5 DRGs, purify nociceptor neuron using tdTomato, and then single-cell RNA seq them. And one of the thing that we found is that, well, there was a unique population of neuron in a melanoma-bearing animal, and there's a lot of differentially expressed genes across different subset of neuron. But really, this unique population of neuron were actually expressing ATF3. ATF3 is a key transcription factor that's expressed specifically in injured neurons. So this is very classic. If you have nerve injury, ATF3 is absolutely essential to allow neuron to actually regrow in the nerve stump. So finding this ATF3 in our tumor innervating neuron was very cool, so wanted to follow up on this. So first of all, we use a ATF3 reporter animal to confirm that, yes, tumor innervating neuron were actually expressing ATF3. But most interestingly, we wanted to see what happen if you flux out ATF3 from nociceptor neurons. If we make them resistant to injury, what happen? So we found that there were smaller tumor growth and smaller tumor weight. And then we ask ourself, how is this actually happening? So we decided to profile immune cells inside of those tumor, and we found that in our injury-resistant mice, we found there was higher expression of, or higher infiltration of interferon gamma positive CD8 T cell. And we also did single-cell RNA seq of this tumor. And what we found is that there's lower level of LAG3 expression of T cell, but also that tumor-associated macrophages, their potential to be immunosuppressive seems to be less, meaning they express lower level of IL1B, CD86, and CD80. Because of time, I'm going to just skip this one. But why is this actually interesting is because Moran had a population of patient, a cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma patient that were treated or not with anti-PD-1.And he had sample before, during, and after treatment. And of course, the patient might respond or not to the treatment. But the really cool part is that in non-responding patient, he found that there's a lot of perineural invasion. Perineural invasion, as it was discussed by Andreas, is basically, the tumor will kind of engulf the nerve, and that will lead to actually potentially injury to the nerve. And really this is what we actually found. We characterize those perineural invasion, and we're able to find that in the non-responder, they seem to overexpress ATF3. So both in our mice, but also in our patient that do not respond to treatment, ATF3 seems to overexpress in these neuron that have perineural invasion. So then we decided to create a signature for these injured neuron, and we wanted to see, well, is this nerve injury signature correlate with poor or bad prognosis for patient? And across different cancer type, including our cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma, PD-1 treated melanoma patient, gastric cancer treated with PD-1, as well as another cohort of melanoma patient treated with PD-1. In every cases, nerve injury seems to be correlated with poor prognosis for the patient. So based on this, we went back to our cutaneous squamous cell carcinoma patient, and we decided to do Visium transcriptomic on these slides. So we had three different gene profile. One that's nerve injury in green, one that's immunosuppression in red, and one that's good, so meaning good anti-tumor immunity in purple. And we find a very great overlap between nerve injury and immunosuppression. And when there's no nerve injury, we found really good presence of anti-tumor immunity. Meaning that, again, it seems that this nerve injury seems to be very bad for anti-tumor immunity. Again, not showing you all the data due to time, but what we found is that during tumor growth, including melanoma, the nerve become injured. They overexpress ATF3, this injury marker. Downstream of this, the nerve will overexpress galanin. We found that galanin actually drive T cell exhaustion, but we also found that the nerve overexpress interferon-1 and IL-6, which then will act on tumor-associated macrophages. So another cool part, the paper was published last year, but what was really cool to see that in the same issue, a different group completely found that also nerve injury was present and seems to be bad for glioblastoma progression. So it seemed that this nerve injury signature, it's pretty constant across tumor type and also perhaps in glioblastoma. So I think I'm out of time here. Just concluding, yeah, I'm just going to stop here, actually. All right. Thank you, guys. I'm going to thank the people that did the work in my lab. Mohamed, Mariam, and Tuani, our collaborator, Alex in Madison, Wisconsin, Moran at MD Anderson, Payver Mir in SUFA, Ronit Rapkin at UPenn, Nicole Schiff at Pitt, Vijay Kuchroo at HMS, Karen Dixon in Basel, and our student, Elisa Pretto. So on this, I'm going to welcome any questions. Sorry to went over a little bit longer. Really interesting talk. Is it true of the liver also, and is it the same mechanism, Ramp1 CGRP? It's a great question. Liver is a bit of a weird organ, actually. We don't see too much sensory neuron innervation in the liver. If you do, actually, I disco, at least I did some of that during my post-doc. I did not see too much sensory neuron innervation in the liver. That said, there's other cells that produce CGRP, so potentially that CGRP Ramp1 could also be present in liver cancer or liver in general. Second question was about Nav1.8 and whether it's another kind of neuron, and does it overlap with the Ramp1 axis? Yeah. So sorry. So Nav1.8 is a classic marker of nociceptor neuron. It labels about 80% of them. And within those Nav1.8 neuron, about 25% are CGRP positive, so the one that would act on Ramp1. So the one that would act on Ramp1 is a smaller subset of the Nav1.8. Thank you. Thank you. Yes. I wanted to write that down. Sorry about that. I hate to open the can of worms of T cell exhaustion- Yep ... but I was curious about your CGRP co-culture and how you defined CD8 T cell exhaustion, if you had a subset or a gene set. Yeah. In our case, we looked at PD-1, Tim-3, like 3 positive, interferon gamma negative, but, I guess, as you said it's a bit of a chemo war. One of the experiment that I liked, I think was the best one to show that it was a B16F10 ova OT1 CD8 T cell co-culture plus minus CGRP, and then that was actually decreasing by 50% the elimination of the cancer cell. So whether it's true exhaustion. So the way we rolled that is effect immuno surveillance, so it's kind of a little bit broader than, I guess, true or absolute exhaustion. Yeah. Quick mechanistic question. ATF3 can be activated through different pathways. Do you have an idea which pathway is responsible in this case? That's a great question. This is something we haven't really looked into. Yeah, I think that's really open to be tested. Yes. Thank you. Sorry. Yep, go for it. Talk about this tumor cells pumping various autoantibody exosomes. Yep. And in this case, the neural tumor cells can also exosomes. Yeah. And did anybody look at them? What are those, are those exact exosomes between the two-way transfer? Yeah, so Payver Mir actually had a Nature Comm paper where she showed that head and neck tumor were innervated because they were secreting exosome, and that was actually driving the innervation. And Moran had a 2021 Nature paper looking at exosome as well in head and neck, but he looked at a subset. It was a microRNA, which I don't remember right now which one it is, but if you look him up, he did look at a specific microRNA. That I'm sorry. Okay, thank you. So I just want to thank the speakers

Auto-generated captions

This transcript is Vimeo auto-generated English. Expect misheard names and technical terms. Use the ripgrep/search approach for exact quotes.

Okay. Thank you everyone, and welcome to this both technology and biology-focused session on spatial and single-cell genomics at scale. And it's really a session focused on, I think you'll see, decoding the ecosystem of tumors. And I think many of you guys will appreciate that there's been a wealth of new technologies that have really recently come to bear on the ability to measure transcripts at scale within tissues. I'm a big science fiction fan, and Arthur C. Clarke has these three laws, and one of them is, "To discover the limits of what's possible, you have to venture into the impossible." And you might be able to tell that many of these technologies that we have, being able to measure the whole transcriptome within cells and tissues would have been maybe impossible to consider just maybe a decade ago. And so it's my pleasure to chair this session and introduce myself. I'm from the Broad, Dana from Sloan Kettering, and then Itay from Weizmann, who will talk about three different aspects of this. And actually, unfortunately, due to some of the geopolitical circumstances, Itay couldn't make it out here, but he pre-recorded his talk. All right. So we'll just dive right in. If I can move... Okay, great. Yeah. So, my lab has really been focused on developing tools and technologies and thinking about what questions we can answer with these technologies, especially with respect to measuring the transcriptome within tumor ecosystems. And one, we've both been interested in the spatial context and the temporal context. And this is going to be clear to many of us, but cells really only make sense in context. For example, this is a zoomed-in H&E image of one cell, and you might be able to see some features. It has this funny-looking nuclei. But really, it isn't until you see it in the context of the tissue, for example, this is the Hodgkin lymphoma's tissue H&E specimen, you might appreciate that it's this large, multi-nucleated cell surrounded by many other cells of the microenvironment. And what we've been doing in genomics for a long time is a little bit like zooming in to that cell and looking at each cell in its individual context. And it's been focused on dissociated cells. And it's only been recently that we've been able to bring the full power of molecular measurements directly within the context of tissues. The other thing I would just say is that these measurements are snapshots. You have to kill the sample, or maybe the sample's already dead, when you make the measurement, and they're destructive snapshots. But in fact, to really understand maybe mechanisms, you might need to understand the progression and the cellular history to understand how we arrived at the present state. For example, this Hodgkin's lymphoma sample might have been a healthy lymph node in the past, but there are some evolution of lineage and exposure that arose this. And we really have also been quite interested in developing tools to measure this cellular history directly in the context of tissue. So I'll touch on both of these in my talk. And we've been building a variety of technologies for bringing genomics to tissues, including ways to measure transcriptomes, genomes, and analysis tools. I won't talk about this. I just want to say one thing. A class of these technologies have been built on these bar-coded arrays. You can see that here. And this is pretty old now. This is something we developed six or seven years ago, actually eight years ago, where we put tissues onto these arrays that have bar-coded beads, and the beads have XY locations that are encoded by DNA barcodes, and RNA or DNA can be captured onto these beads. And then you know where those RNA and DNA came from by the DNA barcodes. And this, obviously, many of you guys have used technologies. Takara has commercialized this under this seeker technology we call the Slide-Seq, and then Visium HD is very similar. But most recently, a couple of years ago, I feel like we've developed a version of this technology that we use regularly, and I want to just briefly touch upon it today, called Slide Tags. And we think it has many advantages. In fact, we think of it as a kind of a universal platform to move any single-cell measurement, whether that is DNA, RNA, epigenomes, directly into the spatial context. And so how does Slide Tags work? It works by using these same bar-coded arrays, but instead of trying to capture the molecules onto the arrays, we invert the process. Now, we put the tissue onto these arrays, and these beads have photo-cleavable DNA barcodes. And then when you cleave these DNA barcodes, they diffuse into the tissue, allowing these barcodes to be associated with the nuclei. And this is a little bit like GPS for cells, because each cell picks up more than one barcode. It picks up a distribution of barcodes nearby. And with that, we can localize the cell with very high precision, actually higher than the 10-micron resolution of the beads. And it's true single-cell resolution. We can encode basically the location of each cell that we sequence with an XY, or the majority of cells we sequence with an XY location. And it's compatible with any single-cell approach. And so a lot of the data that I'll show today is with 10X, either Phi Prime or Flex. And so here you can see this fancy UMAP, where each individual cell in this UMAP, this is from mouse hippocampus, is placed into the context of space. And what does this really give you? Well, one thing is it gives you really high-quality, true single-cell data. You don't have to deal with segmentation or other sorts of things thatLike result in mixing of cells. And actually, this is comparisons between single-cell RNA-seq or single-nucleus RNA-seq and Slide-Tags, and you can see the cell type proportions, the number of molecules, which is in the thousands, and the counts are all the same. And most importantly, this technology has been commercialized by Tecan Tecara. I don't have any financial interest into Tecara, but they licensed the technology, and they've made it compatible with FFP through 10x Flex. And we've just been consistently very impressed by the data from this Flex in this spatial tagging of FFP samples. Here is a melanoma specimen. And on the exact same paired specimen, we ran it on Visium HD, and you can here see the median UMIs per cell, and genes per cell, for the single-cell technology versus, well, Flex versus Visium HD. And I think you can really appreciate that the true single-cell resolution in combination with molecular resolution gives you much, much better separation between cell types and states. That's all I'll say about the technology. We've been using this as a workhorse and it's readily available for you all. And so, I think a question that many of us, and you'll see in this series of talks we'll try to answer is, how are tumor cells and immune cells organized and shaped by their microenvironment? We're quite interested in how cell-intrinsic states are shaped by their neighborhood and the niche of the cells that they live in. And for example, tumor cells obviously have some dynamic evolution through the course of the tumor, whether that's genomic evolution through genetic and epigenetic means, as well as transcriptomic adaptations to their local environment. And that evolution is actually, through the course of the tumor, is in some equilibrium with the environment, right? It's driven in many part by the immune cells and stromal cells. And many of you guys here know this and are appreciative of this because it's very therapeutically relevant. Because many of our ways of modulating the immune system actually needs to take advantage of what our understanding of this equilibrium and evolution. Also targeted therapies as well. And so for example, response to checkpoint blockade in melanoma is highly bimodal, and it's really unclear what drives this bimodality. We speculate it is something to do with the immune microenvironment. There are many papers around it. But how do we actually understand if cell states within the cancer are associated with the microenvironment? And so we've been looking at spatial niches within the melanoma microenvironment, in particular in metastatic melanoma, using Slide-Tags. We actually did this in our original Slide-Tags paper. I'll show you one tissue as an example, and then I'll generalize these observations over many samples. So here is one of our first Slide Tag specimens on a melanoma. You can see there are these two histological regions of the tumor. And when you perform single-cell RNA-seq, here is the UMAP. You can see very fine-grained resolution of cell states, and then you can place the majority of these cells back into space here. And actually, if you just look at, this is tumor cells, you can see that they adopt a couple of transcriptionally distinct states that are also spatially distinct. And actually, these distinct transcriptional states, they turned out to actually also have kind of different CNVs that represent different evolutionary histories of these two clones, and they have very distinct cellular neighborhoods. Here's just a very, very simple analysis where blue represents the kind of depletion of cell types in the local microenvironment, while red represents the enrichment. And you can see generally, tumor cells in state one are relatively depleted in immune cells in their neighborhood, and then there's a particular enrichment in T cells in tumor cells with state two. And actually, you can go and use, here we used 10x Phi Prime to map the TCR sequences in single cell, but now we have the spatial localizations of those TCR sequences. And you can see here this particular T cell clone that's actually driving this enrichment to state two and depletion in state one. Here, the gray represents all T cells in this spatial context, and purple represents this particular clone. And you can, without any statistics, you can just see by eye that there's this strong tumor state and T cell clone association. So what's driving both this clone dependence and this T cell depletion? And we had a couple theories, one of which is that melanoma dedifferentiates during the course of progression, and as along to this more mesenchymal-like or neural crest-like phenotype. And along the way, then it can lose both its endogenous antigens or maybe it can drive a more immunosuppressive niche. And you can kind of already see that in the H&E. And this is something that clinicians see all the time that melanomas are often pigmented before treatment, but during treatment they lose their pigment. But in this particular sample, you can see that the two lobes, histological lobes of this metastasis actually have differential pigmentation. And indeed, when you look at just the transcriptome scoring for these mesenchymal-like states, you see this difference where tumor one has adopted this more mesenchymal-like state and lost endogenous antigens. And so, this is just one sample. We've then have been systematically profiling many metastatic biopsies, 27 or approximately 30 so far actually now. And I'm skipping a lot of the analysis and data, and I just want to show you two highlights for what we see. One is that this dedifferentiation trajectory actually promote different niches correlated with the cancer cell state. Here you can see-On the rows of this heat map, different states of tumor cells, whether they're melanocytic or this neural crest transitory phenotype, and I haven't shown the fully undifferentiated here. But in particular, we observe that the neural crest transitory state is strongly associated with a particular immune suppressive neighborhood consisted of this SPP1 positive macrophage and this fibroblast that's post-N positive. So this is an immunosuppressive macrophage population, and then a tumor-associated fibroblast population. And association with this is exactly anti-correlated with many, basically effector CD8 T cells and also associated macrophage populations that we term an immune effector population. And when you're next to an immune effector population, we see that the cancer cells generally actually are interferon stimulated and dying. So, basically de-differentiation to this neural crest state causes this association with this immunosuppressive niche that also is anti-correlated with the effector status. And actually, not only is it anti-correlated with these cell types, the T cell clones are suppressed in the niche associated with SPP1 max and post-N fibroblasts. So, in those niches, if you look at T cell clonality, most T cells are singletons, or many more are singletons versus inside of this effector niche, many more are expanded, meaning they're dividing. Okay. And so what's going on with this? Well, we know SPP1 is one of these wound-associated macrophage factors, and it's probably a wound-healing program that also suppresses the local immune response. And we did some functional interrogation of... These are secreted factors, right? So post-N is a secreted factor from this fibroblast. As you could see, we really have, again, there's asynchrony, so this is not a perfect thing, but you could really see that within the asynchrony, we're capturing a temporal cascade. And we could ask what, again, are the big things that are changing along this temporal cascade? We see the cancer cells are expressing all sorts of chemokines, these stress chemokines, these interferon-induced chemokines, and importantly, this is exactly what the lymphocytes are trained to sense. The lymphocytes, the NK cells, and the T cells have the receptors for exactly these chemokines, and they emit the interferon signature. And interferon gamma really hypercharges this entire thing, really bringing in the T cells and the NK cells. So now, Thomas didn't want to stop there. It's like, let's push our functional mice even crazier. So I don't know how to explain this crazy cassette, but Thomas is back there, so don't ask me questions about this. But I know what it can do for me, and what it can do is my dream. It can take the basal cell and do a CRISPR for a specific gene just in the basal cell. So we're taking in vivo, and we're saying let's limit ourselves to that 4% of basal cells and remove CSF2 just from that 4% of cells in vivo inside a tissue. And lo and behold, this phenocopies the entire basal ablation phenotype. So just CRISPRing out CSF2 just in the basal cells phenocopies collapsing and killing the basal cells. And lo and behold, we have suddenly CD3s coming in if we remove this CSF2 signal and just remove that specific signal from the basal cells, collapsing the tumor by either removing the basal cells or disrupting their CSF signaling, that really builds this immunosuppressive niche. So our model is this basal cell, the master architect of the tumor niche, that PDAC is so well known for, and that pushes all therapy away. It calls the proliferative MYCAFs that really protect it, the fibrotic one, the immunosuppressive myeloid cells, and T cells cannot enter. The basal cell goes away, the immunosuppressive niche goes away, and in come these hero lymphocytes to clear the tumor. And so across both early and late disease, malignancy is really sustained by these plastic states. The oncogenes tumor charge the plasticity, but it's really the plastic states that organize and maintain the tumor ecosystem that makes cancer the nasty thing it is. So finally, acknowledgments. The first story was Jose and Scott. Andrew built SEGER, and I recommend you use it. Doron built Wormhole, and we're using it, and we love it. Sam did the computation in my lab with the amazing team from Thomas's lab, and Sail in our lab really helps collect all this amazing data. And thank you. Hi there. Impressive methods and results. So I have one question about the cellular neighborhood map you're showing, the latent plots where you mention one dot is one cellular neighborhood. Mm-hmm. So I have a two-part question. First is that how is each dot being... So like for example, for a cell neighborhood, are you separating, for example, 100 cells, grouping 100 cells, and then call that as a cell neighborhood? Or are you looking at one cell and the 100 cells around it to be considered as a neighborhood? Yeah. One cell and 100 cells around it. And I'm not collapsing at the cell type, so I'm basically imagine having a matrix. Mm. A little sub-matrix of 100 cells-By all their transcripts, so 100 cells by 480 transcripts. There's a little bit of collapsing to gene programs, but 100 cells by their rich gene expression, a little mini matrix. And as I showed in the wormhole algorithm, we are reasoning about that entire unit at once without losing the information. Yes. So in that case, if two cells are similar or close to each other, will those two, the neighborhood overlapping then? So the neighborhood, yes, there is some overlapping features in these neighborhoods, but that gives robust statistical signal. As people who've used spatial transcriptomics knows, these things are very sparse. So actually having many similar units gives a little bit more robustness. But yes, this is not completely disassociated neighborhoods. But basically, we have an anchor cell, and much of our analysis, we actually reason about, here is the anchor cell, here's its neighborhood. And of course, many of these neighborhoods overlap because, just the math of it. Got you. Thank you. Hey, Donna. A very interesting talk. I had a question about the wormhole data you showed on the gastric tissues, where you estimated the progenitor cells and the more differentiated cells. So differentiated cells were more in the ducts, the circular structures. But the progenitor cells were in the ducts, and they were also out in the stromal areas. And so I was wondering what you thought about those distributions. So again, I discretized it and said progenitor and gastric because unlike computers that can learn complex functions, we're humans, and I can't say in one word, "Here is all the continuum of cell states." But within the progenitor cells and within the gastric cells, there's a very rich variation, and that's why I'm really pushing for this continuous representation. And we learn a lot from the continuous representation. And we actually played a bit, and we said, "What happens if we discretize the data to progenitor cells and gastric cells?" And that doesn't cut it. You really need this continuum, and I just can't talk continuum, so I give it names. Okay. Hi. Really great talk. And just to, a little bit of clarification, when you present a matrix for the niches, you said only the rows are permutated, right? Yeah. So would it be helpful to consider the SVD-based methods to do the reduction instead of doing optimal transport? Well, again, any way you try and collapse it-- And you could do SVD with inside each row, but if you try and do SVD for the entire matrix, you lose the cell identities. Anything that sort of averages across cell identities and collapses and says, "Okay, let's take an average of a myeloid cell, a fibroblast, and a T cell," there's some people in this audience which would not be happy if I tried to do that. Thank you so much. Hi. I was just curious if you had benchmarked SEGER against other transcript-aware methods like PROSEG, for example. We've benchmarked it like crazy. I want to give you the intuition. And so one, in performance, it performs better by the metrics you care. But also, PROSEG, for example, it's the second best. It still tries to solve a geometric problem. It still tries to find a boundary. So you look at the PROSEG cell membranes, and you have all these deep notches that goes like this to try and avoid including transcripts in these-- It looks like a macrophage that's just trying to pull this thing to pull that transcript. It's really psychopathically shaped. And PROSEG is pretty good because it actually uses a lot of very similar reasoning to us about learning cell states and what genes go together, but it still insists on drawing a boundary. And we just say forget the boundary, assign transcripts to cells as link assignment, and that's our big difference. But actually, PROSEG works really well. We work better, but PROSEG gets a lot of good marks, except for the fact that it has psychopathically shaped cells. Hi there, and thank you very much for your talk. Always inspirational. So my question is a bit naive maybe, so apologies for this. I really like this concept of working in this embedding space with niches, no longer cells. So I was wondering, if we want to go from cells to patients, does it make sense to think in the embedding space for patients where we start even to use the geometry and do some clustering according to these common niches, to ways that these patients possibly get together, not in the canonical imagination that we have at the single biomarker level? So I'll give a quick answer to that, even though I have a longer answer because Faye is trying to pull me off the stage. Multiscale is the answer. You have small niches, you have entire lesions, you have entire tissues, and you have entire humans. And I think the way we need to build embeddings is these multiscale thing where you also have an embedding at the level of a patient-- But this patient is a multiscale embedding that you could go deep into finer and finer spatial resolution. We're working on that, but not quite ready with that. Thank you. Thank you. And last but not least, we have Itay Tirosh joining us from virtually. And he's going to talk about spatial transcriptomes and single-cell transcriptomes in head and neck cancer. And he's very sad that he can't make it today, but due to the geopolitical climate. Hi, my name is Itay Tirosh, and first I want to apologize that I was unable to come to San Diego and present this in person. But I want to thank the organizers for both inviting me and for the flexibility to allow me to record this talk. So I will tell you about our work on using spatial approaches to understand the organization of tumors, both in glioma and in head and neck cancer. And we are generally quite interested in the diversity of cells within tumors, trying to understand the entire ecosystem, but in particular, we are focused on the states of the cancer cells. And after doing a lot of single-cell RNAseq analysis to define those states, we've been working in the last few years to better understand how these cells are organized in the tumor. This allows us to better understand what generates the different states and perhaps also to start to understand their functions. And we are using two main technologies. The first one is Visium, spatial transcriptomics. Here we have a glass slide in which each spot has its own unique barcode. And this is producing very good data, and we learned a lot from it. But of course, one important challenge is that the size of the spots is still 55 microns in the first version, which means that in a given spot, we have somewhere between 5 to 20 cells. So understanding the pattern within a spot is still quite challenging. The second technology that we've been using is spatial proteomics, the CODEX platform, also known as PhenoCycler, and this is highly complementary to the Visium, both because it gives us the protein information, but also because this produces a real single-cell resolution. Now, this is antibody-based, and so we've constructed a specific antibody panel for glioma, as you see here, as well as another panel for carcinoma. And we've been using both of these technologies to understand the organization of both gliomas and head and neck cancers. And I'll start with glioblastoma. So in glioblastoma, our single-cell analysis in the past have shown that in a given tumor, there's typically four different states of cancer cells. And many of the cells are somewhere in the middle, but the diversity is really captured by these four different cell states. And these cell states recapitulate many patterns from development of the brain. So some of the cells, one state resembles neural progenitors, another resembles oligodendrocytes progenitors, a third state resembles astrocytes as well as their progenitors, and finally, we have a state that resembles mesenchymal-like cells, and this is the state that is the most responsive to the microenvironment. So we've shown in the past that this mesenchymal-like state can be induced by macrophages as well as by hypoxia. And when we see cells in a mesenchymal state that also express many hypoxia response markers, we call this mesenchymal hypoxia, and we know that this indicates that the cells are in hypoxic regions. So we recently applied Visium as well as CODEX to 32 glioblastoma samples, and here you see two of them. In this data, we can identify all of the major expression programs that we saw in the single-cell data. So you can see on the left all of the programs that we defined. The bold ones correspond to the cancer cell states, and the others correspond to the microenvironment. And we can assign each spot in the Visium to the main signal that we see in that spot, and this is how two of those tumors look like. But of course, there was still this challenge with the resolution of the spots. So each spot contains approximately 10 cells, and we wanted to better understand what is happening within those spots. So to address this, we went into the CODEX data to see what happens within a given spot. And what we saw is that even though a typical spot is indeed a combination of multiple cell states or cell types, typically, and more specifically in 64% of the spots, we see that one cell state or one cell type controls the vast majority of the cells in a given spot. So the Visium data still gives us a good amount of information about the main signal in a given spot, which is often sufficient to really understand the organization of the tumor. This also tells us a lot about the biology of glioma, that the cells are really clustering together. And we wanted to better understand to what degree the cells are clustering, not just within one specific spot, but in larger areas than that. So we expanded from analyzing individual spots to looking at adjacent spots, and we defined this measure of spatial coherence, which is basically asking, after we assign each spot to the dominant state, how many of the neighboring spot for one specific spot are still dominated by the same state? So we see variation in spatial coherence between different cell states, for example, higher coherence for this mesenchymal hypoxia state in yellow. We see variation between different regions of the same sample, and we see a lot of variability between different samples. And surprisingly, this was actually the strongest effect that we saw. So there were some samples in which overall, we saw high spatial coherence. So almost wherever you look in this particular sample, you see that spots are surrounded by other spots, often with the same color. This is what we call a structured sample. And in other samples, we see very limited spatial coherence. This is what we call a disorganized sample.And overall, we could divide the vast majority of the samples to either mostly structural or mostly disorganized, and there were very few cases that showed both of these behaviors within one sample. So we next wanted to better understand what is creating this dichotomy of structured versus disorganized. And the main difference that we saw between those samples was, again, the presence of this mesenchymal hypoxia state. And this suggests that whenever we have a high degree of hypoxia, not only the immediate cells in that region are affected and express this mesenchymal hypoxia state, but also the entire tissue becomes more organized, suggesting that hypoxia might have a long-range effect on the organization of the tissue. So to better understand the organization that emerges in these cases, we next asked what was the colocalization between pairs of cell states or cell types. So in this graph, each node is a cell state or a cell type, and the edges corresponds to a significant degree of colocalization across all of the data sets. And as you can see, this analysis divides all the cell states and cell types into five different groups or five different layers, such that all the edges are either within a given layer or between adjacent layers. And this, again, is consistent with the role of hypoxia in organizing the tissue. So the first layer is where we see the actual mesenchymal hypoxia spots and also the necrotic spots, the necrotic regions. The second layer corresponds to other mesenchymal states and inflammatory macrophages that are adjacent to the hypoxic regions. Then in the third layer, we see a lot of vascular cells, macrophages that secrete VEGF, and so this appears to be the layer that is trying to resolve the hypoxia. And then in the fourth layer, we see many more of the cancer cells in a neurodevelopmental state that is presumably more dependent on oxygen. Finally, in the fifth layer, the furthest away from the hypoxia, we begin to see the infiltration of the tumor to the normal brain, where there are many normal brain parenchymal cells, like oligodendrocytes, astrocytes, and neurons. So this suggests a model for the organization of GBM that consists of five different layers. Of course, we are not suggesting that they are very clean layer. It's more of a probabilistic shift in the abundance of different cell types and cell states. And here you see an example of this from the Codex data, where we start in the left from a region that is highly hypoxic with this mesenchymal hypoxia state. And then gradually, we see more of the other mesenchymal state, macrophages, vascular cells, and towards the end, we begin to see more of the neurodevelopmental cell states and the normal cells. So overall, what we see is that in GBM, there are many regions that are quite disorganized, but as we get close to the hypoxic regions, we begin to see more structure emerging, both in terms of cells being surrounded by cells that are similar to them, as well as this approximate structure of five different layers. So this work in GBM was already published, and after finishing this, we began to look at the second major type of glioma, which are IDH mutant glioma. And so we profiled both by Codex and by Visium, 34 IDH mutant samples covering both astrocytomas and oligodendrogliomas of different grades. And when we analyze the degree of structure in those samples, we see that there's overall less structure in the IDH mutant cases than in the GBMs, and there is more structure in the high-grade cases, which are more similar to GBM compared to the mid-grade cases. So this is still very consistent with the role of hypoxia, because hypoxia occurs mostly in the high-grade cases. And so far, this is quite consistent with what we saw in the GBM work. But what then surprised us is that when we looked at low-grade cases, we saw much more structure than the mid-grade and even the high-grade cases. And in the low-grade cases, there was almost no hypoxia and almost no necrosis, suggesting that something else is driving the organization of these samples. So in high-grade IDH mutant glioma, as well as in GBM, we see these approximate layers in which, as you can see in the bottom, the tumor really consists of these small patches that are dominated by specific cell states or cell types. In mid-grade cases, we begin to lose this organization. There is still some degree of organization, but much lower. And then in the low-grade cases, again, we see more structure, but it's not the same structure. We don't see again those patches. Rather, we see pairs of cell states that are correlated in their localization. So there's a different type of structure, and we are trying to understand what is driving this structure, which it probably not hypoxia. And what we are starting to see is that in those low-grade cases, the normal structures of the brain are still maintained to a large degree. These normal structures have been eroded in the high-grade cases, but in low-grade, they are still there, and they appear to influence the organization of the tumor. And I'm going to show you one example of this, which is the division of the tumor to white matter, gray matter, and the junction between them. So the normal brain is divided into white and gray matter, as well as other regions. And in the tumor, we can still see that division quite nicely in the case of low-grade tumors.Not only do we see white and gray matter, we also see a very sharp junction that separates them. And the fact that this is such a clean and sharp structure suggests that this has been maintained despite the growth of the tumor. So next, we wanted to see how this influences the cells around that junction. So we counted the number of cells moving from the white matter through the junction and to the gray matter, and we saw that this actually serves as a barrier for the growth of the tumor. So the density of cells drops dramatically as we switch from the white matter to the gray matter. And this was surprising for us to see because in the context of glioma, we normally think about tumors that diffuse in the brain and that expand almost with no interruption. And here we see that this junction between white and gray matter is in fact a barrier for the growth of the tumor. So not only the overall density of cells dropped at this junction, but also the fraction of cells that are malignant further dropped, suggesting that this is really stopping the growth of the tumor. At the same time, there are changes in the microenvironment. We see, of course, many more neurons in the gray matter, and we see almost no macrophages as we pass from the white matter to the gray matter. We can go deeper into this and ask not just about the overall amount of malignant cells, but about the specific states of the malignant cells. And we see that as we go through the junction, we see an enrichment of OPC-like cells, a further depletion of astrocyte-like cells. And just around the junction, we see some enrichment of undifferentiated cells. And even for the state that is enriched after the junction, the OPC-like cells, we can go deeper into this and look at specific markers, and we see that almost all of them are changing significantly. So even for a given cell state, we see more subtle changes in the degree of differentiation as cells move from the white matter to the gray matter. And so to summarize the analysis in glioma, we see two different behaviors. We see in high-grade cases, as well as in GBM, that hypoxia and necrosis appear to organize the tumor. But in low-grade cases where there is almost no hypoxia and necrosis, it seems like residual brain parenchymal structures are organizing the tumor. And specifically, this junction between the white and gray matter serves as a barrier for the growth of the tumor. And around this barrier we see significant changes in the composition of cell types and cell states, and specifically the OPC-like cells are the ones that appear to be most capable of migrating along this border, which is very consistent with the ability of OPC-like cells to migrate during development. So now I want to switch from glioma to head and neck cancer. So also in head and neck cancer, we see specific cell states that are commonly observed in many tumors. Here I'm showing just one tumor as an example. These main cell states include cell cycle related states, stress states, states reflecting epithelial differentiation and senescence. And one state that I'm going to come back to because it's particularly important clinically is a state that resembles epithelial to mesenchymal transition with dementin, podoplanin, TGF-beta responsive genes, and others. Now, this is a very partial form of EMT. The cells do not lose expression of epithelial markers. They also do not gain expression of canonical EMT factors like SNAI, ZEB, and Twist. But this partial EMT is still associated with metastasis as well as with poor overall survival. So we applied Visium as well as Codex to 28 head and neck cancer samples covering different sites and different genetic classes. And again, with the Visium data, we are able to identify all of the main patterns that we expect to see in those tumors directly from the Visium data. We divide the spots into the malignant spots, those where we see a strong signal for chromosomal aberrations, and to the non-malignant spots where we don't see this signal. And again, overall, we see high consistency between the single-cell data and the spatial data. But there was one interesting exception, which is that in the malignant spots, we see a program that we call the inflammatory response that consists primarily of genes that are often cytokines and chemokines that we know from the single-cell data are expressed not by the cancer cells, but actually by myeloid cells, either macrophages or neutrophils. So this indicates, and we can validate this with the Codex data, that there is a strong colocalization of cancer cells with myeloid cells that are active and produce many cytokines and chemokines. And I will get back to this program later on. So next, we wanted to better understand the organization of head and neck tumors. So again, we asked about the colocalization of these different cell states and cell types. And what we saw, unlike glioma, is a global division into immune-rich compartments, stromal-rich compartment, and cancer-rich compartment. Again, with this exception of inflammatory response of myeloid cells embedded in the region that is mostly cancer-rich. And next, we wanted to better understand the organization within the cancer compartment. So we defined another analysis that we called a zonation analysis.In this case, every spot that is dominated by immuno stromal cells is considered in the non-epithelial zone. After that, all the spots that are dominated by cancer cells but are bordering the non-epithelial zone are considered as the tumor edge. The spots that are dominated by cancer cells and that then border the tumor edge are the mid-tumor. And finally, the spots dominated by cancer cells that are only bordering the mid-tumor are called the core of the tumor. And so basically, we are dividing all the spots based on how far away they are from the stromal regions. And here you see an example of how it applies to one specific tumor. So we apply this to all of the tumors, and then we can ask for every cell state, how is it distributed across these different zones. And I'm going to focus on the analysis of this partial EMT that I highlighted a few slides ago. So here you see in black the overall pattern of partial EMT across all samples, and the thinner lines in the background correspond to individual tumors. So you can see that the average pattern doesn't really reflect what's happening in individual tumors. And the individual tumors can actually be separated into two main patterns. In some samples, we see EMT enriched at the edge of the tumor, and this is consistent with a lot of literature about EMT. But then in other samples, we see EMT mostly enriched at the core of the tumor. And we could validate this by staining for LAMC2, which is a top marker for this partial EMT program. And importantly, when we analyze multiple samples of the same tumor, we see that this result is highly consistent. If a tumor has EMT at the edge in one sample, it's usually going to have the same pattern in other samples of the same tumor. So this suggests that we are seeing two different subtypes of tumors. And so we asked what else is different between them. And some of the main differences that we saw include more lymphocytes in tumors with EMT at the edge and more of this inflammatory response, more of these myeloid cells in tumors where EMT is at the core of the tumor. And this suggests that perhaps this inflammatory response might be inducing partial EMT at the core of the tumor. So to ask this, we went back to this colocalization analysis, but now we cleaned each of the edges based on whether this colocalization is seen in all samples or whether it's seen only in cases where EMT is at the core or at the edge. And what we see is that partial EMT actually has two opposing interactions. When the EMT is located at the edge of the tumor, it's colocalized with the fibroblast, as you see with the yellow edge. And when partial EMT is located at the core of the tumor, it's instead colocalized with this inflammatory response. And this suggests that there might be two different mechanisms for microenvironment-based induction of partial EMT. And we search for potential ligand receptor interaction that might explain this. The top prediction from the fibroblast was TGF-beta, which is, of course, a well-known inducer of partial EMT. And for the inflammatory response, the top prediction was oncostatin M. So next, we treated two different head and neck cancer cell lines with both oncostatin M and TGF-beta. And we saw that both of these cytokines indeed are able to induce many of the partial EMT genes. Now, TGF-beta was more effectively inducing partial EMT in this in vitro analysis. But in vivo, we see the same partial EMT program when it's at the core and at the edge, suggesting that perhaps there are other mechanism and that there is convergence to the same partial EMT program. So to summarize, we see in head and neck cancer a global division to immune-rich, stroma-rich, and cancer-rich compartment with this exception of myeloid cells in the cancer-rich compartment. We see two main patterns of partial EMT. At the edge, it seems to be induced by fibroblasts, and at the core of the tumor, we believe that this might be induced by the myeloid cells and specifically by oncostatin M. And in those cases, we see an even lower amount of T cells and B cells, suggesting that perhaps EMT at the core of the tumor might have a stronger effect of immunosuppression. So right now we are trying to better understand what determines the separation into patients with EMT at the edge and those with EMT at the core, and whether that would have any clinical implications. For example, it's easy to imagine that EMT at the core might have a stronger immunosuppressive effect, going back to what I mentioned about lower amount of lymphocytes. And perhaps EMT at the edge might be more clearly linked to invasion and metastasis. So this is some of the questions that we are trying to answer now. So finally, I want to thank everyone that contributed to this work. In my lab, the glioma work was led by Alisa, Reuven, and Noam, and this was a great collaboration with Mario Suva's lab and specifically with Chris Mount. And the work on head and neck cancer was led by Dor Simkin in my lab, together with Sid Pouram's lab and specifically with Tom Barrett. And thank you again for listening. All right. Thank you. Well, I guess you can email your questions to Yitai, and thank you for joining this session.

Our program is about to begin. The AACR Annual Meeting is the focal point of the cancer research community, where attendees gather to share the latest advances in cancer science and medicine. With the theme of Precision. Partnership. Purpose.: Advancing Cancer Science to Save Lives Globally, the AACR Annual Meeting highlights the work of the best minds in cancer research from around the world. Welcome to San Diego. Good morning. Welcome everybody to our early morning plenary session on artificial intelligence. Thank you very much for coming. Please join us. There's plenty of free space over here. My name is Jakov Catsa. I'm an oncologist and I'm doing AI research in Germany, and I was part of this year's AACR scientific committee, responsible for some of the AI content. We've had tremendous artificial intelligence content at this conference, and this is our crown jewel. This session here is where we are presenting some of the most exciting advancements in artificial intelligence. So before I call the first speaker here on the stage to join me, I'm going to present you with a very short introduction on the topics that we are going to cover here today. These are my disclosures, and I just have one slide here to outline the evolution of the artificial intelligence techniques as they are applied to cancer research, as they have evolved over the last decades. Many years ago, in the 2000s, we already had methods that we now call classical machine learning methods. These methods allow us to analyze structured data, tabular data, features that we extracted from images. But for complex data such as image data, we needed more capable methods. So in the 2010s, deep learning came along and allowed us to really extract patterns from more complex data. And this was supercharged by the advent of another technology, foundation models, just a couple of years ago, whereby you have a large data set, you can train a big model one time on this large heterogeneous data set, and then you can repurpose it for many downstream tasks. Another type of foundation model is large language model, the technology that powers all of the chatbots that everybody's using. But one of the most exciting applications of large language models is that they can reason about complex procedures, and this enables us to build AI agents around them that can solve complex procedures. So the two technologies that we will focus on in this session from a technological point of view is foundation models and AI agents. And here's just a bit of terminology on these. Foundation models are trained on large amounts of data, and their purpose is to provide you with embeddings of the data, so compressed representations of the data by which you can solve many downstream tasks. Agents can be single-agent systems or multi-agent systems that help us solve complex multi-step procedures. And of course, you can put both of these technologies together, and have agents that use foundation models as tools that can really do great things, as we will see in the upcoming talks. So thank you very much. This was my short introduction, and now I'm very pleased to introduce our first speaker. Our first speaker is Dr. Jure Leskovec. He's a computer scientist and a professor at Stanford University. His team was a pioneer about AI agents applied to biomedicine, specifically in cancer research. Jure's team published Bi Omni, which was the first and the most widely used collection of tools for AI agents in biology, and these tools are where the magic happens and where agents get the capabilities to solve problems in cancer research. So without further ado, let me welcome Dr. Leskovec here on the stage. Thank you very much. Good morning. So I'm here today very excited to talk to you about what's new in AI and in particular, what is new in agentic AI. What I'll talk about is how do we go from AI as chat agents like ChatGPT that everyone here knows, but really think about developing copilots and co-scientists that allow us to do science better, faster, and more reliably. If we think about scientific discovery, it really drives the civilization forward. Not only drug diagnosis and clinical diagnosis and drug discovery, but also agriculture, manufacturing, health, and so on. And all these are extremely complex processes that require super advanced and sophisticated human teams. And really, if you think about it, the pace of discovery is limited by our human bandwidth. There are petabytes of new data that is left unanalyzed. Scientists have many ideas, but it takes them time to test them out. So really, we are limited by our ability to analyze this data, act on our hypothesis, and test them out. So the question is: how can we close this gap? How can we fulfill this gap that is opening between the demand for discovery and the supply of human experts that we are able to provide?So the goal for this talk is for me to walk you through our research journey on developing an AI agent that helps us to simulate and scale the scientific discovery process. So this is about building a co-scientist, a partner to a human researcher that allows the human scientists to make progress faster and speed up the rate of discovery. What I want to contrast this with is the advanced AI tools that have been recently developed. So we are not talking perhaps about a model or a tool that somebody can use, but we are actually talking about an agent, a co-scientist, an active partner in research that helps us plan, act, debug our experiments, verify them, and also iterate. That we go from observations to hypothesis to experimental validation of those hypotheses. And we close this loop and we can run it faster, more reliably, and with greater transparency. So the goal is to speed up scientific discovery dramatically. Create a virtual scientist that helps us automate scientific research, suggest and explore novel hypothesis, perform tasks much faster, and importantly, tackle many tasks at the same time. So really parallelize and speed up the entire discovery loop. And if we look at how scientists do research and discovery today, how we work, it's actually extremely fragmented.
