So these models were made publicly available and have been downloaded over four million times and have been used at this point in over 2,000 different studies. So this really accelerated the utility of these models show that how important self-supervision is and how important representing data into meaningful representations can be. So these studies were focusing on representing... regions of pathology slides, but we also wanted to scale this to the entire slide. So last year we published Titan, which is a foundation model that focuses on representing the entirety of a whole slide image into a singular vector or representation. And this used a number of different bells and whistles, including iBOT-based training and using what's commonly used for training large language models, where we train short and test long, and train on a limited region of the slide and testing on a large region of the slide. But we also used additional layers of training, which includes using text, both from the report and a generative model that had been developed in our group. And we tried to show that we can improve slide level representations in contrast with some of the other foundation models that were out there. Also, we assessed what the scaling laws looked like. And as our models are getting better, our benchmarks are also getting more complex and difficult because all of the problems that we were trying to target back in 2024, these models already perform almost perfectly on those tasks. So we tried to represent the whole slide, and we made these models publicly available as well. But text is a very subjective modality, so we also wanted to explore that can we contrast with additional modalities such that it will improve image representation? And there's a lot of more objective information about these cases that we have available to us. So we started contrasting with molecular information. We started by looking at IHCs, contrasting with IHCs to see if the representation would improve, and then doing the same with molecular data or transcriptomics in a really toy-based setting. So this is just by using the TCGA. And we showed that you could really improve few-shot performance quite a lot. That means using very, very few labels or very, very few samples for training these models, and still converging to a clinically useful result. So this was early indication that this is an approach that we should scale, and that's where we started to develop Threads, which is a model that uses all of the molecular data that was available to us at MGB as well as at Dana-Farber, where we tried to contrast between H&E images and corresponding molecular data. To improve representation, we showed that you could focus on or target more difficult problems like treatment response prediction directly from the histology slide. So this is a study that will come out in the coming months, and we do have plans to make this model publicly available as well. We also try to expand this to spatial proteomic data. So this is a model for spatial proteomics that we developed in the group using large amounts of data and self-supervision. The goal is the same. Can we represent proteomic data into meaningful representations that can then be used for a host of different downstream tasks? This includes tissue phenotyping, looking at artifact classification and so forth, but also using it as a search engine to retrieve similar regions within spatial proteomic data, as well as for spatial biomarker discovery. So we have an earlier version of this model that was already made available, and if people would like to get access to the newer version of the model, there's a QR code that you can use to sign up for the new version that will be coming out. And my colleague, Shizun, will be giving a talk about this, and we also have a poster on this foundation model, and hopefully the study will also come out later this year. But as we have continued to develop these models, we started by looking at regions within a pathology slide, which we tried to contrast with other modalities to improve image representation. We scaled it to the entirety of the slide, and then we can represent the whole slide. But something that we've been trying to do for the past three years or so is trying to represent the entire patient. So now it's commonly referred to as virtual patient representation, but at the time, we just called it representing the entire patient's record. The goal was that can we use everything digital that we have about the patient and represent the patient into a singular vector that can then be used for a lot of different downstream applications? And these applications can be predictive. They can be related to diagnosis, prognosis, treatment response prediction, next event prediction, hospital operations. But just having something that represents the patient into a meaningful representation would be incredibly valuable. And we wanted this to be dynamic and continuously updating because we have a lot of information about the patient at any given point in time, but that information also continues to evolve as we get more and more data into the system. So we used all of the data that was available to us at Mass General Brigham. This includes about 12 hospitals, and this is data from about 7.2 million patients that were used to develop this model, and it has about 18 different modalities. And the goal is that as more and more data will become available about the patient, we will represent it into a singular vector or singular representation for that patient. So the representation would evolve over time, and we'll also have a patient trajectory as to how the patient and its representation evolves. So once we have this representation, we can look at risks, predictions, similarity searching, statistical analysis, other kinds of treatment response predictions. So the single vector would be incredibly useful for us, right? So these are all downstream tasks or applications that we can potentially look at. But once we have these representations, we can look at how the different concepts in medicine cluster together. This is a very nice plot where we have an entire atlas of medicine being learned on its own from these representations. And you can look at the fact that particularontologies that we know from literature all clustered together, even though they were not given to the model during training. The model is unaware of all the literature that we have about these different ontologies, and yet it manages to cluster these ontologies all together. And then you can also go in and study different relationships that exist across modalities. These are all ways to see how rich these representations are and how meaningful representations does the model learn? We can also look at individual embeddings. So in this case, each dot represents the embedding of the entire patient, or everything that we know about the patient, including structured and unstructured data, and it's colored by age. And then once you have these embeddings and these representations, you're also able to look for similar patients. So in an entire record, in a large record, are you able to find similar patients? Because similarity search or patient matching is a problem that can solve a lot of issues that we have, both in oncology and in medicine in general. This includes looking at patients who might respond to a clinical trial, looking at rare disease diagnosis, and so forth. So here we have examples for how well the model does in finding similar patients, and here's some examples for oncology, and we have a baseline that's for the last progress note. So just embedding the last progress note versus embedding the entire patient's record. We can do similarity search based on text. So we can use text to find if there's a similar patient in the entire record, or we can also use other modalities. Because it's a multimodal model, you can start with an image or text or any other modality to see whether you'll be able to find any similar patients. And there's also a score for how similar the corresponding patient might be. So obviously, this model is very new, and we're still exploring what the capabilities of the model are, but image search is definitely, or patient search is definitely one of those applications that we are very interested in and we continue to devote a lot of effort towards. We can also look at preclinical evidence. So I think one of the basic promises of machine learning and medicine is early diagnosis. And we've seen a host of different studies over the past five years showing that you can use all these different auxiliary modalities to predict disease risk. For example, looking at retinal images, you can predict cardiovascular and cancer risk and so forth. And so in this case, what we have is that we have 18 different modalities all merged into a singular vector or a representation for the patient, and then we use that representation in a more supervised problem downstream to try to see if we were able to predict those diseases early on. And for many of these diseases, we do see that we can predict them earlier. We can also look at disease progression, and trying to see what the progression of the disease would be. The baseline here is just an age, sex baseline, so a very simplistic baseline. But we show that using this representation that includes both structured and unstructured data, you can improve both early diagnosis of disease as well as disease progression. And then you can also look at treatment outcome predictions, because I think this is important. We want to know which drugs the patient would respond to. And you could do that in a retrieval setting where you're finding similar cases, but here it's being posed as a supervised problem. And then you can also, because you have representations of patients, you can also look at clinical operation management as a whole as well. And then here are just some results for cancer survival and progression, and also some baselines for what happens when you use structured and unstructured data, as well as some very fundamental age, sex baselines as well. You can also stratify patients into distinct risk groups. This is just by using the representation itself, and we also studied that these stratifications are also well calibrated. So once we have these representations and we've used them in some kind of supervised downstream tasks, then we can also go back and assess the interpretability of these supervised models as well as those representations. But we want to see that what the model uses in making some of these predictions and how the risk of the patient evolves over time, and this is an example here that we can study how the risk of the patient is evolving over time and what is responsible for that risk evolution. So you can study this at the level of the patient, but you can also study this at the level of the large cohorts, so that can lead to discovery of additional information, additional knowledge. This is something that we are still exploring and will take more time for us to see whether it has any discovery potential. So this is just a flavor of what's coming. This is a very early stage study, and we've been working in this direction for a while, but we will continue to work to validate this model and see what the capabilities of the models are. So you can download a preprint using this QR code, and the preprint would also be available on arXiv in the coming days. So I'll stop here in the interest of time, and I'd like to thank all the PhD students and postdocs who have contributed to this work over the years, as well as all the funding that we've received to make this work possible. Thank you so much. Thank you very much. It's truly an AI revolution in cancer research. Thank you very much for joining today's plenary session. Please come back next year. There's much more to come, and I wish you a nice conference. Thank you.

Welcome everyone, to those in the room and those joining us online, to this major symposium, Clonal Hematopoiesis: Aging and Drivers of Both Blood Cancer and Solid Tumors. My name is Jyoti Nangalia. I'll be chairing the session. I'm a hemato-oncologist based at Cambridge University Hospital, but also the Wellcome Sanger Institute, where I do my research. We have three speakers today. I'm one of them. We have Siddharth Jaiswal, who I'll introduce first. He's a current associate professor of pathology at Stanford? Associate. Associate at Stanford. One of the first people, together with Ben, to describe the concept of clonal hematopoiesis. So we're really fortunate to have amazing speakers with us today. His lab focuses on understanding the biology of aging, of the hematopoietic system in particular, and how these mutations associated with clonal hematopoiesis contribute not only to cancer, but also to age-related phenotypes. So first up, we'll have Dr. Jaiswal, then myself, and after that, Ben Ebert. All right. Over to you, Sid. Thank you, Dr. Nangalia, and it's my great pleasure to be back at AACR presenting our latest work. These are my disclosures. So clonal hematopoiesis is a premalignant expansion of hematopoietic stem cells, typically due to acquired somatic mutations in a handful of driver genes. And we know from first principles, clonal hematopoiesis should be very common with aging. Thanks to great work from the Sanger Institute, we can estimate that there are about 50,000 to 200,000 hematopoietic stem cells in adult humans. And we also know that these HSCs acquire about one protein coding mutation every 10 years. Which doesn't sound like a big number, but if you multiply these two figures together, you can calculate that by the age of 70, there will be about 1.4 million protein coding mutations within the HSC pool of each of us. And if just one of these mutations is sufficient to confer a fitness advantage to a hematopoietic stem cell, then these clonal expansions should be common with aging. And indeed, that is what we see. And so I thought it'd be useful to spend one minute just talking about the terminology of clonal hematopoiesis, because it is a bit confusing. So clonal hematopoiesis, as I mentioned, is any clonal expansion due to a fitness-increasing mutation in a hematopoietic stem cell. And we know that clonal hematopoiesis, by this definition, is ubiquitous in all humans. Clonal hematopoiesis can be further subdivided into CH with known cancer-associated driver mutations. So that's how we first identified this state, is by looking in genes that were recurrently mutated in heme malignancies, and then going back to healthy individuals to see if they had those mutations. However, there is also clonal hematopoiesis with unknown driver mutations, and we don't really understand why these mutations expand. But we know that this is almost as common as clonal hematopoiesis with known drivers. And then within the known driver clonal hematopoiesis space, there's what we have defined as CHIP, clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential. That's based on a variant allele fraction of greater than 2%. And then clones that are smaller than this are sometimes called micro CH or microCHIP. These are very common, because only a subfraction of these small clones go on to develop into large clones. And then within the CHIP pool, there's CHIP due to single nucleotide variants or indels, so think mutations in TET2 and DNMT3A, and then there's also mosaic chromosomal alterations. So surprisingly, there haven't been that many studies that have reported the prevalence of these different kinds of clonal hematopoiesis all in a single population, mainly because you need whole genome sequencing data to identify clonal hematopoiesis with unknown drivers. It's typically identified because there's an accumulation of passenger mutations, which doesn't occur, at least is not detectable from whole blood sequencing, unless there is an expansion event. But we've done this in a few cohorts now, and this is the prevalence of the different kinds of clonal hematopoiesis as a function of age. So you can see that in those under the age of 60, it's relatively uncommon, about 10% in total. And this rises to about 80% of all individuals who are age 90 or older have a large detectable clone. And you can see that clonal hematopoiesis with indels or single nucleotide variants is almost as common as clonal hematopoiesis with unknown drivers. And one of the bigger surprises in the initial surveys of clonal hematopoiesis was the spectrum of genes that we typically see mutated. And if you think about typical oncogenes, things like RAS signaling pathway or tumor suppressors, like TP53 loss of function mutations. We do see these in clonal hematopoiesis, but they're relatively uncommon. Only about 10% of the total. Instead, the other 90% seems to be genes that are involved in epigenetic regulation, like DNMT3A, TET2, ASXL1, or spliceosome factor mutations.And so why are these particular genes that don't seem to have an obvious link to oncogenes or tumor suppressors, why are they positively selected? And we hypothesized that we could make headway into this question by studying it directly in humans. And specifically, if we could identify a way to calculate the clonal expansion rate in a large number of people, we could do large-scale association studies to try to figure out why these particular genes are mutated. And so we developed a method that we call passenger approximated clonal expansion rate. So this is a method that uses the total number of passenger mutations in a clone to infer how old that clone is. So basically, these passenger mutations are accumulated linearly with respect to time, and so it's like a timestamp for when that clone was born. And once we know how old that clone is, we can infer how quickly it's been growing using a simple linear regression model, as shown here. And what we hypothesized was that the residual, so if you plot the passenger mutations versus the input variables for each individual, which is shown by a dot here, the residual, which is the difference on the y-axis from the line of best fit to their number of passenger mutations, that should be a measure of the fitness of that clone in that individual. And so we went on to validate this method in several ways. And one of the things that we found was that the specific driver mutation itself is a pretty large determinant of clonal fitness. So these are our PACER fitness estimates for the most common drivers seen in CHIP. These are all shown relative to DNMT3A mutations. And what you'll note is that most of the drivers have a higher fitness than DNMT3A. So DNMT3A, somewhat paradoxically, despite being the most commonly mutated gene, also has one of the lowest fitness scores. The highest fitness scores were seen in the spicy som genes, U2AF1, SRSF2, and SF3B1. JAK2 was also quite high. And then in the middle, you see a lot of genes that are common, TET2, PPM1D, ASXL1, et cetera. So we know that driver mutation is a major determinant of growth rate, but we wanted to know, using our method, what environmental and genetic factors may also drive positive selection of these clones. So we turned first to environmental factors. And this is data taken from the UK Biobank, as well as some other cohorts. So we first measured biomarkers or demographic factors that were available in this data set and asked, did any of these associate with clonal expansion rate? And you can see that of these commonly assessed demographic variables, including sex, smoking, diabetes, BMI, inflammation, and air pollution, only smoking was associated positively with clonal expansion rate. This was a little surprising given the amount of animal model data supporting things like obesity or inflammation as being drivers of clonal expansion, at least in mice. However, we did not see these associations in humans. The reasons for that difference are not entirely clear. We've also looked at this in other ways. This is a collaborative project with Alex Bick's group at Vanderbilt. And what his group did was to create polygenic risk scores for different protein levels that you might have in your body, and then asked if you have a higher genetic risk of having certain proteins circulating in your body, does that associate with clonal expansion rate? And what we found generally was that genetically predicted cytokine levels were not very predictive for clonal expansion rate. The one exception being there was a modest association between predicted IL6 levels and the rate of growth of DNMT3A clones. And then there were a handful of other TNF-like factors that were also modestly associated with DNMT3A clonal expansion. So overall, what our findings have seemed to indicate thus far is that of the measured environmental factors that we can assess, it's really only smoking that seems to have a strong correlation to growth rate. And so we then hypothesized that perhaps we could do a genome-wide association study or a GWAS to look for germline variants of clonal expansion rate to reveal genes or pathways that may be associated with fitness advantage. And this is the result of our first survey. So this was done in the TOPMed cohort. This finding has been replicated now in additional cohorts. And what we found was that there was a single locus that reached genome-wide significance in the survey. The lead polymorphism in that locus is called RS2887399. It's a single nucleotide polymorphism in the promoter of a gene called TCL1A. The reference allele is a guanine. The alternative allele is a thymine. And what we observed is that the alt allele was associated with slower clonal expansion in several non-DNMT3A driver genes, including TET2, ASXL1, and some splicing factors.TCL1A is an interesting gene because it has been studied in the context of heme malignancies before. It was originally cloned by Carlo Croce's lab back in the 1990s because it was found in a translocation in a rare malignancy called T-prolymphocytic leukemia. That's a leukemia of mature T cells. And this translocation causes the TCR alpha locus to come into proximity with TCL1A to drive aberrant expression of TCL1A in the mature T cells, and it's thought to be the causal driver of that malignancy. However, there was no known link between this gene and myeloid malignancies or HSC biology. TCL1A is a bit of an enigmatic protein in the sense that it's not really very clear what it's doing. It's a tiny protein. It's 14 kilodaltons. It forms an obligate homodimer with itself, and early studies show that it was able to bind to the PH domain of AKT and potentially activate AKT via an unknown mechanism. And so what we went on to show in our published work, through a variety of experiments, was that we think TCL1A is a major driver of clonal expansion in hematopoietic stem cells. What we showed was that the TCL1A locus is normally closed or lowly expressed in hematopoietic stem cells. And in fact, the only cell types in adult humans where TCL1A is expressed are B cells, plasmacytoid dendritic cells, and progenitors of sperm cells. And so in this sense, TCL1A might actually be a very good therapeutic target because you might predict that you'd be able to block its function without really affecting normal tissues very much. However, if you now acquire a mutation in one of these driver mutations that we showed was associated with the polymorphism, we believe that this de-represses the TCL1A locus. So now the gene goes from off to on. This promotes TCL1A protein expression and we think is a driver of clonal advantage for these mutations. And the reason we were able to find this serendipitously was that there happens to be a subset of the population that has a thymine at this TCL1A promoter at this SNP. And we think that having this thymine variant prevents the chromatin from opening and abrogates the clonal advantage, and therefore reduces prevalence of CHIP in these individuals. So what is the full spectrum of driver mutations in CHIP that might be associated with TCL1A? And so what we can do now that we have this polymorphism that we know is strongly linked to TCL1A expression, is to systematically ask what driver mutations are enriched or de-enriched if you have the T allele at this locus. And if the prevalence of the driver mutation is below the dashed line, we would predict that these driver mutations are somehow dependent on TCL1A for their clonal expansion. And so we did this in the UK Biobank dataset, and we replicated our previous findings, which were that ASXL1, TET2, SF3B1, and SRSF2 mutations were strongly depleted in individuals who carried this T allele. But we found a number of other surprising things, such as NRAS mutations, IDH2 mutations, and JAK2 mutations may also be depleted in carriers of the T allele. And furthermore, we found that clonal hematopoiesis with unknown drivers, so this large class of clonal expansions where we don't really know why it's happening, it turns out the strongest genetic hit, so if you do a GWAS for clonal hematopoiesis with unknown drivers, the strongest hit is in this TCL1A polymorphism, suggesting that many of these mysterious clonal expansions may also depend on TCL1A expression. So we think that TCL1A is a critical factor for the development of clonal hematopoiesis, and it was found using GWAS. And many of you in this room may note there have been many polymorphisms, many genes that have been linked to clonal hematopoiesis through GWAS. But what I would say is distinct about TCL1A is that it is the only gene of all the GWAS hits that goes from off to on in hematopoietic stem cells when a somatic mutation in one of these driver genes is acquired. And this suggests that this is not just a modulator of clonal expansion, but it may be a major causal driver, so the reason that these mutations are actually selected. And if this model is true, there are two predictions. So one is that ectopic expression of TCL1A should be sufficient to cause clonal expansion phenotypes in vivo, in a model system, for example, by altering key HSC biology. And a second prediction is that TCL1A expression should promote the risk of at least some CHIP-related phenotypes, such as hematologic malignancy. And so we decided we would like to study this in an animal system. And as many of you in this room know, there are many models for these common CHIP driver mutations, including loss of function, TET2 alleles, TET2 catalytic domain mutants, truncating mutations at the C-terminus of ASXL1, and then point mutations in SF3B1 and SRSF2. So these have all been built in mice.And they variably show a clonal expansion phenotype at the HSC level. The majority of these mice show things like anemia, but only a couple of these models actually develop malignancy. And when they do develop malignancy, it's typically at a very late stage. And we looked in all of these models, and in none of these models could we see that TCL1A became expressed in the HSCs. So unlike what we see in humans, if you introduce these mutations into human HSCs, TCL1A goes from off to on. It doesn't seem to happen in the mouse. One reason for that is that if you look at the promoter region of TCL1A, this is where the polymorphisms that I described lie. You can see that there is generally poor conservation between humans and other species at this locus. And so we think that maybe because the promoter is not really conserved at this region, mice do not have the same effect. So even if you put the mutation in the mice, it doesn't lead to the de-repression at this locus. And so to get around this, what we decided to do was to build a transgenic mouse model where we could enforce expression of TCL1A in a tissue-specific manner. And so we introduced the TCL1A human open reading frame into the H-11 locus. It's a safe harbor locus in mice, and the promoter is separated from the open reading frame with box stop lux cassettes. And so what we can do is cross these mice to various Cre-expressing strains to get tissue-specific expression of TCL1A in the mice. And so we have done this using Bav1 Cre mice as well as Tau1 Cre mice. And what we find is that these mice, for most of their life, look largely normal. So we followed their CBCs up to a year, and you can see that there's really no difference in the white blood cell count, in the red blood cell parameters, in the platelet counts, or in the differential up to nine months. We did note that by midlife, there was a marked HSPC expansion in the bone marrow of these mice, and this was particularly evident in the long-term hematopoietic stem cell fraction of the bone marrow and less evident in the myeloid progenitors. So we think that TCL1A, as perhaps is expected, does lead to some sort of fitness effect on the hematopoietic stem cells and causes some sort of expansion in this model. We've also done competitive transplants, where TCL1A was forced to be expressed in some HSCs and then competed against wild-type HSCs, and you can see that over time, the TCL1A-expressing HSCs take over. So there is this competitive advantage as well. In terms of the mechanism of why TCL1A may cause clonal expansion of these HSCs, that's still being worked out. But we suspect that there is increased proliferation, so increased cell cycling of these HSCs and also resistance to apoptosis. So, we thought that these mice would probably not have a very exciting phenotype beyond what I just showed. But much to our surprise, when we kept the mice alive for up to a year, we found that there was 100% mortality in the TCL1A transgenic mice. So you can see that by one year in both Cre crosses, all of the mice have died. And we observed there's a pronounced splenomegaly and a pronounced hepatomegaly, as well as an expansion of HSPCs in the moribund mice. The phenotypes at death range from pancytopenic, that's the majority of the mice, to marked leukocytosis. And we further characterize what are these mice dying of, and it looks like the majority of the mice are developing a myeloid leukemia phenotype, characterized by sheets of abnormal myeloid cells in the bone marrow that express an abnormal phenotype. They're Kitlow CD11b positive, so they're myeloid, as well as CD34 positive and negative for lymphoid markers. So is this relevant potentially in human myeloid malignancies as well? And so we've asked if individuals who have this T allele, the one that prevents TCL1A expression, do they have any alteration in their risk of developing myeloid malignancy? And we can see that indeed that is the case, that carriers of the T allele are less likely to develop any myeloid malignancy, and an especially strong protective effect for CMML, chronic myelomonocytic leukemia. And finally, we've asked, is TCL1A still expressed in the hematopoietic stem cells from patients with myeloid malignancies? And we've looked at this in a couple of different ways. First, using publicly available single-cell RNA-seq data from healthy or malignant hematopoiesis. We can see that healthy HSCs, as expected, there's essentially no TCL1A expression. However, if we look in the HSCs from patients with CMML or MDS, so each dot represents a single patient, we now see TCL1A is expressed in these HSCs, confirming that it may actually play a role in the malignancies as well as clonal hematopoiesis.And we've also looked at this at the protein level using flow cytometry. So this is gated on a HSC fraction. You can see that in healthy donors, there's, as expected, essentially no TACE1A expressed, whereas we do see robust expression in these high-risk MDS cases. So to summarize, clonal hematopoiesis becomes ubiquitous with aging, but the factors leading to positive selection of these drivers is incompletely understood. Of the environmental factors we've studied so far, smoking seems to be the strongest promoter of clonal expansion. And genetically, we think that expression of TACE1A seems to be a major driver of clonal expansion of clones of both known and unknown drivers. And we hypothesize that TACE1A may be a therapeutic target for myeloid malignancies arising from antecedent clonal hematopoiesis. And I'd like to acknowledge all the people that did the work. The majority of the studies that I've showed today were done by a very talented postdoc, Isaac Tingestdal, and an MD-PhD student, JK Gopalkumar. Thank you for your attention. Beautiful talks. Thank you. The talk's now open for questions. Can I ask people to come to the microphones because this is being live-streamed, and for those joining us online to use the QR code and ask questions via the online chat so we can ask the speaker. Hi, Tim Ley from Wash U. Sid, beautiful work. I must have been shocked to see those tumors arise in those mice late. The long latency suggests that there's either cooperating mutations. I wonder if you know what they are or whether there's some kind of transcriptional earthquake associated with escape. Yeah, Tim, great questions. So we are trying to sequence the bone marrow from these mice now to determine if there are any recurrent cooperating mutations that to be determined. The thing that is a little bit surprising is the very narrow window in which these mice all seem to die. So they seem to be pretty healthy up to about nine months, and then by 12 to 13 months, they're basically 100% dead. So I don't quite understand at this point why that window is very short, and it would be a little bit surprising if they all acquired the same cooperating mutations within that time frame. So I'm starting to suspect it's some sort of epigenetic state or something else that goes wrong around that time point. Are they transplantable? Yes, they are transplantable. Yes. Very interesting presentation. I have a couple questions, actually. Now that you can measure fitness, if we measure the fitness of the non-clonally involved hematopoietic stem cells in a patient who has clonal hematopoiesis, are they as fit as normal or less fit than normal? Yes, a good question. So the method that I talked about, we can only assess the fitness of the expanding clone. So I think you're asking, can we assess the fitness of the other HSCs that are not part of that clone? I'm by no means an expert on this, but I was always wondering, is the clonal hematopoiesis the result of the background failing from aging? Yeah. So now you can see the clones because they are the only ones left contributing. Yeah. Or is it really that they are more effective, that's why they are succeeding more and becoming more prominent? The other question was, when we say they are more fit, is it because they are more constantly dividing or more actively dividing, meaning is it the amplitude or the time? Can we distinguish these two? Because we say it's fit, but is it fit as a result of the constant firing, or is it fit because it does a lot when it fires? Yeah. So for your first question, we don't know for sure what the reasons are. Sorry, could you repeat the first question? We've been always told in oncology, this is an activated mutation. Yeah. Okay? I'm now trying to ask, is it more potent, the mutant, or is it more constantly on, and as a result, you end up having more function? So here, the same thing, the fitness, is it because of more proliferation per unit of time, or is it proliferating more than normal, so it ends up being represented more than normal? Can we distinguish these two scenarios? So we could try to do that using the mouse models. So far, we have observed an increased proliferation rate using things like BrdU over short time points. It increases the risk and there needs to be another stimulus. In the case of cardiovascular disease, that could be a high cholesterol exposure, or in the case of gout, it's uric acid crystals, and that inflammatory response is exaggerated in the case of the Tet2 knockout. So here we used a classic stimulator of myeloid inflammation, which is zymosan from a yeast cell wall, and then harvested cells from the peritoneum, which becomes very inflamed in this circumstance. And we actually looked at the bone marrow and the peritoneum, looking specifically not just for clonal expansion broadly, but for genes that mediate inflammation and accumulation of guides in the peritoneum. When we did this, we were struck that a very large percentage of the guides related to lipid metabolism, and particularly one of the key regulators of the lipid metabolic pathway is ACLY, as well as OGT, which I'll talk about in a little bit. It also reminded us of some of the very early studies that we did, that Sid did, that showed sheets of macrophages, foamy macrophages in mice with Tet2 knockout exposed to a high-fat diet. So if you look at some of the individual genes that hit in this screen, they include ACLY, which is a regulator of conversion of citrate to acetyl-CoA, a number of genes that are critical regulators of cholesterol and fatty acid metabolism. And each of these individual mutations takes the level of inflammation in the peritoneum from increased inflammation with Tet2 compared to wild type back to baseline. So the same effect of the inflammatory stimulus in the Tet2 knockout and the wild type. If you do lipid profiling of these mutant cells, both in human cells and in mouse cells, you see a very dramatic increase of accumulation of triacylglycerols, diacylglycerols, as well as cholesterol esters in neutrophils, macrophages in mice and in human macrophages that have been edited at the Tet2 locus. And if you stain these cells, these green droplets are lipid droplets that we see in the Tet2 knockout cells much more than in wild-type cells. And in humans as well, using a different stain, you can see these lipid droplets in Tet2-edited HSCs, HSPCs, compared to wild type. So there's a quite profound metabolic defect related to lipid metabolism in these Tet2 knockout cells. If you look by gene expression profiling in the Tet2 knockout cells exposed to this inflammatory stimulus, it's quite marked compared to wild-type cells. But if you knock out ACLY, one of the critical regulators, you largely return the gene expression profile to the wild-type state. I mentioned that OGT was one of the other hits. That struck us because OGT is one of the primary binding partners of Tet2, and OGT is a regulator, is actually a sensor of metabolic state in cells, and it adds a sugar moiety, glycan acylation, to many different proteins in the cell in response to metabolic stimuli.We tried to look at that interaction between TET2 and OGT and map it. We did a base editing screen, tiling all of TET2 and found some hits right where we predicted the binding interaction between TET2 and OGT to be. And then we developed a TR-FRET assay to look directly at the interaction of the TET2 with OGT right at this location, and you can see there's a nice interaction here with wild type TET2 interacting with OGT. And if we mutate the critical amino acids shown here, we lose the interaction between TET2 and OGT. So we think there's a very specific interaction that occurs at this locus between TET2 and OGT. If TET2 is gone, OGT is liberated from that interaction. So there's a lot more to be worked out there, but we think that TET2 mutations result in a major metabolic defect and it's related to OGT and its metabolic sensing. If you interrupt, so if you knock out TET2, OGT is liberated from its interaction with TET2, it results in glyco-N-acylation that's aberrant. It results in this lipid accumulation. If you block AOLY, you remove that lipid droplet formation. Lipid droplets are known to cause inflammation, and that, again, can be inhibited by various inhibitors of lipid metabolism. It also aligns with findings from our lab and a number of labs that have shown mitochondrial defects in TET2 knockout cells as well, which we think are probably related to the substrates going into the mitochondria. And then quickly, I just wanted to note prediction of outcome for CHIP, because this is critical for us to think about how we are going to intervene in individuals with CHIP who might have these various outcomes. We did this in the UK Biobank in 500,000 individuals. If you look at instant myeloid malignancy in individuals with CHIP, you see a huge variation in the risk of progression, DNMT3A heterozygous mutations being among the lowest, splicing factor mutations being among the highest. This aligns very well with the PACER analysis that Sid showed us, though there are exceptions like PPM1D, which had a higher rate of progression in the PACER analysis but has a very low risk of developing a myeloid malignancy. DNMT3A mutations, though they have a very low risk compared to the others, still, of course, increase the risk of progression to myeloid malignancy. It's just much smaller than the others, at least for the heterozygous DNMT3A mutations. By putting the various factors that we observed together, which are quite simple, what the genotype is that's driving, how many mutations are present, how big the clone is, RDW, which in all studies have been very powerfully associated with all the adverse outcomes, MCV, cytopenias, and age, get a very simple score that really subdivides the risk. High-risk individuals, which fortunately is only about 1% of individuals, have getting close to an inevitability of progressing to a myeloid malignancy, and there are already multiple clinical trials underway to intervene on risk of progression, specifically in this subgroup. Again, that's only 1% of individuals, which is good. 90% of individuals are in green in the very low-risk group. Only a threefold increased risk of developing a myeloid malignancy, which is a very low baseline, so the absolute risk is very low. And then the intermediate risk has an intermediate, about a 35-fold increased risk, but still a relatively small overall risk. And even though we built this model for progression to myeloid malignancy, it correlated very powerfully with overall survival. The high-risk group having about 50% overall survival, low risk and no CHIP having about a 95% survival. And this has been validated now in a number of cohorts, but illustrating that even in this cohort that was very different from the UK Biobank, in that it was older and less healthy, the absolute risk of heme malignancy is most affected by this risk group, but the total mortality is still driven by cardiovascular disease as the major cause of death, though solid organ malignancy also was significantly elevated, particularly in the high-risk group. So just wanted to note that, again, CHIP is extremely common, associated with overall mortality, increased risk of a variety of inflammatory diseases, and that TET2 inactivation exacerbates these inflammatory phenotypes and alters lipid metabolism, and intervening on that lipid metabolism removes the inflammatory phenotype. And risk of progression to malignancy or to overall mortality is affected by individual genetic alterations and can be predicted by this and other clonal hematopoiesis risk scores. And again, highlighting the seminal work that Sid did, as well as various members of the lab. The work I talked about today was led by Peter Kim and Chris Hergot here. Happy to take any questions. Yeah, go ahead. Beautiful talk. I was wondering, when you see infection, cancer, or anything other than autoimmune, you start to wonder about sex effects. Mm-hmm. And so I was wondering, do you have a component for mosaic loss of sex chromosomes in your risk score? And to what extent is there an overlap between the effect of any given clonal hematopoiesis-associated allele? It's a great question. Minus Y is included in there, but there is clearly an effect of sex on each of these individual mutations. The vast majority of mutations are much more common in males than females. DNMT3 mutations are slightly more common in females than males. And we've actually been able to recapitulate some of that in animal models by just modulating hormone exposures and estrogen-driving clonal advantage in DNMT3A. Very cool. Thank you so much. Hey, Tim. Ben, great talk. Fantastic work, as always. Clonal hematopoiesis of indeterminate potential. Since the algorithms are so good now, is it time to drop IP and just call it- Yeah ... clonal hematopoiesis? I suppose every human disease has some indeterminate potential. We were trying to align with MGUS, which also has almost an inevitable component to it. But it's still a smaller percentage that fully progress, which is the idea. It's a good question. My question's related to the ACLY component. Yeah. Do you see the same dependency in earlier, less mature cells being MPPs and HSCs, or is this lipid accumulation phenotype restricted to these different- Great question. We're doing that now, and it is not a trivial experiment because ACLY is essential for all cells, and so doing that genetically carefully is hard. There are some ACLY inhibitors, some of which have been moved forward clinically, but they are developed to have their primary activity in the liver, to modify lipid metabolism. And so, understanding the tet2 specificity is not trivial, but we think it's there. But we're still working our way through those experiments. Good question. Thanks. Question? Yeah. Wonderful talk. Just a quick question. Building on what you mentioned about the lipid metabolism, do you think there's a role to investigate CHIP on tumor microenvironments and how it would evolve, like response to immunotherapy and things of that line? Absolutely. I think the most elegant work has been done in lung cancer, where infiltrating tet2 mutant clones seem to increase the risk of lung cancer. That also aligns with the striking finding of the CANTO study, in which a large number of patients, about 10,000 patients in a randomized controlled clinical trial, were treated with an IL-1 beta inhibitor called canakinumab, and the risk of lung cancer was approximately halved in the individuals who got canakinumab. And when mature lung cancers were treated with canakinumab, it didn't have great efficacy. So it may be in those very earliest stages where there's an initial mutation that the inflammatory microenvironment that CHIP is part of, can lead to whether that clone becomes established, expands, and then ultimately progresses to lung cancer. So, yes, I think at least in the case of lung cancer, that seems to be true and may be true in other cases as well. Yeah. Thank you very much. Great work again. I just remember from the very first paper of DNMT3A that Dr. Lei published in the "New England Journal." Yeah. There were two mutants that were recurrent. Yeah. The rest were one hit each. Yeah. Now with more sequencing, maybe this is not completely true. So the question is, are they all relevant or only some that are recurring and have functional impact? Yeah, great question. It's a loss-of-function mutation, but as Tim showed and has held up both in CHIP and in mature MDS and AML, there are hotspot mutations, and those hotspot mutations that are dominant negative mutations. And so if you look at those mutations, specifically, the risk of progression is greater than a heterozygous loss-of-function mutation and associated with worse outcomes as well. So in the model, when they say DNMT mutation, any one counts or only the hotspots? Yeah. We have lumped them together, which is an apples and oranges. It's probably true for many mutations, P53 as well. They're hotspot mutations that act as dominant negatives. So, we do sometimes lump just because even with these huge data sets, you start to get into sample size problems when you get down to individual types of mutations. Thank you. Great talk. My name is Amulia Singh. We work on blood tests to detect lung cancer, and so almost everything you all said was fascinating in that light. For your COPD phenotype, do you see it sort of differential or kind of a differential diagnosis where you have individuals who have COPD but don't get lung cancer, and what does that look like relative to those who do? Yeah. It's not something that we've worked on ourselves, but that's a great question. We certainly haven't looked at that at all. But that's a good question because that is the at-risk population and whether there are other stimuli that lead somebody in a more oncogenic direction versus airspace disease or whether that's a stochastic event. So, great question. Thanks. Great. We can now open the floor for a panel discussion, for the last five minutes actually, because there are quite a lot of questions online, and if there are questions for any panel members, please come to the microphones. So the first one is for you, Sid. Is expression of TCL1A increasing with age in the healthy population? That's a great question and one that we're looking at right now. So I don't have any data yet, but that's something that we're going to want to look at. It could be complicated because, as I mentioned, clonal hematopoiesis with unknown drivers seems to be strongly associated with the TCL1A SNP. So if you start to look at older individuals, many of them will have these unknown expansions. Maybe could I ask Jodi a question? In your methylome analysis, have you seen any TCL1A promoter hypermethylation? Yeah. Well, we'll check when we get back. Now, I'm looking at Shin in the audience, who's probably going to be very keen to check. We haven't looked. Question for both of you, actually. Were there any protective environmental factors for CH expansion that either of you have come across? Pradeep Natarajan published a paper showing that a vegetarian diet actually had a lower risk of CHIP, so that's one that I can think of. But as Sid said, the exact relationship between CHIP and inflammation from a human genetic standpoint has been difficult to see. Yeah, I don't have anything additional beyond what I showed. Smoking seemed to be the strongest risk factor, so not smoking is protective. But yeah, I'm not sure. And perhaps, I think there are sex hormone differences that are driving clonal selection in ways that we don't understand yet, or hematopoiesis in ways, and we've always known that there's differences in blood count parameters between males and females, so there's some interaction there. Perhaps the most powerful selective pressure that we see on a routine basis in all of our cancer centers is chemotherapy and radiation, which has an extremely powerful selective pressure for p53 and p53 pathway mutations, which ends up being the basis of therapy-related malignancies, ultimately. And I suspect the protective factors will be very much gene dependent. So, with JAK2, for example, you can do these polygenic risk scores for all your different blood counts. Are you likely to have a high hemoglobin or a low hemoglobin in the population? And for example, if you're likely to have a low platelet count in the population and you acquire a JAK2 mutation, you're much less likely to develop an MPN, and you're more likely to have just clonal hematopoiesis due to JAK2. So your germline polygenic risk scores, as you've also shown, can sort of influence selection on specific drivers. There is an interesting question here online. In germline carriers of DNA repair defects, do you see more CHIP? We don't at the moment, but we haven't looked in detail. Any thoughts on that? So there are, for all of the really powerful germline predisposition to leukemia disorders, clonal hematopoiesis does develop early in life and is a predictor. So patients with RUNX1 mutations or Shwachman-Diamond syndrome, and the particular mutation that is inherited does, to a large degree, dictate what those initiating mutations are. So individuals who inherit one RUNX1 allele mutated will acquire a mutation in their second RUNX1 allele. Patients with Shwachman-Diamond syndrome will develop p53 mutations as one of their initial drivers. So the inherited allele does have a powerful effect on the initiating mutation. And sometimes what's growing out in that context can be maladaptive. But occasionally, what's growing out in that context can be germline rescue. Yeah. So it can be a really powerful tool for discovering what actually reverses the germline defect because those good clones will also grow out in addition to the maladaptive clones. It could be a powerful discovery engine. Some more questions on the floor? A quick question about GATA2. Very famous epiallele, right? Because when you methylate the wild-type allele and the mutant allele is expressed on the other one, it's associated with progression to monoMAC and AML. Did you look at GATA2 in your studies to see whether it was affected early on? Sorry, didn't quite catch the gene. Which one? GATA2. GATA2. It hasn't come out in our unsupervised screens. We will do a more supervised screen on known drivers. So far, what we're finding is we're finding some early signals in known tumor suppressor genes where there's promoter methylation early in life. What's tricky is knowing which segment in the promoter is critical. So there might be five segments in the promoter, one of which has shown this beautiful allelic methylation in association with the lineage. Is it changing gene expression? We don't yet know, but we will check out GATA2. We haven't looked at it directly. It's very susceptible to allele-specific methylation. It just might be a place to look because there's something very special about it. We should be able to. We have genome-wide coverage. Yeah. Thank you. My question, in general, is I guess related to clinically, we now sequence all of our cancer patients and find their CH incidentally, or their primary care found them. And obviously, we shouldn't be changing people's chemo exposure at this point without a randomized controlled trial to suggest that avoiding doxorubicin prevents therapy-related myeloid neoplasms. But I'd just like put it to you three experts on where you think we should be going and what types of questions we should be asking, and how do we incorporate this data in our care of cancer patients over the next five years? And I can start. So, we've looked at the effect of chemotherapies, lots of different chemotherapy agents, both for solid tumors and liquid tumors in normal blood cells. And sometimes you find quite interesting things. You can find that two agents within the same class that actually have quite similar efficacy, one is mutagenic to the blood cell and one isn't. So in some scenarios like that, clinicians may be quite happy to switch. Um, we found that long-term alkylator use can be mutagenic. So you can have two routes. You can have direct mutagenesis to cells, or you can just have clonal selection, such as on PPM1D and TP53. I think what will be quite interesting is to survey that before you start. So if you have someone who has a history of chemotherapy use and is about to get more treatment, surveying what proportion of TP53 selection there is already in the marrow may be quite useful. So not only might be useful in the future in terms of making our chemotherapy regimes a bit safer, but it could be useful for predicting how damaged wild-type hematopoiesis is following the first bout. I don't know if there's anything to add. Yeah, we see it a lot because it's in the sequencing reports. I think the vast majority of cases it wouldn't give it a thought in the midst of therapy, but as those patients become cancer survivors, it becomes perhaps a bigger issue or to identify the people who might be at greatest risk of a therapy-related malignancy or something. So, they end up in our survivorship clinics and thinking about it. And the other point is that the tumor-infiltrating clonal hematopoiesis may be a little bit different than just identifying the mutations in the blood, and the associations with lung cancer most powerfully with the individuals where the cells are at a higher percentage in the tumor. So, I think we're probably too early to know how to change therapy. And as you said, you would never change therapy without evidence from a randomized trial first. In your descriptive... So the question's around whether we've stratified by hormone therapy. We're looking at a cohort to look at just that question right now, but don't have any answers yet. Okay, probably the last question. Thanks. Oh, just a quick question, more of a technical question. Thank you for the great talk. For the epigenetic phylogenic trees, did you use short-read sequencing, and have you done it with long-read sequencing? You know, because that has better- So it's Illumina short-read sequencing. So with long-read sequencing, you need large DNA input, whereas we have two nanograms of DNA. Okay. So you can do long-read sequencing, but it's going to be on the whole sample. So it's useful for phasing the germline, for example. But we can phase about 15% of sites on short-read sequencing. Gotcha. Thank you. Great. Okay, well, with that, thank you all very much for attending in person and I'll close the session. Thank you to the speakers.

This transcript is Vimeo auto-generated English. Expect misheard names and technical terms. Use the ripgrep/search approach for exact quotes.

Welcome to the session of Decoding Cancer's Complex Ecosystem. My name is Hoifung Poon. I'm from Microsoft Research. Very excited to welcome you to this session. And so, as we all know, cancer, one of the really primary challenge is that it's very robust, right? And so the first generation chemotherapy tried to target mitosis, tried to kill dividing cells. Toxicity is high, and efficacy is low. Then came the genomic revolution and the targeted therapy, leading to the notion of precision medicine and precision health. But still, cancer has the blessing on natural selection, and often find out ways to compensate, to escape, to actually get roaring back, right? So leading to all the relapse and so forth. Immune system is one health system that also have natural selection on its side. So, immunotherapy is a really promising direction for taming cancer once and for all, right? So indeed, we have seen, obviously, many of you know way better than I do, right, that when immunotherapy works, oftentimes the response is much more durable. The challenge still is that right now, a lot of the immunotherapy is still a blunt instrument, right? So checkpoint just released the brake, and the overall response rate is still far too low. And the current companion like PD-L1s and TMB, they are not that good at actually stratifying patients, right? And so the question is how can we actually go much, much better and to do much, much more precise stratification of the patient? Now, tumor microenvironment is really one kind of 80/20 ways to actually start to unraveling a lot of those kind of secrets about why can the patient respond or not responding, right? And when we look at the tumor microenvironment, it's a very complex ecosystem of immune cell, tumor cells, stromal elements, and so forth. So there is lots and lots of clones and heterogeneity, and also there is a lot of temporal complexity, right? So the tumor microenvironment constantly changing in respond to immuno pressure, in respond to treatment pressure, right? So understanding this kind of tumor microenvironment grammar thereby could really start to shed light on how we actually can understand the cancer response, treatment response, and eventually figure out ways to actually make immuno-oncology much more precise. So, the goal for this session is try to overview all this complexity, right, from mechanical to temporal complexity, and then try to discuss a little bit about how artificial intelligence can potentially provide us some of the very powerful new tools, equip a human expert with some of the new capability to try to uncover this kind of tumor microenvironment grammar. So, I'm very excited to have the first speaker of this session, Dr. Ken Pienta, who lead the Cancer Ecology Center at Johns Hopkins. So he will basically introduce this eco-evolutionary lens for understanding the tumor microenvironment. Now, unfortunately, Dr. Pienta has a family emergency, so he couldn't actually come here. So he actually recorded a video, so I will play that video now. So, again, apology that we cannot do a live Q&A with Dr. Pienta here, but he is more than happy to communicate with you guys offline, right? So after Dr. Pienta give his talk introducing the tumor microenvironment ecosystem, I will talk a little bit about how AI might be able to help decode that tumor microenvironment grammar. So that will be the plan for the session. So now, let's play the video from Dr. Pienta. Hello, everyone, and thank you so much for allowing me to present this talk to you by video conference. I'm very sorry that I can't be there today with you, but I really appreciate your indulgence in letting me present to you virtually. I'm going to give you a talk today about tracing the eco-evolutionary path of tumors to understand cancer, but really what I'm trying to do is set you up for the next talk by your chairman. So here we go. I have really no relevant disclosures to this discussion except to say that I'm a professor at Johns Hopkins University, and none of the entities I consult for are relevant to this talk. I wanted to say welcome from the Cancer Ecology Center at Johns Hopkins, where we're harnessing ecology and evolution to redefine cancer risk detection and treatment. The issue we have is that 20 million people a year around the world are diagnosed with cancer. 10 million of those patients are cured with local therapy, but 10 million patients progress with metastatic and therapy-resistant disease and ultimately die of this disease.What is this idea of convergent evolution and how do these different cancers, all of which start independently in different people, converge to this lethal phenotype? Well, convergent evolution is the independent evolution of similar features in separate species and, or at different periods of time. It leads to analogous structures that have similar form or function but were not present in the last common ancestor. Good examples of this are eyes, teeth, wings and especially stress response, which is important for us here today. The convergent lethal phenotype of cancer leads to 10 million deaths per year worldwide. What is that convergent lethal phenotype? Well, number one is metastasis. Cancer spreads from the primary tumor to other parts of the body and the second part of the lethal phenotype is therapy resistance. Cancer is resistant to all known forms of systemic treatment even before it's been exposed to those treatments. So we try to look at this problem a little differently. Generally, we think of cancer as a disease of mutations, but cancer is no more a disease of cells than a traffic jam is a disease of cars. A lifetime study of the internal combustion engine would not help anyone understand our traffic problems and tumors are the same way. This was a very famous quote by David Smithers from 1962. So what is cancer? Well, cancer is a disease of uncontrolled proliferation by transformed cells subject to evolution by natural selection. We think about this because nothing in biology makes sense except in light of evolution. But nothing in evolution makes sense except in light of ecology. Evolution is change in heritable variation over generations, but ecology are the external forces that influence adaptation. Evolution acts upon phenotype, not genotype. The evolution that we observe in each patient is a result of cellular adaptation to those changing ecological forces, i.e. the tumor microenvironment and the patient macro environment, that cells that adopt a successful phenotype outcompete those with a less optimal phenotype. So our challenge is to integrate evolutionary principles to improve patient care. Remember the ecology. What selective forces are at play in a patient? How do they change over time and space? What adaptive cellular phenotypes are selected for? With intervention, how do we change the ecology of the adaptive landscape of the tumor? And don't forget, treatment kills more than just cancer cells. So what is an ecosystem? An ecosystem as defined by Eugene Odum in the '30s is that any unit that includes all the organisms, i.e. the community in a given area interacting with the physical environment so that a flow of energy leads to defined trophic structure, biodiversity and material cycles. Ecosystems do not exist independently, but interact in a complex web of ecological relationships connecting all ecosystems to make up the biosphere. Way back in 2008 now, we first defined tumors as ecosystems, that cancer cells as a species coexist in a complex habitat with other host cells. These cells interacting with their habitat create an ecosystem, and this ecosystem in turn exists within a larger environment. The host patient is the tumor's biosphere. And we created these tables that everybody's now familiar with looking at how we can think about man in a ecosystem like living on the land with cancer cell, living on the extracellular matrix, interacting with all organisms as a man, all cells with cancer. Our community is, for us, an ecosystem, whether we live in a city or a farm. The cancer cell community is the microenvironment, creating meta communities, metastases and living within the host biosphere or the patient. Cancer has several strategies to evolve traits in response to stress that it's constantly feeling in response to how the tumor microenvironment is changing. And these strategies we're going to talk more about, but they include tumor cell heterogeneity, proliferative quiescence, evolutionary triage, and self genetic modification. But the bottom line is that cancer creates a new ecosystem that now we refer to as the tumor microenvironment. We need to understand how, we need to understand how to disrupt this process because remember, it's easier to drain the swamp than swat a billion mosquitoes one at a time. And cancer cells are actually ecologic engineers, and there's two kinds of ecological engineers that result in niche construction. Allogeneic engineers modify environments by mechanically changing materials from one form to another. Think about beavers that construct dams. Autogenic engineers modify environments by changing themselves. Oak trees, as they grow, provide more and more living space for various birds and small mammals.Cancer is both an allogenic and autogenic engineer. Think about prostate cancer modifying the bone matrix, and the growing cancer alters the environment. Cancer creates its own beaver pond, attracting new species like tumor-associated macrophages and cancer-associated fibroblasts. Does this engineering affect genetic evolution, causing an increased rate of clonal selection? Well, if you look at ecological inheritance in increasing the rate of clonal selection, a feedback relationship between natural selection and niche construction, when organisms affect their environment, that change can cause a shift in what traits are being naturally selected for. The effect of niche construction is especially pronounced in situations where environmental alterations persist for several generations, introducing the evolutionary role of ecological inheritance. One example of this on Earth are yam cultivators in West Africa. They cut clearings in forests to grow crops, but that resulted in much standing water, which attracted mosquitoes and increased the rate of malaria. This caused a modification to the selection pressure for the sickle cell allele that protects against malaria. So does the cancer swamp increase the rate of clonal selection? Do we see that the rate of intrinsic genetic instability changes due to ecological inheritance? So let me run you through a few examples of how the cancer swamp increases or accelerates clonal selection. Gatenby and Gillies pointed out what's called the breeder's equation applied to somatic evolution, where they showed that harsh TME conditions like hypoxia, acidosis, and a heterogeneous extracellular matrix creates steep fitness gradients. Alvarez and colleagues pointed out that if you looked at in vitro versus in vivo, clonal selection through barcoding, that there were about 17,000 stable barcodes in vitro, but if you find those in tumors, there was a 73% reduction in clonal complexity versus the starting population and the 300 times expansion of the top clone. There have been, again, four converging mechanisms that have been documented. The steep fitness gradients, for example, through the hypoxia, immune-mediated pruning, acidosis-driven mutagenesis, and positive feedback loops because selected clones remodel the tumor microenvironment to entrench their advantage. So environmental stress can drive monoclonal dominance. You see this in even precancerous lesions, as shown by Zhang et al., where they demonstrated a polyclonal lesion with multiple completing clones, selection pressure through the tumor microenvironment leading to monoclonal dominance. So in summary, the swamp does drive selection, and there have been multiple examples of this across time. And this is why it's so important to think about how we can model this, as you'll see in the next talk. The tumor microenvironment is not merely a bystander. It is a primary engine of cancer evolution. So I want to switch gears a little bit and bring this home with thinking about why is lethal cancer lethal? Why do we die from cancer? This is a patient that died from prostate cancer, had all these lesions in their liver, but they had normal liver function. People don't die in general of organ dysfunction because the cancer metastases grow and overtake that organ. The tumor microenvironment kills us. At death, we estimate that a kilogram of tumor is lethal for a patient. But that kilogram of tumor is spread out across the patient in metastases. And that kilogram represents one to two trillion cancer cells of the total of 50 trillion cells in the human body. It's not about cancer cell mass. We need to understand the context within cancer occurring. That context is the human patient host. And so I want to remind you that cancer has no negative feedback loop. As long as it has enough energy to grow, it doesn't turn off like a normal cell does. So without a negative feedback loop, the healthy pond devolves into a swamp. Why do we die from cancer? Cancer poisons the biosphere of the patient, through cachexia syndrome, through thrombotic syndromes, through skeletal pain, through respiratory failure, and the common theme here is all of these are a result of cytokine overproduction. And we call this cytokine overproduction the miasma of cancer. MiasmaWhat a great word. It's a highly unpleasant or unhealthy smell of vapor. And so when you think about swamp gas, we all have heard the stories of fires in the swamp lighting because of flammable ecologic swamp gas. But it's really methane from dying algae and other fermentation. But lethal cancer swamp gas is a result of many cytokines leading to these different syndromes. So again, we actually published this almost 20 years ago now, looking at the different cytokines that contribute to what we call cancer swamp gas. IL-6, produced by macrophages, T cells, muscle cells, osteoblasts, adipocytes, and cancer cells. TNF alpha, otherwise known as cachexin. Look at all these cells that make TNF alpha. Cancer cells barely make this list. It's the cells of the tumor microenvironment. Matrix metalloproteinases made by macrophages and cancer cells. And all these cytokines lead to things like the cachexia syndrome, where the cells are released from the tumor microenvironment, causing lipolysis of fat and muscle wasting, et cetera. So what I want to leave you with here is this idea that the cancer swamp, i.e. the tumor microenvironment, poisons the patient. That's why we need to understand and be able to intervene in this better. So our challenge is integrating evolutionary ecology principles to improve patient care.
