Morning, everybody. My name is Bill Heit, and I'm honored to serve currently as the AACR Chief Scientific Advisor, but it's really my even greater honor to introduce today's symposium in honor of my friend and colleague, Barney Clarkson. And we welcome you to the AACR Bayer D. Clarkson Symposium on Plasticity in Cancer Progression: Mechanisms and Consequences. You probably know that this symposium has been held annually for many years, and it recognizes Dr. Clarkson's contributions to cancer research, and especially in the areas of cancer stem cells. Dr. Clarkson always attended this symposium, and even in more recent years when he became more frail, he always watched it on live stream. He always maintained his curiosity and passion for cancer research, and that's reflected in his really unbelievable scientific legacy. He was an expert in the field of heme malignancies for more than 50 years. His laboratory studied the growth and differentiation of normal leukemic and cancer progenitor cells. His research has added significantly to our understanding of hematologic malignancies and has been pivotal in the development of improved treatment strategies. He and his colleagues were among the first to develop curative chemotherapy for adults with various types of acute leukemias and lymphoma. They were also the first to show that an intensive chemotherapy regimen could induce remissions in patients with chronic myelogenous leukemia. In more recent years, Dr. Clarkson's research focused on characterizing and understanding leukemic stem cells with the goal of identifying specific drugs or treatment paradigm to target these quiescent cell populations that are often not eliminated by traditional chemotherapeutics. Barney was a member of the AACR for more than 60 years. He showed an unwavering commitment to advancing the organization's mission, and he served the AACR in numerous influential capacities. In fact, Dr. Clarkson is the only individual to have ever held four major AACR leadership positions. He served as a member of the AACR Board of Directors, he was AACR president, and he was AACR treasurer for an unprecedented five terms. I, as the immediate past treasurer for AACR, have a full appreciation of the importance of this role, and I'm grateful, will be forever grateful for Dr. Clarkson's leadership. And finally, Barney was president and founding chair of the AACR Foundation Board of Trustees, and he spearheaded the initiation of the AACR Foundation and served as its president for many years. In 2007, in recognition of his immense lasting impact on cancer research, patients, and the AACR, the AACR Board of Directors decided to name a symposium in his honor. Dr. Clarkson died on December 30th, 2025, and so today's AACR Bayer D. Clarkson Symposium, which is titled Plasticity in Cancer Progress: Mechanisms and Consequences, will honor his remarkable life and legacy. Chaired by one of our AACR Annual Meeting 2026 program chairs, Dr. Lynn Marie Postovit, this session will explore the mechanisms underpinning induced plasticity, with particular emphasis on stress-induced plasticity and the role of epigenetic dysregulation. The speakers will also discuss how plasticity may be a therapeutic target for the treatment of advanced cancers. We thank our chair, Dr. Postovit, and additional speakers, Dr. Matthew Loupiain, Hongjun Ji, for presenting their work and for honoring the member of Dr. Clarkson. Thank you for your attention, and I'd now like to invite Dr. Postovit, to begin the session. Thank you for the introduction, and thank you all for being here today. It's my pleasure to begin this session and to introduce, first, some concepts around plasticity. So in the background here, you see an African michaela zene butterfly. And why would we start a cancer session with a butterfly? It's because this particular butterfly undergoes a pretty dramatic phenotypic plasticity. And so in response to its environment, whether it's a dry or it's the wet season, in Africa, it'll actually change its wing patterns in a fairly dramatic way. This isn't genetically regulated. It's an epigenomic and transcriptionally regulated process. And so plasticity, in the case of the butterfly, is really the ability of the organism to change its phenotype in response to the environment. And today, we're going to be talking about cellular plasticity in the context of cancer, where cancer cells can also change their phenotype non-genetically, and most often in response to the microenvironment. In cancer, we can assume that plasticity should confer a tremendous selective advantage, should allow cells to evade the immune system, to spread, and to evade therapy, and so it's a very important problem in cancer.So what does plasticity look like, and how do we understand it? The first is really histologically in a loss of structure function. It's first seen well over 150 years ago now with the advent of the first microscopes by Kannheim and Geronte, and then Virchow. It's really the loss of structure function. And so this would be the loss of glands, tape structures, et cetera, and the acquisition of what looks increasingly like embryonic-like structures within the tissue. We see this, and we'll see it today with adenosquamous type conversions, as well as a number of malignancies or transformations during malignancies, such as neuroendocrine prostate cancer. Below, I'm showing you a picture of something I'll be talking about, dedifferentiated endometrial cancer, where you can see in stark contrast to the fairly well-differentiated areas here, we have very poorly differentiated areas right next to it. In addition, there's functional plasticity, which is more of a coordinated program wherein cells can actually behave like other cell types. One of my favorite examples of this is from my previous mentor, Mary Hendrix, in work that was done in 2002. In this particular study, they took melanoma cells, so very aggressive melanoma cells, labeled them with an RFP protein, and then injected them into the ischemic limb of a mouse. And so in an ischemic limb model, there's neovascularization, as you can see here, with a green dextran and beads that can move through it. And what is truly remarkable is that the red melanoma cells were forming chimeric vessels with the endothelial cells. So these weren't melanoma cells becoming endothelial cells, but rather co-opting certain features of those cells, in this case, the expression of VE-cadherin. And finally, we have the movement between cellular states and fates, which is sort of where we are right now with concepts of lineage plasticity. This was described many years ago now with EMT and then MET, so epithelial-mesenchymal transition and then the opposite, where it's thought that cells can actually acquire mesenchymal phenotypes, spread and metastasize, and then colonize with epithelial phenotypes. And as you can see in this cartoon here, overlaid on a Waddington's epigenetic landscape, it can also be simply heterogeneity and cells moving through different epigenomic patterns in order to display plasticity. And so we do consider and understand plasticity in the context of epigenetics. So here I'm showing a cartoon of Waddington's epigenomic landscape that was co-opted by Dr. Yamanaka several years ago now. And so within this, we have what would be considered a totipotent cell at the top of the hill. And during development, in response to developmental cues and microenvironmental factors, there's cell fate specification until you eventually lead to the various cell types within the body. It was considered very difficult to transdifferentiate or move between these epigenomic states, and even more difficult to move back up the trajectory. And of course, Dr. Yamanaka showed that this is actually quite easy and can occur with just three or so factors. And since then, we've shown that this can occur with cocktails within the microenvironment. Superimposed upon this, I added my small addition, which are the lightning bolts, which is a context of cancer wherein we have mutations. And certain mutations, like the loss of P53, can actually dramatically increase the ability of cells to reprogram and move up that hill. So collectively, those results suggest to us that dedifferentiation isn't actually dedifferentiation. It's not the acquisition of an embryonic phenotype, but rather the inability of a cell to sit in a set state. Right. Hi, everyone. So, thank you to everyone who came to our session, and I'll be very, very brief. The session, as you can see, is about AI and the meeting point between AI and spatial transcriptomics, to see if and to what extent we can predict spatial gene expression or any other interesting things that one can think of predicting directly from the histopathology slides. And we will have three talks. The first two talks will be by two amazing superstar scientists in this bridging field of AI, computational biology, and spatial transcriptomics. The first speaker will be Mingyao Li, Dr. Mingyao Li from UPenn. I'm sure many of you are aware of her cutting-edge work. The second speaker is James Zou from Stanford. A general AI leader and so on, but James regrettably is under the weather, but we have his talk recorded. Then the third speaker will be myself. And after that, Mingyao and me, we will be happy to take questions and have discussion. Also, if you can see the barcode, or how is it called? I don't know. The thing, the QR thing. You can scan it, and then you can put questions into that link, and presumably, I'm supposed to see them somewhere and answer. But if not, just raise your hand because I'm technologically challenged. Okay, guys? So without further ado, we will hopefully start on time. Dr. Li, please. Looking forward to your talk. Thank you so much for the very kind introduction, and thank you for the invitation. It's a great pleasure to be here. So today, I'm going to share our recent work on digital tissue twins, and in particular, how to turn histology into spatial omics at the population scale. Spatial omics technologies, including spatial transcriptomics and spatial proteomics, have transformed our understanding of tumor ecosystems. However, despite their power, the current spatial technologies remain expensive and slow, and this makes them difficult to scale across the full clinical enterprise. So for example, just mounting a small piece of tissue can easily cost you a few thousand dollars. But on the other hand, many of the spatial omics platforms allow the generation of a histology image from the same tissue slice. And oftentimes, these histology images are very high resolution, high quality, and importantly, these histology images are very inexpensive, and indeed, they are already routinely being generated for nearly every cancer patient in the clinic. So this highlights a fundamental data tradeoff issue in spatial biology. On one hand, spatial omics is molecular information-rich but is expensive and slow, difficult to scale. On the other hand, digital pathology is common, cheap, and fast, but contains no molecular information. So a central question that the field is facing right now is: how can we bridge this gap? And this central question has motivated our development of what I call the digital tissue twins, where our goal is to transform those routine H&E slides into spatially resolved and molecularly informed digital representation of human tissues at the population scale so that we can link spatial biology, AI, and clinical outcomes together to enable risk prediction, patient stratification, and eventually therapeutic decision-making. So in the last few years, my lab has been developing this AI-powered ecosystem to help us build what I call the digital tissue twins. In this ecosystem, we start from H&E stained histology images. We have developed the tools that can conduct the H&E QC and the cellular resolution tissue masking, and the cellular resolution histopathology image segmentation. And leveraging these processed histology images, we also have developed tools that can help researchers to automatically select the most informative samples and the regions of interest for the expensive spatial omics experiments. And after the spatial omics data are generated, we can further leverage these histology images to enhance the quality of the spatial omics data. And after all of this data preparation is being done, we will build AI models to virtually predict the spatial omics data at the population scale. In the meantime, we also perform multi-modal data integration so that we can have a comprehensive representation of every single tissue section in every single patient. And throughout this inference and integration process, we use rigorous statistical modeling to ensure that the AI models that we build are reliable and are trustworthy. So the core idea behind building digital tissue twins is teaching AI to see molecules within a histology image. And this is based on a simple but powerful observation that is similar histology implies a similar molecular profile. So this means that if we can ask the AI to learn this link, then the histology images can become proxies of the spatial molecular marvelous that people typically obtain in the expensive spatial omics experiment. So our work in this space started back in 2021. We were among the first to treat the histology as a primary modality in spatial omics analysis.And then later we developed the iSTAR, where we used a hierarchical vision transformer to extract image features out of a histology image. And this mimics how a pathologist examines a histology slide under the microscope. Okay, I think it's time to get started. Thank you very much everyone for coming. And this is a session about microenvironmental determinants of tumor evolution and immune escape, another component of tumor microenvironment. And we will be your chairs for today, and we will have seven exciting talks in the program. And we will get started right now. Remember that please actively contribute to the discussions and questions, and our only requirements for speakers, try to stay on time. It's a 10-minute talk and five minutes questions. You will see the timer on the screen. When it's 10 minutes, it will be yellow color and your talk is supposed to end. When you run out of 15 minutes, it will be a red color and no more time for questions, unfortunately. And without further ado, I think we will have our first speaker, Yi Zheng from Columbia University, and he will talk about neuroinflammatory memory in gastric tumorgenesis. Thanks for the introduction. Good afternoon, everyone. I'm Yi from Columbia University. Today, I will talk about vagal sensory neuron inflammatory memory. We all know that H. pylori eradication reduces the risk of gastric cancer. However, a large RCT with up to 26 years of follow-up revealed important limitation. Even after a successful eradication, gastric cancer still occurred in about 2.6% of treated individual. A risk that remains potentially higher than that of general population. Interestingly, patients with dyspeptic symptoms derive little to no benefit from eradication therapy. Together, these findings suggest that eliminating the pathogen alone is not sufficient. Instead, they raise the possibility that a form of persistent inflammatory memory, potentially involving the gut-brain axis, remain after bacterial clearance. So before going further, let me briefly define what do we mean by inflammatory memory. Inflammatory memory can be defined as tissues or cells retaining a memory of inflammatory injury that acquisition to react more quickly and broadly to subsequent diverse secondary stimuli. In the pancreas and Crohn's, epithelial memory of inflammation limits tissue damage in subsequent episodes of acute inflammation while promoting tumorigenesis. So this brings us back to a central question. Can neuron themselves store inflammatory memory? For example, in a DSS colitis model, reactivation of insular cortex neural activity during primary inflammation is sufficient to induce secondary Crohn's inflammation. And these findings indicate that the nervous system can encode and reactivate information about prior inflammatory states. However, while a similar neural memory exists in the stomach and how it might influence long-term disease outcomes remains unknown. To study inflammatory memory in a physiologically relevant manner, we employed a set of complementary gastric regeneration and tumor model. For gastric regeneration, we primarily use a high-dose tamoxifen model, which induces parietal cell loss and chief cell loss, and triggers PEN, a kind of metaplastic response, and normally resolve back to histological baseline within three weeks. Using the high-dose tamoxifen model, we observed a striking memory phenotype in the stomach. We use immunofluorescence for parietal cell, chief cell, and spin cell, and proliferation. Mice that had experienced a single prior injury and fully returned to histological baseline displayed a markedly accelerated regenerative and metaplastic response upon a second injury. Importantly, the enhanced recall response was not transient. The memory effect persists for at least six months after the initial injury. A similar phenotype could be observed in a clinically relevant manner. In mice previously infected with H. pylori and subsequently eradicated, we induced the HDD injury. Although gastric histology appeared comparable to control before injury, mice with an inflammatory history showed significant accelerated regeneration and metaplastic response during recall with increased parietal cell and metaplastic cell. However, this accelerated recall response comes at a cost.While inflammatory memory enhances regeneration, it has deleterious consequences in the context of cancer. The memory effect accelerated orthotopic ACKP tumor progression, and a similar phenotype can be observed in multiple spontaneous cancer models, including the intestinal type and diffuse type. These findings indicate that the memory, although beneficial for tissue repair, creates a permissive microenvironment for tumor progression. So next, we sought to link the memory phenotype to the sensory nerve system. Of course, both regeneration and tumor model recall injury was consistently associated with an increased CGRP positive density fibers at the lesion site. In parallel, we observed a selective CGRP increase in the Trpv1 positive sensory neuron within the nodose ganglion, while neurons of dorsal root ganglion origin were not comparably engaged. To directly test whether vagal sensory neurons are required for the memory phenotype, we selectively transected the anterior vagal trunk, denervating the anterior gastric wall. Indeed, when we introduced our target neutrophils, those subcutaneous tumors significantly became resistant to immune checkpoint blockade, suggesting that our target neutrophils mediate resistance to checkpoint blockade in vivo. To investigate the molecular mechanisms, we carried out pathway analysis using differentially expressed genes and then crossed the species to identify conserved activation of the pathways.And we found that inflammation-related pathways were highly upregulated in our target neutrophils. And further computation analysis implicated IL-1 receptor pathway as a key mechanism. To explore this possibility, we initiated co-culture of our target neutrophils with activated CD8 T cells in the presence or absence of CD1 receptor blockade. Indeed, immune suppression mediated by our target neutrophils were significantly reduced following IL-1 receptor inhibition. To test the relevance in vivo, we developed intraosseous prostate cancer and treated the cohort with immune checkpoint blockade in the presence or absence of IL-1 receptor antagonist. Consistent with human data, immune checkpoint blockade alone showed minimal efficacy, shown in blue. And IL-1 receptor inhibition also didn't show significant impact. However, when we combined these together, tumor growth significantly reduced, suggesting that IL-1 receptor blockade can enhance immune checkpoint blockade efficacy in intraosseous prostate cancer. Lastly, to investigate clinical perspective, we analyzed a published symposium consortium data, including bone biopsies. We stratified the patients using our mature neutrophil signature scores, and we found the elevated target neutrophil signature scores are highly associated with reduced survival, shown in gray versus red. Moreover, our target neutrophil signature scores also significantly correlate with increased immune suppression, as well as inflammation-mediated immune suppression, suggesting that our preclinical findings well align with those patient perspective. In summary, our lab has identified a distinct mature neutrophil expressing elevated IL-1 beta transcript in prostate cancer bone metastases. These neutrophils are functionally immunosuppressive, and the blockade of inflammatory signals, particularly IL-1 receptor, enhance the efficacy of these therapeutic options. An elevated IL-1 beta high mature neutrophil signature scores correlate with inferior survival. With that, I'd like to thank Dr. Larry Fong for his unwavering support and mentorship, and I thank our lab members and longstanding collaborators. And last but not least, I thank our funding sources, particularly Prostate Cancer Foundation, for supporting this presentation. Thank you for listening and happy to take questions. Yeah. I have a question. Is it black and white, SPP1 macrophages under the skin or orthotopically work, and then IL-1 beta neutrophils work in the bone and there is no role for SPP macrophages there? Yes. So the question, if I understand correctly, whether SPP1 high Macs are more restricted to primary tumors, whereas our target neutrophils are limited to the bone metastases. Am I understanding correctly? Yes. So other metastatic sites need to be further explored when I compare primary tumors versus bone metastases. Although I found multiple neutrophil subpopulations, I couldn't find these IL-1 beta high mature neutrophils in primary tumors, suggesting that those neutrophils, at least in the context of prostate cancer, may be more limited to bone metastases compared to other sites. Thank you. Please. Hi, I'm Amy Leslie. I'm from Stanford. And because we're talking prostate cancer, we got to talk about AR. And so thinking back to Amy Moran's and Felix Swings' paper on how enzalutamide and targeting AR changes the immune microenvironment and activates MHC-1, how do you think that recapitulates in terms of AR positive and AR negative and how that affects the immunosuppressive microenvironment, especially in terms of neutrophils? Are they affected by the AR signaling access or not? That's a great question, and it needs to be determined, at least for SPP1 macrophages. When I looked into AR expression in those macrophage populations and across the myeloid populations, their transcriptional expressions were quite marginal, suggesting that they may not be highly impacted by AR. But in terms of IL-1 beta mature neutrophils, I haven't done that analysis or experiment yet. So, thank you for the great question. Thanks. Mm-hmm. So conditioning with... Over to this mic. Tony Letai, NCI. Conditioning with cytotoxic chemotherapy is generally found to be necessary to have an effective CAR T cell treatment. It's often considered that this cytotoxic therapy is necessary for lymphocyte reduction. Do you think instead it could be an important effect is myeloid cell reduction? So if I received the question correctly, so whether these- I'm just saying we always give cytotoxic chemotherapy- Mm-hmm. ... to condition people before they get CAR T cells. Yes. And if we don't do that, they don't work well. Mm-hmm. Typically, it's thought that we need to give that chemo to do lymphoreduction, lymphodepletion. Mm-hmm. Is it possible, based on your findings- Mm-hmm ... that myeloid depletion is every bit as important as lymphodepletion, and that we're actually doing myeloid depletion with some of these chemotherapy regimens? Well, as a myeloid cell immunologist, not all myeloid populations are bad. During the disease progression, myeloid cells are reprogrammed into suppressive phenotypes. So I am relatively against the concept of broad ablation. I would rather more focus on how to reprogram bad myeloid populations into initially good, as part of innate immunity, myeloid populations. But I don't have experimental evidence, so I cannot say this confidently. But I think ablating myeloid cells could be playing a role there. Thank you for the question. Maybe I was just going to comment on this last question. I think one of the things we've seen, like even with checkpoint inhibition, actually, most of the efficacy that we see is in combination with chemotherapy. And I think for many folks studying immunotherapies, that's always been a bit of a conundrum. People think about potentially debulking the tumors, but there may be a myeloid reset that is associated with that. It may be a blunt tool to do that, but it's a provocative idea. Yes. Agreed. So prostate cancer isn't the only cancer that metastasizes to the bone. Breast cancer patients often have this happen. Do you think that what you're observing is restricted to prostate cancer, or would we expect some of these changes in, say, breast cancer? Yes. So, I would say the enrichment of our target neutrophils may not be restricted to prostate cancer. However, relative recent articles suggested that other subsets of neutrophils, inflammatory neutrophils expressing chitinase, particularly in the context of triple negative breast cancer. Phils may not be restricted, but it's not frequent or observed in at least bone trophic breast cancer. Okay. Thank you. So I'm charged with providing a summary, and I will be blessedly brief. I think we've heard some incredibly good talks, very exciting and future-directed, I think. And what impresses me the most is, even though this session was entitled "Microenvironmental Determinants," which is true, I'm struck by the systemic nature of the talks that we heard today in terms of how things like obesity, the nerve, brain stress, the microbiome, sleep deprivation, all of these clearly systemic events, inflammation, change from primary tumors to metastatic tumors, are affecting the tumor microenvironment, and I think that this has really opened up far more ideas than we originally thought of when we think about cancer hallmarks. There is going to be some great additions from the system, and I'm particularly intrigued myself with psychological stress and the role of nerves. But I'm impressed today with the incredible presentations that we saw on a variety of other factors as well. So I hope you all take home some new ideas and think about the systemic nature and control of the tumor microenvironment. And thanks to all the speakers. I'm really impressed with the quality of the presentations. We both are very happy with what we learned, and I hope you are too. So enjoy the rest of the evening, and thanks to all our speakers.

It's my pleasure to be the chair for this session, which is on single-cell multi-omic technologies to understand genotype and phenotype relationships. And I'll kick things off with the first talk, and that'll be followed by Charles Gewirtz and Andrew Attie. I don't have any disclosures that are relevant to the stuff that I'm talking about today, but I just wanted to mention some of the SABs that I serve on, just to be transparent. So first I'll talk about some of our efforts to develop single-cell DNA and RNA sequencing methods to understand how mutations and copy number alterations lead to phenotypic changes in cancer cells. Chuck will be giving the second talk on high-content single-cell multiomics to resolve molecular determinants of cancer cell phenotypes. Chuck has been working in the single-cell DNA field for quite a long time on hematopoietic cancers and has founded a company, BioScribe, which many people use and collaborate with these days. And then Andrew's going to give the third talk on advances in single-cell DNA methylation and multi-omic technologies analysis. And Andrew's really a pioneer in technology development, especially around combinatorial indexing methods and studying epigenomics both in cancer and in normal development and neurological systems. So we have a really great lineup of talks today. I'm excited to hear from all of them. So just to introduce the topic a little bit, this is a PubMed search I did for single-cell sequencing papers. It's a field that's just been growing tremendously over the years. It's a very common practice in research today, and there's a severely outdated analysis I did of papers in the field from 2015, but I think they're still about correct today. The cancer field is still a very large one where these technologies are being applied a lot, as well as fields like neuroscience, developmental biology, and other areas like immunology. So one of the limitations for single-cell technologies is that although many of them have been commercialized now, we have great methods to do single-cell DNA sequencing, especially copy number analysis, but also to look at mutations. We have great methods to do single-cell RNA sequencing that are scalable, high throughput, 10x genomics, also combinatorial indexing methods. And many of these have been commercialized now as well, Pars Bio, Scale Bio as well, and even great methods to do single-cell epigenomics, DNA methylation, ATAC sequencing, CUT&Tag methods. Most of these are unimodal. There's a few now that have been commercialized, like there's a DNA and ATAC-- Sorry, RNA and ATAC method from 10x Genomics. But the majority of methods are unimodal, and they do great. But that's a limitation because a lot of times we do want to understand how these modalities relate to each other and lead to biological phenomenon. So I just wanted to brainstorm a little bit about some of the questions we can ask if we have really great multimodal technologies, and the biology that we can study with them, especially in cancer. So one of the first ones is really just understanding the central dogma of biology. How do things like mutations and copy number changes result in changes in the transcriptome or the epigenome, affect protein translation and protein abundance, and then ultimately affect the phenotype of the cell? Another one is really to understand the relationship between the genotype and the phenotype. And so how genetic alterations like mutations and copy number can lead to changes in the cell's proliferation, properties, the cancer hallmarks like EMT or invasion, hypoxia migration. And so really if we can get multiple measurements from the same cell at scale, we can understand these relationships. Another important question has to do with cancer evolution, and we know that we can reconstruct genetic lineages of cancer cells and understand how different subclones evolve in the tumor over time. But a real question is whether these phenotypes that we just mentioned in cancer, are they encoded by the genetics or which ones are plastic? We know things like EMT, for example, doesn't have a lot of known genetic mutations or copy number alterations. And so with this type of data, you can reconstruct lineages, map phenotypes onto those lineages, and understand about plasticity in cancer. Another important question is to understand kind of cis and trans impacts of genetic alterations on things like gene expression. In other words, when you have a copy number gain or loss or even a mutation, how does it impact the genes in those regions, and how does it also impact genes across the genome? And how can that affect regulation that affects the phenotype of the cell? And so by looking at things like subclonal alterations in cancer, you can start to get and study at some of these relationships. Another one is understanding cells of origin in cancer. So in many cancers, we don't actually know what the cell of origin is. It's usually an epithelial cell, or in sarcomas, it might be another type of cell. But with these methods, we can link the programs of the cells directly to their genetic profiles, and that can teach us a lot about cells of origin. In breast tissues, we have three different types of epithelial cells, luminal cells that form the lumen inside, the myepithelial cells around the outside. And there's big questions about whether these give rise to ER positive or negative breast cancers, which are the two main subtypes. And a final question that I think we can address here is are there DNA alterations in non-cancer cells? In other words, can you acquire mutations, copy number events in cells like stromal cells or immune cells, and can they also help promote a cancer progression? This is also very understudied in the cancer field. There was a nice paper by Fuqiao Tang's group not too long ago showing that fibroblasts in colorectal cancer often have this chromosome 7 amplification across patients. And they suggested that that might contribute to more of a CAF-like phenotype that promotes cancer progression. But for most cancers, we really don't know whether these alterations exist or not and whether they promote cancer progression.So, some of the first techniques that were described to look at DNA and RNA in a cell, which I'll talk about a lot in my presentation today, included things like GNt-seq. This was by Thierry Voet's group, and DR-seq from Alex van Oudenaarden. These important studies showed that it's technically feasible to measure both modalities from a cell, but they were quite difficult to perform. GNt-seq, you have to physically separate DNA and RNA from a cell before amplification. DR-seq, the bar coding is quite difficult. So they are low throughput. They were expensive and very high costs, but they were pioneering for the time. This is really around the time that the first single-cell DNA and RNA methods were being described. There have been another series of papers, work from Fuchou Tang. Also more work from Thierry Voet's group. Also DEFENSEC from Peter Sims' group, and some methods like GOT from Dan Lundahl's group. And these are all methods that allow you to look at DNA and RNA simultaneously in cells. They still have some challenges. For example, DEFENSEC doesn't completely lyse chromatin, so the complexity of the DNA is low. GOT is really looking at mutations in transcriptomes, so that's affected a lot by expression, RNA editing. And these methods are still relatively low throughput. So there's still a lot of work to be done here, I think, to be able to scale this up. And so we really want to be able to scale these co-measurements up, have better high-quality DNA library complexity that you can look at, better genomic resolution, and then streamlined protocols that you can perform in the same reactions or tubes so that they can be adapted for micro droplets or nanowells. In my own lab, over the years, we've developed a lot of unimodal technologies. So, starting with some of the early single-cell DNA sequencing methods that use things like DOP-PCR, methods that use things like MDA to look at mutations across the genome at base pair resolution. We've also developed some methods to do single-cell RNA sequencing. And then more recently, we've been using tagmentation chemistries to look at single-cell DNA alterations. But they've all been unimodal so far. More recently, we've tried to really develop multimodal methods, and so we have a few methods developed now that are in papers that are published or coming out. One of them is WELL-DAC that looks at DNA in ATAC. It does essentially two rounds of tagmentation, one with the chromatin ATAC, one with it removed. This is now on bioRxiv. I won't talk about this today, but you're welcome to look at this paper. Another paper called WELL-DR or WELL DNA and RNA sequencing. This was published in "Cell," and this is one of the first methods we published to do the chemistries. It's a DNA first chemistry, so we do tagmentation of DNA initially, followed by the RNA chemistry. And today, I'll talk a lot about a new method called ARCH-DR or archival DNA and RNA sequencing. And this is a new method where we can look at copy number alterations, mutations, and RNA simultaneously in thousands of cells at the same time. So I won't talk about the WELL-DR study too much because it's already published. It does allow you to scale up things quite a bit. In nanowells, you can look at thousands of cells, usually about 1,800 to 2,000 cells per experiment. It did have very good genomic DNA resolution. The RNA quality, I would say, is moderate, and so that's something that we've been improving on a lot. But it requires fresh cells, so that's quite a limitation for clinical samples. It can't really look at mutations. And yeah, as I mentioned, the RNA quality was kind of moderate. So, today, I'll be talking about the new method, ARCH-DR, and how we apply this to study esophageal cancer. And this is a collaboration and work that was done through Rui Yi, a postdoc in my laboratory, Kyler Wang, former postdoc, now a PI in Shanghai, and Steven Lin, who is an oncologist in the Radiation Oncology Department. So esophageal cancer or EAC is one of the most common forms of esophageal cancer, esophageal adenocarcinoma. The major risk factors are acid reflux that you get, as well as smoking, alcohol use, and there's about 21,000 new cases per year in the US. The five-year survival rate is only 20%, so we really need better treatment modalities here. And, interestingly, it has a much higher incidence in China, Iran, and Central Asia. These cancers are interesting from a genomic perspective because they have lots of extrachromosomal DNA. We also see more intratumor heterogeneity and aneuploidy in these cancers and many other types. And there have been some driver genes identified, including things like CDKN2A, KRAS, ERBB2, TP53, EGFR, and PIK3CA. So the questions we're interested in studying here is really what's the cell of origin for EAC, and is there switching of cell lineages during cancer and clonal evolution? Which are the ecDNAs that arise, and how are they inherited through the genetic lineages? And which driver and copy number and mutational events lead to gene expression differences? And finally, are different phenotypes inherited in the genetic lineages, and which are plastic? So, some of the technical challenges then is that this extensive intratumor heterogeneity exists, and so, we need to use single-cell DNA methods. We want high genomic resolution, so we can detect really focal events that are ecDNAs that might only be a few hundred kilobases. We need a co-assay method to look at DNA and RNA, and we want to be able to link the cellular epithelial lineages and identities to the genotypes. And we also want to be able to look at frozen and FFPE materials because fresh materials are not always available and don't have long-term clinical outcome data available. And we want to look at mutations and copy number events. So in this method that we've developed, archival DNA and RNA sequencing, we can look at RNA species, copy number alterations, and mutations all at the same time in the same cells. We've done a lot of work to look at QC metrics, and we've shown that things like overdispersion is very low, similar to our previous methods and things like DLP from Saurabh Jha's group. The breadth of coverage is very high, so similar to what we see in our unimodal methods for single-cell DNA sequencing.And for our RNA-seq, we see very high gene counts, which is great, higher than what we see for 10x version three, and much better than our older Well DR chemistry or what we see with Defense EQ. This is just an example of a human tumor sample where we took the same tissue, we made a cell suspension, we snap-froze the tissue, and we embedded it in FFPE, and then we ran the same assay on all three samples. And at least at the cell type level, you can see that the cell types overlap very well by the fixation method or preservation method, and it suggests that we're still getting a really great RNA quality from these tissues, even despite fixing them or freezing them. So in this study, we looked at 12 patients. We dissociated the fresh tissues, we ran ArcDR, and then we were able to look at RNA copy number and whole exome mutations at the same time. We looked at about 34,000 cells in total with these co-measurements and investigated some of the questions that I mentioned earlier. Just looking at the RNA data, you can see that we typically see that the patients have patient-specific clusters. That's largely due to copy number alterations, which create gene dosage effects since every patient has kind of a different overall global transcriptome profile. In the other cell types, we see that they overlap quite a lot between patients, so that's good. So first, we wanted to look at the different cell lineages. And so in esophageal cancer, the three major lineages are esophageal, there's actually two separate ones, gastric, and then intestinal, we have three different types. We leveraged some data from the Human Atlas projects for the GI as a reference, so we can really distinguish all these different lineages very well. And then in our own data, we saw that the patients clustered a lot by the lineages, which were different across different patients, as shown over here. And this plot over here shows you that within one patient, there typically isn't a single lineage. You see one patient will often have multiple lineages that are present. And I'll show that in a few slides after this as well. So interestingly, when we look at copy number data from a single patient, this is one of the patients here, we can look at all genomic alterations and identify subclones in this heat map. In this particular patient, we had a separate subclone that was very different, didn't share any of the copy number alterations and really looked like an independent lineage. Now, when we looked at the mutations, actually found that there were a few shared variants, although that lineage down here has a lot of mutations that are different as well. And in a subclonal tree, you can see that that divergent lineage or independent lineage was kind of out here, an outbranch, and it had gastric epithelial cell type, really looking like a different cell type. On the other hand, the other subclones were over here, and they have kind of intermixed lineages, as indicated in the colors here, some of the intestinal populations over here, and some of the esophageal populations over here. But interestingly, when we see this in patients, there are about three or so. When there's a divergent genetic lineage, it typically has a different cell of origin as well. But as you can see, most of the subclones have multiple lineages associated, suggesting that there's pretty high cellular plasticity here for the epithelial markers. Next, we looked at extrachromosomal DNA events, and in EAC, we see quite a lot of these. The easiest thing is if you look at this line plot down here, you see these very thin lines. These are high copy number events. Interestingly, in this patient, there were two separate subclones. One subclone had high EGFR amplification, the other one had high ERBB2 amplification, and that was indicated in the lineages here. These subclones over here have ERBB2, these have EGFR. If we look at gene expression, it correlates very well. The subclones on the top have high ERBB2, and they have low EGFR. And on the other lineage, they have low ERBB2, high EGFR. This is actually important because in the ecDNA field, it's still unclear how these things are inherited in genetic lineages and whether it kind of follows what you would expect for a kind of mitotic inheritance and segregation, or whether it's just random dispersion. And so we really see that it does follow the segregation pattern. We use methods like Amplicon Architect to reconstruct and assemble the reads across the subclones and show that these are really circular species that exist at a high copy number level in the cells. Interestingly, we looked at the gene expression for different ecDNAs and overall across all the patients. And we found that for ecDNAs, the gene expression really saturates around 20 copies or so. You kind of see this linear increase with copy number as you go from zero to 20. But once you approach 20 copies, it's fairly flat. And so that allows us to understand and interpret that perhaps cells just can't tolerate really, really high levels of ecDNA or expression. We also looked more globally at the correlation of gene expression and copy number events. And we found that overall, there's about 51% of the genes that when you have a copy number gain or a copy number loss, follow that pattern. And there's about 50% genes that don't agree with increased expression or lower expression in copy number regions. And based on that, we can classify genes into dosage sensitive or dosage insensitive. And it's interesting to look then at a lot of the EAC driver genes. Some genes like CDKN2A really has this linear increase and gene dosage relationship, as well as KDM6A, another event that's common in EAC. But other genes, even ones that you in other cancers you know correlate a lot with expression, in EAC like MYC doesn't seem to correlate with copy number and increased expression levels. And that's also true for ARID1A. And so we can classify all the genes based on whether the data is sensitive or insensitive. Next, we can also look at mutations. And so mutations, it's also very interesting to understand the relationship with gene expression. Overall, these were the variants that we found and looked at. We found that about 20% or so correlate with differences that happen in gene expression. And so we're showing you some examples here. So interestingly, if you look at P53, we compare wild type subclones versus mutant subclones. The ones with the mutations have much higher gene expression levels. But if you look at copy number in EAC, actually, there's no difference.CDKN2A as well, when you find a mutation, there's a very high difference in gene expression. And then SMAD4, this is an inactivating loss of function mutation. And so when you have this one, you see that actually the expression goes way down, whereas there's no difference in copy number. So overall, we found that about 20% of somatic mutations actually had an impact on gene expression, which is different, of course, than what we see for copy number. Finally, we looked at these questions around genetic hardwiring and plasticity in the lineages. And so what we do is we take all the single cell profiles. We can take a consensus and look at different subclones as shown over here, and then we can reconstruct a copy number lineage. This is with a method called MEDIC2, which is based on copy number events. And it has a bifurcation here into these two major lineages, and then within those, there's differences in the subclones. And so we found that some genes like MDM2 are very heritable, so you see them only express high in one lineage. This is MYC over here. It's also expressed mostly in one lineage, but other genes like cyclin E1, you can see that it's expressed across the lineages. And so we would call this a more plastic type of gene. So we can do this across all the patients. So we can look at pathways now and signatures that follow the genetic lineage or are independent of it. And so we find some pathways and signatures that seem to be very genetically heritable. In this case, I'm showing you this example of wound healing, where you can see it's very constrained to the genetic lineages across multiple patients, and following here, also this lineage. And other phenotypes, things like mitoses. We also saw DNA repair. These look to be much more plastic, and so you can see that they exist across multiple lineages. It's high over here as well and here as well across the lineage. And so, those seem to be much more plastic or maybe more transient programs that occur within lineages and are not always tied directly to genetic events. And then finally, we looked at the non-cancer cells. And so, in this study, we were looking across all the cell types that are essentially not the tumor cells or aneuploid cells. And we found that there are chromosome X losses, and they're very common, mostly in the T cells. We don't see those in other cell types. And of course, we looked at this mostly in the female patients, where there's two intact chromosomes. Interestingly, when you lose the X chromosome, there's really no difference in expression. That's probably because you're losing that inactivated allele that's been inactivated by Xist. In contrast, for the Y chromosome loss, when we see that male patients lose the Y chromosome, there's a big difference in the expression of genes. And we can also map both of those events very granularly to different cell states. We did this in T cells, and so we see some different distributions across the T cell populations, but actually Y and X are occurring pretty much across all of the T cells. And I think the loss of Y chromosome is very interesting. There's been more attention to this paid recently in the cancer field, showing that sometimes loss of Y chromosome can affect cancer progression and also T cells in patients. So, to summarize this data, we developed a high-throughput method that's compatible with fresh, frozen, and FFPE materials. It's pretty scalable. We can look at thousands of cells. We find that even though EACs have this clonal origin, so at the genetic level, they really start from just a single cell. However, they're able to switch, and they're very plastic during progression in terms of the lineages they represent from the expression level. ecDNAs are common. They're segregated, usually in genetic lineages. And we see that they saturate in expression around 20 copies. And about 51% of the genes are dosage sensitive, so they correlate with gene copy number, but many genes are also not. And about 20% of mutations result in expression changes that we can see in the single cells. And so the EAC patients have both plastic and genetically inherited genes. And as we look at more patients, I think this will give us a better understanding of events that are caused by genetic differences versus non-genetic differences. And just on my last slide here and to set the stage for the next talks. Really, I think the ultimate goal here is to be able to measure many modalities from single cells. Hopefully, in the next five to 10 years, we'll get there. This is a fast-moving area. So in addition to DNA and RNA, which I mostly talked about today, we'd like to be able to look at epigenetics, look at methylation, ATAC, Hi-C conformations, certainly protein abundance modifications as well. And I think what's missing a lot too right now is imaging data. So if we have ways to do high cellular imaging, we can also get morphometrics, look at subcellular differences as well, and to be able to do this all modalities at high scale. And then we can really learn a lot about cancer phenotypes, cancer hallmarks, how these things ultimately interact together to affect cancer and cancer progression, and then how we can target that to improve cancer treatment and diagnosis. So I think I'll end it there. And a big thanks to everyone in my lab that did this work. I especially want to recognize the work from Rui Yi, who did a lot of the technology development here, Kyler Wang, and our collaborators in the clinic, especially Stephen Lin for this project. And I think I have a little bit of time, so I'll take some questions. Thank you. Thank you for the presentation. John Schatz, University of Miami. I'm wondering, when you looked at the non-tumor cells, if you did any analyses of the state of the microenvironment relative to the tumor genotype/phenotype relationships that you established? For example, loss of antigen presentation machinery leading to depletion of CD8 T cells, that sort of thing. Yeah. So with this RNA data, we can look at all these cell states in quite granular detail. And so I was just showing some examples for the X and Y chromosome losses that occurred. And-We see a lot of changes at the RNA level, obviously. So, for fibroblasts, we see a lot of CAFs in tumor, in endothelial cells, we saw a lot of tumor endothelial cells. But we don't always see genetic events that are associated with those phenotypes. So far, I think, at least the data we have in EAC doesn't show a strong correlation with those tumor-associated cell states and genetic events that we have. But it may be cancer type specific. Certainly, the work Fuchou Tang did in colon cancer showed that a very common gain on chromosome 7, I believe it was, leads to CAF states in those cancers. So I think we have to look at a lot of cancers and try to understand, and see if there are genetic events that also drive things over in the stroma or the immune cells. Thank you. Andrew? Hey, Nick. The gene dosage work is super cool. Do you see instances where you have, in some patients, gene dosage sensitivity and then others where it's not? So, like a patient-specific, whether that gene is affected by dosage. Yeah. So those are really interesting questions, and I think what you're getting at is differences potentially at the epigenetic layers that might be regulating those things, knowing your background. But, yes, no, we try to really classify things across patients. So there was also a lot of patient variability, too. I think we're missing the extra layer. It'd be great to look at methylation or ATAC data that could help us understand those 50% of transcripts that are not correlated. When I try to think about things more longitudinally, I imagine that there's a lot of aneuploidy occurring early on in progression, and so at that time, probably gene dosage is very highly correlated, I think, with the copy number events. But cells have to respond. You can't tolerate thousands of genes being upregulated or downregulated. And so I think that's where the epigenome comes in and regulates things. And so by the time we see the tumor, which of course is after millions and millions of cells, I think there's a lot of biology that's already happened to try to do gene regulation and get these cancer cells into their high fitness programs that lead to the expansion and everything. But yeah, thanks for the question. Thank you. Over there. Sandy Markowitz at Case Western. There's a GitHub with lots of tutorials, and the goal of this was really to make it a kind of one-stop shop for single-cell DNA methylation analysis. Our goal here was to get the analysis tools in the hands of the biologist that's doing the data. So to that end, we really put a lot of work into the visualization tools so that biologists can get their raw data, take it through this workflow, and start to look at the genes of interest and understand the biology of the methylomes. I like these plots in the middle here. There's PBMCs on the left where the rows are the different cell types, and then brain on the right. And the blue are these hypomethylated regions. And you can see there's high cell type specificity, and these black boxes are the differentially methylated regions that were called. So it's a really nice way to visualize and interact with the data. And I think it's really important to be able to develop those tools to really allow the biologists to really be digging into the data. Using AMETHYST and SKI-MAPv3, I'm going to touch on a vignette here. And I mentioned non-CG methylation is not present in most cell types. That's true, except in neurons. So I know this is a cancer meeting, but this is a cool vignette where seminal work by Joe Ecker showed that when you're born, your neurons, you actually don't have any of this non-CG methylation, but through the first several years of life up to adolescence, it actually accumulates in your neurons. So it's this postnatal maturation of your neurons during this peak window of synaptogenesis. And we really wanted to study this. So in mice, this corresponds to P7 to P28. So we took these regions in the mouse brain, five microdissected regions, sorted for neurons and profiled them using our SKI-MAPv3 technology. And we were able to produce this really comprehensive atlas of postnatal neuronal maturation. So this is about 240,000 high-coverage single-cell methylomes, where we're able to show all of these branching lineages of early neurons and then differentiating out into these very specific neuronal subtypes. And just a vignette that I think highlights how you can use this single-cell methylation data that's applicable across all sorts of tissue types and certainly cancer, where there's a lot of evolution in cell state dynamics. As an example of looking at the pseudo temporal ordering of the progression of methylomes in this branch from MGE-derived GABAergic neurons. So these are inhibitory neurons branching either into parvalbumin or somatostatin. And you can see here's a couple genes here where in the parvalbumin branch, we're getting dramatic increase in methylation as we go through pseudoage.With a lot less in somatostatin. And conversely, here at this gene, we get a clear hypomethylated window that is not the case in progressive increasing in methylation in the other branch. So you get clear branch-specific methylation patterns. And these concepts can be applied across any dynamic system. And we have lots of other kind of really novel, exciting discoveries in this that really get into the neuroscience, but I'll leave that for those of you that are interested in neuroscience and can look up the preprint, which will be coming out hopefully in the next few weeks or so. So finally, I wanted to touch on how we've taken this to the multi-omics space. So we have our process for doing our nucleosome disruption and taking it through combinatorial indexing with tagmentation for single-cell whole genome sequencing, right? Well, work also by Ryan Mulqueen showed that we can actually tack on this step. It's almost like a freebie processing step for generating Hi-C, which could probably be compatible with Chuck and Nick's technologies too, I would imagine, where you add on this restriction digest and religation, and it allows you to capture 3D chromatin structure. So we showed this is, again, in pancreatic cancer. We can get our single-cell genome plus 3D chromatin, and this is showing the 3D plots here. And we were actually able to identify a translocation. So this is a balanced chromosomal rearrangement. So you can't pick it up from copy number alterations and copy number profiling, but it's a subclone-specific balanced translocation. And indeed, we can apply this to methylation. So this is actually data from a very small snippet of a very large data set on mouse embryo development, where we can take a single cell and look at our 3D chromatin structure. But we also get our whole methylome profiles, and that's what this UMAP is looking at the methylation. And then our chimeric reads give us this 3D structure. And where we're really driving this, the ability to look at the 3D structure in Hi-C from single cells is low because it's not super high coverage. But what you can do is aggregate over these methylation clusters and really capture that. And then lastly is coupling ATAC with methylation. So first ATAC with whole genome. We did this stepwise tagmentation. So we found if you do initial tagmentation with one index complex and then do the nucleosome disruption, and then do another tagmentation with a different index, you actually get whole genome sequencing where a subset of those reads are actually tagged with a different index that allows you to get chromatin accessibility as well as whole genome profiling. And also if you use a different set of indexes, you can actually multiplex different samples together, which is kind of nice because you often don't want thousands of cells for a single sample when you have to sequence really deep for whole genome sequencing. So it allows sample multiplexing. And in general, though, the copy number profiles are a little more noisy than what you would get. I don't know if you're seeing that too, Nick, with your dual tagmentation. Maybe not, because you're doing it where you're isolating the DNA fully after. But we do see more noise. And then same with the ATAC, we get a little more noise than the assay on its own. But we can also apply this to DNA methylation, where we're profiling DNA methylation and ATAC from the same cells. And this was in our publication on the SkyMapv3 approach. We were able to look at nice high-quality ATAC profiles for our neuronal subtypes, as well as methylation from the same cells. Slightly less quality for each of these compared to the assay on their own, but still pretty good and able to do de novo analysis on each of these modalities. But typically, we're using this in a bridging sense. So in new data that we're working on in collaboration with Ted Brown and Geronimo Dimja, we're working towards a large AML project, where we can look at DNA methylation and ATAC. This is the co-assay. If you analyze it for methylation, we get nice cell type separation. Same with ATAC. Thank you. Yeah. Sorry. But we can get nice profiles for each of these modalities on their own. And this is actually a small subset of data from human hematopoiesis, where we've got these different lineages that are branching out from bone marrow samples. There's 140,000 cells, where about 8% of these are actually done with the co-assay. So we have a subset of these cells that are actually co-assayed and have that ATAC signal as well. And we can use this to integrate with other unimodal ATAC data. So it allows us to do that bridging. And we're starting to expand this into bridging with RNA as well. And with that, I want to thank those involved and take any questions. A simple technical question. Will the methods work on frozen tissue, or does it need to be fresh tissue? What's really nice with the methylation is that the first step is fixing cells. So it works with fresh, it works with frozen, it works with banked fixed cells. We haven't done FFPE yet. But I imagine there are ways you could certainly get it to work. It's really robust to input, which is one of the things that's really nice about it. Yeah. I'm kind of fascinated by the non-CpG methylation. Yeah. Have you looked more broadly in your data sets? Could things that were neural crest-derived or somehow related to the nervous system or maybe just other cells within tissues have non-canonical? So there's a great study on that from Joe Ecker's group. It's, I think, in bioRxiv. I don't know if it's published in full yet, but they look at that. It's really, really low levels in other tissues. I think it's hard to delineate between just off-targetMethylation. So, the DNMTs, it's DNMT3A that does it in the brain, and that's also active in a lot of tissues. And if it can do non-CG methylation, chances are if it's really active doing CG methylation, it can do some off-target CH methylation maybe. But the levels are very, very low in other cell types, except embryonic stem cells, where it's a very different patterning than in the brain, and that's a cell type that's turning over, and we have no idea what is going on with that. So that's another area that we're starting to explore. Okay, cool. Andrew, really great talk. I was wondering if you could tell us a little bit more about, I guess, using methylation data to separate out cell types and cell states and when you show the data on the brain, it looks beautiful, like you have very differentiated cell types and they separate very well. But then I think the last slide or two you showed, you can see that- Yeah ... cell types are really close together. You can still distinguish what they are, but there's a lot of overlap, and it's something I think we've been struggling with a little bit too with breast cancer type of data where it's actually quite hard to distinguish cell types. And I was wondering any ideas why that is and- Mm-hmm ... whereas at the RNA level, it's usually very straightforward. And strategies, I guess, to choose subset specific markers, do more supervised analysis or... Yeah, absolutely. So a couple things. One, in the brain, we can leverage that CH methylation, which is a really, really powerful high information content kind of modality. It's almost like a separate modality. With CG specific cell types, yeah, it's more challenging. In this one, this is a progression. This is actually not the most up-to-date UMAP, and we actually have more sequencing on these cells now. And it separates a bit better. But we do expect a continuum in this context. And we are capturing what we expect. But yeah, it's definitely challenging. I think a couple things. One, we need to get better at some of the computational tools to address this. A tool like MethScan I think we've seen works really well. We have our AMETHYST tool, but the dimensionality reduction is just one small step, and we actually encourage people to use a variety of tools to see what works best with their data. But I think there's more that can be pushed forward in that space. And it is relatively sparse data, so accommodating that I think is important. And then, yeah, doing the cell typing, I know that's a challenge. One of the challenges there is that a lot of the genes that are great marker genes for RNA might not be great marker genes for methylation. And the best strategy I have is look at the genes that define the lineage and if they're lineage-defining as opposed to where that gene gets maybe activated earlier on in the lineage specification. Those tend to be more indicative. But it's a variety of factors. But yeah, it's more challenging. It's a newer modality. I remember going through all these headaches with single-cell ATAC-seq when that was new. But now that's much more straightforward, and I think we're moving towards that now. Thanks. You mentioned that the front end of this is the 10X ATAC-seq technology, which is incorporated into their multi-ome technology where you get ATAC-seq plus expression. I'm wondering if you've been able to do expression plus methylation at the single-cell level. Yeah. So we have some ways where we're working towards that. To get it to work with the multi-ome, there's potentially ways to do that. One of the challenges, doing the nucleosome disruption well can really ruin your RNA. So you have to find a balance there. There's the Peterson's, the DEFENSEQ, they do that with RNA and whole genome where they capture that co-assay where they do a nucleosome disruption. It's one of the other ones that we had worked on a long time ago, and it's trickier, but it's possible. The one we like to use for methylation, it tends to destroy the RNA, so it's not really compatible with something like the multi-ome kit. But it is compatible with the combinatorial indexing. If we have some upfront processing of the RNA in certain ways, we can retain it. So we're working towards that, and we do have some datasets where we have it, but it's not as robust as we would like right now. Thank you. Thanks. All right. Thanks, everyone. Let's give the speakers another round of applause. And that ends our session. If there are any extra questions, just come up here and talk to us. Thanks.
