Hello everyone. Welcome to ACR session on agentic AI as the cancer researcher autonomous discovery in oncology. AI agents are really an exciting new type and class of artificial intelligence systems that can contribute to cancer research as partners to human researchers. These systems can plan multi-step analysis, potentially retrieve, organize cancer research and clinical data sets, use various kinds of tools and analysis, and adapt their actions based on human feedback and experimental results. And so in this role, they can help researchers explore large hypothesis spaces, gather and connect evidence across different data sets, and support iterative cycles of analysis and experimentation. In this session in particular, we will examine agentic AI systems in cancer research. We will also discuss some of key challenges for their use in practice, including how to apply agents to real-world data for clinical trials, what regulatory considerations are necessary for autonomous AI discoveries, and translational research aspects of agentic AI with a focus on pathology and a few other data modalities and translational aspects of agentic AI in cancer research. The first speaker will be Dr. Daniela Bittermann from Brigham and Women's Hospital. Dr. Bittermann is physician scientist at the Dana-Farber Cancer Institute in Boston and Brigham and Women's Hospital, with unique expertise in AI and natural language processing. Her research is dedicated to incorporating technological advances in AI into intelligent electronic health record systems to improve data-driven cancer care. And in her talk, Dr. Bittermann will focus on late-stage discovery, touching on agents applied to real-world data and clinical trials, and she will also discuss some of regulatory considerations for autonomous AI discoveries as part of her topic. So I'll now welcome Dr. Bittermann to present on agentic AI for clinical development in oncology. Thank you. Thank you so much, Dr. zitnick, and thank you everyone for being here and the opportunity to present. Here are my disclosures. So as likely most people in the audience know, there have been persistent bottlenecks to oncology clinical development. There is a massive amount of investment upfront by biopharmaceutical companies in research and development. But as you go from initial investment to the pre-clinical phase, early phase one, phase two, phase three, you ultimately get to a point where only about 10% of compounds that enter a clinical trial advance to FDA approval. And each time a drug fails to make it successfully from phase two to phase three, we lose an opportunity to improve care for patients. The patients who've enrolled on those trials would not have had the opportunity to be a part of a potentially more successful trial, and all of the investment that went into that one drug ends up being lost because it was diverted away from other potentially promising compounds. And so if we could advance this whole process, improve the efficiency, improve the likelihood that we can either rapidly identify that a drug is unlikely to demonstrate benefit in a phase three trial or improve the efficiency with which we're able to conduct a phase three trial, we'll really accelerate the pace of improving management in cancer care. And so there are multiple bottlenecks that contribute to this process. Here I'm highlighting just a few key points. One is patient selection. We tend to take a fairly blunt approach to identifying cohorts for clinical trials. This is due to limitations in our ability to risk stratify patients based on pre-clinical data and real-world evidence. This leads to diluted signal and limited information to drive go/no-go decisions. If we're able to more precisely select patients, we can potentially run a clinical trial with fewer patients due to improved signal-to-noise ratio. Another challenge is access. Many clinical trials are run at large academic medical centers that don't necessarily reach all of the patients that are treated every day in cancer in the community. If we're able to unlock all of the community sites where the full diversity of cancer patients receive care, we'll have a much broader base to recruit from. Execution is a challenge. It takes multiple weeks to start up a study at a clinical site. Activation and staffing all delay studies and require a lot of resources, which is challenging in an increasingly resource-limited setting. And finally, there's bottlenecks in our ability to rapidly access clinical data, both for real-world evidence generation to guide development decision-making, as well as to proactively and rapidly identify signal for our clinical trials. This is because clinical data are highly fragmented in silos. Patients are treated at many different sites, and it's very difficult to integrate technologies to extract information from EHR warehouses, and get that information that's documented on patients to the clinical monitorsSo there's a lot of potential of AI in general to improve clinical development processes and in particular agentic AI. So I'm just going to take a quick step back and define what I'm talking about when I say agentic AI, because there are multiple different definitions of it. And I'd like to highlight a really wonderful paper by Dr. Truin that goes through the differences between single LLM, single AI, all the way to autonomous agentic workflows. So we're all likely familiar with the standard large language model approach, where a human puts in a query into a large language model. This could be a question, what is a high value drug to proceed to clinical trial? Or it can be, can you tell me what this note says about a patient? And there's a single output. You can use this to answer questions, summarize text, or draft new text. Sometimes you can extend this a little bit further where you have a large language model iteratively interact with a human in a conversational setting, and that human might be able to access tools or instruct the language model to use tools. This can allow a system to perform more complex tasks, but still requires quite a lot of human input and is not fully automated, still presenting challenges with efficiencies. An autonomous LLM agent is where a large language model, or it can be other machine learning models, plans multi-step tasks, execute tasks, iterates, refines, and determines whether or not a tool is needed to be called so that it can explore an environment with agency to answer an input query. This allows these models to solve much more complex tasks, with a lot more clinical nuance, because you can more rapidly embed clinical information into these environments that these agents interact within. So really a high potential for general clinical oncology automation and in particular clinical development. So why is agentic AI particularly exciting for the clinical development workflow? And I think this is because a lot of our challenges is not just challenges with our ability to access data or collect data, but really there are multi-step workflow challenges that require really deep coordination and iteration across many different fragmented systems that hold different data types. As I previously mentioned, clinical data are fragmented, non-standardized, and require a high level of clinical reasoning to reason over effectively. Decisions regarding clinical development must keep pace with a really rapidly evolving biomedical literature base, and relying only on human review makes it challenging to ensure that you're, for example, selecting the most appropriate comparator for your experiments. Clinical development workflows are multi-step inherently and require a lot of coordination, so are a natural fit for agentic AI. And insights to clinical development are not a one-stop kind of, we found this finding, and this is the answer, but it actually triggers timely action. So, for example, you have an insight where you have a patient that's developing early signal of an adverse event. You don't just stop saying this patient's having early signal of adverse event. Ideally, you have an action where the clinical trialist then acts on that adverse event per protocol. Agentic AI can play a lot of roles throughout the clinical development continuum. Here I'm highlighting just a few examples. Agentic AI is really critical to use currently human expertise to define the goals to go after when triggering an agentic investigation into a challenge. Agentic AI can be used to help develop the evidence base to guide clinical development decisions. You can use AI to rapidly assess prior literature of the standard of care and predictors. You can use it to generate real-world evidence, and you can use it to develop biomarkers for better patient selection. That can then go to inform clinical development strategy ranging from what is the optimal trial design, what patient stratification options can be used, what endpoints should be selected, and what's the appropriate regulatory pathway for your clinical trial. Then moving to execution, agents can then take the evidence and strategy and automatically draft a protocol or regulatory submission pre-drafts. Agentic AI in the future with high integration with clinical sites can be used to automate site activation, for example, to automatically help set up EDCs for a given trial. Patient matching has received a lot of attention with agentic AI, and agentic AI can be used to automatically monitor patients for outcomes that need action. All of this can go to inform decision-making about the dosing schedule, eligibility criteria, safety adverse events, and go/no-go decisions to accelerate clinical development. And ideally, all of this works in a cycle where agentic insights then go into inform what is the next evidence that we need to further refine our trial design or further refine our next drug decisions. Now I'm going to quickly go into an example of how my lab has been using agentic AI for one part of this workflow, which is monitoring of adverse events in real time from electronic health records.So a current bottleneck for real-world data abstraction as well as for clinical trial curation is that we currently rely largely on manual abstraction for a lot of the information that's documented in the EHR. This is because all data in the EHR tend to be highly non-standardized, and a lot of it's entered in the clinical notes, which require manual review historically. And it requires providers to pore through large amounts of clinical records to determine what happened to a patient at a given point in time. This is time-intensive, expertise-intensive, costly, and has a high degree of inter-annotator agreement, where two expert oncologists might disagree on whether the same event occurred on a given patient. To address this challenge, we developed an agentic AI system that takes in clinical notes and extracts adverse events, specifically immunotherapy-related adverse events, from those notes. It first determines whether an event is present in a clinical note, grades the severity of the notes according to CTCAE definitions, determines whether that adverse event is attributed to the immunotherapy, and determines the certainty with which that adverse event is attributed to the immunotherapy. This leads to a pipeline that goes from a fully unstructured clinical note that historically would have required human review to structured output in a JSON file that clearly delineates whether an IRE is present, the grade attribution, and the underlying clinical evidence for the attribution. Our system achieved a macro F1 of 0.93. It takes a human 10 minutes to do the careful curation for all adverse events present in a clinical document, and it takes our LLM system two cents to review a note for all this evidence. Because our agentic system is able to extract the underlying text that provides evidence for the adverse event, as well as provide a reasoning summary for why the determination was made, we're able to develop an interactive system that our research staff can use to oversee the system and make edits if needed. Our research staff found that highlighting this text was particularly helpful in guiding their review and saving time in the process. We conducted a randomized user effect study where we randomized clinical research staff to using our agentic system versus manual curation and found that using our system reduced the time needed to curate adverse events by 40%. It led to similar accuracy in adverse event determination compared to an expert oncologist, and I think really importantly, significantly improved the inter-annotator agreement or consistency with which two research staff will agree on the adverse event. So we are making this process more efficient. We're not leading to decrements in accuracy or data quality, and actually we're improving the consistency, so reducing noise in adverse event determinations. So we found this to be really promising, and just as kind of a step back, where could we go from here in terms of using an agentic system, focus on adverse event detection to really better understand the role of adverse event and predict adverse events to guide clinical development. So drawing back from our adverse event extraction system, you can imagine a much broader system that, for example, uses real-world data and AI-assisted literature review to allow us to better anticipate adverse event rates and determine imaging or biomarker-based predictors of adverse event risk to better guide patient selection. This could then inform a strategy into risk-adapted cohorts to improve the signal-to-noise ratio and allowing for a more precise determination of who is most likely to benefit with the fewest risks for a given treatment strategy. Moving on to execution, I think using our system just to extract those adverse events more reliably and faster would really make it easier for clinical sites to run these clinical trials. An agentic workflow could also pre-position adverse event management in the SOPs and allow for continuous monitoring for early intervention of an adverse event to reduce the risk that an early adverse event progresses to a grade three or four or five event. Finally, this could improve decision-making about clinical development. By improving detection of an emerging adverse event signal, you could facilitate grade triggered holds and more precise causality assessment, which is a really persistent challenge in determining the risks and benefits of a new management strategy, especially as patients are treated with many modalities over long periods of time as patients are living longer and longer after their initial cancer diagnosis. Now, there's one really persistent challenge with using large language models in general and agentic systems in particular in any high-risk critical setting and any highly regulated site setting, such as clinical development, of course. Our current standard approaches for evaluating the performance of these large language models largely relies on types of multi-choice question answer exams that can be automatically assessed. You ask a question of an agentic system and give it multiple options to select from, and it can choose the right answer, and then you can calculate the accuracy.The challenge is this does not necessarily reflect the type of real-world applications that we would really want to use these agentic AI systems in. And we don't know if performance in these multi-choice question answer settings really translates to similar performance in real-world applications. Real-world applications, like this example showing here, are often have generative output and rely on faithful reasoning steps across agentic systems and reliable extraction from the correct evidence base. All of that requires a much higher level of coordination of monitoring and benchmarking strategies themselves. Sound scientific judgment and multi-step reasoning abilities are currently not covered by our evaluation strategy, which I think is a really high priority for future research in order to ensure that agentic insights that inform clinical trial design and determinations are fully auditable and reportable when presenting ultimately to regulatory bodies. Now, a lot of focus with large language models and agentic AI systems currently is on retrospective performance on prior data sets. We have models that really do perform impressively well. Like the agentic system I previously showed, it got an F1 of 0.93 that's very, very high sensitivity and positive predictive value for determining and fully phenotyping adverse events documented in EHRs. But that doesn't necessarily mean that these systems are ready to just turn on and use to extract information or provide high-value insights for clinical development. That's because currently the challenge with agentic systems is not the performance of the models, in my opinion. It's all the other work that has to go into making agentic systems a reality. Data integration with agentic systems is super important. You can think of agentic systems like workers using tools on a conveyor belt. The workers need to be able to anticipate what type of data that they are pulling from in order to do their job. If you don't have high-quality data integration, standardization, harmonization, that conveyor belt approach is going to fall apart really rapidly. You need to ensure value to demonstrate the need and return on investment of building the agentic workflows and its surrounding governance approach. Monitoring model drift and data drift, as I previously mentioned, is really important for any highly regulated setting, in particular this, and governance bodies need to be set up to ensure that the ethical approach and safety are being governed in a responsible way. All of this requires a lot, currently the lion's share of effort for implementing agentic AI in clinical systems. And finally, patients are really the core of what we do and need to be deeply engaged in any conversation about clinical research and clinical trials, including the use of AI in clinical trials and clinical development. This is a survey that was run by Cancer Nation of cancer survivors assessing their comfort and trust in AI as part of their cancer care. Here, they bucketed responses by age group. Overall, a minority of patients for any use case were very comfortable with AI being used in their care and were predominantly comfortable with the use of AI for administrative tasks, much less comfortable with the use of AI for clinical tasks. Clinical trials must engage our patients in the conversation of using AI to ensure conduct and trust and ongoing patient participation and engagement in trials. There are risks of both hype and underestimating any technology, and there's a lot of hype about agentic AI right now. There are risks of moving too fast. You can't move fast and break things in healthcare. That's a cliché. But there are also risks of not moving fast enough. Premature adoption and overpromising will cause backlash when performance falls short, and therefore unrealized benefits due to backlash and slower long-term uptake and inadequate implementation. On the flip side, dismissing innovation and having unrealistic performance requirements slows progress and can potentially push people to using AI inappropriately and in non-regulated settings. So to summarize, agentic AI has potential to accelerate and augment evidence generation, strategy, operational execution, and decision-making in clinical development. Near-term use cases include biomarker development, patient stratification, patient matching, automated outcome monitoring, and document preparation. Data integration, infrastructure monitoring, and governance require upfront effort but will compound value as models continue to advance. And rigorous evaluation, benchmarking, and scalable oversight strategies are top priorities for responsible, safe, and regulatory-grade deployment of these systems in clinical development. So I'd like to thank my collaborators and my funders, and thank you for the opportunity to present here today. Thank you, Dr. Peterman. We have time for one question. Does it work? Yep. Go ahead. Hi. Very nice talk. I was wondering, clinical trials are really multifactorial. You have many things you have to do to make them happen. I was wondering, you mentioned in one of your slides that you were working on matching patients to trials, so kind of probably use agentic AI to improve accrual. I was wondering if you could comment on your progress on that side. So, my group is not working on agentic AI for trial matching. There is a lot of ongoing effort in this space on trial matching. I will say our immune-related adverse event project, which is focused really on more accurately collecting adverse events, is currently being prospectively tested by evaluating whether it improves accrual to an immune-related adverse event biobank, in which, in that case, that special case, the immune-related adverse event is an eligibility criteria. But that's a fairly simple protocol with only a few eligibility criteria. It's performing really well. But there's many other groups that are tackling this challenge of patient matching. It's really hard in oncology because we have these really lengthy, complex eligibility criteria that are written in a non-standardized way. I think to really accelerate this, kind of upfront standardizing eligibility criteria will really make it much easier to implement. And there's a lot of great work, I see my colleagues out here, coming out of the NCI and CBIT in standardizing eligibility criteria to make that a more realistic reality. Thank you. Thank you. We'll have a bit more time for the general discussion at the end of this session, but for now, we need to proceed with the next speaker, and this will be Dr. Sebastian Firsch from University Medical Center Mainz in Germany. Dr. Firsch is physician, scientist, and pathologist at the Institute of Pathology at University Medical Center Mainz. His research focuses on applying AI to digital pathology, particularly for cancer diagnosis, prognosis, and clinical decision support. And in his talk, he will present on translational clinical research aspects of agentic AI with a particular focus on pathology. Okay, I look forward to this presentation. Yeah. Thank you so much for the kind introduction and also for this invitation to the organizers. It's my first time at AACR, and San Diego has been nothing but wonderful. So for the next 20 minutes, I'm going to talk to you about AI agents in clinical tissue medicine and research. These are my conflicts of interest. And I want to use this first slide to sort of convince you that clinical tissue medicine, and what I actually mean by this is sort of just pathology, is really at the center of precision oncology. So if you're thinking about a typical cancer patient, the truth is that the diagnosis for the majority of cancer patients is either done by a pathologist or confirmed by a pathologist. So this is really important to take into consideration when you want to include patients into your clinical trials. And it's also important for when you're doing tissue-based research that it's a good idea to have a specialist look at your tissue because we all know, no tissue, no trial. The second thing is that precision oncology is getting increasingly more complex. If we're thinking just about one particular sort of entity, it used to be the case that in earlier guidelines, it would be based on morphology and then some clinical parameters to make your treatment decisions. And with an increasing number of tissue-based prognostic and predictive biomarkers, this changes rapidly, and most of the analyses are actually done in pathology, looking at, for example, molecular testing really, really early on, and other technologies such as immunohistochemistry. And artificial intelligence could help navigate some of that complexity, but it paradoxically can also potentially contribute additional complexity when we're moving from morphology to multi-omics analyses. Gene expression profiling is common in lymphoma for over 25 years now, and we're still not great at bringing that into the clinic. And so I think we have some work to do. This whole meeting, I think, as you peruse different titles and sessions, has been a meeting where there's been a ton of talk about AI, and I think here is a question that's really quite relevant to this problem is can we use AI tools and foundation models to scale findings that we're learning from spatial transcriptomic data? I think we, along with other people, are trying to develop pathology foundation models, and we have developed a lymphoma-specific foundation model that we're calling LymphoVision that does better than the general pathology models. The only reason I bring that up is that I think if we're going to do this, we're going to have to use these models because they outperform general pathology foundation models. And so if we use specific models, we can then start to think about how do we bring them into the spatial transcriptomic and spatial biology area, and that's by pairing the data with those images. And so I think there's two approaches. These are all papers that are out in preprint, and basically there's two approaches, right? There's one where you can basically start from scratch, where you have paired transcriptomic data on all your cases in the paired image data, and you train it from scratch with image and spatial data. The other way, which is that last paper, the SEAL method that came out of Dr. Mahmoud's lab at Harvard, takes a little different approach. It starts with a well-trained foundation model and then fine-tunes it with spatial data to make it a spatially aware foundation model. And they have shown that you can, whatever task, it doesn't have to be a spatial transcriptomic task, but once you have a spatially aware foundation model, it does better in almost every task that you ask it to do. And so then you could think about taking that and then training or fine-tuning it on a true spatial prediction task. And so these are the kind of things I think we're going to have to think about and how we bring things like this into the clinic and democratize the findings into something that is answering a clinically relevant question. And with that, I will invite you to Rochester to see our amazing Corn Tower, if you ever want to go there. And I'll stop there. Yes, take any questions. Thanks. Thank you, Eric. Great talk. So do you have any questions from the audience? Thank you so much for the great conclusion summaries. So I'm wondering how to improve the statistical sound of the spatial technology since the tumor can be much bigger and each slide's only about five to 10 micrometer, and it is relatively really expensive, and normally the lab could just get a few slides. And even though we say from the second paper, the "Nature Genetics," they say the T cells have less exhaustion marker than the B cells. Is it possible just from that one slide or they conclude from many slides? Yeah. So those were done on tissue microarray cores across all the things. So I think that was an inference from across the entire set. But your point is well taken, right? Especially in an example like follicular lymphoma or AITL, where there's a lot of heterogeneity across a tissue, and now if you're basing all your analysis on two TMA cores per case or whatever, I think you could get into some issues. And then, of course, in the clinic, if you're doing things-- we are doing things on just tiny little needle core biopsies, and trying to infer some spatial data from that, I think we can also start to run into problems. Yes. So regarding that, is there a certain workflow we can follow? Like from Professor Yana Kikmoto, and she started from the transcriptomics data, like bulk data, and then followed a final signature. Then we look at specific signature from the spatial transcriptomics and validate with the spatial proteomics. So, if we already have certain marker that we can focus on, maybe can reduce a bias. Is there a certain workflow you could recommend? Thank you for your question. I think the bias and the pathological or insights are quite very difficult to discriminate is what I'm thinking. Because I focus on-- I would like to ask Ron and Eric because I am focusing on angioinvasive T-cell lymphoma, because classically, angio is very important because it is the origin name. So there should be something that angio-- Because when we collect the angio proliferative sample, then it is AITL, so it should be important, is my pathological insight. But how we can discriminate this pathological insight from a bias? Sorry, I think my question was not clear. So, I think you made a good example, the workflow from spatial started from the bulk RNA-Seq. Yeah. So we can be more focused. My question is, do we recommend the spatial transcriptomics, the technique always followed after the bulk all single-cell RNA-Seq, so we can be more- Ah, yeah ... focused, but not just from one slice? Thank you. For that issue, myself, I'm confident that we should do single-cell RNA sequencing before we do spatial transcriptomics, because each specimen has the thickness, so we cannot avoid the segmentation issue completely. So we are pretty sure that we should do single-cell RNA sequencing before, and then we identify new cells, and we determine the mapping. Is my stance. How Rong is doing? I'm not a pathologist. I'm afraid I can not make any kind of expert recommendation, but I want to share what Mina told me. So often, if you get a fine needle biopsy, often she needs to order 10 IHC slides. You pretty much would exhaust the entire tissue, and then you put a patient at risk, right? If you don't get a good result back for those IHC and you cannot make a diagnosis and the patient cannot be treated, that's a real problem. And so that's why Mina demands, "Okay, can you get all the information from exactly the same tissue section or adjacent, now 10 of those, and then I can make sure I don't put a patient at risk, and I can get a sufficient amount of information to make a proper diagnosis." I think that no matter bulk single-cell sequencing or bulk genome sequencing, I think FoundationOne is widely used, but still it got to consume a lot of tissue specimen. I would say it depends. So my goal is you don't need to do that, and you get a sufficient amount of info. But the sampling variability, that's a problem I think pathologists, oncologists, they know for decades. You cannot sample entire tumor. But I know for prostate cancer, they know how many cores you need to take to get a relatively good representative of the tumor. That has been investigated. I don't think the very informative spatial omics technology is going to address that question that has been intended to be addressed during the past couple of decades. But at least that single piece of tissue, if you can get much more information, that should help, yeah, in making the whole thing compatible with pathology. Don't try to ask them to take a different tissue processing protocol. That's not going to happen. That's not going to happen very soon, maybe. Thank you. Thank you so much. So it's time, so we would like to wrap up the session. Thank you for coming. Thank you. Yeah. Thank you. Fabulous talk, you guys. Thank you.

This transcript is Vimeo auto-generated English. Expect misheard names and technical terms. Use the ripgrep/search approach for exact quotes.

Good afternoon, everyone. We're going to start our session, Immune and Stromal Reprogramming Across the Tumor Micro and Macro Environment. So the field of the microenvironment, and I see many of the people involved in this research, which is the closest to my heart and my main topic, has been around for several decades, and I think for now, we don't need to convince anyone that the microenvironment is important after decades of research. But it also has become very clear that there's more to it. Tumors are ecosystems, and they're part of an entire organism, and there's also a lot of what we call now macro environment factors that affect tumor growth, metastasis, and very important, response to therapy. And this is what we're going to try to integrate. It's a huge amount of topics, but we're going to try and taste and integrate this in this session. And we have two speakers. Yuval Shaked will tell us about the host response to immunotherapy and how it changes the microenvironment, specifically ECM. Mitchell Fain from Fox Chase will tell us about a very important systemic factor at the level of the organism, which is aging, that affects tumor growth, and mostly it affects metastasis, as Mitchell will tell us. And then we'll finish with my presentation talking about stromal and immune interaction in organ-specific metastasis, and again, I hope you all enjoy it. What I didn't say is that at the end of each talk, you can ask questions, but you can also... There it is, the barcode. If you're too shy or if you're online, scan the barcode, and then text the questions. Okay. Let's start our session with our first speaker, Yuval Shaked. Thank you very much, Netta. I'd like to thank the organizers and the chair of this session for inviting me to this meeting. Today, I'm going to talk about immune checkpoint inhibitors and their association with the extracellular matrix, and all with respect to host response to treatment. So my lab in the last, I would say, two decades, is interested in resistant to treatment. And while the majority of studies focusing on how tumor cells are being affected by the treatment, we were more interested to see how the therapy affects many different host cells. They can be at the bone marrow or other organs, and they can be even at the tumor microenvironment. These are not side effects that we are talking about. I call it silent side effects. They are changing the tumor microenvironment, sometimes, as I will show you, to the tumor advantage. I call it the host response to anticancer treatment. By way of example, if you take non-tumor-bearing mice and you treat them with chemotherapy, and then you extract the plasma from these mice, and after that, you look into a different variety of assays that looking at the characteristics of cancer cells, what you can find is sometimes that the tumor cells become more aggressive when they are cultured with plasma from treated mice compared to plasma from control. So something in the plasma, in response to the treatment, promoted the activation of cancer cells. They are becoming excited. They are becoming proliferative and invasive. Another way to show it is that if you prime non-tumor-bearing mice with chemotherapy and then inject tumor cells to the mice, the mice that will show higher mortality rate are those that were first treated with chemotherapy. Again, there is something in the host in response to the treatment that promotes the aggressiveness of tumor cells. And these effects is not only in preclinical models. We can actually find them in the clinic, in samples from patients. Indeed, what we've done is we took plasma samples from colorectal cancer patients before and after treatment with FOLFOX chemotherapy. Before baseline and after treatment, it's 24 hours after the first treatment, and we did the same assay that I just showed in mice. 70% of the patient will show increase in metastatic properties of the tumor cells by means of invasion and filtration throughout the Boyden chamber, as you can see here. So this means that the host, in response to the treatment, promotes a lot of regenerative factors and proliferative factors that support the growth of the tumor. It can explain tumor relapse and metastasis. And throughout the years, we have done work not only with chemotherapy but also with radiation and targeted drugs such as bortezomib, anti-angiogenic drugs, surgery, and more recently, with immune checkpoint blockade. In each and one of these treatment modalities, we do see these effects. There is infiltration of a lot of immune cells into the tumor, and not only immune cells, but here we show only the immune cells. They secrete a lot of different factors that makes the tumors more immunosuppressive, and that could actually help tumors proliferate and metastasize. But one component that we neglected so far was the extracellular matrix. And we ask, what happened to the extracellular matrix? And the reason why it's important, because there is a huge interplay between different cell types and the extracellular matrix.Cancer-associated fibroblasts that support ECM remodeling. The cancer cells themselves. Immune cells, mostly myeloid cells that also support. And the interconnection between all these cells can promote ECM remodeling. And why ECM remodeling is important, because we know that it's pro-tumorigenic. It promotes resistant cell death. It escape the immune system. It is being used as a barrier, as a physical barrier, not allowing T-cells getting into the tumor, promote invasion and metastasis, and induce angiogenesis. So really, we're interested in the ECM. And when we say ECM remodeling, is not only the expression, the novosynthesis of different micromolecules that support the ECM, that make the ECM, but also post-translational modification of enzymes. And many of these enzymes are known to degrade the matrix. These are the MMPs, cathepsin, ADAMs, heparans, and others. They will degrade the ECM, the macromolecules. But in addition to them, so far in the world literature, we know about two enzymes that assemble the ECM. This is the lysyl oxidase, which is five members of one family, and the BMP1, which is upstream to LOX. They are known to assemble the ECM to cross-link collagen and elastin. And indeed, we found that there is increase in LOX expression in the lungs of mice that underwent chemotherapy. And this could explain why after chemotherapy, we do see sometimes more metastasis in mice that have been first treated. Long story short, what we showed in a previous study is that chemotherapy can induce ECM remodeling, and this support the seeding of cancer cells in the lungs due to the stiff tissue in the lungs. What we found is that CD8 T-cells expressing lysyl oxidase are the one that support chemotherapy-induced ECM remodeling. And when we talk about CD8 T-cells, what questions that we really were interested then was what happened when you give immunotherapy. Would you get a similar effect or changes in the ECM? And the story that I'm going to tell you is about the immunotherapy-induced ECM remodeling. And why it's important? It's important because we know that only 30 or 40% of patients will benefit from immunotherapy, and the other patients will not. And there are many different reasons for resistant mechanisms for immunotherapy. Among them are those that are associated with immunosuppression activity. The ECM is immunosuppressive. It stores a lot of factors that are immunosuppressive. And also, as I mentioned, it serves as a physical barrier at not letting T-cells infiltrating the tumor. So we really were interested to study whether immunotherapy induced ECM remodeling. So in order to do it in an unbiased manner, we were looking for a homogeneous population of patients, cancer patients, that we have paired samples before treatment, usually at biopsy, and after immunotherapy, usually when you have tumor debulking. And we found in triple-negative breast cancer, a study that was published in "Nature Medicine" a few years ago. And we found 12 paired samples that we have the same patients. So we looked at the immune cells within these tumors and the expression, the differentially expressed genes between before and after treatment. And what we found that there are about 3,000 genes that are differentially expressed when you look at the whole immune system. And among these biological pathways that are enriched in these cells are usually cell matrix adhesion, of course, immune modulation, ECM remodeling, and epithelium development. And what really struck us was the fact that we found that the majority of the ECM remodeling and cell matrix adhesion were found in the T-cells. So we really were interested to see whether ECM remodeling can be recapitulated in animal models. So we used the 4T1, the triple-negative breast cancer syngeneic tumors, and we asked what happened when you give anti-PD-1. What happened to the ECM in the tumor? As you can see here with Sirius Red staining, there is dense ECM collagen I and III staining after anti-PD-1 compared to the IgG control. Here is another tumor model, such as Lewis lung carcinoma. You can see again these fibers, massive dense fibers following anti-PD-1 compared to control. Since our suspect are the T-cells based on the single-cell RNA sequencing, as well as based on the previous studies we have done, and the fact that it's anti-PD-1 treatment, we ask what happens when you don't have T-cells. We use SCID mice that are lacking B and T-cells, and we did the same experiment. As you can see here, after anti-PD-1, there is no changes in ECM in the tumors. And in fact, when we now adaptively transfer T-cells from normal mice into these SCID mice, you can restore the ECM remodeling after anti-PD-1 therapy, suggesting that T-cells indeed responsible, either directly or indirectly, to the ECM remodeling. So we wanted to study what could be the reason, and we looked at the different enzymes, post-translational modification of the ECM, and we found that BMP1 and LOX are upregulated in the T-cells.We validated it by looking into conditioned medium of CD8 T cells, but we also find it systemically. We found that also in the plasma of anti-PD-1-treated mice, we have higher levels of BMP1. What is BMP1? It's a bone morphogenic protein 1. It plays a role in the formation and development of the extracellular matrix. How it does that? It does it in a variety of ways. It cleaves procollagen, usually I, II, and III, into active collagen, fibrillar collagen. It also cleaves pro-LOX, make it active LOX, then it can cross-link collagen and elastin, and it also release TGF-beta from the ECM. BMP1 in tumors, overexpression is known to be pro-tumorigenic and support metastasis. And there is an inhibitor for BMP1, a small molecule that developed by Pfizer, for fibrosis, not for cancer, and it's called UK-383367. I will call it from now on UK. So the obvious experience that one would like to try is to see what happens when you combine anti-PD-1 with the BMP1 inhibitor. So the BMP1 inhibitor as a small molecule and short half-life, you need to give on a daily basis, whereas the PD-1, you give twice a week. And again, you use the 4T1 breast cancer model that is resistant to anti-PD-1. But once you use this combination, now you can see the tumors become sensitive to anti-PD-1 therapy. And why they are sensitive? They are sensitive because if you look at the ECM, there is reduced ECM in the combination treatment compared to the anti-PD-1. And what else you can see, that there is more infiltration of activated T cells into this tumor, suggesting that blocking BMP1 in combination with anti-PD-1 can actually make resistant tumors sensitive tumors to therapy. But we wanted to really, because we saw that in the plasma there is increase in BMP1, so there is systemic increase in BMP1, but not only in T cell. We really wanted to figure out whether the BMP1 in T cell is as responsible. So what we did next was we did an experiment where we basically took the SCID mice, and we adaptively transferred T cells either expressing or not expressing BMP1 using CRISPR-Cas9, and so you can see that there is knockdown of BMP1, and then we gave anti-PD-1 treatment. And you can see that when you don't have BMP1, there is no ECM remodeling in these tumors. Suggesting that it's sufficient to block BMP1 just in T cells in order to get the effect on the ECM. So it doesn't necessarily have to be a systemic effect. It could be really local effect with the BMP1 in the T cells. And we figured out the mechanism, how actually it works. So if you have anti-PD-1, it actually activate the T cells. In the granules, you have stored BMP1 that is secreted after activation. The BMP1, as we said, act on the ECM and makes collagen, activate LOX, and therefore, make more ECM or ECM remodeling. But it also, as I mentioned, release the TGF-beta from the ECM. And once it release it from the ECM, it can bind back to the receptor, the TGF-beta receptor, that now will exhaust the T cells. So when we have kind of a positive loop that will inhibit the activity of T cells once you give anti-PD-1. And to prove that, here I'll show you that when you take T cells, dump them cells in vitro, and you add anti-PD-1, you get activation of the T cells. But if you do it on the experiment when you have ECM in the culture, then you see that after anti-PD-1 treatment, there is no activation of CD8 T cells. But you can restore the activation if you block either the TGF-beta receptor or you block BMP1 activity by the enzyme, as I mentioned. So what you have here is not only inhibition of the physical barrier, but you also have ignition of the T cell, making sure that they not undergo exhaustion and actually work better in this case. So due to these studies, we decided to develop an antibody-drug conjugate. I call it the first-in-class antibody drug conjugate because usually the antibody drug conjugate, what do they do? We have three components that are very important. The first one is the specificity, which is based on the antibody that you use. You have a linker that is very important to know how many payloads you put on each antibody and if there is a steric interference with the antibody. And you have the payload that, in our case, is a BMP1 inhibitor rather than a cytotoxic drug. Currently, most of the ADCs that are in the clinic are based on payloads of tubulin inhibitors and DNA-modifying agents, which are cytotoxic agent. So what we decided to do is to use an enzyme inhibitor as a payload, and that we will know that we'll harness the immune system and will reduce the frequency of drug administration. We don't need to give the UK on a daily basis. It's on the antibody, so it may stay for a longer time. So then we tried the same treatment, but this time using the ADC. And you can see that just by adding the ADC, you get, again, tumor growth retardation in this 4T1 tumor model. We've tried additional models such as melanoma and Lewis lung carcinoma. And why it happens? It happens because it reuses the ECM content or the remodeling in the tumors with the ADC, and you get ignition of-Or a full activation of the T cells that infiltrate into these tumors. So you don't have the physical barrier, and you have more activation of the T cells due to this ADC. Last but not least, what we were also interested in is to see, like this is all preclinical models, what happened in clinical situation. So we were collaborating with Roche on a clinical study that was done in Essen, by Sven Brandau, and we actually looked at small number of patients where we, again, have a biopsy and after treatment with immunotherapy of head and neck squamous cell carcinoma. And you can see that almost all patients show higher levels of ECM remodeling after treatment with immunotherapy. And if you look on the immune cells, you can see that CD8 T cells express higher levels of BMP1 after treatment, suggesting that what we have seen in preclinical model might be relevant to the clinic. And this is, I would like to conclude that ECM remodeling after immunotherapy is associated with ECM remodeling. This is done due to de novo synthesis. I didn't show you, but we have done also work on showing that there is more fibrillar collagens that is highly expressed and activation of post-translational modification by enzymes. In addition to cancer-associated fibroblasts, myeloid cells are also known to support ECM remodeling. But here we show that also CD8 T cells can generate factors that can remodel the ECM. Blocking BMP1 in combination with immunotherapy, it can sensitize tumors that are otherwise resistant to immunotherapy. And tumor ECM remodeling was found also in clinical samples using head neck squamous cell carcinoma. And we propose here first in class, first time antibody drug conjugate that encompass a PD-1 with an inhibitor of ECM remodeling enzymes, the BMP1, in order to make resistant tumors to immunotherapy become sensitive. And I would like to thank the people that were involved in this work. First and foremost, Bar and Josephine, that equally contributed this work. Josephine already a post-doc in the UK, but she continued working on this work. And many collaborators from the Technion, that have done the work on the single-cell RNA sequencing, Sven Brandau, Keren Yitzhak, and also Karbian Odivalla-Dilke, that has done some of the staining that I showed with the tumor samples from the UK. With this, I would like to thank you for your attention. Thank you, Yuval. We have time for questions. Please go to the microphone if you have questions, and introduce yourself before asking. Maybe by the time people are walking in, I'll start with a question. Yuval, did you check whether the thing that you're seeing with the changes is specific to any organ? Did you look at different metastasis, for example, because 41 will metastasize to the lungs, but it can also metastasize to the brain. So did you see whether this mechanism is specific to a certain organ, or is it general response? So in this study, we looked at the tumor, at the primary tumor. But I can tell you that indeed, we looked also on other organs. We look at the lung, and in the lung, we also see changes in the ECM. And in fact, if you look at studies, these are reviews that were published, clinical reviews. They started to say that after immunotherapy, there is a pulmonary fibrosis in some patients. So this could explain what we see here, could explain this. So we looked at the lungs, and we found it. And in the lungs, the reason we think that in the lungs you will see it mostly is because the lysyl oxidases need oxygen to work. So that's why this perfused tissue, oxygenated tissue, where you will see mostly the effect. So in the lungs, we do see this effect. Okay. And we have a question there. Hi. Very interesting data. I am Devashish Sain from Washington University, St. Louis. I was just wondering that, have you checked whether this PD-1 treatment leads to also changes, like through T cell, leads to changes in fibroblast phenotype in the tumor microenvironment? No. This, we haven't done that, and I'm sure that Netta will say that I need to do it as well. Yeah. So we haven't done that. So we haven't looked into what happened to the fibroblast, and I'm sure that also will go some kind of changes, but we haven't looked into that. Thank you. Hi. Xavier Tecpley from Oslo University Hospital. Very interesting talk, looking at different interaction between different cell type and cell states. I had a question about BMP1 expression across different T cell state indeed, and if you had the chance to look if in different single-cell RNA sequencing or different datasets, which T cell may express BMP1. Yes. And as a continuation of that, within the dataset that you basically mined in the initial single-cell RNAseq experiments, did you look if the responders versus non-responder had a different expression of ECM-related genes? So yeah. Thank you for these questions. Yes, we have done that. So first of all, most of the T cells that express are in the states of memory T cells that express that. That's where you see BMP1, but I have to say BMP1 is not highly expressed on these cells, so it's really only after the activation that you can start to see the BMP1 expression. And regarding the other question, yes, we have looked also into BMP1 levels and maybe by BMP1 levels, predict response or non-response to immunotherapy. I don't have a clear conclusion. That's why I didn't put it on the slides, because I think that we don't have enough samples to test it, because we had to look to samples that when you have the same patients before and after. You cannot just look at the levels of BMP1 because it could vary between a patient and between samples. So it was very important to look before and after the same sampling, and we didn't have many of those, so we didn't get into conclusive results about that. That's why we don't want to say that. Thank you. Thank you. Charles Earnshaw from Cancer Research UK, Manchester. I really liked the story and the BMP1 idea from CD8 T cells to TGF-beta. Obviously, TGF-beta activation from the latent band form is known to involve things like GARP and integrins as well, possibly on other cell types. Do you think there is a link between the CD8, a physical link, maybe tumor cells, fibroblasts, or monocytes that might be also involved in the activation step that you're seeing? This is an interesting view. We haven't looked into that, but I will go back to the board and look into that. Thank you. Thanks. Yeah. Last question. Matt Maxwell. I'm a postdoc at Tempus AI. I was curious if you've looked at clinical data to see if, not just non-responder versus responder, but is BMP1 predictive of hyperprogression following ICI treatment? So not just not responding, but rapidly progressing. Yeah. We have a lot of studies we have done on hyperprogression as well, not with respect to this study. And, so again, I don't have answer for that, for these questions. But I do want to mention, remember that even in the patient data that we showed with the head and neck squamous cell carcinoma, we showed that the majority of the patient show higher levels of BMP1 in the T cells. Okay? Majority of the patients, even though they responded to treatment. So I'm not sure that we can count on this as a biomarker. However, remember that also the treatment was a very short time of treatment, because it's before tumor debulking, so the immunotherapy is given, I think once, and after six weeks you get the surgery. So, maybe if you give consistent treatment of immunotherapy, maybe then it start to kick in and then you will see differences, but we don't have an answer for that. Great. Wonderful talk. Thanks. Thank you. Thank you, Yuval. And our next speaker is Mitchell Fain from Fox Chase, and he's going to tell us about the role of aging in immune-mediated reactivation from metastatic dormancy. Go, Mitch. Yes. Thank you so much for that introduction. It's a real pleasure to be here. We opened our lab about three years ago, so yeah, I'm very excited to talk about the role of aging in metastatic dormancy progression, particularly in melanoma. So I have nothing to disclose, and if there's one thing that you can take from the talk that I'm giving today, I hope it's the fact that cancer is indeed a disease of aging. We see that aging is one of the highest prognostic risk factors for the majority of cancer, and if we simply just look at cancer incidence over time, for a large number of cancers on the left here, and then we have melanoma specifically on the right, which is what I'm going to be focusing on today. You can see past the age of 30, we start to get this really rapid increase in cancer incidence. But what's also really interesting and what I got interested in when I first started the lab is that once you get to around the age of 85, you actually have this inflection point where the majority of cancers actually start to decrease with age. So we got really interested in this difference between these middle-aged patients versus these geriatric patients. And, unfortunately, I won't have time to talk about this decreasing trend, but my postdoc, Dr. Kelly Coton, is speaking right after this in the aging micro and macro environments and tumor progression and therapy session in ballroom 6A. She's a great speaker and has a really, really interesting story. So go check that out if you're interested. But today I'm going to be focused on more on the role that middle age plays in driving this increase in incidence, progression, mortality, and all of these different factors, particularly within melanoma. So who cares about aging? It's interesting statement. A reviewer has actually said this to me before, and if you look at healthy aged tissues, so no cancer or anything like that, what you tend to see over time in the lung, in the liver, these really common metastatic sites in healthy aging is you get dysfunction of a huge amount of different stromal cells. So fibroblasts change the soluble factors that they secrete with age. They change the way in which they remodel the extracellular matrix. We get really dramatic differences in angiogenesis. And what I'm going to mainly focus on today is this dysfunction in immune cells with age. And when we look at, and as I said, in a normal healthy human, these dysfunctional phenotypes that we see in these stromal cells almost mimic exactly what we see in a very aggressive tumor microenvironment, be that a primary tumor or even a metastatic tumor as well. And one of the reasons why this is a particular issue in the field is that I would say about 90% to 95% of studies are done in preclinical animal models in these eight to 12-week-old mice. This is the clinical equivalent of a 20-year-old human for a disease where the median age of diagnosis is 65. So there's a famous saying, we could treat and cure cancer in mice, but we can't do it in humans. And I think one of the reasons why translation is so abysmal is because we're putting these therapies into these young mice that have a fully intact immune system, don't really have any of these age-related deficits. Whereas when we see in the clinic, a lot of these patients are in their 60s to 70s, and they have that age-related dysfunction. So that's something that I wanted to really start looking at when we set up the lab. The other issue is that there's often not very good models to look at colonization or metastasis across a wide variety of different organs.Particularly in melanoma, the majority of studies are done in the lung because there are some syngeneic melanoma cell lines that will disseminate into the lung, and you can study for metastasis, or you could do a very simple tail vein injection and the cells will go to the lung as well. A very understudied site in melanoma is the liver because there aren't great models of colonization. And one of the reasons why this is important is there are studies now in the clinic that show if patients have localized liver metastasis only versus patients that have localized lung metastasis only, the patients with liver metastasis will actually respond much worse to immune checkpoint blockade compared to those with lung metastases. So it's important to look at multiple different organs to really increase the ability for us to give personalized patient care, particularly with regards to age. We showed that astrocytes that are induced by interferon gamma, so the AP astrocytes, can actually uptake and process antigens. But they also need to, in order to be professional antigen-presenting cells, they need to be able to uptake, process, and present to T cells. So we also did a series of experiments, again, showing you just a little bit of it, so I can show you the highlights. We showed that AP astrocytes induced with interferon gamma can activate CD4+ T cells that they are co-cultured with, and these CD4+ T cells were isolated from vaccinated mice that were vaccinated with tumor cell lysate. So they can present antigen to CD4 T cells in a tumor antigen context. And we saw this by proliferation of T cells, expression of CD44, and also secretion of interferon gamma by these activated T cells. But can they actually interact? So we used image stream analysis to see whether astrocytes that are isolated from brain metastasis can be physically associated with T cells. And what we found is that, yes, AP astrocytes can be physically associated with T cells. And then we looked in patient samples from melanoma, breast cancer, and lung cancer, and to see whether we can kind of catch them in action. And we did. So this is the quantification. What we found is that AP astrocytes, but not astrocytes that are not expressing MHC class II, like we said, this is just a subpopulation, are more likely to be found in contact with T cells in brain metastasis. And so because we, like I told you, also did single-cell analysis of T cells, again, finding, I'm not going into this, but finding many subpopulations of T cells, we looked at the predicted interactions of T cells with AP astrocytes, and we found that these neuroprotective astrocytes, which are the population that contains the AP astrocytes, are most likely to form many interactions with T cells. And so we wanted to see whether this would have any functional consequences for tumor cell killing. So we did this ex vivo assay, again, with T cells isolated from vaccinated mice with breast cancer cells, and we co-cultured them with AP astrocytes or with normal astrocytes, CD4 T cells that I showed you are activated by astrocytes, and CD8 cells, and we looked at tumor cell killing. And what we found is that CD8 T cells that were cultured with AP astrocytes enhanced their secretion of granzyme B, interferon gamma, and TNF alpha, which shows that they are activated. And when we culture them then with cancer cells, this really significantly enhanced the killing of cancer cells by these AP astrocyte-activated T cells. But until now, everything I showed you, all these ex vivo assays, were with astrocytes that we induced by interferon gamma. What happens if we isolate astrocytes from end-stage metastasis? And there the plot thickened. What we found is that when we isolate astrocytes from late-stage metastasis, they were actually immunosuppressive. They suppressed the proliferation of T cells, and they started expressing high levels of checkpoint ligands such as PD-L1 and CD155, suggesting that something is suppressingTheir function as AP astrocytes. And indeed, when we looked at the correlation between MHC expression and brain metastatic burden, we found that the expression of MHC was correlated with low brain metastatic burden. So something is happening at later stages. I'm not going to go into what is happening. I'll just tell you that it looks like the secreted factors from tumor cells are suppressing the antigen presentation by astrocytes. So we wanted to see the bottom line, and these would be my final pieces of data. What happens if we manipulate AP astrocytes? Are they good? Are they bad? Do they enhance or inhibit brain metastasis? So for that, we created mice that had MHC II knockout specifically in astrocytes by crossing GFAP-Cre mice with MHC Lox mice, and then we injected these mice with cancer cells and looked at their metastasis. And what we found is that AP astrocytes actually inhibit brain metastasis, because in these mice where we knocked out MHC class II specifically in astrocytes, so we inhibited the antigen presentation by astrocytes, they now had a lot more brain metastasis. Suggesting, again, that AP astrocytes are important. So just to summarize what I've shown you, that antigen-presenting astrocytes can orchestrate antitumor immunity in brain metastasis. Their expression of MHC class II is induced by interferon gamma, which is a hallmark of neuroinflammation in the brain, and they activate T cells, enhance tumor cell killing, but later, as metastasis prevails, tumor secreted factor, I didn't show you that part for lack of time, inhibit the expression of MHC class II, causing immune suppression and progression of metastasis. So I want to thank all the members of my lab and our collaborators and, of course, funding and Yael is really-- So the crown moved, but Yael is really the queen of this project. And one very last thing that I want to keep on while we have a discussion is I want to encourage you to attend the MRS meeting, the Metastasis Research Society that will be on June 28th in Utah. It's going to be an amazing meeting. There's still early bird registration, and I encourage you to attend, and I'm happy to take any questions. I have a couple of quick question. First one, I may be missing. When you knock down lipocalin 2 and show very nice and strong effect on metastasis and survival, what happens with primary tumor? So we knocked out lipocalin 2 using the experimental metastasis model. So the data I showed was when cells were injected intracardially, but we also did this with the primary tumor, and there was no effect on primary tumor growth. It's actually published, so it's in the paper. No effect on primary tumor growth. Okay. Very interesting. It was a specific mechanism for brain metastasis. And just related to that, so effect on astrocytes, it's clear. What happens with their counterpart in other tissues like fibroblast on effect on macrophages? Do you see something different? It's only this astrocyte-specific effect of lipocalin, or it's little bit more than that? So it is a little bit more than that. Lipocalin is actually secreted also by fibroblasts in the primary tumor. It has different effects on organ-specific metastasis. We focused on brain metastasis, but there are other papers showing that lipocalin 2 has effects also in other organs, just different effects. Yes, and that effect is anti-tumor? The other papers. No. No? It's always pro-tumorogenic. It's pro-inflammatory, yeah. Okay, thanks. Okay, Sergey. Yeah, very nice talk. About astrocytes early and astrocytes late, did you look at their interactions with Tregs among other CD4 T cells? Yes, we have, and they do interact with Tregs, but I don't think we compared early and late. So we did this only in late metastasis. Yes. Thanks for the presentation. My question is, precedes the metastatic organ or tissue, the niche is not solved yet. But for the research purpose and the clinical study, any good idea or suggestion in terms of how to choose the organ? What timeline is the best to figure out those changes of the niche? Mm. A lot of resources, energies were put on it. So any idea about it? Yes. So when working with mouse models, it's an important question. Thank you for that. It needs to be carefully calibrated to find what are the important time points and how to define early and late.And this changes with the cancer type, the organ, it really changes in each system, and it's important to calibrate it in each study before you call this early and this late. But it's very important to do that. It's just very specific to tumor type and metastasis site. Thanks. Yes. So it was just about the LMC2 buildup. Is there an actual buildup in the primary tumor before you reach a threshold that's able to activate these astrocytes in the brain? Or does the tumor have to grow to a certain size before you're actually getting the astrocyte activation, or is it something else? Yeah. So it is secreted from the primary tumor, and it's gradually increasing in the blood. And at the time when we resect the primary tumor, we see a decrease in the blood in LCN2, but the astrocytes are already activated, and then the main source is actually granulocytes that are recruited to the brain, and the blood levels go up again. So I guess the ask is, is there anything changing in the tumor to increase this, or as soon as the tumor starts, the primary tumor, you're already getting that LCN2 into the blood? Yes. Okay. And it gradually increases as the tumor grows. Thanks. Yes. Thank you for the talk. Have you looked at the blood-brain barrier? How does it react? How T cells and tumor cell, how do they get in there? Yeah. So this is not our studies, but many people have looked, and one of the hallmarks of brain metastasis and of neuroinflammation is breakdown of the blood-brain barrier that allows recruitment of granulocytes and T cells from the periphery to brain metastasis. So this is something that is known, and we also saw it in our system. Thank you. Thank you for the very interesting talk. I was just wondering, have you compared this antigen-presenting ability of AP astrocyte with the professional antigen-presenting cells? I was just wondering why they are coming and- Are you reviewer number two? I'm still a PhD student, so no. Yeah. So it's a cool question, and we're doing it now because we were asked by one of the reviewers to do that. Okay. Thank you. Welcome. I want to ask a question. I know the time is up. Okay. But you are the chair, so you can- Yeah ... choose to continue. One last, last question. So new role for astrocytes, APC astrocytes. So do we have dendritic cells in the brain? And if yes, what do they do? There are dendritic cells in the brain when there is brain metastasis. I'm guessing that they do the same, and this comparison is exactly what we're trying to do now. Mm-hmm. It's a really good question. Thank you. Okay. So thank you all for listening and for a great discussion, and thank you for our speakers, and enjoy the rest of your day.
