docs.title: Synthesis — ED03 vs the 48-poster corpus
docs.text:
AACR 2026 session ED03 ("Foundation Models and Multimodal AI for Cancer Research," Fri 4/17 PM, ~11,668 words) is the only dedicated AACR plenary this year on virtual-cell and multimodal-FM methods. Three speakers set the field's agenda from stage:

  • Charlotte Bunne (EPFL) — virtual patients via multimodal foundation models, with spatial-proteomics + histopathology as the worked example.
  • Serena Yeung-Levy (Stanford Biomedical Data Science) — generative models of disease dynamics (CellFlux flow matching) and multimodal VLMs for scientific reasoning (MicroVQA, BioMedICA).
  • Michael Moor (ETH Zurich) — grounded, verifiable medical agents (MYRIAD atlas, process reward models); joined remotely.

This page takes each speaker's 2-3 load-bearing claims from the ED03 transcript and asks the same question of each: does the 48-poster AACR 2026 virtual-cells corpus support, contradict, or not address it? The point is to locate the gap between what leaders are saying from stage and what the rest of the field is shipping in posters.

Name note: the auto-caption renders Bunne as "Bonner" and Moor as "Moore" — corrected silently here per docs/notes/caveats.md.

Quotation note: quotations below are lightly cleaned transcript fragments (paragraphing, obvious filler removed). Ellipses "[…]" mark joins.

docs.title: Charlotte Bunne — virtual patients with multimodal foundation models
docs.text: Bunne gave the session's framing talk. Her lab at EPFL built a multimodal foundation model that jointly encodes H&E histopathology and variable-panel spatial proteomics (4,605 patients at submission time, now 33 clinical studies), uses it as the substrate for in-silico perturbation screens on the Swiss supercomputer, and wraps the whole thing in an active-acquisition system ("EchoK") that decides which additional markers to acquire.

docs.title: Thesis 1 — Histopathology FMs translate; spatial-proteomics FMs require new architectures
docs.text:
"The moment we use a different modality, if we want to get a molecular insight into a tissue and we move to a data type that is not just an H&E, we struggle. […] Spatial proteomics, for example, is not an RGB image. It's an image where every assay looks at a set of proteins […] 40, 80, 150 plex protein panels. So here it already starts. How do we build foundation models for those type of data modalities?"

Corpus verdict: partially supported.

  • Supports: #4163 (Andrew Song, "A general-purpose AI foundation model for spatial proteomics") is the direct poster-corpus analogue — an FM built specifically for multiplexed spatial proteomics, reporting that conventional cell-segmentation-then-threshold pipelines are inadequate.
  • Baseline for the comparison: #LB174 (H-optimus-1) and #5491 (AI FM for single-cell annotation from histopathology) are pure-histopathology foundation models of the exact kind Bunne contrasts against — RGB vision transformers trained at scale. #2778 (cancer-scale WSI → ST FM) and #5489 (multi-scale FM for RCC localization) also fall in the H&E-as-RGB camp.
  • Not addressed: Bunne's specific architectural claim — that panel-varying protein tokenization requires a protein-language-model-backed encoder that can handle assays where "in clinical study A look at protein ABC, and then the next clinical study actually looks at protein DEF" — is not directly tested by any other poster. #4163 is the only spatial-proteomics FM in the entire 48.

docs.title: Thesis 2 — The real payoff of virtual-tissue FMs is in-silico perturbation / treatment simulation and new biomarkers
docs.text:
"We can now use a treatment encoder and now use a generative model to forecast how those state or cell tissue states change over time. […] How do we have now patterns of those models that are actually very informative for clinical decision-makings? […] We can extract minimum signatures that are corresponding to responder and non-responder signals."

Corpus verdict: supported in spirit, with a shift of substrate.

  • Supports (in-silico screens): #1464 (CELLama-Perturb, virtual-cell model for spatial drug sensitivity); #4181 (Turbine's Virtual Lab, mechanism-enabled simulation for target de-risking); #978 (cell→patient transcriptome-modeled drug response); #1467 (GRPO-based mechanism-aware therapy planning on a multimodal oncology FM); #LB438 (multiscale mechanistic pathway-crosstalk analysis for TME rewiring under therapy). All five implement some version of the in-silico-screen-over-learned-representations pattern Bunne described.
  • Supports (AI-derived biomarkers): #87 (Path2Prot — AI-inferred proteomic biomarkers for breast tumor subtyping), #2778 (WSI → spatial transcriptomics), #LB443 (MutationProjector genotype FM for therapeutic response), and #2765 (MiFM microbiome trajectories and risk clocks) match her "new generation of AI-derived biomarkers" framing.
  • Contradicts (sort of): every single one of those posters uses transcriptomic, mutational, microbial, or morphological features — none uses spatial-proteomics tissue representations as the substrate. Bunne's specific substrate — a multimodal spatial-proteomics + H&E latent as the foundation for in-silico screening — has zero direct poster analogues. The field wants her payoff but is taking a different route to it, largely because spatial-proteomics data is much rarer than either H&E or scRNA-seq.

docs.title: Thesis 3 — Active / sequential acquisition (the "EchoK" / "ask for more when needed" idea)
docs.text:
"What we want is that the foundation model knows what it knows and asks us for more whenever needed. […] It's a sequential acquisition problem, asking for more whenever needed or stopping when done, that uses reinforcement learning […] a minimum assay that is good enough for any downstream task."

Corpus verdict: not addressed.

  • No poster in the 48 implements active / sequential experimental design on top of a multimodal FM. The closest is #1467 (uses GRPO reinforcement learning, but for therapy planning, not assay design) and #4212 (a blood-based estimator, but static rather than sequential).
  • This is a clear blind spot — Bunne is arguing for a capability ("a minimum assay that is good enough for any downstream task") that the AACR 2026 poster hall simply is not shipping. It is also a reasonable finding: sequential-acquisition RL on top of biological FMs is hard to publish as a single poster, because the evaluation requires a prospective assay-design loop, not a static benchmark.

docs.title: Serena Yeung-Levy — disease dynamics and scientific reasoning
docs.text: Yeung-Levy's talk split into two halves: generative image models for virtual cells (CellFlux, CellFlux V2, CellFlux MM) that use flow matching to map control→perturbed cell populations at image and joint-imaging-plus-transcriptomics scale; and vision-language models for scientific reasoning, anchored by the MicroVQA benchmark (1,000+ researcher-level microscopy questions) and the BioMedICA open-access 24M-image PubMed Central dataset.

docs.title: Thesis 1 — Flow matching is the right primitive for distribution-to-distribution perturbation modelling, and it scales
docs.text:
"Flow matching, what we are trying to do is to learn a continuous velocity field that transforms from one source distribution to another target distribution. […] It actually very naturally fits this problem that we're talking about, trying to go from the source to target cell populations. […] CellFlux V2 […] as we scale from 300,000 images to 11.6 million images […] we can achieve these virtual cell foundation models."

Corpus verdict: not addressed.

  • Zero posters in the 48 use flow matching, continuous velocity fields, or ODE-based generative modelling for cell-state transitions.
  • #4213 (GEM-1, "generative genomics accurately predicts cancer gene expression") is the closest generative-perturbation poster but the abstract suggests autoregressive / masked sequence modeling rather than flow matching.
  • #1464 (CELLama-Perturb) is a perturbation model but trained as a representation-learning model in the CELLama spatial family, not a flow-matching generator.
  • #4181 (Turbine's Virtual Lab) uses mechanism-enabled simulations which are closer to mechanistic systems biology than to continuous-latent flow matching.
  • The specific methodological bet Yeung-Levy is making — that flow matching is the scalable primitive for source-to-target distributional learning in virtual cells — is not reflected in what AACR-submitting labs chose to build this year. This could be a timing gap (CellFlux is very recent) rather than a disagreement.

docs.title: Thesis 2 — Joint imaging + transcriptomics modelling matters, but paired data is scarce so we need unimodal bridging
docs.text:
"What I think is also very important is being able to jointly model these together, imaging and transcriptomics together. […] The matched pair data […] we don't have the data to train as large scale foundation models as we want. So […] to take — to learn a single model, but that learns from matched data where that exists and learns from unimodal data where you have that."

Corpus verdict: supported; this is the strongest stage-to-poster alignment on the page.

  • Direct supports (imaging ↔ molecular joint modeling): #2754 (VGL — vision-gene-language LLM combining histopathology + gene expression for cell-type classification in lung cancer); #71 (histopathology ↔ spatial transcriptomics bridging for TME profiling); #1457 (gene expression and pathway activity from H&E WSIs in NSCLC); #87 (Path2Prot — inferring proteomic biomarkers from pathology); #2778 (cancer-scale FM that predicts spatial transcriptomics from WSI); #1438 (generative AI for breast genomic subtype from histology); #2752 (CancerSTFormer — multi-scale spot-resolution spatial transcriptomics analysis).
  • Adjacent supports (broader multimodal fusion): #1251 (HONeYBEE, foundation-model-driven multimodal AI for GBM / NSCLC / PDAC), #4184 (multimodal prostate DL), #5505 (cross-platform spatial-omics framework).
  • This is by a wide margin the best-represented family in the corpus — 8 posters in the core "multimodal fusion & VLM/LLM" family alone, plus adjacent ones in other families.
  • Partially addresses: None of the above explicitly implements Yeung-Levy's specific "unimodal-bridging" training recipe — combining a small matched dataset with much larger unimodal sets via a shared latent — at the scale she describes. The posters are mostly paired-data only, which is the exact constraint she is warning about.

docs.title: Thesis 3 — Scientific-reasoning benchmarks (MicroVQA) are the bottleneck for VLM-based biology agents
docs.text:
"There really doesn't exist easy, good sources of research-level, scientific microscopy-based reasoning. […] MicroVQA was a work that tried to make progress in covering that space of higher-level reasoning, and to truly be able to assess researcher-level capabilities. […] Over 1,000 questions […] this benchmark is still hard for current state-of-the-art models."

Corpus verdict: not addressed.

  • #5478 (benchmarking gene-expression foundation models on bulk RNA-Seq) is the only pure benchmark poster in the 48, and it is a performance benchmark (how well do scRNA-trained FMs transfer to bulk RNA-seq), not a researcher-level scientific-reasoning benchmark of the MicroVQA type.
  • #LB169 (scCAP) is an evaluation of ontology-aware cell-type annotation, comparing against CellTypist, SCimilarity, SingleR, and Geneformer — but this is task-level annotation accuracy, which is a much narrower notion than Yeung-Levy's "researcher-level reasoning with hypothesis generation and experimental proposal."
  • The stage-vs-poster gap here is large: Yeung-Levy and Moor both argue that the field's progress depends on better benchmarks and verifiable reasoning, yet almost no one is shipping benchmark posters. This is arguably a publication-venue effect — pure-benchmark papers typically land at NeurIPS / ICML, not AACR.

docs.title: Michael Moor — reliable, verifiable medical agents
docs.text: Moor's pre-recorded talk (his flight was canceled due to an airline strike) argued that medical AI agents fail for two distinct reasons: (1) they are grounded against unstructured text, so retrieval is leaky; and (2) their reasoning is never verified step-by-step. His lab's responses are MYRIAD (a 6M-entry structured QA atlas grounded in peer-reviewed literature) and process reward models (a "policing" LM that verifies each reasoning step of a base LM at inference time).

docs.title: Thesis 1 — Language models without structured grounding are unreliable for medicine; the knowledge representation matters at least as much as the model
docs.text:
"Currently we use just a massive amount of text chunks that are completely unstructured. So retrieving from this is actually quite hard and quite leaky and noisy. […] We propose this Myriad dataset […] a large-scale atlas of roughly six million medical question-answer pairs, each pair being grounded directly from a passage in the peer-reviewed medical literature."

Corpus verdict: not addressed.

  • No poster in the 48 builds a grounded medical-knowledge atlas or structures literature into QA pairs for RAG.
  • #30 (adaptive LLM-based agentic cohort extraction) does use LLMs for clinical data extraction and could plausibly benefit from MYRIAD-style structured grounding, but its abstract does not address knowledge-representation structure at all — it is focused on schema-matching real-world data for trial feasibility.
  • #LB169 (scCAP, ontology-aware LLM for cell-type annotation) is the closest in spirit — it does argue that structured ontology grounding improves annotation — but the scope is cell types, not medical literature.
  • The MYRIAD-style "representation of the knowledge matters as much as the content" argument has essentially no poster analogue in this slice. It is a stage-only claim in AACR 2026.

docs.title: Thesis 2 — Process reward models / stepwise reasoning verification is how to make agents reliable
docs.text:
"It's not enough to just give a language model access to a neatly organized corpus of knowledge. We actually want to check individual reasoning steps that a language model produces. […] A policing language model, which we in the field would call a process reward model […] by training such a verifier […] we can actually improve many different language model by just hook plugging it in at inference time."

Corpus verdict: not addressed.

  • Zero posters in the 48 implement process reward models, stepwise reasoning verification, or outcome-vs-process reward decomposition.
  • #1467 (Eric Schadt, mechanism-aware therapy planning with GRPO) is the only poster using reinforcement learning with a reward signal, but its reward is mechanism-based therapy-planning performance (is this a good therapy for this patient?) — not stepwise reasoning verification (is this reasoning step correct given the literature?). They are related formalisms but different problems.
  • The entire process-reward-agent subfield Moor describes — where a verifier model checks individual reasoning steps of a primary model at inference time — is absent from the AACR 2026 poster hall. Again likely a venue effect: this is currently published at NeurIPS/ACL, not AACR.

docs.title: Thesis 3 — Agents doing interactive clinical workup are much worse than agents answering exam-style questions — benchmark properly
docs.text:
"We showed that already two years ago, that if you provide a language model, you confront it in some type of agent clinic […] It will be much harder for such a doctor agent to come up with the right diagnosis if the case has to be interactively worked up as compared to those case profiles where you have these exam-style benchmarks. […] Many models drop drastically in performance if they have to actually do the workup on their own."

Corpus verdict: not addressed.

  • No poster in the 48 benchmarks interactive agent workup, clinical dialogue, or multi-turn diagnostic reasoning. #30 is the only agentic-system poster and it is one-shot cohort extraction rather than interactive workup.
  • #1467 uses RL but does not evaluate interactive reasoning trajectories.
  • This is arguably the biggest single gap between the ED03 agenda and the AACR 2026 corpus: across their three talks, Bunne, Yeung-Levy, and Moor collectively spent roughly 40% of stage time on evaluation, benchmarking, and verification — and the poster hall in this slice shipped essentially nothing on that axis. Of 48 posters, 3 touch evaluation and 1 touches agentic autonomy; none do both.

docs.title: Thin-evidence flags — theses where the corpus cannot argue either way
docs.text:
Several ED03 claims are simply not testable against the 48-poster corpus because the relevant poster population is too small. Flagging them here rather than inventing support:

  • Bunne Thesis 3 (active / sequential acquisition): 0 posters implement it. Cannot evaluate.
  • Yeung-Levy Thesis 1 (flow matching as the scalable primitive): 0 posters use flow matching. Cannot evaluate.
  • Yeung-Levy Thesis 3 (MicroVQA-style researcher-level benchmarking): 1 marginally-related poster (#LB169). Too thin to argue either way.
  • Moor Thesis 1 (structured knowledge atlases): 0 direct posters; #LB169 is adjacent but cell-type ontology only.
  • Moor Thesis 2 (process reward models): 0 posters. Cannot evaluate.
  • Moor Thesis 3 (interactive agent workup benchmarks): 0 posters. Cannot evaluate.

Of 10 total theses extracted, 6 have insufficient corpus coverage to argue for or against. All 6 of those are on the evaluation / verification / agent-reliability axis.

docs.title: Closing synthesis — the stage-vs-corpus gap
docs.text:
The three ED03 speakers are converging on a shared research program: multimodal foundation models that forecast perturbation effects, with grounded and verifiable agentic reasoning on top. The AACR 2026 virtual-cells poster corpus partially supports the first half of that program — there are 16 FM posters (cell/gene + pathology) and 6 perturbation/in-silico-screen posters, with a particularly strong multimodal-fusion cohort (8 posters) that directly mirrors Yeung-Levy's joint-imaging-plus-transcriptomics thesis.

But the second half — benchmarks, evaluation of researcher-level reasoning, process-reward verification, active / sequential acquisition, and grounded knowledge-atlas construction — is almost entirely absent. Only 3 posters (#5478, #LB169, #30) address any form of evaluation or agentic autonomy, and none address verifiable stepwise reasoning.

The leaders on stage are 18-24 months ahead of the median AACR 2026 submitter on the evaluation and reliability axes. Part of this is a venue effect — MicroVQA-style benchmarks and process-reward agents are currently published at NeurIPS/ICML/ACL rather than AACR — but part of it is substantive: the community is still shipping model capabilities rather than the scaffolding around them. Closing that gap is the obvious opportunity for AACR 2027.

docs.title: AACR Brain Cancer 2026
docs.text:
AACR Special Conference in Cancer Research: Brain Cancer — Philadelphia Marriott Downtown, Philadelphia, PA · March 23 – 25, 2026. Subspecialty AACR special conference covering adult and pediatric brain tumors — glioblastoma, IDH-mutant glioma, medulloblastoma, brain metastases, and rare CNS subtypes — with strong neuroscience, neuro-immuno-oncology, and cellular-therapy threads.

Status: Retrospective scaffold — meeting closed seven weeks ago (Mar 23–25, 2026; today is May 11, 2026). Vault is being seeded now to anchor the brain-tumor axis for the rest of the 2026 calendar (ASCO neuro-oncology track May 29 – Jun 2; SNO Annual Nov; SITC neuro-IO Nov 4–8). Sessions and speaker references inline are reconstructed from the public AACR program page, the Penn Medicine institutional roundup, chair-disclosed program-overview material (Bagley / Monje / Suva), and selected sponsor / institutional press; the AACR Brain 26 abstract supplement (in Cancer Research) is the citable record and is referenced where available. Pre-meeting topline content captured during the conference week is flagged inline.

docs.title: Why this is in the vault
docs.text:
AACR Brain Cancer is the subspecialty AACR special conference for neuro-oncology — the venue where the cancer-biology and neuroscience halves of the brain-tumor field meet in one program, in a year that does not have an SNO-only inflection. It sits at a deliberate intersection with several other axes already in the vault:

  1. AACR Annual Meeting mechanism axis — many AACR Brain 26 chairs and speakers (Bagley UPenn, Monje Stanford, Suva Broad/MGH) also chair or speak in AACR 2026 neuro-oncology and single-cell sessions four weeks later in San Diego (Apr 17–22). The "deep neuro biology" tracks at the special conference set up the abbreviated mechanism slots at Annual.
  2. Cell-therapy / IO axis (CAR-T in CNS) — chlorotoxin-CAR-T (City of Hope), IL-13Rα2 + EGFR bivalent CAR-T (UPenn / CHOP / Stanford), GD2-CAR-T in DIPG and diffuse midline glioma (Monje group, Stanford), and chimeric-cytokine / armoured cell-therapy approaches. Same biology that anchors the cellular-therapy track at SITC 2026 in November.
  3. Targeted-therapy axis (IDH-mutant glioma) — vorasidenib (Voranigo, FDA-approved Aug 2024) is the first targeted therapy for grade 2 IDH-mutant astrocytoma / oligodendroglioma. INDIGO follow-up plus vorasidenib-combination signals (TTF, immune, radiation) thread through the program. Counterpart trials feed forward to ASCO 2026 and SNO 2026.
  4. Pediatric oncology / medulloblastoma axis — molecular-subgroup-specific therapy (WNT, SHH, Group 3 / 4), CAR-T for relapsed disease, and DIPG / DMG cell-therapy. Strong CHOP / Stanford / St. Jude / DFCI representation.
  5. Single-cell / spatial neuro biology — Suva, Tirosh, Bernstein, Patel-aligned labs at the discovery edge of glioma cell-state mapping, with direct methodological overlap with the AACR 2026 single-cell / spatial topic.

Hybrid per-talk template (and the design decision behind this vault): Brain Cancer 26 is neither pure-clinical (ASCO) nor pure-tools (EuroBioC) nor pure-trial (SABCS) — like SITC and ASHG, it programs neuroscience-mechanism, cellular-therapy clinical, targeted-therapy biology, and single-cell methods in the same room, often back-to-back. The unit of analysis is the talk, not the trial or the tool. We're using the ASHG-style hybrid per-talk template (see talks/index.md) with an explicit Anchor type field that resolves to one of: cell therapy / trial, targeted therapy / trial, cohort / readout, mechanism / biology talk, tool / pipeline, award lecture.

docs.title: Program shape
docs.text:
AACR Brain Cancer 2026 ran Monday March 23 – Wednesday March 25, 2026, three days, Philadelphia Marriott Downtown. Co-chaired by Stephen J. Bagley (UPenn), Michelle Monje (Stanford), and Mario L. Suva (Harvard / Broad / MGH). Structure followed the AACR special-conference pattern:

  • Plenary keynotes — bookending the meeting. Mario Suva and Simona Parrinello (UCL) delivered named keynote talks; the latter on "The role of injury programs in gliomagenesis." Additional keynotes (TBA in our reconstruction) framed neuro-immuno-oncology and pediatric-CNS-tumor sessions.
  • Concurrent thematic sessions — clustered around: GBM CAR-T and cellular therapy; IDH-mutant glioma biology and clinical; pediatric brain tumors (medulloblastoma molecular subgroups, DIPG / DMG); brain metastases (lung / breast / melanoma); neuroscience of gliomas (neural circuits, dopamine signaling, microglia, neurogliogenesis); blood-brain-barrier delivery; single-cell and spatial CNS tumor biology; tumor heterogeneity and resistance.
  • Poster sessions — translational and discovery posters across all of the above; full abstract list on the AACR Brain 26 abstracts page.
  • Mentorship / career sessions — AACR special conferences include an early-career investigator program.
  • Press / media — limited press program; trade-press editorial recaps in the OncLive / Neurology Live / Targeted Oncology cadence.

Tracks dominating the corpus (per the program page + chair public statements):

  • Cellular therapy for CNS tumors — CAR-T for GBM (chlorotoxin, IL-13Rα2 single-target, IL-13Rα2 + EGFR bivalent / bicistronic, EGFRvIII, B7-H3); CAR-T for medulloblastoma and DIPG / DMG (GD2, B7-H3); locoregional / intraventricular delivery; engineered T-cell biology (next-gen designs, TGF-β-resistant constructs, cell-state-directed engineering); endogenous-immune-system interplay.
  • IDH-mutant glioma — vorasidenib (Voranigo) post-INDIGO biology and combinations; IDH-mut-specific immunotherapy (vaccine, neoantigen); 2-HG biology and downstream epigenetic targeting; high-grade IDH-mut clinical experience.
  • Glioblastoma biology — cell-state plasticity (AC-/MES-/OPC-/NPC-like, per Suva / Tirosh / Bernstein single-cell framework); resistance mechanisms; intratumoral heterogeneity; clonal evolution under therapy.
  • Pediatric brain tumors — medulloblastoma molecular subgroups (WNT / SHH / Group 3 / Group 4) and subgroup-specific therapy; DIPG and DMG (H3K27M, ONC201, GD2-CAR-T); ependymoma; ATRT; targetable fusion-driven low-grade glioma (BRAF / RAF / MEK; DAY101 / tovorafenib).
  • Brain metastases — incidence trends (CNS-active ADCs, targeted-therapy effects on CNS pattern); HER2 brain mets (T-DXd CNS activity, tucatinib); melanoma + lung; leptomeningeal disease; intrathecal regimens.
  • Neuroscience of gliomas — neural-circuit integration (Monje lab thread); activity-dependent glioma growth; dopamine / serotonin signaling in glioma; microglia and tumor-associated microglia / macrophages (TAM); astrocyte-glioma crosstalk; peripheral-nerve cancer biology.
  • Blood-brain-barrier penetration — BBB / BTB-aware drug design; focused-ultrasound BBB opening; convection-enhanced delivery; PK / PD modelling for CNS-penetrant agents; ADC CNS activity question.
  • Single-cell and spatial CNS biology — scRNA-seq / snRNA-seq atlases of glioma; spatial transcriptomics in glioma and pediatric brain tumors; integration with neuroscience markers; 3D / volumetric methods.
  • Tumor heterogeneity and 3D / spatial genomics — strategies to reconcile bulk and single-cell readouts; 3D-genome organization in glioma.
  • Next-generation diagnostics / biomarkers — CSF ctDNA / cfDNA in glioma and pediatric CNS tumors; methylation classifier (DKFZ MNP) updates; liquid biopsy for response monitoring.
  • Neuro-immuno-oncology beyond CAR-T — checkpoint blockade in GBM (the persistent unmet niche), oncolytic virus, vaccine approaches.

docs.title: What's different from AACR Annual Meeting, SITC, and SABCS
docs.text:
• Smaller, denser, more neuro-pure. ~600–900 attendees vs AACR Annual's ~22,000. Every session is neuro-oncology; no breast, no GI, no GU, no non-cancer biology. Tighter cross-talk between cancer biologists, neuroscientists, and clinicians than at Annual.
  • More neuroscience than other special conferences. The Monje thread (neural-circuit integration, activity-dependent glioma growth) and the microglia / TAM thread are bigger here than anywhere else in the cancer-meeting calendar. Closer to the Society for Neuroscience (SfN) end of the spectrum than SITC or SABCS.
  • Earlier-phase clinical than SABCS. Most cell-therapy and targeted-therapy readouts here are Ph1/2 cohorts and dose-escalation updates, not randomized Ph3. The randomized vorasidenib INDIGO readout was at ASCO 2023 — by 2026 the work is biology, combinations, and post-marketing.
  • Pediatric component is substantial. Unlike most adult-cancer meetings, the pediatric brain-tumor track is roughly co-equal with the adult-GBM track in airtime. Medulloblastoma and DIPG / DMG content is comparable in volume to glioblastoma content.
  • Single-cell biology load-bearing. Suva / Tirosh / Bernstein / Patel-aligned labs essentially defined glioma single-cell biology; the special conference is where their lineage-and-state framework gets updated. Direct overlap with AACR 2026 single-cell topic.

docs.text:

  • AACR 2026 single-cell / spatial topic — Suva-lineage glioma biology overlaps heavily.
  • SITC 2026 — IO half of the cell-therapy axis. CAR-T solid-tumor cell-therapy threads (GBM, pediatric CNS) appear in both; SITC's larger cellular-therapies track is downstream in November.
  • ASCO 2026 — clinical-translation counterpart. Vorasidenib follow-up, INDIGO post-hoc analyses, and CNS-active ADC readouts have ASCO 2026 trial counterparts (May 29 – Jun 2).
  • SABCS 2026 — brain-metastases overlap (HER2 brain mets, DESTINY-Breast12 update, HER2CLIMB-05) where the breast and brain communities meet.
  • ASHG 2026 — methodology overlap on single-cell, spatial, and cohort genomics. Hybrid per-talk template borrowed from ASHG.
  • AGBT 2026 — upstream platform layer (long-read CSF ctDNA, single-cell methods used in neuro-onc).
  • JPM 2026 — financing layer. CAR-T-in-CNS sponsors (CARGO Therapeutics, Mustang Bio, City of Hope spinouts) and targeted-therapy sponsors (Servier vorasidenib, Day One DAY101) framed brain-tumor pipelines at JPM.
  • Conferences timeline — Brain 26's position in the year's neuro-oncology cycle (JPM Jan → AGBT Feb → AACR Brain Mar → AACR Annual Apr → ASCO May–Jun → SITC Nov → SNO Annual Nov).

docs.title: Format & embargo
docs.text:
AACR special-conference sessions historically use:

  • Plenary keynotes — typically 3–5 named keynote talks bookending the program; Mario Suva and Simona Parrinello (UCL, "Role of injury programs in gliomagenesis") confirmed for 2026.
  • Concurrent thematic sessions — clustered around major tracks (cellular therapy, IDH-mut, neuroscience of gliomas, pediatric, brain mets, single-cell / spatial, BBB delivery, diagnostics / biomarkers).
  • Poster sessions — one or two poster sessions running across days 2 and 3; abstracts on the AACR Brain 26 abstracts page.
  • Educational / forum sessions — typically a single shorter educational block for early-career investigators.
  • Industry sessions / sponsored research presentations — Servier (vorasidenib), Day One (tovorafenib), Chimerix (ONC201), Novocure (TTF), cellular-therapy sponsors.
  • Trainee / early-career awards — AACR-sponsored travel awards and trainee posters; results visible in Cancer Research supplement.

Embargo policy: AACR special-conference abstracts publish to the Cancer Research online supplement on or around the day of presentation. Sponsor topline press releases for the larger clinical programs (e.g., Servier, Day One, Chimerix, CARGO, 2seventy) frequently precede embargo. Detailed 2026 embargo timing was implemented per AACR press-program standard; trade-press recaps in OncLive / Targeted Oncology / Neurology Live / CancerNetwork landed Mar 23 – Apr 4.

docs.title: Top 5 anticipated themes — pre-meeting watch list (reconciled retrospectively)
docs.text:
Reconstructed from the public AACR Brain 26 program page, chair public statements (Bagley / Monje / Suva), Penn Medicine institutional roundup, and the cross-cutting threads in the field as of Q1 2026. Each entry is followed by a short reconciliation note for the post-meeting update.

  1. GBM CAR-T architecture convergence — single-target vs bivalent vs bicistronic. UPenn ICV bivalent (EGFR + IL-13Rα2) Ph1 update (Bagley / O'Rourke / June lab; published in Nature Medicine 2024 / PMC 2025) vs City of Hope locoregional IL-13Rα2 single-target Ph1 (Brown / Badie / Forman lab; Nature Medicine 2024) vs chlorotoxin-targeted (Brown / Badie) vs EGFRvIII single-target lessons-learned. The 2026 question: which architecture / route / target combination beats single-target antigen escape, and where do "armoured" constructs (TGF-β-resistant, IL-7 / IL-15) and logic-gated designs (SynNotch dual-signal) fit. Reconciliation: track which Ph1 cohorts had cohort-expansion announcements during the meeting week.
  2. GD2-CAR-T in pediatric DIPG / DMG — the inflection signal. Monje + Mackall + Stanford / partner-site Ph1 in H3K27M-mutant DMG showed 9/10 evaluable clinical benefit in earlier reads; the 2026 update is the expanded cohort + biomarker / mechanism data. Practice-defining for pediatric DMG (a disease that has had essentially zero practice-changing readouts since ONC201 / dordaviprone entered the picture). Reconciliation: tie to ONC201 / dordaviprone H3K27M Ph2 + Ph3 trajectory and to Chimerix FDA filing window.
  3. Vorasidenib (Voranigo) post-INDIGO — combinations and high-grade extension. First-in-class brain-penetrant mutant IDH1/2 inhibitor approved Aug 2024 for grade 2 IDH-mut astrocytoma / oligodendroglioma. The 2026 biology + early-clinical question: what's the combination partner (TTF per the Terasaki / Novocure CDA program; RT; immune; vaccine)? Does it extend usefully to grade 3 / 4 IDH-mut (high-grade) glioma (the CURE-reported safety + tolerability signal points this way)? Reconciliation: track Servier post-marketing surveillance + Ph2 combination registrations.
  4. IDH-mutant glioma neoantigen / peptide vaccine signal. Platten / Sahm / Schumacher-aligned DKFZ IDH1R132H peptide vaccine (NOA-16 paradigm extended) is the most-watched neuro-IO + IDH-mut combination strategy. Cross-link to broader neoantigen-vaccine field at SITC 2026 (Cathy Wu Smalley Lecture). Reconciliation: any 2026 cohort-expansion or vaccine + checkpoint data.
  5. Neuroscience of gliomas — neural-circuit integration and microglia. Monje-thread (neuron-glioma synaptic integration, AMPAR-driven proliferation, activity-dependent growth) + dopamine signalling (Venkatesh / Monje-aligned) + microglia / TAM (Bowman / Joyce / Quail-aligned) converging into a single neuro-immune-circuit framework. The 2026 update tests whether the framework yields druggable nodes (e.g., gabapentinoid / glutamate-modulator clinical signals; CSF-1R inhibitors; specific microglial-reprogramming approaches). Reconciliation: any window-of-opportunity / Phase-0 trials testing circuit-modulator + standard-of-care.

docs.title: Sponsor map — who's on the Brain 26 stage
docs.text:
The major neuro-oncology pipelines anchoring 2026 content:

  • Servier — vorasidenib (Voranigo) — INDIGO follow-up, high-grade IDH-mut, combinations. FDA-approved Aug 2024.
  • Day One Biopharmaceuticals — DAY101 / tovorafenib — pediatric LGG BRAF post-FIREFLY follow-up. FDA-approved Apr 2024.
  • Chimerix — ONC201 / dordaviprone — H3K27M-mutant DMG Ph2 / Ph3 + FDA filing.
  • Novocure — Tumor Treating Fields (TTF / Optune Gio) — GBM SOC + vorasidenib + RT combinations.
  • CARGO Therapeutics / Mustang Bio / 2seventy / academic spinouts — CAR-T-in-CNS clinical programs (UPenn IL-13Rα2 + EGFR bivalent, City of Hope IL-13Rα2 single-target + chlorotoxin, Stanford GD2 for DMG, Seattle Children's B7-H3).
  • Bayer / Pfizer / Roche / AstraZeneca / Daiichi Sankyo — brain-mets-active ADC and small-molecule franchises (HER2 brain mets via T-DXd, T-DM1, tucatinib; lung / melanoma brain-mets data from EGFR / ALK / BRAF / MEK programs; CDK / TROP2 ADC brain-mets analyses).
  • MSD / BMS — checkpoint approaches in CNS (the persistent unmet niche; window-of-opportunity Ph0).
  • BioMed Valley Discoveries / Stemline / Kazia / various IDH small-molecule sponsors — IDH-mut combination programs.

JPM 2026 day-by-day digests in ../jpm-2026/ flagged several of these as Q1–Q2 2026 readouts (Day One commentary, Chimerix filing posture, CARGO updates).

docs.title: Cross-cutting themes (for themes.md, deferred until per-talk pages are populated)
docs.text:
To synthesize across talks/ once populated:

  1. CAR-T-in-CNS readout convergence. ICV bivalent (UPenn EGFR + IL-13Rα2) vs locoregional single-target (City of Hope IL-13Rα2, chlorotoxin) vs IV + ICV GD2 (Stanford DMG) vs B7-H3 (Seattle Children's) — the 2026 question is which design / route / target combination wins where. Cross-link to SITC 2026 solid-tumor cell-therapy track.
  2. Vorasidenib combination signal. Post-INDIGO, the question is whether IDH-mut targeted-therapy works as monotherapy in higher-grade disease (CURE follow-up suggests safe + tolerable) and which combination (TTF, RT, vaccine, immune) shifts the curve. The 2026 readout shapes the 2027–28 Ph2 / Ph3 design space.
  3. GD2-CAR-T pediatric inflection. The Stanford DMG signal is the most-watched CAR-T signal across all of pediatric solid-tumor oncology. Brain 26 is where the design + biomarker work feeds forward to expanded multi-site Ph2. Bridges to AACR 2026 Annual pediatric track and SITC 2026.
  4. Single-cell glioma cell-state framework consolidation. Suva / Tirosh / Bernstein-aligned labs continue to refine the AC-/MES-/OPC-/NPC-like framework; the 2026 update integrates spatial transcriptomics, lineage tracing, and clinically-paired specimens. Cross-link to AACR 2026 single-cell topic.
  5. Neuro-immune / microglia framing. TAM-targeting plus neural-circuit-glioma plus neuro-IO is converging into a single conceptual frame. The 2026 update brings spatial-immune and single-cell-microglia work into clinical-correlation territory.
  6. BBB-aware drug discovery. Phase-0 / window-of-opportunity trials + FUS BBB opening + CED + BBB-penetrant chemistry. The 2026 reframing of "CNS drug discovery starts with the BBB" reaches mainstream-oncology consciousness via ADC brain-mets data (cross-link to SABCS 2026 brain-mets section).
  7. Pediatric brain-tumor molecular classification standard. DKFZ MNP v13 update + CBTN / OpenPBTA atlas — the diagnostic + research substrate for pediatric brain-tumor work in 2026 onward.
  8. Brain metastases as cross-cancer practice question. HER2 brain-mets (DESTINY-Breast12, HER2CLIMB-05) and lung / melanoma brain-mets activity from CNS-penetrant targeted therapy is reshaping ADC + small-molecule positioning. Cross-meeting bridge across Brain 26 → AACR 2026 → ASCO 2026 → SABCS 2026.

docs.title: City of Hope IL-13Rα2 / chlorotoxin CAR-T for recurrent high-grade glioma
docs.text:
Locoregional single-target IL-13Rα2 CAR-T plus the chlorotoxin (MMP-2-binding) CAR program at City of Hope — adult recurrent high-grade glioma Ph1 updates.

  • Speaker(s): Christine E. Brown, PhD; Behnam Badie, MD (neurosurgery); Stephen J. Forman, MD (lab); session also folds in the chlorotoxin-CAR thread led by the Brown/Badie group
  • Affiliation: City of Hope (Beckman Research Institute / Department of Neurosurgery)
  • Anchor type: cell therapy / trial
  • Day / session: Day 2 (Tue Mar 24, 2026), Cellular Therapy for GBM session
  • Status: post-meeting; details captured from AACR Brain 26 program notes and the published Nature Medicine 2024 IL-13Rα2 locoregional report; updated AACR Brain 26 cohort numerics TBD pending abstract supplement

docs.title: Headline finding
docs.text: Extended follow-up of the City of Hope locoregional IL-13Rα2 CAR-T program in adult recurrent high-grade glioma — the single-target lineage benchmark for IL-13Rα2 CARs — plus an early cohort update from the chlorotoxin-CAR program, which uses a peptide ligand (rather than an antibody scFv) to recognize MMP-2/glioma surface determinants. The Nature Medicine 2024 report established the safety and signals of response for IL-13Rα2 locoregional delivery; the Brain 26 update extends cohort N and durability. Specific 2026 numerics TBD.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology
docs.text: The IL-13Rα2 construct uses a mutein IL-13 ligand binding moiety with a 4-1BB costim domain, delivered via dual intratumoral + intraventricular catheters. The chlorotoxin CAR replaces the antibody scFv with the chlorotoxin peptide, which binds an MMP-2-associated surface complex broadly expressed on glioma and offering a non-antibody targeting mode that may evade classical antigen-escape mechanisms. Both programs rely on locoregional CSF / intratumoral delivery rather than IV.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology deep dive
docs.text:
Underlying biology. IL-13Rα2 is a decoy IL-13 receptor preferentially overexpressed on glioma (in contrast to the more ubiquitous IL-13Rα1/IL-4Rα signaling complex on normal tissue), enriched in mesenchymal-like glioma cell states. Chlorotoxin, a 36-amino-acid scorpion-venom peptide, binds an MMP-2 / annexin A2 / ClC-3 surface complex broadly expressed across glioma irrespective of IL-13Rα2 status, giving a complementary target with a different escape profile.

Therapeutic design. The IL-13Rα2 CAR uses a mutein IL-13 (E13Y / R109K-class) ligand-binding domain to bias affinity toward IL-13Rα2 over IL-13Rα1, fused to a CD8α hinge/transmembrane, a 4-1BB costimulatory domain, and CD3ζ (per the City of Hope Nature Medicine 2024 construct). The chlorotoxin CAR substitutes the scFv with the chlorotoxin peptide as the antigen-binding domain; costimulatory composition for the current Ph1 construct TBD. Delivery uses dual intratumoral (resection cavity catheter) plus intraventricular (Ommaya) infusions; weekly re-dosing schedules have been reported.

Resistance / failure modes. Antigen loss / heterogeneity is documented (single-target IL-13Rα2 leaves antigen-low cells); local-only response with distant CNS progression has been observed, motivating ICV plus intratumoral combined delivery. T-cell persistence in CSF is short, raising the resistance role of repeated dosing rather than persistence.

Translational gaps. Whether chlorotoxin's broader-target profile actually reduces antigen-escape relapse vs IL-13Rα2 in matched cohorts is unresolved; manufacturing scalability and ex-US site replication of the dual-catheter procedure are unproven.

docs.title: Where it fits in the corpus
docs.text:
• AACR 2026: City of Hope cell-therapy team also presented in the Annual Meeting cellular-therapies sessions in San Diego.
  • SITC 2026: solid-tumor CAR-T track — the IL-13Rα2 single-target lineage is the comparator against bivalent / multispecific designs.
  • Related Brain 26 entries: upenn-icv-bivalent-cart.md (bivalent counterpart), monje-gd2-cart-dipg.md, neuroscience-of-gliomas-tam.md.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Does chlorotoxin's broader surface-determinant targeting reduce antigen-loss relapse vs IL-13Rα2 single-target — public cohort data is still small.
  • Optimal locoregional regimen (intratumoral catheter vs ICV vs both) and re-dosing frequency remains a design question shared with the UPenn ICV bivalent program.

docs.title: DKFZ IDH-mutant glioma peptide / neoantigen vaccine update
docs.text:
IDH1R132H peptide vaccine — the DKFZ-led neoantigen IO program for IDH-mutant glioma, extending NOA-16 toward combination and post-vorasidenib positioning.

  • Speaker(s): Michael Platten, MD; Felix Sahm, MD, PhD; aligned with the Ton N. Schumacher (NKI) and DKFZ Neuro-Oncology team
  • Affiliation: DKFZ / Heidelberg University Hospital (Department of Neurology + Neuropathology)
  • Anchor type: targeted therapy / trial (neoantigen vaccine)
  • Day / session: Day 1 (Mon Mar 23, 2026), IDH-mutant Glioma session
  • Status: post-meeting; details captured from AACR Brain 26 program notes, the NOA-16 Nature 2021 first-in-human report (Platten et al.), and DKFZ follow-up; expanded 2026 cohort numerics and any vaccine + checkpoint combination data TBD pending abstract supplement

docs.title: Headline finding
docs.text: Updated cohort and follow-on data from the DKFZ IDH1R132H peptide vaccine program — the most-watched neoantigen-IO + IDH-mut combination strategy. NOA-16 (Nature 2021) established that the IDH1R132H peptide is genuinely immunogenic and produces mutation-specific CD4 T-cell responses with a tolerable safety profile in newly-diagnosed grade 3/4 IDH-mut glioma. The Brain 26 readout extends cohort N and brings vaccine + checkpoint (PD-1/PD-L1) combination signals into view, plus the practical question of how to sequence with vorasidenib. Specific PFS, immune-response rate, and combo-cohort numbers TBD.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology
docs.text: The vaccine is a long-peptide formulation of the IDH1R132H neoepitope, presented through HLA-DR class II to drive a tumor-selective CD4 T-cell response (the IDH1R132H mutation is a shared, truncal driver, making it a near-universal target across IDH-mut glioma). Combination arms layer PD-1 or PD-L1 blockade on top of vaccination to overcome the strongly immunosuppressive D-2-HG-driven TME — a logic that intersects with vorasidenib's ability to lower 2-HG and potentially "open" the TME for IO.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology deep dive
docs.text:
Underlying biology. The IDH1R132H point mutation creates a tumor-restricted neoepitope spanning the mutated arginine-to-histidine residue, presented promiscuously on multiple HLA class II alleles (notably HLA-DR1 / DRB1 broadly) — making it one of the few truly "off-the-shelf" shared neoantigens across IDH-mut glioma. The mutation is truncal (present in essentially all tumor cells), and homozygous expression on all malignant clones makes immune editing / antigen loss biologically constrained — losing IDH-mut would also lose the oncogenic driver.

Therapeutic design. A 20-mer synthetic long peptide spanning the IDH1R132H mutation (NOA-16 construct: p123–142 IDH1(R132H)), formulated with Montanide ISA-51 adjuvant and topical imiquimod (TLR7 agonist) at the injection site to drive class-II–restricted CD4 helper responses. Subcutaneous prime-boost schedule; combination arms add anti-PD-L1 (avelumab/atezolizumab-class) per the public NOA-16 and follow-on protocols. Specific 2026 combination cohort schedule TBD.

Resistance / failure modes. Documented: pseudoprogression (vaccine-driven immune infiltrate mimicking tumor growth on MRI) requiring careful Rx-response distinction; modest durability of peripheral T-cell responses without boost. Anticipated escape: HLA class II downregulation on tumor cells; D-2-HG–driven local immunosuppression limiting effector trafficking; outgrowth of IDH-mut–retaining but antigen-presentation-defective subclones.

Translational gaps. Optimal sequencing with vorasidenib (does 2-HG suppression enhance or reduce neoepitope presentation?), durability of response, and whether a class I–restricted booster could add CD8 effector activity remain undefined.

docs.title: GD2-CAR-T for pediatric DIPG and diffuse midline glioma — Stanford Ph1 update
docs.text:
Practice-defining pediatric CAR-T cohort update: autologous GD2-targeted CAR-T (IV + intracerebroventricular) in H3K27M-mutant diffuse midline glioma and DIPG.

  • Speaker(s): Michelle Monje, MD, PhD (also Brain 26 co-chair and gave the neuroscience-of-glioma plenary thread); Crystal L. Mackall, MD (cell-therapy lead)
  • Affiliation: Stanford University (Department of Neurology & Neurological Sciences; Center for Cancer Cell Therapy); Howard Hughes Medical Institute
  • Anchor type: cell therapy / trial
  • Day / session: Day 2 (Tue Mar 24, 2026), Pediatric / DIPG session
  • Status: post-meeting; details captured from AACR Brain 26 program notes, prior Stanford Ph1 reports (Nature 2022 / Nature Medicine 2024 follow-ups), and Monje/Mackall public statements; expanded 2026 cohort numerics TBD pending abstract supplement

docs.title: Headline finding
docs.text: Updated, expanded cohort of autologous GD2-CAR-T (4-1BB costim) in H3K27M-mutant DIPG and diffuse midline glioma (DMG), extending the earlier Stanford report (~9/10 evaluable clinical-benefit signal) into a larger multi-site Ph1 with longer survival follow-up and biomarker correlates. This remains the strongest CAR-T efficacy signal in any pediatric CNS solid tumor, in a disease (H3K27M DMG) where nothing has been practice-changing since ONC201 / dordaviprone emerged. Specific updated cohort N, PFS, and OS from the Brain 26 talk TBD.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology
docs.text: Autologous patient T cells transduced with a GD2-directed CAR (4-1BB / CD3ζ); GD2 is uniformly and highly expressed on H3K27M DMG. Initial cell dose is delivered intravenously after lymphodepletion, followed by intracerebroventricular re-dosing via Ommaya to address CNS pharmacokinetics. ICANS-class neuroinflammatory toxicity is managed proactively given tumor location in brainstem / thalamus. Biomarker workup includes CSF cytokine profiles, TCR-seq of expanded CAR-T product, and serial MRI volumetric response.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology deep dive
docs.text:
Underlying biology. H3K27M mutation in histone H3.3 / H3.1 globally reduces H3K27me3, locking DMG cells in an OPC-like / neural-precursor-like state with uniformly high GD2 disialoganglioside surface expression — a developmentally restricted antigen otherwise largely absent from postnatal CNS at high density. The H3K27M-driven OPC-like state also confers responsiveness to neural-circuit / activity-dependent inputs (the Monje thread linking neuron-glioma synapses to growth).

Therapeutic design. Autologous patient T cells lentivirally transduced with a GD2-CAR using the 14g2a-derived scFv, a CD8α hinge/transmembrane, 4-1BB costimulatory domain, and CD3ζ (the Mackall lab construct also used in pediatric neuroblastoma). Manufacturing is standard 9–14-day expansion. Lymphodepletion with fludarabine + cyclophosphamide precedes a single IV dose, followed by Ommaya-administered ICV re-doses at escalating cadence. Tocilizumab, anakinra, and intrathecal steroids are pre-positioned for tumor-inflammation-associated neurotoxicity (TIAN), a Monje-defined entity distinct from classical ICANS.

Resistance / failure modes. Documented: TIAN-driven brainstem swelling requiring aggressive steroid / anakinra and occasional EVD placement; partial / transient radiographic responses; on-treatment progression without clear antigen loss. Anticipated escape: cell-state drift away from OPC-like (toward AC-like / MES-like) reducing GD2 surface density; T-cell exhaustion in CNS TME.

Translational gaps. Multi-site replication of Stanford manufacturing and TIAN management capacity remains the key barrier; sequencing with ONC201/dordaviprone, RT, and re-irradiation TBD.

  • Combinatorial space: where do ONC201 / dordaviprone, RT, and GD2-CAR-T sequence — and does cell-state plasticity (Suva framework) create predictable escape via antigen / lineage drift?

docs.title: Neuroscience of gliomas + microglia / TAM — cross-cutting synthesis session
docs.text:
Hybrid synthesis of the Monje neural-circuit-integration thread with the Bowman / Joyce / Quail microglia and tumor-associated-macrophage (TAM) work — the convergence into a single neuro-immune framework.

  • Speaker(s): Michelle Monje (Stanford); Humsa V. Venkatesh (Harvard / BWH; dopamine + neural-circuit-glioma); Frank Winkler (Heidelberg; tumor microtube networks); Johanna A. Joyce (Lausanne), Robert L. Bowman (Yale), Daniela F. Quail (McGill; microglia / TAM reprogramming); Dolores Hambardzumyan (Emory)
  • Affiliation: Stanford / Harvard / Heidelberg / Lausanne / Yale / McGill / Emory
  • Anchor type: synthesis (cross-cutting mechanism / biology cluster)
  • Day / session: Day 2 (Tue Mar 24, 2026), Neuroscience of Gliomas + Neuro-immune / TME concurrent sessions
  • Status: post-meeting; details captured from AACR Brain 26 program notes and the public Monje / Venkatesh / Joyce / Quail / Bowman published corpus; specific 2026 unpublished data from each speaker TBD pending abstract supplement

docs.title: Headline finding
docs.text: The two halves of glioma neuro-biology — (a) neurons-to-glioma synaptic integration (Monje thread: AMPAR-driven proliferation, neural-activity-dependent growth) plus dopaminergic and other neurotransmitter inputs (Venkatesh) plus tumor-microtube networks (Winkler) and (b) the microglia / TAM reprogramming axis (Bowman / Joyce / Quail single-cell + spatial TAM atlases, CSF-1R-class targeting, microglial-state reprogramming) — converge on a single neuro-immune framework where neural activity, TAM state, and tumor cell state co-determine progression. The session question is whether this framework yields druggable nodes beyond gabapentinoids and CSF-1R inhibitors.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology
docs.text: Methodology spans patch-clamp electrophysiology in tumor slices (neuron-glioma synapses), optogenetic / chemogenetic perturbation of cortical activity in glioma-bearing mice, intravital imaging of tumor-microtube networks, single-cell and spatial atlases of TAM states across glioma grades and treatment status, and TAM-reprogramming pharmacology (CSF-1R inhibitors, complement / TREM2-class targets). Window-of-opportunity / Phase-0 trials testing circuit-modulator agents alongside standard of care are referenced as the clinical translation layer.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology deep dive
docs.text:
Underlying biology. Two converging axes: (1) Neurons form bona fide AMPA-receptor-mediated glutamatergic synapses onto glioma cells (Monje, Venkatesh, Winkler 2019 Nature trio), with electrical activity also coupling glioma cells via connexin-43–containing gap junctions in tumor-microtube networks (Winkler). Activity-dependent secretion of NLGN3 and BDNF drives proliferation. Dopaminergic and serotonergic inputs (Venkatesh) extend the framework beyond glutamate. (2) Microglia and tumor-associated macrophages (the dominant immune infiltrate, 30–50% of GBM mass) occupy a spectrum of disease-associated states (Joyce, Bowman, Quail single-cell atlases) characterized by TREM2, SPP1, APOE, MARCO, and CSF1R-dependent survival programs.

Therapeutic design. Circuit-modulator side: gabapentinoids (gabapentin, perampanel — AMPAR antagonist), levetiracetam (SV2A), tested as add-on to standard of care in window-of-opportunity / Phase-0 designs. TAM side: small-molecule CSF-1R inhibitors (pexidartinib, BLZ945-class), TREM2 antibodies, complement (C1q, C5aR) blockade, and antibody-drug conjugates against TAM markers; combinations with CAR-T (TAM reprogramming as adjuvant to relieve CNS T-cell exhaustion) are an early translational layer.

Resistance / failure modes. CSF-1R monotherapy has failed in randomized GBM trials (BLZ945, pexidartinib) due to TAM-state plasticity — depletion is incomplete and surviving TAMs re-skew toward immunosuppressive phenotypes. Circuit-modulator trials are limited by single-agent effect size and seizure-confounded endpoints.

Translational gaps. Whether neural-circuit + TAM combinations are additive vs redundant, and whether either translates to a randomized PFS/OS signal, remains unresolved.

  • Does TAM reprogramming work synergize with CAR-T (e.g., relieving CAR-T exhaustion in the CNS TME), or are they parallel programs that compete for the same patients?

docs.title: Simona Parrinello keynote — the role of injury programs in gliomagenesis
docs.text:
Plenary keynote reframing glioma origin and progression in terms of wound-healing / injury-response transcriptional programs hijacked from normal CNS biology.

  • Speaker(s): Simona Parrinello, PhD
  • Affiliation: UCL Cancer Institute (Samantha Dickson Brain Cancer Unit), University College London
  • Anchor type: study (mechanism / biology keynote)
  • Day / session: Day 2 plenary (Tue Mar 24, 2026); title "The role of injury programs in gliomagenesis" confirmed on the public AACR Brain 26 program page
  • Status: post-meeting; details captured from AACR Brain 26 program notes and the confirmed keynote title; specific model-system and dataset specifics from the talk itself TBD pending abstract supplement

docs.title: Headline finding
docs.text: Plenary keynote arguing that glioblastoma growth, invasion, and recurrence are organized by injury-response / wound-healing transcriptional programs — the same programs that normal astrocytes, oligodendrocyte-lineage cells, and microglia run after CNS injury — co-opted by tumor cells and their TME. The framing places gliomagenesis on a continuum with reactive astrogliosis and CNS repair rather than treating it as a purely cell-autonomous oncogenic program, and predicts that surgery, radiation, and chemotherapy themselves create the injury context that drives a fraction of recurrence. Specific datasets and quantitative claims from the Brain 26 talk TBD.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology
docs.text: Mouse models of glioma initiation and recurrence, paired with single-cell and spatial profiling of human glioma specimens, used to identify injury-program transcription factors and downstream effectors active in tumor cells, reactive astrocytes, and TAMs. The Parrinello lab's prior work on perivascular niche and stem-like glioma cell biology feeds the model. The keynote frames neurosurgical resection cavities and radiation-injured peritumoral tissue as a permissive niche for residual disease.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology deep dive
docs.text:
Underlying biology. Normal CNS injury (stab wound, stroke, demyelination) activates a stereotyped transcriptional program across astrocytes (reactive astrogliosis: GFAP, vimentin, LCN2), oligodendrocyte-lineage cells (OPC mobilization, PDGFRA re-expression), and microglia/TAMs (DAM-like states: TREM2, APOE, SPP1), governed by core TFs including STAT3, AP-1 (FOS/JUN), C/EBP family, and NF-κB. Parrinello's model: gliomagenesis hijacks these same programs — the MES-like glioma state in the Suva framework is, mechanistically, an injury-program state — and surgical / radiation injury at the resection cavity creates a permissive niche that selects for and expands injury-program-positive residual tumor cells.

Therapeutic design. Not a drug per se but a target-discovery framework. Tractable nodes nominated by the Parrinello lab and aligned work include: STAT3 (clinical-grade inhibitors available), C/EBPβ, AP-1 modulators, and injury-niche–restricted ligands (e.g., osteopontin/SPP1, CHI3L1). The peri-surgical / peri-RT window is the proposed clinical entry point — interrupting injury-program induction during the 2–4 week post-op window.

Resistance / failure modes. Injury-program activation is functionally redundant (multiple TF inputs converge on overlapping effector programs), making single-node pharmacology likely to be evaded; injury-program-positive cells are also intrinsically more resistant to chemo/RT (slow-cycling, stem-like).

Translational gaps. No clinical trial yet specifically targets the peri-surgical injury window with an injury-program inhibitor; biomarkers to identify injury-program-high tumors prospectively are unproven.

docs.title: Where it fits in the corpus
docs.text:
• AACR 2026: the injury-program framing dovetails with Suva-lineage cell-state biology and the Monje neural-circuit thread.
  • SITC 2026: TME / wound-healing programs intersect with TAM-targeting and microenvironment-reprogramming IO concepts.
  • Related Brain 26 entries: suva-glioma-cell-states.md, neuroscience-of-gliomas-tam.md, monje-gd2-cart-dipg.md.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Which injury-program nodes are pharmacologically tractable in the peri-surgical window — and does interrupting them at the cavity actually reduce local recurrence?
  • How do injury programs intersect with the AC/MES-state axis (Suva framework) — is MES-like simply the injury-program state by another name, or genuinely distinct?

docs.title: Mario Suva keynote — glioma cell states, lineage, and therapeutic implications
docs.text:
Plenary keynote anchoring the single-cell cell-state framework (AC-/MES-/OPC-/NPC-like) that underpins much of the rest of the Brain 26 program.

  • Speaker(s): Mario L. Suva, MD, PhD (also Brain 26 co-chair)
  • Affiliation: Harvard Medical School / Broad Institute / Massachusetts General Hospital
  • Anchor type: study (mechanism / biology keynote)
  • Day / session: Day 1 plenary (Mon Mar 23, 2026)
  • Status: post-meeting; details captured from AACR Brain 26 program notes, the chair-disclosed keynote topic, and the Suva-lab published corpus (Patel/Suva Science 2014; Tirosh/Suva Nature 2016; Neftel/Suva Cell 2019; subsequent perturb-seq and lineage-tracing work); specific Brain 26 dataset specifics TBD pending abstract supplement and any accompanying paper

docs.title: Headline finding
docs.text: Plenary synthesis of the glioma cell-state framework: AC-like (astrocyte-like), MES-like (mesenchymal-like), OPC-like (oligodendrocyte-precursor-like), and NPC-like (neural-progenitor-like) states defined by single-cell RNA-seq across primary and recurrent glioma, plus new perturbation / lineage-tracing data showing how these states interconvert under therapy. The 2026 update integrates spatial transcriptomics, clinically-paired (pre/post-treatment) specimens, and perturbation-derived state transitions. Specific datasets and new state-transition rules from the keynote TBD pending the supplement.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology
docs.text: Single-cell and single-nucleus RNA-seq of fresh tumor and matched recurrence specimens, framed by the Neftel et al. four-state model; layered on top: spatial transcriptomics (Visium HD / Xenium-class), CRISPR perturb-seq to map state-determining transcription factors, and lineage-tracing (DNA barcoding) to test whether the same clone can occupy multiple states. The framework explicitly connects to developmental neural lineages, and integrates microenvironmental context (hypoxia, TAM proximity, neural-circuit input) as state-biasing signals.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology deep dive
docs.text:
Underlying biology. The Neftel/Suva four-state framework holds that malignant glioma cells occupy a continuum bounded by four developmentally-informed transcriptional states — AC-like (astrocyte-lineage, e.g., GFAP, AQP4), MES-like (mesenchymal / wound-healing, e.g., CD44, CHI3L1), OPC-like (oligodendrocyte-precursor, e.g., OLIG1/2, PDGFRA), and NPC-like (neural-progenitor, e.g., DLL3, SOX11) — biased toward specific states by recurrent genetic drivers (EGFR → AC; NF1 → MES; PDGFRA → OPC; CDK4 → NPC) and by TME inputs (hypoxia / necrosis → MES; neural-circuit input → NPC/OPC).

Therapeutic design. Not a therapeutic per se, but a target-selection framework: dictates which surface antigens (IL-13Rα2 enriched in MES; EGFR/EGFRvIII enriched in AC/OPC; GD2 enriched in OPC/NPC; DLL3 in NPC) are tractable and where antigen-loss escape will land. Perturb-seq screens nominate state-master TFs (e.g., NFIA/B for AC; CEBPB/FOSL for MES; ASCL1/OLIG2 for OPC/NPC) as state-stabilizing or state-locking pharmacological nodes.

Resistance / failure modes. Plasticity itself is the resistance mechanism: therapy (RT, TMZ, IDH-i, CAR-T) reproducibly shifts cell-state distribution toward MES-like / stem-like programs, mediating recurrence without classical genetic resistance.

Translational gaps. Whether state transitions can be pharmacologically blocked (rather than just observed) is unproven; the framework was built on adult IDH-wt GBM and its fit for pediatric DMG and IDH-mut glioma is still being calibrated.

docs.title: Where it fits in the corpus
docs.text:
• AACR 2026: Suva is a chair / speaker on the Annual single-cell / spatial-omics topic four weeks later; this keynote sets up that thread.
  • SITC 2026: cell-state-directed CAR-T target selection — the link from atlas biology to therapeutic engineering.
  • Related Brain 26 entries: parrinello-injury-programs.md, monje-gd2-cart-dipg.md, neuroscience-of-gliomas-tam.md, vorasidenib-post-indigo.md.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• Which state transitions are deterministically therapy-induced (TMZ, RT, IDH-i, CAR-T) versus stochastic, and which can be blocked pharmacologically?
  • How tightly does the AC/MES/OPC/NPC-like framework hold for pediatric DMG / DIPG and IDH-mutant glioma — both have lineage features the adult-GBM framework wasn't built around.

docs.title: UPenn intracerebroventricular bivalent CAR-T (EGFR + IL-13Rα2) for recurrent GBM
docs.text:
Ph1 update of locoregional bivalent EGFR + IL-13Rα2 CAR-T delivered into the CSF via Ommaya for adult recurrent glioblastoma.

  • Speaker(s): Stephen J. Bagley, MD, MSCE; co-investigators Donald M. O'Rourke, Carl H. June (lab and clinical team)
  • Affiliation: Abramson Cancer Center / Perelman School of Medicine, University of Pennsylvania
  • Anchor type: cell therapy / trial
  • Day / session: Day 1 (Mon Mar 23, 2026), Cellular Therapy for GBM session; Bagley also co-chaired the meeting
  • Status: post-meeting; details captured from AACR Brain 26 program notes, Penn Medicine institutional roundup, and the published Nature Medicine 2024 / PMC 2025 dataset that the cohort expansion extends; specific Brain 26 cohort numerics TBD pending Cancer Research abstract supplement

docs.title: Headline finding
docs.text: Updated Ph1 cohort of locoregionally delivered, bicistronic CAR-T co-targeting EGFR and IL-13Rα2 in adult recurrent GBM, building on the Nature Medicine 2024 first-in-human report that documented rapid, transient tumor regressions in the index patients. The 2026 update reads out an expanded, ICV-dosed (intracerebroventricular, via Ommaya reservoir) cohort with longer follow-up. Exact ORR, durability, and DLT numbers from the AACR Brain 26 talk TBD pending the abstract supplement.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology
docs.text: A single bicistronic CAR construct co-expresses two scFvs — one against EGFR (wild-type and variant III) and one against IL-13Rα2 — paired to a 4-1BB costimulatory domain (per the Nature Medicine 2024 construct). Cells are delivered into the CSF via Ommaya reservoir rather than IV or intratumoral, exploiting CSF circulation to reach multifocal disease and limit on-target/off-tumor systemic EGFR toxicity. Dual antigen targeting is designed to blunt single-target antigen escape seen with EGFRvIII-only CAR-T.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology deep dive
docs.text:
Underlying biology. EGFR (wild-type and the tumor-specific variant III deletion) and IL-13Rα2 are two of the most consistently overexpressed surface antigens on adult GBM, with largely non-overlapping expression patterns across single-cell-defined tumor cell states (EGFR skews toward proneural/OPC-like; IL-13Rα2 toward mesenchymal). Single-target EGFRvIII CAR-T (Penn 2017, Nature Translational Medicine) cleared antigen-positive cells but left an antigen-negative reservoir, motivating the bivalent design.

Therapeutic design. A single bicistronic lentiviral construct co-expresses an EGFR-directed scFv (the Penn group's anti-EGFR(806)-class binder, recognizing both wild-type and vIII conformational epitope) and an IL-13Rα2 binder, each linked to a 4-1BB / CD3ζ signaling cassette. ICV delivery uses an Ommaya reservoir; single or limited-dose schedule reported in the Nature Medicine 2024 first-in-human; lymphodepletion regimen and re-dose schedule for the expansion cohort TBD.

Resistance / failure modes. Documented: rapid cytokine-driven neuroinflammation requiring tocilizumab/anakinra; transient response with re-growth, mechanism not yet defined but candidates include (i) loss of both antigens via cell-state switch, (ii) T-cell exhaustion in the CSF/TME, and (iii) intrinsic resistance in NPC-like / proliferative-stem subpopulations.

Translational gaps. Re-dosing cadence via Ommaya, optimal lymphodepletion for CSF delivery, and whether bivalent ICV is genuinely additive over single-target IL-13Rα2 ICV in a matched cohort — none publicly defined. TBD whether CAR-T persistence in CSF correlates with durability.

docs.title: Where it fits in the corpus

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
• How does durability of the bivalent ICV approach compare to single-target IL-13Rα2 locoregional (City of Hope) in matched recurrent GBM cohorts, and does dual targeting actually reduce antigen-escape relapse?
  • Optimal lymphodepletion and re-dosing schedule via Ommaya — single dose vs serial intraventricular infusions — is not yet defined publicly.

docs.title: Vorasidenib (Voranigo) post-INDIGO — biology, high-grade extension, and combinations
docs.text:
Post-INDIGO update for vorasidenib in IDH-mutant glioma, anchoring the AACR-Novocure CDA-funded TTF + vorasidenib program plus RT, vaccine, and immune combination signals.

  • Speaker(s): Ingo K. Mellinghoff, MD (MSK; INDIGO co-PI); Patrick Y. Wen (DFCI); Timothy F. Cloughesy (UCLA); Zhaohui Wang, PhD (Terasaki Institute; AACR-Novocure CDA recipient for TTF + vorasidenib)
  • Affiliation: MSK / DFCI / UCLA; Terasaki Institute for Biomedical Innovation (TTF combination arm); Servier (sponsor)
  • Anchor type: targeted therapy / trial + tool (post-marketing biology + combination design)
  • Day / session: Day 1 (Mon Mar 23, 2026), IDH-mutant Glioma session
  • Status: post-meeting; details captured from AACR Brain 26 program notes, the published INDIGO Ph3 (NEJM 2023), CURE-reported high-grade safety follow-up, and the AACR press release naming Wang's TTF + vorasidenib CDA; cohort-level update numerics TBD pending abstract supplement

docs.title: Headline finding
docs.text: Three threads in one session: (1) post-INDIGO biology and post-marketing surveillance of vorasidenib (Voranigo) in grade 2 IDH-mutant astrocytoma / oligodendroglioma — the first targeted therapy approved in this indication (FDA Aug 2024); (2) extension into higher-grade (grade 3 / 4) IDH-mut glioma, building on the CURE-reported safety/tolerability signal; and (3) the combination program — TTF (Tumor Treating Fields) per the AACR-Novocure CDA-funded preclinical + Ph1 design (Wang, Terasaki), plus RT and vaccine combinations. Specific updated PFS/biomarker numbers from the Brain 26 talk TBD.

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology
docs.text: Vorasidenib is a brain-penetrant dual mutant IDH1 / IDH2 inhibitor that suppresses oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HG), driving downstream re-expression of methylation-silenced tumor-suppressor and differentiation programs. The TTF combination rationale (per the CDA award) is that low-intensity alternating electric fields disrupt mitosis and may synergize with IDH-inhibitor-induced differentiation pressure; the program is preclinical-to-Ph1. Vaccine combinations leverage the IDH1R132H peptide (see dkfz-idh-vaccine.md).

docs.title: Mechanism / methodology deep dive
docs.text:
Underlying biology. Mutant IDH1 (R132H most common) and IDH2 produce the oncometabolite D-2-hydroxyglutarate (D-2-HG), which competitively inhibits α-KG-dependent dioxygenases including TET2 (DNA demethylation) and the KDM family (histone demethylation), producing the hypermethylator (G-CIMP) phenotype and a differentiation block. D-2-HG also suppresses local T-cell and NK function, contributing to an immunologically cold TME.

Therapeutic design. Vorasidenib (AG-881) is an orally bioavailable, brain-penetrant dual allosteric inhibitor of mutant IDH1/IDH2, designed for CNS exposure that ivosidenib (IDH1-only) and enasidenib (IDH2-only) lack. INDIGO (NEJM 2023) used 40 mg QD in non-enhancing grade 2 IDH-mut glioma post-surgery; combination arms layer (a) TTF at 200 kHz (Optune-class) per the Wang CDA, (b) RT timing studies, and (c) IDH1R132H peptide vaccine + checkpoint.

Resistance / failure modes. Known: incomplete D-2-HG suppression in tumor core, intra-tumoral heterogeneity of IDH activity, and second-site mutations / dimer-interface mutations conferring inhibitor resistance (documented for ivosidenib in AML, plausible in glioma). Anticipated: clonal selection of IDH-wild-type-like glioblastoma transformation under prolonged inhibition.

Translational gaps. Optimal sequencing with RT/TMZ in higher-grade IDH-mut, biomarkers for vorasidenib responders beyond IDH-mut status, and whether 2-HG suppression genuinely improves vaccine immunogenicity are all open. TTF + vorasidenib remains preclinical → Ph1 with no efficacy readout yet.

docs.title: AACR Pancreatic Cancer 2026
docs.text:
AACR Special Conference in Cancer Research: Pancreatic Cancer — Hilton San Diego Bayfront, San Diego, CA · September 25 – 28, 2026. The AACR subspecialty meeting where the pancreatic-cancer field (basic + translational + clinical) convenes between AACR Annual and the late-year clinical-readout cycle.

Status: Scaffold — meeting is ~4.5 months out as of today (May 11, 2026). Structure is being laid down now so the abstract submission cycle (typical AACR Special Conference window: ~June deadline, late-breaker ~August), pre-meeting program release (August–September), and live-coverage build (Sep 25–28) can be staged. Talk titles, the late-breaking slate, and named-lecture assignments are not yet public; anything in this vault dated before its embargo lift is reconstructed from prior-year (Pancreatic 2024 Boston, Pancreatic 2025) AACR programs, AACR 2026 Annual pancreatic-track content, sponsor pipeline guidance, and analyst preview notes — flagged inline.

docs.title: Why this is in the vault
docs.text:
AACR Pancreatic is the field-level convening venue for PDAC research between the Annual Meeting (April) and the late-year clinical readouts (ESMO Oct, ASCO GI Jan). Two characteristics make it distinct from the broader AACR 2026 Annual Meeting:

  • Single-disease depth. The room is pancreatic-cancer-specialist-dominated — basic biologists (KRAS signaling, stroma, metabolism), translational scientists (PDX / organoid models, ctDNA / cfDNA biomarkers), and medical/surgical oncologists run cross-disciplinary discussions that the Annual Meeting's parallel-track format dilutes. Discussion sections after talks routinely run long; the small-room culture is a feature.
  • Hybrid format. Unlike SABCS (clinical-readout-driven) or EuroBioC (per-tool methods talks), AACR Pancreatic mixes practice-changing clinical readouts (Phase 1b/2 KRAS-inhibitor data, mRNA vaccine durability updates), mechanistic talks (stromal biology, immune evasion, metabolic vulnerabilities), and platform / model-system talks (organoids, GEMMs, spatial atlases). The per-talk template in talks/ is hybrid — each entry resolves to a trial anchor (clinical readout), tool anchor (model / platform / assay), or study anchor (mechanism paper / dataset).

The field is in an unusual moment. The KRAS-inhibitor wave that crossed the bar at AACR 2024–2025 (sotorasib / adagrasib for G12C; daraxonrasib pan-RAS at AACR 2025) is feeding the first wave of pancreatic-specific combination Phase 2 / 3 readouts. mRNA neoantigen vaccines (autogene cevumeran / BNT122) reported the first long-term recurrence-free survival signal at ASCO 2024, with follow-up readouts in the AACR Pancreatic → ESMO 2026 → ASCO GI 2027 cycle. Early-detection biomarker work (CA19-9 successors, microbiome signatures, MRI/CT AI) is moving from biomarker discovery to interventional trials. AACR Pancreatic 2026 is the venue where these three threads converge with the basic-biology audience.

Strong overlap with AACR 2026 Annual — the pancreatic-specific clinical-trials and KRAS sessions at Annual feed forward to expanded Phase 2 readouts at Pancreatic. Lighter overlap with SITC 2026 (PDAC immunotherapy track), ESMO 2026 (clinical Phase 3 pancreatic readouts), and ASCO GI 2026 / 2027 (GI-specific Phase 3).

docs.title: Program shape
docs.text:
AACR Pancreatic 2026 runs Friday September 25 through Monday September 28, 2026, four days, Hilton San Diego Bayfront. Co-chairs:

  • Andrew J. Aguirre (Dana-Farber Cancer Institute) — KRAS biology / functional genomics / PDX
  • Florencia McAllister (MD Anderson) — microbiome, immune microenvironment, prevention/interception
  • Kenneth P. Olive (Columbia / Herbert Irving) — stroma biology, GEMMs, drug delivery
  • Eileen O'Reilly (Memorial Sloan Kettering) — clinical pancreatic-cancer trials lead
  • Diane M. Simeone (UC San Diego) — early detection, cancer stem cells, host institution lead
  • Colin D. Weekes (Mass General / Harvard) — translational clinical, KRAS-directed trials

The structure (per the 2022 / 2024 / 2025 recurring pattern):

  • Plenary / keynote lectures — opening keynote (typically a field-defining figure: prior years have included Pasca di Magliano, Vonderheide, Tuveson, Hingorani); named lectures bookend mornings.
  • Major symposia (typically 6–8 across the meeting) — thematic sessions of 4–6 invited + abstract-selected talks. Common 2024/2025 themes: tumor evolution, KRAS-directed therapy, the immunosuppressive microenvironment, metabolism, early detection / interception, models for translation, health disparities.
  • Mini-symposia / proffered-paper sessions — abstract-selected short talks, typically 4–6 per session, distributed across thematic afternoons.
  • Poster sessions — typically two large evening sessions; abstract floor ~400–600 posters.
  • Forum / interactive sessions — career development, trainee networking, advocacy / patient-perspective sessions.
  • Press program — informal; selected presentations get AACR press-release coverage when a sponsor topline is timed to the meeting.

Expected tracks dominating the 2026 corpus (based on prior-year load + 2026 pipeline state):

  • Pan-RAS and KRAS-selective inhibitors — daraxonrasib (RMC-6236, Revolution Medicines) pan-RAS Phase 2/3 PDAC data; zoldonrasib (RMC-9805, KRAS-G12D selective) Phase 1/2; the broader RMC tri-complex portfolio (RMC-6291 G12C(ON), RMC-5552 mTORC1, RMC-4630 SHP2); next-generation Mirati/BMS G12D agents; Astellas/Boundless RAS portfolio; Amgen / Frontier Medicines KRAS-mut combinations.
  • mRNA neoantigen vaccines — BNT122 / autogene cevumeran (BioNTech / Genentech) Phase 2 randomized data; the parallel Moderna / Merck mRNA-4157 individualized program if PDAC arm reads; T-cell receptor / TCR-T cellular therapies targeting shared neoantigens (KRAS-G12D / G12V class-I HLA-restricted).
  • Stromal biology and the immunosuppressive microenvironment — CAF heterogeneity, TGF-β / IL-6 / CXCR4 axis, the LIF / JAK-STAT pathway, mechanical-tension biology, stromal reprogramming with focal adhesion / hyaluronidase / sonic-hedgehog-pathway updates. Strong AACR Pancreatic franchise per the Olive / Tuveson lineage.
  • PDX / organoid / GEMM models — co-clinical trial designs, organoid-based drug screening platforms (Tuveson / Tiriac), patient-derived xenograft sensitivity portfolios, GEMM-derived combination screens for KRAS-resistance.
  • Early detection and biomarkers — CA19-9 successors (multi-analyte serum panels, methylation-based assays from Guardant / GRAIL / Exact Sciences), microbiome-based detection (oral / stool signatures), MRI / CT AI for sub-2-cm lesion detection, intercept strategies for high-risk cohorts (BRCA / Lynch / familial / new-onset diabetes).
  • Metabolism, hypoxia, autophagy — autophagy / lysosomal targeting (DC661 / hydroxychloroquine class), glutamine / pyrimidine metabolic vulnerabilities, MAPK-pathway-induced metabolic rewiring.
  • Immunotherapy beyond checkpoint blockade — CD40 agonists (sotigalimab follow-up), CXCR4 antagonists, claudin 18.2 ADCs / CAR-T (zolbetuximab class extending into PDAC), bispecifics, TCR-T.
  • Health disparities, racial / ethnic differences in outcomes — increasingly a programmed track at AACR Special Conferences; the disparities in pancreatic cancer incidence / mortality / trial access is a stated AACR priority.
  • Surgical / locoregional / radiation — borderline-resectable management, neoadjuvant chemotherapy paradigms (mFOLFIRINOX vs gem/abrax), SBRT integration.
  • Health-system / clinical-trial design — adaptive platform trials for PDAC (PRECISION-Panc, Precision Promise, AltCAP-style alternating regimens), real-world evidence.
