docs.title: MPI Low Concentration Reconstruction Challenge — ISBI 2026
docs.text:
Field-free-line magnetic particle imaging reconstruction at low tracer concentrations — the clinical-translation bottleneck for MPI, with explicit oncology and cardiovascular imaging applications flagged in the challenge description.

  • Speaker(s) / Authors: MPI Low Concentration Challenge organizers (TBD pending challenge-results writeup)
  • Affiliation(s): TBD (MPI community is centered around Lübeck / Würzburg / Berkeley groups)
  • Anchor type: challenge
  • Track / day: ISBI 2026 challenge results session (Sat Apr 11)
  • IEEE Xplore: TBD (challenge summary paper typically indexed within ~4 weeks post-meeting)
  • Status: post-meeting

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Magnetic Particle Imaging (MPI) is an emerging tracer-based molecular imaging modality that directly visualizes the spatial distribution of superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticles with zero ionizing radiation and zero background signal from tissue. Clinical translation has been gated by reconstruction quality at low tracer concentrations — the regime needed for both oncology (tumor-specific tracer payloads, sentinel-lymph-node mapping) and cardiovascular imaging. This challenge benchmarks reconstruction algorithms specifically at the low-concentration regime using field-free-line MPI (FFL-MPI) setups.

docs.title: How it works / methodology
docs.text: Participants submit reconstruction algorithms — classical (Kaczmarz / regularized least squares), model-based with learned priors, or end-to-end deep learning — that map raw FFL-MPI measurement data to tracer concentration images. Evaluation focuses on image quality (PSNR / SSIM against high-concentration reference reconstructions), spatial resolution recovery, and quantitative concentration accuracy in the low-tracer regime.

docs.title: Headline benchmarks
docs.text:
• FFL-MPI dataset (specific phantom / in-vivo composition TBD)
  • PSNR / SSIM / concentration-quantification metrics; top-1 reconstruction algorithm and any methods paper introducing a new MPI DL prior are candidate tool-page entries
  • Specific top-1 numbers TBD pending challenge writeup

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Core idea. Magnetic Particle Imaging directly reads the spatial distribution of superparamagnetic iron oxide nanoparticle (SPION) tracers via their nonlinear magnetization response to a driving magnetic field. The reconstruction problem maps raw multi-coil time-domain measurements (the "system function" formulation) to tracer-concentration images. At low SPION concentrations the inverse problem becomes increasingly ill-posed; this challenge benchmarks reconstruction at exactly that regime.

Inputs / outputs. Inputs: raw field-free-line MPI measurement data (time-domain induced voltages across receive coils for a given drive-field excitation pattern), plus the calibrated system matrix. Outputs: 2D or 3D spatial maps of SPION tracer concentration (typically expressed in mmol Fe/L or relative units).

Key innovation. Field-free-line MPI geometry (a 1D zero-field region scanned across the FOV, vs the more common field-free-point geometry) trades scan-time efficiency for sensitivity per voxel — well suited to low-concentration imaging. The challenge surfaces methods that combine classical regularization (Tikhonov, total variation, Kaczmarz) with learned priors (deep image prior, diffusion-prior posterior sampling, end-to-end CNN reconstructors), comparing against high-concentration reference reconstructions as a proxy for ground truth.

Parameters. Method-dependent. Classical regularized least squares: regularization strength, iteration count. Deep-learned reconstructors: typical parameter counts in the low-millions for U-Net-class architectures, with patch-based training to handle volumetric data.

Canonical example. A FFL-MPI phantom containing tracer inserts at decreasing concentrations (e.g., 10, 5, 2, 1, 0.5, 0.1 mmol Fe/L) is scanned. Participants submit reconstructions; evaluation reports PSNR / SSIM vs the high-concentration reference, spatial resolution from edge-spread / line-pair phantoms, and quantitative concentration accuracy (estimated vs known per-insert concentration) — with explicit emphasis on the lowest-concentration inserts where clinical oncology applications (sentinel lymph node, tumor-targeted tracer payloads) live.

docs.title: Where it fits in the corpus
docs.text:
• AACR 2026: indirect — molecular imaging axis; MPI is not yet in AACR clinical dossiers but is a candidate emerging modality for tumor-targeted tracer studies
  • MICCAI 2026: MPI is ISBI-overweighted; MICCAI cousin coverage is sparse
  • RSNA 2026: clinical-translation watch — if any MPI system reaches first-in-human at an oncology indication, RSNA is the deployment venue
  • CVPR 2026: not direct — inverse-problems methodology could cross-pollinate via CVPR FMV / generative-modeling workshops

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: ISBI is the home venue for MPI methods (MICCAI underweights this modality entirely). The explicit oncology translation goal in the challenge framing is the load-bearing reason this entry sits in the cancer-relevant filter — MPI's value proposition for cancer imaging is tumor-targeted tracer accumulation at concentrations below current reconstruction-quality thresholds, which is exactly what this challenge attacks. Watch for TBME Special Section invitation of the top methods paper.

docs.title: RIVA Cervical Cytology Challenge — ISBI 2026
docs.text:
Pap smear precancer detection challenge with nucleus-level annotations across Bethesda categories — direct cervical-cancer-prevention axis with 959 FOVs and 26,158 nucleus annotations, scored on detection + multi-class classification with expert-agreement evaluation.

  • Speaker(s) / Authors: RIVA Challenge organizers (TBD — full author list pending challenge-results writeup)
  • Affiliation(s): TBD (multi-institutional consortium typical for cytology challenges)
  • Anchor type: challenge + dataset
  • Track / day: ISBI 2026 challenge results session (Sat Apr 11)
  • IEEE Xplore: TBD (challenge summary paper typically indexed within ~4 weeks post-meeting)
  • Status: post-meeting

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: RIVA targets the cervical-cancer prevention pipeline: from a Pap smear field of view, detect and classify cervical cells (nuclei) into Bethesda System categories (NILM, ASC-US, LSIL, HSIL, SCC, atypical glandular cells). The dataset — 959 fields of view with 26,158 nucleus-level annotations — is a direct downstream evaluation substrate for general pathology FMs and a focused training corpus for cytology-specific models.

docs.title: How it works / methodology
docs.text: Two-task structure: (1) nuclei detection (bounding-box or centroid localization), (2) multi-class cell classification across Bethesda categories. Evaluation uses standard detection mAP plus class-balanced classification metrics, augmented with an expert-agreement evaluation — a fairness / inter-rater check that compares model predictions against multiple expert annotators to flag where model "errors" are within human inter-rater variance. Patient-level data splits prevent leakage.

docs.title: Headline benchmarks
docs.text:
• Dataset: 959 FOVs, 26,158 nucleus annotations, Bethesda category coverage
  • Per-class F1, detection mAP, expert-agreement-normalized accuracy — specific top-1 winner numbers TBD pending challenge-results paper
  • Top-1 and (if code released) top-3 winning models are candidate tool-page entries

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Core idea. RIVA frames cervical-cytology AI as a two-stage detection-then-classification task at the nucleus level (not cell or FOV level), with explicit Bethesda-system categorical structure and an expert-agreement-normalized fairness metric — a more clinically faithful evaluation than older slide-level cervical-AI benchmarks.

Inputs / outputs. Inputs: Pap smear fields of view (typically 1024x1024 to 2048x2048 pixel crops from whole-slide scans at 20x or 40x); outputs: per-nucleus bounding box / centroid + Bethesda-category class label (NILM, ASC-US, LSIL, HSIL, SCC, AGC).

Key innovation. Three load-bearing design choices: (1) nucleus-level annotation density (26,158 nuclei across 959 FOVs — roughly 27 nuclei per FOV, dense relative to other public cytology datasets), (2) Bethesda-faithful multi-class structure rather than binary normal/abnormal, (3) expert-agreement evaluation that compares model predictions against multiple annotators and penalizes only the model errors that fall outside human inter-rater variance — flagging where model confusion is genuinely human-disagreed.

Parameters. Submission-dependent; typical winning entries are likely Mask R-CNN / Cellpose / SAM-medical-adapted detectors paired with a tile-classifier head (ResNet / Swin / pathology-FM tile encoder). Per-class F1 + detection mAP are reported alongside expert-agreement-normalized accuracy.

Canonical example. Input a Pap-smear FOV containing ~30 cells of mixed Bethesda categories. The pipeline detects each nucleus, classifies into Bethesda category, and the leaderboard reports (a) detection mAP at IoU 0.5, (b) per-class F1 (NILM / ASC-US / LSIL / HSIL / SCC / AGC), (c) overall accuracy weighted by expert-agreement (predictions matching majority-expert vote score 1.0; predictions matching any expert vote score partial credit; predictions outside the expert-vote envelope score 0).

docs.title: Where it fits in the corpus
docs.text:
• AACR 2026: direct downstream-evaluation use case for CHIEF and UNI (zero-shot transfer to cytology); intersects with cancer-prevention / screening axis
  • MICCAI 2026: likely COMPAY workshop cousin papers from challenge participants
  • RSNA 2026 / CVPR 2026: less direct — cytology is pathology-side, but generalist medical-FM evaluations may include RIVA

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Cervical cytology is one of the rare cancer-screening modalities with a mature, label-rich, public benchmark — RIVA fills a gap MICCAI underweights. Expert-agreement evaluation is a methodologically interesting fairness flag worth highlighting. Watch challenge GitHub for dataset release license and winning-model code drops May–July 2026.

docs.title: Segmentation Foundation Models at ISBI 2026 — Synthesis
docs.text:
Synthesis dossier covering SAM-3 / MedSAM / SegVol successor models surfacing across ISBI 2026 main proceedings and the FAIBI + Exploring-FM-in-Medical-Image-Analysis workshops — the segmentation-FM axis that bridges CVPR architectures to MICCAI medical adaptation.

  • Speaker(s) / Authors: Multiple — main-proceedings authors + workshop presenters across FAIBI 2nd ed. and Exploring FM in Medical Image Analysis (organizers Gu / Chen / Yang / Zheng / Zhou / Shen)
  • Affiliation(s): Multi-institutional — Tohoku, Sheffield, Emory/GT, Liverpool, UCL, ShanghaiTech, plus Stirling/MD Anderson/Imperial (FAIBI co-organizers)
  • Anchor type: synthesis / methods
  • Track / day: ISBI 2026 main proceedings (Thu Apr 9 – Fri Apr 10) + Fri Apr 10 PM workshop + Sat Apr 11 PM workshop
  • IEEE Xplore: TBD (multiple Xplore DOIs across main proceedings + workshop volumes — individual papers get their own tool pages where artifacts released)
  • Status: post-meeting

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: This synthesis tracks the SAM-3 / MedSAM / SegVol successor line at ISBI 2026 — promptable segmentation foundation models adapted for medical imaging. The axis covers (a) SAM-3 medical adaptations (continued from SAM / SAM-2 lineage), (b) MedSAM successors with expanded modality coverage (CT, MR, US, microscopy, pathology), (c) SegVol-style volumetric promptable segmenters, (d) text-promptable medical segmentation models. Cancer-relevance is via tumor segmentation across modalities — the backbone use case for radiotherapy planning, radiomics, treatment-response measurement.

docs.title: How it works / methodology
docs.text: The shared recipe: pretrain a large image encoder (often initialized from SAM / DINOv2 / a medical FM checkpoint), pair with a prompt encoder (points / boxes / masks / text), train on large multi-modal medical segmentation corpora (often >1M masks across CT / MR / US / pathology), evaluate on held-out tumor / organ / lesion segmentation benchmarks. Variations cover prompt modality (interactive vs text vs auto), 2D vs 3D, supervised vs self-supervised pretraining, generalist vs modality-specific specialization.

docs.title: Headline benchmarks
docs.text: TBD — synthesis-level. Anchor benchmarks across the SAM-medical line: BraTS (brain tumor MR), KiTS (kidney CT), LiTS (liver CT), TotalSegmentator (multi-organ CT), MSD (Medical Segmentation Decathlon), AMOS (abdominal multi-organ). Specific ISBI 2026 paper-level deltas extracted into per-tool pages once IEEE Xplore indexes proceedings (~early May 2026).

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Core idea. Promptable segmentation foundation models replace per-task / per-dataset segmentation training with a single large model that produces segmentation masks conditional on a prompt (point, box, mask, or text). Medical adaptations (MedSAM, SegVol, SAM-3-medical successors) port this promptable paradigm to CT / MR / US / pathology / microscopy, where the prompt encodes clinician intent (point at a tumor, click on an organ, describe an anatomical structure).

Inputs / outputs. Inputs: an image (2D slice or 3D volume) plus one or more prompts (points with positive/negative polarity, bounding boxes, coarse masks, or natural-language descriptions like "left kidney"). Outputs: a binary or multi-class segmentation mask aligned with the prompt; for some variants, ranked candidate masks with quality scores.

Key innovation. Three shifts from per-dataset U-Nets: (1) pretraining on >1M masks across heterogeneous medical modalities so the same model handles CT, MR, US, and pathology, (2) prompt conditioning that decouples model capability from task specification, (3) zero-shot generalization to anatomical structures never explicitly labeled in training. SegVol-line models extend this to native 3D promptable volumetric segmentation, closing the 2D-to-3D gap that hampered earlier SAM-medical adaptations.

Parameters. SAM-3 / MedSAM scale: ViT-H/16 image encoder (~600M parameters), small prompt encoder (<10M), mask decoder (~10M). SegVol-class 3D: typically 100–300M parameters with patch-based volumetric processing. Training compute: thousands of GPU-days on multi-million-mask corpora.

Canonical example. Tumor segmentation on a 3D liver CT: clinician places a single positive point inside the tumor and an optional negative point on adjacent vessel; SegVol returns a 3D tumor mask in seconds; mask quality measured against the LiTS / KiTS held-out annotation. BraTS brain-tumor canonical example: text prompt "enhancing tumor" applied to a 3D MRI → segmentation mask scored against BraTS multi-region ground truth.

docs.title: Where it fits in the corpus
docs.text:
• AACR 2026: indirect — tumor segmentation feeds radiomics and treatment-response endpoints; no direct pathology-FM crosswalk but cross-modal generalist medical FMs may overlap
  • MICCAI 2026: strong sibling — most ISBI 2026 segmentation-FM papers will have MICCAI cousin papers (Sep 27–Oct 1); BraTS / KiTS / AMOS challenge results land at MICCAI
  • RSNA 2026: clinical-deployment counterpart — radiotherapy / treatment-planning systems use these segmenters; RSNA tool index gets the deployed-product entries
  • CVPR 2026: architecture upstream — SAM-3 line originates at CVPR / NeurIPS, ISBI adapts ~6 months later

docs.text: This is a synthesis page, not a single-tool page — individual named-model papers (specific SAM-3 medical successors, specific MedSAM v3 / SegVol v2 releases) get their own tool pages once IEEE Xplore indexes the proceedings. The synthesis exists as a navigation anchor in the vault for the broader segmentation-FM axis that spans ISBI main proceedings, both relevant workshops (FAIBI Sat Apr 11 PM, Exploring FM in Medical Image Analysis Fri Apr 10 PM), and the MICCAI 2026 cousin-paper pattern.

docs.title: Diagnostic Radiology AI — Bram van Ginneken (Radboud)
docs.text:
ISBI 2026 plenary keynote on diagnostic radiology AI — lung CT, mammography, and the Grand Challenge platform — directly bridging into the RSNA 2026 clinical-deployment axis with concrete cancer-screening applications.

  • Speaker(s) / Authors: Bram van Ginneken
  • Affiliation(s): Radboud University Medical Center (Diagnostic Image Analysis Group, Nijmegen)
  • Anchor type: keynote
  • Track / day: ISBI 2026 main plenary (day TBD — Thu Apr 9 or Fri Apr 10)
  • IEEE Xplore: TBD (keynote — no Xplore paper)
  • Status: post-meeting

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: Van Ginneken's keynote covers the Radboud DIAG group's two-decade-long line of work on diagnostic radiology AI, anchored on lung CT (nodule detection, COPD, lung cancer screening) and mammography (breast cancer detection AI, the LUNA / DREAM challenge legacy). The talk is the most cancer-direct keynote on the ISBI 2026 slate after Mahmood — both lung cancer screening and breast cancer mammography AI are core RSNA / clinical-deployment topics.

docs.title: How it works / methodology
docs.text: The DIAG-group pattern emphasizes (a) large-scale curated datasets (LIDC-IDRI, NLST-derived, OPTIMAM mammography), (b) benchmark challenges hosted via the Grand Challenge platform (grand-challenge.org — van Ginneken co-founded), (c) clinical-validation studies with reader-study designs that compare AI to radiologist performance, (d) regulatory-facing translation toward CE-mark / FDA-cleared products. Methods themselves are typically CNN / transformer hybrids tuned for clinical-deployment metrics (sensitivity at fixed FP rate, AUC vs reader panels).

docs.title: Headline benchmarks
docs.text: TBD — keynote-level synthesis. Anchor numbers from the DIAG-group published line: lung nodule detection on LIDC-IDRI (FROC sensitivity), mammography AI vs reader-panel AUC. Specific ISBI 2026 keynote deltas not in program-notes.

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Core idea. Diagnostic radiology AI succeeds clinically when it is built on large curated public datasets, benchmarked against radiologist readers via challenge platforms, and validated for the specific operating points clinical workflows demand (sensitivity at a fixed false-positive rate, not just AUC). Van Ginneken's two-decade DIAG-group line operationalizes this end-to-end.

Inputs / outputs. Lung CT inputs: full chest CT volumes (typically 0.5–1.0mm slice thickness); outputs: nodule candidate locations with malignancy probabilities, plus lung-cancer-screening LDCT triage scores. Mammography inputs: 4-view digital mammograms (CC + MLO, bilateral) and/or DBT volumes; outputs: lesion locations, BI-RADS-aligned probability scores, and case-level malignancy probability.

Key innovation. The Grand Challenge platform (grand-challenge.org — van Ginneken co-founded) institutionalized fair reader-study-grade comparison across teams: hidden test sets, standardized evaluation, multi-reader multi-case (MRMC) study designs, and regulatory-grade audit trails. The methodological gain isn't a single architecture — it's an infrastructure layer that made medical AI benchmarking reproducible.

Parameters. Tool-specific; the DIAG-group line spans 3D CNNs for nodule detection (tens of millions of parameters typical), DenseNet / EfficientNet-class mammography classifiers, and increasingly transformer hybrids. Operating-point selection is parameter-equivalent in importance to architecture.

Canonical example. Lung-nodule CAD on LIDC-IDRI: sliding-window 3D CNN over a chest CT volume produces candidate locations, false-positive reduction stage filters, FROC sensitivity reported at fixed FP-per-scan rates (1, 4, 8 FP/scan). Mammography canonical pipeline: per-view CNN feature maps fused across CC + MLO via attention, case-level malignancy score benchmarked against reader-panel AUC on MRMC datasets like OPTIMAM.

docs.title: Where it fits in the corpus
docs.text:
• AACR 2026: indirect — lung cancer screening and breast cancer prevention axes overlap with AACR clinical sessions
  • MICCAI 2026: strong sibling — DIAG-group work appears across MICCAI main proceedings and challenge tracks
  • RSNA 2026: direct crosswalk — Grand Challenge platform, lung CT and mammography AI are core RSNA deployment topics; van Ginneken keynote bridges ISBI methods → RSNA clinical translation
  • CVPR 2026: indirect — architecture upstream

docs.text: Of the five ISBI 2026 keynotes, van Ginneken's is second only to Mahmood's in direct cancer-screening relevance (lung + breast). The Grand Challenge platform itself is a vault-relevant infrastructure asset — many of the challenges referenced across the MICCAI / ISBI tools index are hosted there. Keynote does not yield a separate tool page; any named tool announced in the talk would warrant either an RSNA tool entry (clinical deployment) or a MICCAI cousin-paper entry.

docs.title: WBCBench2026 — Leukemia Diagnosis Benchmark
docs.text:
Hematopathology benchmark for white blood cell classification with patient-level test separation — direct leukemia-diagnosis axis testing robust morphological discrimination under severe class imbalance.

  • Speaker(s) / Authors: WBCBench2026 organizers (TBD pending challenge-results writeup)
  • Affiliation(s): TBD (multi-institutional hematopathology consortium typical)
  • Anchor type: challenge / benchmark
  • Track / day: ISBI 2026 challenge results session (Sat Apr 11)
  • IEEE Xplore: TBD (challenge summary paper typically indexed within ~4 weeks post-meeting)
  • Status: post-meeting

docs.title: What it does
docs.text: WBCBench2026 evaluates fine-grained white blood cell classification on peripheral-blood and bone-marrow smears — the substrate for leukemia and lymphoma diagnosis. The benchmark distinguishes itself by enforcing patient-level held-out test splits (preventing the common pitfall where multiple FOVs from the same patient end up across train and test) and by surfacing severe class imbalance characteristic of clinical hematopathology (rare blast morphologies, atypical lymphocytes).

docs.title: How it works / methodology
docs.text: Single-cell crops or full-FOV bone-marrow / peripheral-blood images labeled across WBC morphological categories (neutrophils, lymphocytes, monocytes, eosinophils, basophils, plus blast / atypical categories relevant to leukemia diagnosis). Patient-level separation in train/val/test prevents information leakage. Evaluation uses class-balanced metrics (macro-F1, balanced accuracy) to ensure rare-but-clinically-critical blast classes drive the leaderboard.

docs.title: Headline benchmarks
docs.text:
• Patient-level held-out split (specific patient counts TBD pending writeup)
  • Class-balanced F1 / balanced accuracy headline metrics
  • Top-1 winner + any baseline-beating workshop paper are candidate tool-page entries (TBD post-IEEE-Xplore indexing)

docs.title: How it works
docs.text:
Core idea. WBCBench2026 evaluates fine-grained white-blood-cell classification on peripheral-blood and bone-marrow smears under strict patient-level held-out splits and class-balanced metrics — two evaluation-discipline choices specifically aimed at exposing the over-fitting / inflated-accuracy failures that plagued earlier WBC-classification benchmarks.

Inputs / outputs. Inputs: single-cell crops or full-FOV images (typically 100x oil-immersion microscopy of stained smears at 224x224 to 512x512 per cell crop, or larger for FOV-level inputs). Outputs: WBC morphological class (neutrophil, lymphocyte, monocyte, eosinophil, basophil, plus blast / atypical-lymphocyte / promyelocyte / metamyelocyte / band-cell categories relevant to leukemia diagnosis — exact class count TBD pending challenge writeup).

Key innovation. Patient-level partitioning of train / val / test (no FOV from the same patient appears in multiple splits) plus class-balanced macro-F1 / balanced accuracy as the leaderboard metric. Pre-2024 hematopathology benchmarks routinely used FOV-level splits — a model could memorize per-patient staining / scanner / cell-density signatures and over-report performance. WBCBench2026 forecloses that shortcut and surfaces rare-blast-class performance, which is the clinically critical regime.

Parameters. Submission-dependent; typical strong baselines are ResNet-50 / EfficientNet / Swin-Tiny classifiers fine-tuned from ImageNet or from a pathology / microscopy FM checkpoint. The benchmark itself is parameter-agnostic — any model that produces a probability vector over WBC classes can submit.

Canonical example. Input a single-cell crop of a candidate blast from a bone-marrow smear. The model outputs probabilities across all morphological classes; the leaderboard scores macro-F1 across classes (weighting rare blast / atypical classes equally with abundant neutrophil / lymphocyte classes). Held-out test patients are drawn from institutions / scanners not present in training, so model robustness to domain shift is implicitly tested.

docs.title: Where it fits in the corpus
docs.text:
• AACR 2026: connects to hematologic-malignancies dossiers; downstream evaluation candidate for general pathology FMs (CHIEF, UNI)
  • MICCAI 2026: likely COMPAY / MILEX workshop cousin papers
  • ASH 2026 (Dec 12–15): clinical-deployment counterpart — winning models may resurface as ASH readouts
  • RSNA 2026 / CVPR 2026: less direct (hematopathology is microscopy-side)

docs.title: Notes
docs.text: Patient-level separation is a methodological best-practice flag worth highlighting — many hematopathology benchmarks pre-2024 used FOV-level splits and over-reported accuracy. WBCBench2026's enforcement is the kind of evaluation-discipline signal worth citing when comparing against older WBC-classification baselines. Watch challenge GitHub for winning-model code drops May–July 2026.

docs.title: ISMB 2026
docs.text:
34th Intelligent Systems for Molecular Biology (ISMB) Conference — Washington Hilton, Washington, DC, USA · July 12–16, 2026. Hybrid (in-person + ISCB Nucleus virtual platform).

Status: Scaffold — meeting upcoming (~9 weeks out as of May 11, 2026); structure landed now so bulk per-tool extraction can run immediately after the meeting closes Jul 16, 2026. Program shape is fixed (day-by-day COSI grid published), keynote slate is announced, accepted-paper list is not yet public.

One factual correction up front: the original task brief listed this as the joint ISMB/ECCB year in Liverpool. That was last year — ISMB/ECCB 2025 ran Jul 20–24, 2025 in Liverpool. ISMB 2026 is ISMB-only in Washington, DC. ECCB 2026 is a separate event (Geneva, Aug 31–Sep 4, 2026, "Biodiversity, AI & Health" theme); we treat ECCB 2026 as a possible future sister vault, not folded into this one.

docs.title: Why this is in the vault
docs.text:
• Methods-and-tools depth. ISMB is the largest computational-biology meeting (~2000–3000 attendees) and the one venue where methods underlying tools like CHIEF, GigaPath, Geneformer, scGPT, Cell2location, SpatialData, SCimilarity, and PerturbNet get peer-reviewed and presented. Many tools we've already documented from EuroBioC2025 / GBCC2025 (msqrob2, edgeR, SpatialData, Voyager, plyxp, Tidyomics, OSTA, signifinder, sosta, footprintR, …) re-surface here with updates, methods papers, or new downstream uses.
  • Formal peer-reviewed proceedings. Unlike EuroBioC / GBCC (community workshops with informal talk selection), ISMB has a real two-round peer-reviewed proceedings track that publishes in Bioinformatics (Oxford University Press) ~1 month before the meeting. Tool entries from ISMB can cite a published DOI — a depth the community-conference vaults don't get.
  • AACR axis fit. Six ISMB COSIs map directly onto the AACR vault's axes: MLCSB (foundation models / scGPT-class), TransMed (translational), BioVis (figure / dashboard tooling), HiTSeq (sequencing methods used in cancer cohorts), VarI (somatic variant interpretation), NetBio (pathway / network methods). MICROBIOME, RegSys, Function, 3DSIG, CompMS, BOSC, and EvolCompGen feed adjacent axes (cancer-microbiome, regulatory genomics, structural drug-target work, proteomics, open-source infrastructure).
  • Cross-vault people overlap. The Robinson lab (Zurich), Love lab (UNC), Carey (Channing/Harvard), Soneson (FMI), Mangiola (Adelaide), Castelo (UPF), Borman (Turku), Marconato (EMBL), and the broader scverse / SpatialData crowd typically split between EuroBioC, GBCC, and ISMB each year. docs.title: Program shape
docs.text:
ISMB 2026 runs Sunday Jul 12 (tutorials + opening keynote) through Thursday Jul 16 (closing keynote). Mon–Thu morning starts with a Distinguished Keynote followed by 11 parallel COSI / special-track sessions in three slots (11:00–13:00, 14:20–16:00, 16:40–18:00). The Sunday day-zero is tutorials + Student Council Symposium + DREAM Challenge.

Counts:

  • 5 Distinguished Keynotes (one per day, ~1 hour each)
  • 22 COSI tracks + 7 special / closed tracks + 1 Open Session ("Bioinformatics in the USA") + 1 equity track + 1 publishing session + Industry Workshop + Pathogen Data Network forum + NIH/ODSS
  • 9 tutorials (IP1–IP9), all Sunday Jul 12, full-day
  • >600 expected scientific talks (per ISCB's own framing)
  • Two posters-and-exhibitors blocks per day (morning + afternoon coffee), Mon–Thu
  • BOSC 2026 nested inside — Jul 14–15, runs as a 2-day COSI within ISMB
  • CollaborationFest (CoFest) Jul 17–18, separate registration, hackathon-style follow-on (sister event to GBCC2025's CoFest)

docs.title: What's different from EuroBioC / GBCC
docs.text:
• Scale. EuroBioC ~250 attendees, GBCC ~300. ISMB ~2000–3000 attendees, >600 talks, 22 parallel tracks. Per-tool extraction will be substantially larger — the constraint is reviewer bandwidth, not source availability.
  • Peer-reviewed proceedings. Every accepted proceedings paper has a DOI before the meeting, so tool pages here will be unusually "complete" — DOI + GitHub + benchmarks + figures — even before talks happen.
  • Domain breadth. EuroBioC = Bioconductor (R). GBCC = Galaxy + Bioconductor. ISMB spans Python, R, C++, Julia, web, cloud, and quantum (yes — Q4LS / Quantum for Life Sciences runs as a Tuesday track). Tool entries cannot assume any one ecosystem.
  • Awards and recognition arc. ISMB hands out four ISCB awards in 2026 (Senior Scientist → Durbin; Innovator → Troyanskaya; Overton → Zitnik; plus career awards for fellows). Keynote treatments need an "award arc" note that the EuroBioC / GBCC keynotes don't have.
  • BOSC + Bioconductor-2026 spillover. BioC2026 is Aug 10–12, 2026 in Seattle — a month after ISMB. Many Bioconductor speakers present at BOSC during ISMB and then again at BioC2026. Tool entries built from BOSC at ISMB will need to anticipate a BioC2026 re-up.

docs.text:
Internal-use working file. Source for the bulk tool-page generation pass that will run immediately after the meeting closes Jul 16, 2026. Not for end-reader consumption — formatting is utilitarian. Compiled from the public ISMB 2026 web pages and the abridged-agenda PDF, fetched 2026-05-11 (~9 weeks pre-meeting).

Tag legend: - [PROC] — proceedings paper (peer-reviewed in Bioinformatics); has a DOI ~1 month before meeting - [COSI] — COSI-invited talk; abstract-only submission, no DOI - [BOSC] — talk in the nested BOSC 2026 program (Jul 14–15) - [TUTORIAL] — Sunday Jul 12 tutorial (9 tracks, IP1–IP9) - [KEYNOTE] — distinguished keynote - [?] — placeholder; populated post-meeting

Sparse-coverage flags: - Accepted-paper list not yet public. Proceedings notifications go to authors May 5, 2026; the Bioinformatics online supplement typically posts mid-June 2026 (~1 month pre-meeting). Until then, per-paper titles + authors are not extractable from a public source. Monitor: https://academic.oup.com/bioinformatics — ISMB 2026 special issue, expected Jun 2026. - Per-COSI speaker rosters trickle in. Microbiome and EvolCompGen COSI pages already list committees; most COSIs publish full speaker rosters in the 4–6 weeks before the meeting.   7. Tutorial syllabi (IP1–IP9). Typically post 3–4 weeks pre-meeting on the ISCB tutorials page; needed for the "Tutorial-as-tool-page" entries.
  8. bioRxiv "to appear in ISMB 2026" preprints — cross-search bioRxiv for the "Comments: To appear in ISMB 2026 proceedings" tag; useful for getting paper-and-code links before the OUP supplement is online.
  9. Slide DOIs (post-meeting). No ISMB-wide Zenodo community; check (a) zenodo.org/communities/bioconductor for BOSC speakers, (b) individual lab sites, (c) ISCB Nucleus on-demand for video links.
  10. CollaborationFest (CoFest) Jul 17–18. Parallel to GBCC2025 CoFest; produces concrete "wrapped tool" artifacts. Worth a 1-day post-conference scan for new Galaxy/Bioconductor wrappers, scverse↔Bioconductor bridges, or MCP-style integrations.
  11. Cross-link map. Build the EuroBioC2025 ↔ GBCC2025 ↔ ISMB 2026 ↔ BioC2026 cross-link table once the ISMB roster is firm; populate the "Mentioned elsewhere" cell on each tool page.
  12. AACR cross-link mirror policy. Decide (see tools/index.md Open Q2) whether AACR posters citing an ISMB-released tool get an AACR-vault stub page or just a cross-link line — applies broadly to Bustamante / Troyanskaya / Zitnik lab spinouts.

docs.title: ISMB 2026 — Tools
docs.text:
ISMB 2026 will run ~5 distinguished keynotes + ~600 scientific talks across 22 COSI tracks + nested BOSC + special tracks (NIH/ODSS, Industry Workshop, Pathogen Data Network, Q4LS) + 9 full-day Sunday tutorials. The subset that yields tool pages is the intersection of (a) Proceedings papers published in Bioinformatics (peer-reviewed full papers with DOIs), (b) COSI-invited talks that announce a named package or method, and (c) BOSC talks that introduce a Bioconductor / Galaxy / scverse / open-source tool. Ecosystem field = Bioconductor / scverse / Galaxy / standalone-Python / standalone-R / web-service / C++ — broader than EuroBioC's R-only and GBCC's R+Galaxy.

Status: Template stub. Per-tool format proposed here for review before bulk extraction runs immediately after the meeting closes (Jul 16, 2026). Once locked, expected ~60–120 entries get populated from the proceedings-paper list + COSI program books.

docs.title: Per-tool entry template
docs.text:
Each tool gets its own page (tools/<package-slug>.md) following this structure. The shape mirrors EuroBioC2025 and GBCC2025 with two ISMB-specific additions (a Proceedings DOI row, a COSI track field):

# <ToolName>

**One-line description** — what the tool does in plain language.

- **Maintainer:** <name> (<institution>)
- **Ecosystem:** Bioconductor / scverse / Galaxy / standalone-Python / standalone-R / web-service / C++ / other
- **Package / source:** [GitHub link]
- **Docs / vignette:** [link]
- **Status at ISMB 2026:** new release / major update / proceedings paper / methods talk / case study / tutorial / BOSC demo
- **Proceedings:** [*Bioinformatics* DOI if applicable — null for COSI-invited / methods talks]

## Talk at ISMB 2026

- **Speaker:** ...
- **Day / COSI track:** Mon Jul 13 / MLCSB · Tue Jul 14 / RegSys · etc.
- **Session slot:** 11:00–13:00 | 14:20–16:00 | 16:40–18:00
- **Slides:** [Zenodo DOI or lab site]
- **Video:** [ISCB Nucleus on-demand link if posted]
- **Abstract / talk page:** [ISMB program link]

## What it does

2–3 sentences: the problem it solves, the key methodological idea, what it consumes/produces, what it's benchmarked against.

## Where it fits in the corpus

- AACR 2026: [link if mentioned]
- EuroBioC 2025: [link if mentioned]
- GBCC 2025: [link if mentioned]
- BioC 2026: [link if mentioned — Aug 10-12 Seattle, likely re-up for Bioconductor speakers]
- Nextflow Summit 2026: [link if mentioned]
- JPM 2026 / RECOMB 2026: [link if mentioned]

## Notes

Free-form impressions, benchmarks claimed, comparisons to alternatives, AACR-axis fit notes.

docs.text:
Placeholder table. ~60–120 entries expected after bulk extraction; the populated table will be sortable by Ecosystem, Domain, or COSI. Slide DOIs and video links typically populate over the 2–4 weeks following the meeting (ISCB Nucleus on-demand is posted incrementally).

Package Ecosystem Domain Speaker Day / COSI Proceedings Slides Video Mentioned elsewhere (populated post-meeting from proceedings list + COSI rosters; see ../program-notes.md for the candidate shortlist)

docs.title: Why this format
docs.text:
• Proceedings DOI is the anchor for ISMB — unlike EuroBioC / GBCC (where slide-deck DOIs are the most stable artifact), the Bioinformatics paper is what survives. Putting it on the same row as the talk metadata keeps the citation chain intact.
  • COSI track is the cleanest sort dimension at this scale. ISMB has 22 COSIs; faceting by COSI gives 30–60 entries per slice instead of 600.
  • Ecosystem field broadened beyond EuroBioC's Bioconductor-implicit assumption — at ISMB, scverse (SpatialData, anndata, scanpy) and standalone-Python (DeepChem-class, foundation-model adapters) tools are first-class and shouldn't be forced into a Bioconductor template.
  • Cross-vault "Mentioned elsewhere" picks up the Bioconductor speakers who run EuroBioC → GBCC → ISMB (BOSC) → BioC2026 in a single year (Soneson, Mangiola, Castelo, Carey, Borman, Marini, etc.) so a reader of any one entry can hop sideways.

docs.title: Open questions
docs.text:
1. Granularity — locked: one page per tool, same as EuroBioC / GBCC.
  2. Proceedings-paper linking — new for ISMB, open: when a tool's ISMB Proceedings paper is also cited in an AACR poster / talk, do we mirror the entry into the AACR vault, or just cross-link with a "Mentioned at AACR 2026" line? Proposed default: cross-link only, full entry stays in ISMB vault — the AACR poster usually treats the tool as a black-box dependency, not the artifact under study. Mirror only when the AACR poster is methodologically central (e.g., a benchmark of the ISMB-released tool on cancer data).
  3. BOSC entries vs. main-program entries — open: BOSC runs as a 2-day COSI inside ISMB. A Bioconductor package introduced at BOSC is "an ISMB 2026 tool" in this vault, but the same package may also surface at BioC2026 in Seattle a month later. Proposed: one tool entry, two talk slots within it (one BOSC, one BioC2026) — the talk-slot block in the template repeats per appearance.
  4. Coverage budget — open: 600+ talks. We don't expand 600 tool pages. Filter: (a) any proceedings paper with code + maintained repo, (b) any COSI-invited talk in MLCSB / RegSys / NetBio / VarI / TransMed / Microbiome / CompMS / 3DSIG / BOSC that names a package, (c) any tool that is an update to an existing-in-corpus entry. Estimated ~60–120 after filtering.
  5. Tutorials as tool pages — open: 9 Sunday tutorials, each ~6 hours, each effectively a hands-on workshop for one tool/stack (Agentic AI, Cytoscape+NDEx, Quantum-for-multi-omics, k-mer biophysical ML, etc.). Proposed: yes, each tutorial gets a tool page treating the tutorial as a Status: tutorial entry — same pattern as EuroBioC2025's workshop entries (OSTA, msqrob2, iSEE, mia, Workshop Platform).

docs.title: JPM 2026
docs.text:
Day-by-day digests and cross-day synthesis from the 44th J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference (San Francisco, January 12–15, 2026) — the largest healthcare investor conference of the year.

Caveat: Unlike the Nextflow and AACR vaults (which have primary transcripts and abstracts), JPM is invite-only — there are no public transcripts. Every claim in these pages is one degree removed from the room, synthesized from trade-press reporting (STAT, Fierce Biotech / Pharma / Healthcare, Endpoints, BioPharma Dive, Evaluate, Pharmaceutical Technology, Clinical Trials Arena, BioSpace) and primary company press releases. Inline citations on every page so claims can be traced.

docs.title: Themes & takeaways — JPM 2026
docs.text:
Cross-day synthesis of the recurring threads, surprises, and named entities across Day 1, Day 2, Day 3, and Day 4.

Source caveat: Unlike the Nextflow vault (which has primary transcripts), JPM is invite-only — every claim here is one degree removed from the room, synthesized from trade-press reporting (STAT, Fierce Biotech/Pharma/Healthcare, Endpoints, BioPharma Dive, Evaluate, etc.) and primary company press releases.

docs.title: 1. AI in pharma — from partnership to ownership
docs.text:
The single loudest theme. JPM26 marked a phase change from "we have an AI collab" to "we own the AI company":

  • Lilly + NVIDIA $1B AI Co-Innovation Lab (Day 1) — largest pharma–AI infrastructure commitment ever announced at JPM; NVIDIA BioNeMo + Vera Rubin compute.
  • AstraZeneca acquires Modella AI (Day 2) — described in trade press as the first big-pharma acquisition of an AI firm; multi-modal foundation models for oncology.
  • Pfizer announced plans to "embed AI across the business" (Day 2).
  • Waystar projected RCM TAM expanding from $20–25B to $55B with agentic AI (Day 1).

The closing-week framing in Alex Hogan's STATus Report: AI is "table stakes" — the conversation has shifted from will you do AI to show us the ROI and the compliance story (echoed by Hogan Lovells on AI compliance + BIOSECURE).

Counterweight: Regeneron's George Yancopoulos publicly questioned current AI applications in medicine on Day 4 — calling for careful oversight. The conference's most prominent scientific voice pushing back on AI maximalism.

docs.title: 2. Licensing displacing M&A
docs.text:
JPM26 had ~$8.3B in announced deals (Pharmaceutical Technology) but no pharma megamerger. The pattern:

  • AbbVie + RemeGen $5.6B PD-1×VEGF licensing (Day 1) — biggest single deal headline of the week.
  • Novartis + SciNeuro $1.7B Alzheimer's antibody pact (Day 1).
  • Novartis + Zonsen PepLib $50M radioligand license (Day 2).
  • AZ + Modella AI — undisclosed terms, tuck-in (Day 2).
  • Boston Scientific + Penumbra $14.5B (Day 4) — the one megadeal, and it's medtech, not biopharma.
  • Pre-JPM Lilly + Ventyx $1B+ acquisition cited as the largest biopharma deal near the conference window.

Fierce Biotech canonical framing: "All the meetings, none of the megadeals." One attendee told Fierce some companies appear to be holding announcements for the TD Cowen Health Care Conference in March.

docs.title: 3. China is the story
docs.text:
Two distinct angles converged:

  • China-origin assets in big-pharma deals — RC148 (RemeGen → AbbVie, Day 1), brain-shuttle Alzheimer's antibodies (SciNeuro → Novartis, Day 1), peptide radioligand (Zonsen PepLib → Novartis, Day 2).
  • Chinese pharma stage time — Hengrui presented on Day 4 with >$3.2B 2025 sales through Q3, 21 NDA/BLA approvals, $1.5B HK IPO, ~$16B cumulative out-licensing (incl. GSK partnership). Kelun-Biotech presented bispecific/multispecific conjugates.

BioPharma Dive's framing: US biotech's "Sputnik moment." Novartis CMO Shreeram Aradhye (Day 3) cautioned against simple speed comparisons — different ecosystem, trial-enrollment economics, payer structure — but did not dispute the trend.

docs.title: 4. Obesity = the gravitational center
docs.text:
Every major pharma had to address it:

  • Pfizer (Day 1, Day 2) — $10B Metsera acquisition anchors 10 Phase 3 starts in 2026; Bourla compared cash-pay obesity demand to Viagra.
  • Amgen — MariTide Phase 2 reveal (Day 1, reprise Day 3): up to 20% mean weight loss in obesity-only, 17% in obesity + T2D; potential first once-monthly T2D therapy; six global Phase 3 underway.
  • Novo Nordisk (Day 2, Day 3) — oral Wegovy ~3,100 patients in first week since Jan 5 launch; Doustdar publicly hungry for M&A "with intention" after losing Metsera bid; pulling back from non-obesity/diabetes indications.
  • Roche (Day 2) — teased entry into obesity as one of three growth pillars.
  • The competition has shifted from drug-data tournament to commercial/distribution warfare: oral GLP-1s, monthly dosing, cash-pay channels.

docs.title: 5. Policy / regulatory headwinds as constant background noise
docs.text:
Threaded through every day:

  • Sanofi Day 3 — RSV recommendation narrowing on Beyfortus, recent FDA rejection, MFN pricing arrangement skirting tariff threats; Sanofi singled out the Dec 24, 2025 CRL on tolebrutinib for "skipped advisory committee" reasons.
  • Pazdur Day 2 — first public remarks since departing FDA, warning on politicization and voucher-program transparency.
  • Mehmet Oz Day 2 — fielded hospital-exec questions on Medicaid and vaccines off-site.
  • Trump MFN pricing — Yancopoulos (Day 4) explained why Regeneron was the only one of 17 companies receiving presidential pricing letters that hadn't yet struck a deal.
  • AI compliance + BIOSECURE — Hogan Lovells flagged as top device-supply-chain concerns.

docs.title: Predictions to watch
docs.text:
From the closing recaps and threaded through the keynotes:

  1. AI bake-off goes from collab to acquisition. Expect more big-pharma + AI-startup acquisitions (vs. partnerships) in 2026 following the AZ–Modella template.
  2. The TD Cowen Health Care Conference (March) may absorb the megadeals JPM26 didn't see — at least one Fierce attendee suggested companies were holding announcements.
  3. Up to ~20 biotech IPOs in 2026 if the Sionna/Maze/Eikon/Aktis/Veradermics windows hold (HSBC's Jonathan Norris). 2025 had <12 IPOs, the lowest since at least 2018.
  4. Obesity competition shifts to distribution. Novo's DTP/oral-Wegovy push, Amgen's once-monthly differentiation, Pfizer–Metsera's combos — the next 18 months are commercial, not data.
  5. Policy risk is structural, not transient. Vaccine politics, MFN pricing letters, BIOSECURE, FDA-process scrutiny — all four will continue weighing on biopharma narratives through 2026.
  6. China-origin licensing is now mainstream. Three of the four top deals at JPM26 had Chinese-origin assets; expect this share to grow.

docs.title: Caveat
docs.text: JPM is invite-only. There are no public transcripts. Every claim above is reconstructed from third-party trade-press reporting and primary company press releases. Where dating to a specific day was uncertain (some outlets bundle the week), the source notes that. Some headlines (notably the rumored Merck/Revolution Medicines $32B deal) stayed rumors through the week and are not represented above. Treat dollar figures and patient counts as best-effort transcription from public reporting, not official tallies.

docs.title: Day 1 — Monday Jan 12, 2026
docs.text:
Source: synthesized from public coverage (see Sources). Unlike the Nextflow vault, this digest has no primary transcripts — JPM is invite-only and most content is reconstructed from trade-press reporting and company press releases.

The 44th J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference opened in San Francisco with an unusually quiet news flow by historical standards: no megadeal M&A and no surprise blockbuster acquisitions. Day 1 was anchored by a $1B Lilly–NVIDIA AI alliance, a $5.6B AbbVie/RemeGen PD-1×VEGF licensing deal, and a ~$1.7B Novartis/SciNeuro Alzheimer's pact — alongside a heavy slate of fireside chats from BMS, Pfizer, J&J, Regeneron, Biogen, Moderna, Alnylam, argenx, BridgeBio, Sarepta, Summit, and CRISPR Therapeutics. Multiple observers (Takeda R&D chief Andy Plump; investor Brad Loncar) flagged the slow Monday cadence as a contrast with prior years.

docs.title: 1. NVIDIA + Eli Lilly — $1B AI Co-Innovation Lab
docs.text:
• Up to $1B over 5 years, jointly funded, to build an AI Co-Innovation Lab in the SF Bay Area co-locating Lilly biology/scientific staff with NVIDIA AI engineers.
  • Built on NVIDIA BioNeMo platform and NVIDIA Vera Rubin architecture; aim is closed-loop drug discovery plus AI applications across manufacturing and commercial.
  • Kimberly Powell (NVIDIA VP, Healthcare) led the press briefing.

Why it matters: Largest pharma–AI infrastructure commitment announced at JPM26 Day 1; sets the tone for the AI/bio convergence theme.

Sources: Lilly press release; Clinical Trials Arena.

docs.title: 2. AbbVie + RemeGen — $5.6B PD-1×VEGF bispecific licensing
docs.text:
• $650M upfront, up to $4.95B in milestones, plus tiered double-digit royalties; ex-Greater China rights to RC148, a PD-1/VEGF bispecific antibody.
  • Therapeutic area: advanced solid tumors (NSCLC, CRC focus); Phase 2 asset.
  • Strategic rationale: combination potential with AbbVie ADCs including telisotuzumab adizutecan (Temab-A).

Why it matters: Largest deal announced on Day 1; another China-origin asset crosses to Big Pharma; intensifies the PD-1×VEGF bispecific race (vs. Summit's ivonescimab).

Sources: AbbVie press release; Fierce Biotech.

docs.title: 3. Novartis + SciNeuro — ~$1.7B Alzheimer's antibody pact
docs.text:
• $165M upfront, up to ~$1.5B in development/regulatory/sales milestones plus royalties. Worldwide license.
  • Asset: de novo amyloid-beta antibody candidates with SciNeuro's proprietary brain-shuttle delivery technology designed to improve BBB penetration.
  • Therapeutic area: Alzheimer's disease; expected close 1H 2026.

Why it matters: Differentiated delivery tech vs. approved anti-amyloid antibodies; positions Novartis in an active neuro-licensing market.

Sources: SciNeuro/PRNewswire; Fierce Biotech.

docs.title: 4. Bristol Myers Squibb — CEO showcases blockbuster pipeline
docs.text:
• CEO Chris Boerner highlighted six multi-billion-dollar candidates: Cobenfy (Alzheimer's psychosis), milvexian (FXIa, J&J-partnered, AFib/stroke), admilparant (IPF), pumitamig (PD-L1×VEGF, BioNTech-partnered), and CELMoDs iberdomide & mezigdomide (multiple myeloma).
  • Pivotal 2026 readouts: three Adept trials (Cobenfy in Alzheimer's psychosis), milvexian, admilparant, both CELMoDs.
  • Targeting >10 new launches by 2030; BD remains a top capital-allocation priority.

Why it matters: Investor narrative for BMS hinges on pipeline diversification past LOEs.

Sources: Fierce Pharma JPM26 Day 1 tracker; Endpoints Q&A with Boerner.

docs.title: 5. Pfizer — obesity strategy on the back of $10B Metsera
docs.text:
• CEO Albert Bourla projected the obesity market reaching $150B by 2030; compared expected demand to the original Viagra rollout.
  • Metsera acquisition (announced Sept 2025, closed Nov 2025) anchors a portfolio built around monthly injectables and oral combos, including PF-3944/MET-097i (ultra-long-acting GLP-1 in Ph2b).
  • Plans up to ~10 Phase 3 obesity trials via the Metsera platform in 2026.

Why it matters: Pfizer's re-entry into obesity after the danuglipron failure; differentiation play vs. Lilly/Novo.

Sources: Pfizer JPM 2026 fireside chat deck (PDF); BioPharma Dive.

docs.title: 6. Amgen — MariTide (maridebart cafraglutide) Phase 2 update
docs.text:
• Monday-evening reveal of Phase 2 obesity and Phase 2 T2D data on the once-monthly GLP-1/GIPR-antagonist peptibody.
  • T2D arm: clinically meaningful HbA1c and body-weight reductions at 24 weeks on monthly dosing; favorable cardiometabolic profile.
  • Tolerability consistent with GLP-1 RA class; six global Phase 3 studies underway.

Why it matters: Reinforces Amgen's positioning as a third obesity major behind Lilly and Novo; monthly dosing as differentiator.

Source: Clinical Trials Arena.

docs.title: 7. BridgeBio — Attruby Q4 commercial beat
docs.text:
• Preliminary Q4 2025 Attruby (acoramidis) net revenue of $146M, ahead of consensus; +35% QoQ.
  • 6,629 unique patient prescriptions from 1,632 prescribers as of Dec 31, 2025.
  • Leerink raised PT to $75; Morgan Stanley initiated Overweight with $96 PT.

Why it matters: Validates ATTR-CM commercial trajectory and BridgeBio's transition to revenue-generating biotech.

Source: BridgeBio investor release.

docs.title: 8. Sarepta — Elevidys re-commitment, prelim 2025 sales
docs.text:
• CEO Doug Ingram doubled down on DMD gene therapy Elevidys despite 2025 safety controversies (two patient deaths, FDA back-and-forth).
  • Preliminary 2025 total sales: $1.86B; Elevidys contributed $898.7M.

Why it matters: Sets the tone for Sarepta's recovery narrative entering 2026.

Source: BioPharma Dive.

docs.title: 9. Biogen — high-dose Spinraza approved by European Commission
docs.text:
• EC marketing authorization for high-dose nusinersen (50 mg/5 mL and 28 mg/5 mL) in 5q SMA, granted same day as Biogen's JPM presentation.
  • Backed by DEVOTE study data in treatment-naïve and previously-treated patients. Already approved in Japan; FDA action by April 3, 2026.

Why it matters: Shores up an aging franchise on the morning Biogen presented its "new Biogen" pivot; CEO Chris Viehbacher emphasized continued immunology build-out via HI-Bio.

Source: Biogen press release.

docs.title: 10. Moderna — 2025 sales beat, 2026 growth guide
docs.text:
• Preliminary unaudited 2025 sales of $1.9B (~$100M above midpoint of guidance).
  • 2026 outlook: up to ~10% sales growth on a "large seasonal vaccine franchise" plus pipeline progression (CEO Stéphane Bancel).

Why it matters: Steadies the Moderna investor narrative post-COVID-revenue cliff.

Source: STAT JPM 2026 Day 1 recap.

docs.title: Smaller items / notable mentions
docs.text:
• J&J fireside chat at 11:15 am ET; pipeline/financial guidance, no headline deal.
  • Regeneron (Schleifer + Yancopoulos) outlined five late-stage near-term readouts across oncology, obesity, complement, anticoagulation, and immunology.
  • Alnylam unveiled "Alnylam 2030" — three pillars: scale with discipline, global TTR leadership, sustainable innovation; cited 300K global ATTR-CM patients with ~80% undiagnosed.
  • CRISPR Therapeutics highlighted CASGEVY global rollout and in vivo cardiovascular/autoimmune programs.
  • Summit Therapeutics presented Monday hours after AbbVie/RemeGen news re-priced the PD-1×VEGF competitive set.
  • Waystar (Matt Hawkins) projected RCM TAM expanding from $20–25B to $55B with AI; touted Iodine acquisition data leverage; processed 7.5B claims in 2025.
  • Advocate Health CEO Eugene Woods cited $1.5B in annual operating savings since the 3-year-old merger.
  • Takeda R&D head Andy Plump publicly noted the absence of major deal announcements Monday morning, hoped for M&A later in the week.
  • Investor Brad Loncar: "This [has] been the slowest JPM for news in a long time."
  • Pre-JPM follow-on financings hit a record $2.6B for the month so far (STAT).

docs.title: Themes emerging by end of Day 1
docs.text:
• AI/bio convergence as headline theme — Lilly–NVIDIA $1B lab framed Day 1; AI also dominated health-tech presentations (Waystar agentic AI).
  • Licensing displacing M&A — Day 1 produced ~$7.3B in announced licensing value (AbbVie/RemeGen, Novartis/SciNeuro) but zero megadeals; multiple commentators flagged a "slow Monday."
  • Obesity remains the gravitational center — Pfizer (Metsera), Amgen (MariTide), and the broader Lilly/Novo backdrop drove a disproportionate share of Day 1 narrative.
  • China-origin assets continue moving west — RC148 (RemeGen) and the SciNeuro brain-shuttle platform both originated in China.

docs.title: Day 2 — Tuesday Jan 13, 2026
docs.text: Day 2 was driven by big-pharma strategy presentations rather than blockbuster M&A, with AstraZeneca, Novo Nordisk, GSK, Bayer, Roche, Pfizer, Sanofi, Gilead and Sandoz on the main stage. Two notable deals broke during the day — AstraZeneca's tuck-in of AI partner Modella and Novartis' $50M radioligand license from China's Zonsen PepLib — alongside multiple mid-cap pipeline updates. The political/regulatory undercurrent was loud: former FDA oncology chief Richard Pazdur made his first public remarks since departing the agency, and CMS chief Mehmet Oz fielded hospital-exec questions at an off-site event.

docs.title: 1. AstraZeneca acquires Modella AI
docs.text:
• AZ buying Boston-based Modella AI; financial terms undisclosed.
  • Builds on a multi-year research collaboration signed in July 2025; CFO Aradhana Sarin called the partnership a "test drive."
  • Modella's multi-modal foundation models and AI agents will be integrated into AZ's oncology R&D for biomarker discovery, clinical-development acceleration, and data-driven decisioning.
  • Described in trade-press coverage as the first acquisition of an AI firm by a big pharma.

Why it matters: Signals big pharma moving from AI partnerships to outright ownership of multimodal-AI platforms in oncology.

Sources: Modella AI release; Pharmaceutical Technology; Fierce Biotech tracker.

docs.title: 2. Novartis licenses peptide radioligand from Zonsen PepLib (China)
docs.text:
• $50M cash upfront to Zonsen PepLib Biotech for an undisclosed peptide-based radioligand therapy asset.
  • Exclusive worldwide license; Novartis takes development and commercialization; PepLib eligible for undisclosed milestones plus tiered royalties.

Why it matters: Extends Novartis' leadership in radioligand therapy and continues the trend of big-pharma in-licensing from Chinese biotechs.

Sources: Endpoints News; BusinessWire.

docs.title: 3. AstraZeneca strategy update — $80B by 2030 reaffirmed
docs.text:
• Revenue up 11% through Q3 2025; oncology contributing roughly half of growth.
  • CFO Sarin called the $80B revenue target "very much within reach."
  • Near-term launch focus: hypertension drug baxdrostat, breast-cancer candidate camizestrant, myasthenia gravis drug gefurulimab.
  • Multiple Phase 3 readouts expected in 2026 across oncology, immunology, respiratory.

Source: BioSpace.

docs.title: 4. Novo Nordisk — "mastering" DTP cash-pay; Wegovy pill ramping
docs.text:
• CEO Maziar Mike Doustdar acknowledged a "difficult 2025"; 2026 priorities = commercial execution, R&D pipeline, organizational focus.
  • Oral Wegovy reached ~3,100 patients since its Jan. 5 launch — first oral GLP-1 for obesity in the U.S.
  • Plans to advance higher-dose injectable Wegovy and "several" new obesity/diabetes assets into clinic in 2026.
  • Novo took ~200 meetings during JPM week. Pulling back from non-diabetes/obesity indications.
  • CSO Martin Holst Lange (recently promoted) said Novo is craving "different flavors" of pipeline innovation.

Source: Fierce Pharma JPM26 Day 2 tracker.

docs.title: 5. Gilead — "unprecedented opportunities"; Kite anito-cel filing
docs.text:
• CEO Daniel O'Day said Gilead has "the most robust pipeline in the almost 40-year history of the company"; up to 10 launches in new/additional indications by end of 2027.
  • Kite confirmed FDA submission of anito-cel (BCMA CAR-T for relapsed/refractory multiple myeloma, partnered with Arcellx) before year-end 2025; targeting differentiated one-time treatment in 2026 with 14–17 day turnaround.

Why it matters: Anito-cel positions Kite to compete directly with J&J/Legend's Carvykti.

Source: STAT News.

docs.title: 6. GSK — 15 "scale launches" by 2031
docs.text:
• Head of R&D noted GSK achieved all five targeted approvals in 2025.
  • Goal: 15 scale launches each with potential peak sales above $2B, fueling growth through 2031.
  • Strong execution narrative and pipeline momentum highlighted.

Source: Evaluate JPM2026 Day Two Update.

docs.title: 7. Bayer — Nubeqa and Kerendia anchor post-Xarelto plan
docs.text:
• 9M 2025 sales: Nubeqa (prostate cancer) ~€1.7B (~$2B); Kerendia (kidney/heart failure) ~€600M (~$700M).
  • Strategy: navigate Xarelto patent cliff while elevating five high-value assets across oncology, cardiometabolic, specialty.
  • Kerendia framed as "next blockbuster in the making."

Source: Fierce Pharma JPM26 Day 2 tracker.

docs.title: 8. Roche — three-pillar growth strategy
docs.text:
• CEO Teresa Graham: maximize current portfolio (17 blockbusters generating $44.5B YTD through Sept 2025), deliver 2026–27 launches, expand into Alzheimer's and obesity.
  • Giredestrant (next-gen SERD) positioned to advance ER+ breast-cancer SOC via combos with PI3K and CDK4/6 inhibitors.

Source: Clinical Trials Arena.

docs.title: 9. Pfizer — Metsera assets and 10 Phase 3 starts
docs.text:
• Plans 10 Phase 3 starts by end of 2026 for Metsera's MET-097i (long-acting injectable GLP-1) following the Metsera acquisition.
  • 2026 priorities: maximize value of recent transactions, deliver R&D milestones, invest for future growth, embed AI across the business.

Source: PharmExec.

docs.title: 10. Lonza — fifth major Vacaville commercial contract
docs.text:
• Lonza disclosed a fifth significant commercial contract at the 956,000-sq-ft Vacaville, CA biologics site (acquired from Roche for $1.2B in 2024).
  • Additional contracts in late-stage negotiation; one of the world's largest mammalian biologics facilities.

Source: Fierce Pharma JPM26 Day 2 tracker.

docs.title: 11. BioNTech — multiproduct oncology by 2030
docs.text:
• Ugur Sahin presented at 2:15pm PT Tuesday.
  • 2026 = "catalyst-rich": 7 late-stage data readouts, 15 Phase 3 trials ongoing by year end.
  • Three-modality oncology strategy: immunomodulators, ADCs, mRNA cancer immunotherapies.
  • Key 2026 readouts: HER2 ADC (TPAM), Gotistobart, BNT113 (HPV+ head/neck), pumitamig (with BMS, June 2025 partnership worth up to $7.6B), personalized vaccine in high-risk colorectal.

Sources: BioNTech IR; Pharmaceutical Technology.

docs.title: Smaller items / notable mentions
docs.text:
• Sandoz (CEO Richard Saynor) framed itself as "the only pure-play generic and biosimilar player with global reach"; biosimilar pipeline of 27 assets targeting ~$200B in originator sales; 400+ generics targeting ~$220B.
  • Acadia — analysts modeling $834M Nuplazid and $621M Daybue revenue.
  • Agios — touting Dec. 23 FDA approval of Acvezmi (thalassemia); $10B+ market opportunity by 2030; AG-181 (PKU) and AG-236 (polycythemia vera) flagged as ~$1B each.
  • Sarepta — doubling down on Elevidys in ambulatory DMD; expanding field force; awaiting Endeavor cohort 8 readout late 2026.
  • Biogen — CEO Viehbacher pitched "the new Biogen": diversified neuroscience, rare disease and revitalized pipeline.
  • Travere — disclosed FDA extended its sNDA review for Filspari/sparsentan in FSGS; new PDUFA April 13, 2026.
  • Mid-cap pipeline progress flagged by Evaluate: Crinetics, Cogent, Nuvalent, Edgewise.
  • Mirador Therapeutics — closed $250M Series B (OrbiMed, Atlas Venture among investors).
  • Off-site policy events: Richard Pazdur's first public remarks post-FDA departure at STAT@JPM (warning on politicization, voucher transparency); Mehmet Oz and Trump health officials briefed hospital execs on Medicaid and vaccines.

docs.title: Themes dominant on Day 2
docs.text:
• AI moves from partnership to ownership in pharma (AZ–Modella as exemplar).
  • China in-licensing pace remains high (Novartis–PepLib, building on AbbVie–RemeGen on Day 1); China-sourced assets are now mainstream pipeline inputs, not bargain bins.
  • Big-pharma narrative is execution and late-stage delivery, not transformative M&A — the rumored Merck/Revolution Medicines $32B deal stayed a rumor through Day 2.
  • Regulatory/political uncertainty is a recurring sidebar: FDA voucher program scrutiny, Pazdur warnings, MFN pricing fallout for Sanofi, RFK Jr. vaccine rhetoric hitting Sanofi's Beyfortus.
  • Obesity remains the most-watched therapeutic area: Novo's commercial recovery vs. Pfizer/Metsera entry vs. Roche teasing obesity entry.

docs.title: Day 3 — Wednesday Jan 14, 2026
docs.text:
Day 3 unfolded as the conference's "final full day" with no megadeal materializing despite morning anticipation among bankers; instead the day skewed toward strategic narratives — AbbVie's post-Humira runway, Sanofi navigating U.S. vaccine policy turmoil, Novo Nordisk telegraphing M&A appetite under a new CEO, and a parade of mid-cap and rare-disease names making their case. Dominant Day 3 threads: policy/politics, China innovation pace, obesity-pipeline jockeying, and rare disease as a pivotal-year story.

Cross-day note: The widely-cited Boston Scientific / Penumbra $14.5B acquisition was announced Thursday Jan 15 (Day 4), not Day 3. See Day 4.

docs.title: 1. AbbVie — "clear line of sight" to growth into the 2030s
docs.text:
• CFO Scott Reents in a Wednesday fireside chat said AbbVie has a "clear line of sight" extending into the 2030s, citing 8% 2025 revenue growth and 19% growth in its growth platform.
  • Issued 2027 guidance of $31B combined for Skyrizi (~$20B) and Rinvoq (~$11B), now three years past the Humira LOE cliff.
  • Came on the heels of AbbVie's Day-1 $5.6B RemeGen licensing deal (RC148, PD-1/VEGF bispecific); Day 3 framing emphasized organic engine, not M&A.

Why it matters: Re-anchors the post-Humira AbbVie story as durable rather than transitional.

Source: Fierce Pharma.

docs.title: 2. Sanofi — vaccine policy and RSV probe dominate the Wednesday press event
docs.text:
• R&D chief Houman Ashrafian and CEO Paul Hudson addressed renewed U.S. scrutiny of immunizations following CDC's narrowed childhood RSV recommendation, which directly touches Beyfortus.
  • Sanofi flagged a recent surprise FDA rejection (last week before JPM) as an outstanding hurdle entering 2026.
  • Hudson also discussed the company's late-2025 "most favored nation" pricing arrangement with the White House, which has temporarily skirted U.S. import-tariff threats.

Why it matters: Vaccines remain a policy-risk asset class for Merck, Pfizer, GSK, and Sanofi heading into 2026.

Sources: Fierce Biotech; Endpoints.

docs.title: 3. Novo Nordisk — M&A "with intention" under new CEO
docs.text:
• Novo's BD team logged ~200 meetings during JPM week; CEO Mike Doustdar laid out 2026 priorities: rolling out semaglutide 7.2 mg, launching oral Wegovy, expanding U.S. cash-pay channels, and improving supply.
  • Novo signaled appetite for novel obesity/diabetes mechanisms, tolerability/dosing improvements, rare blood diseases, and obesity-complication adjacencies.
  • STAT framed Day 3 as the day Novo "has an eye on M&A" after losing the Metsera bidding war to Pfizer.

Why it matters: Confirms Novo is a structural buyer in the obesity ecosystem despite ceding the lead position to Lilly.

Sources: STAT; BioSpace.

docs.title: 4. Amgen — MariTide Phase 2 (mid-week reprise)
docs.text:
• Amgen reiterated Phase 2 MariTide data: up to 20% mean weight loss in obesity-only patients and up to 17% in obesity + T2D.
  • T2D arm: clinically meaningful HbA1c and body-weight reduction at 24 weeks on once-monthly dosing.
  • Six global Phase 3 studies ongoing; a Phase 3 in T2D being prepared; safety profile consistent with GLP-1RA class.

Why it matters: Positions MariTide as a potential first once-monthly T2D therapy and Amgen's anchor in the obesity contest.

Coverage is bundled across mid-week; exact session day not pinned to Wednesday.

Source: Clinical Trials Arena.

docs.title: 5. Regeneron — defends Dupixent strategy, M&A discipline
docs.text:
• CEO Leonard Schleifer defended Dupixent's role: now approved in 8 type-2 inflammation indications with annualized global net sales >$19B (Q4 run-rate).
  • Plans $6B 2026 R&D spend; flagged 2031 as the Dupixent LOE horizon.
  • Said large M&A often results in "value destruction" and that acquirers "in most cases, dramatically overpay."

Why it matters: Regeneron stakes out a discipline posture as peers chase deals through patent cliffs.

Sources: Endpoints; Pharmaceutical Technology.

docs.title: 6. Gilead — broadening virology beyond HIV/HCV
docs.text:
• CMO Dietmar Berger detailed plans to extend Gilead's antiviral footprint to respiratory viruses and pandemic-potential pathogens at a JPM-adjacent event.
  • Builds on lenacapavir momentum; separate Fierce coverage that week framed Gilead as eyeing deals from a "position of strength."

Why it matters: Signals Gilead's intent to convert HIV cash flows into a broader infectious-disease franchise.

Source: Fierce Biotech.

docs.title: 7. Legend Biotech — operating profit guide for 2026, Carvykti scale-up
docs.text:
• Updated JPM presentation guides to company-wide operating profit in 2026; Carvykti franchise hit operating profit in Q3 2025.
  • 10,000+ patients treated globally; Raritan facility expansion targets up to 10,000 patients/year capacity; 279+ sites across 14 markets.
  • ~$1B cash and time deposits as of Sep 30, 2025.

Why it matters: Cell-therapy economics inflecting toward profitability in commercial CAR-T (with J&J).

Sources: Legend Biotech IR; TipRanks.

docs.title: 8. Pfizer / BioNTech — COVID 2025-2026 formula immunogenicity readout
docs.text:
• Phase 3 cohort of LP.8.1-adapted monovalent COVID-19 vaccine met immunogenicity endpoints in adults 65+ and 18–64 with risk conditions; ≥4-fold rise in LP.8.1-neutralizing titers at 14 days.

Why it matters: Supports continued strain-updated COVID franchise amid a more skeptical U.S. policy backdrop.

Source: Pfizer press release.

docs.title: Smaller items / notable mentions
docs.text:
• Biotech CEO Sisterhood second-annual Wednesday meetup drew "hundreds" — attendance roughly doubled from 2025.
  • Novartis CMO Shreeram Aradhye on China speed: cautioned against simple speed comparisons, citing different ecosystem, trial-enrollment economics, and payer structure.
  • IPO market chatter: as many as ~20 biotech IPOs could price in 2026 if windows hold (BioPharma Dive).
  • Rare-disease Wednesday spotlight: Rocket Pharma CEO Gaurav Shah called 2026 a "year of execution"; REGENXBIO CEO Curran Simpson framed it as "really pivotal" pending Hunter syndrome (MPS II) approval; Agios highlighted PK-activator franchise growth.
  • Evaluate Day 3 readout: notable presenters included AbbVie, UCB, Arcus, Disc Medicine, Immunome, Legend, 4DMT, Agios, Anavex, Neurogene, Tango.
  • Lonza added contracts at the Vacaville, CA biologics site it bought from Roche for $1.2B in 2024.
  • No Wednesday megadeal materialized; one attendee told Fierce some companies appear to be holding announcements for the TD Cowen Health Care Conference in March.

docs.title: Themes dominant on Day 3
docs.text:
• Policy and politics threading through pharma narratives — Sanofi's vaccine/tariff overhang, Pfizer/BioNTech's COVID franchise reframe, Moderna's break-even-by-2028 path.
  • Obesity competition shifts from drug-data tournament to commercial/distribution warfare (Novo's DTP/oral-Wegovy push, Amgen's once-monthly differentiation, Pfizer-Metsera looming).
  • Rare disease and cell/gene therapy as the "year of execution" story, aided by FDA's late-2025 plausible-mechanism pathway.
  • Capital-discipline rhetoric (Regeneron) coexisting with active BD pipelines (Novo, Gilead) — few megadeals on Wednesday but strong tone of asset-centric, mid-size dealmaking.

docs.title: Day 4 — Thursday Jan 15, 2026
docs.text: The closing day of the 44th J.P. Morgan Healthcare Conference was, as expected, a wind-down — but with one significant late-week deal: Boston Scientific's $14.5B acquisition of Penumbra. Otherwise the day shifted to small- and micro-cap presenters, Chinese pharma, an interview with Regeneron's chief scientist George Yancopoulos, and end-of-week synthesis from the trade press. The mood reporters distilled at the close was one of "pragmatic optimism" and "restraint" rather than fireworks.

docs.title: 1. Boston Scientific — $14.5B acquisition of Penumbra
docs.text:
• Press release dated Jan 15, 2026.
  • Adds Penumbra's stroke / peripheral vascular / venous thromboembolism thrombectomy portfolio to BSx's interventional cardiology and vascular franchises.
  • Largest single deal of JPM week 2026; only true megadeal of the conference.

Why it matters: The exception that proves the rule — JPM26 was overwhelmingly licensing-driven; this one strategic medtech acquisition stood out against an otherwise megadeal-free week.

Source: Boston Scientific press release.

docs.title: 2. Clover Health — on track for first full-year GAAP profit
docs.text:
• CEO Andrew Toy presented Thursday at 11:15 a.m. ET.
  • Clover said it is on track for its first full-year GAAP profit in 2026.
  • 53% YoY membership growth in the most recent annual enrollment period; ~153,000 members entering the year, with 97% in the company's central PPO.
  • The PPO plan claims a #1 national ranking on core HEDIS quality measures.

Why it matters: Clover joins Alignment Healthcare in a counter-narrative to MA giants pulling back; signals smaller, tech-enabled MA plans may pick up share as larger players retreat.

Sources: Modern Healthcare; Fierce Healthcare.

docs.title: 3. Regeneron — Yancopoulos interview
docs.text:
• STAT sat down with Regeneron co-founder/chief scientist George Yancopoulos on Day 4. (Regeneron's formal JPM presentation was Monday.)
  • Outspoken on the Trump administration's "most-favored nations" drug-pricing policy — explained why Regeneron was the only one of 17 companies receiving presidential pricing letters that had not yet struck a deal at that point. (Regeneron later signed a pricing deal in April 2026.)
  • Voiced skepticism about current AI applications in medicine, calling for careful oversight.
  • On gene therapy, he framed scaling as the unsolved problem.

Why it matters: Highest-profile scientific voice at Regeneron pushing back on both AI hype and federal pricing pressure on the conference's final day.

Sources: STAT — Yancopoulos profile; STAT — Day 4 top stories.

docs.title: 4. Day 4 small/mid/micro-cap presenters
docs.text:
• Inventiva (MASH): Phase 3 for lanifibranor is fully enrolled; Phase 2b F2–F3 data + safety profile cited as setting up 2026 readouts.
  • Precigen: debuted as a commercial-stage company following the 2025 FDA approval of PAPZIMEOS (zopapogene imadenovec-drba) for adult recurrent respiratory papillomatosis; high coverage rates and rapid uptake.
  • Biocon: outlined 2026 launches across biosimilars and GLP-1s; framed itself as moving from post-acquisition consolidation into an "accelerate" phase.
  • Oruka, Vicore: clinical/commercial catalysts in dermatology, rare disease, and IPF.
  • Atea (HCV), Corbus (ADC + obesity), Molecular Partners (radiotherapeutics): each presented as micro-cap update stories.
  • Rakuten Medical: closed the day with a photoimmunotherapy platform update.

Why it matters: These are the catalyst stocks BD teams scout on the quiet final day; Evaluate framed Day 4 as "BD signal day" rather than headline day.

Source: Evaluate Day Four.

docs.title: 5. Chinese pharma — Hengrui and Kelun-Biotech
docs.text:
• Hengrui reported 2025 sales through Q3 of >$3.2B and 21 NDA/BLA approvals.
  • Hengrui flagged a $1.5B Hong Kong IPO and a cumulative ~$16B in out-licensing deals (including a partnership with GSK), alongside its Shanghai listing.
  • Kelun-Biotech presented oncology and bispecific/multispecific conjugate platforms.

Why it matters: Reinforces the week's dominant "China is the story" narrative on the final day.

Source: Evaluate Day Four.

docs.title: Tone: restraint and execution, not fireworks
docs.text:
• Fierce Biotech ("All the meetings, none of the megadeals") and STAT's STATus Report (Alex Hogan) both used the words "restraint" and "fundamentals" to describe the week.
  • C&EN: "Despite few big announcements at JPM, biotech investors optimistic."

docs.title: Capital markets / M&A outlook
docs.text:
• pharmaphorum and Ballard Spahr: no pharma megamergers; many partnerships, smaller tech-tuck-in M&A, and a few IPO announcements. Pre-JPM Lilly–Ventyx ($1B+) acquisition was cited as the largest near-conference deal. (BSx–Penumbra $14.5B medtech was the only true megadeal during the week.)
  • Pharmaceutical Technology: ~$8.3B in announced JPM-week deals; emphasis on oncology (PD-1/VEGF bispecifics, ADCs), obesity, and neurodegeneration.
  • IPO forecast (HSBC Innovation Banking's Jonathan Norris, cited by STAT/BioSpace): up to ~20 biotech IPOs may price in 2026 if conditions hold; <12 priced in 2025 (lowest since at least 2018); most 2025 IPOs trade above offer, with Sionna and Maze more than doubling. Aktis Oncology ($318M), Eikon Therapeutics (~$381M, biggest biotech IPO since 2024) and Veradermics (~$256.3M, NYSE: MANE) were the headline IPO/IPO-target stories.

docs.title: AI: from hype to ROI
docs.text:
• STATus Report (Alex Hogan): AI is "table stakes," exemplified by the Lilly–NVIDIA expanded partnership announced on Day 1.
  • Advisory.com top-5 takeaways and Mondaq/Ballard Spahr both wrote that AI conversations shifted to measurable ROI and compliance rather than promise.
  • Hogan Lovells flagged AI compliance and BIOSECURE as top device-supply-chain concerns.

docs.title: Therapeutic-area winners and losers
docs.text:
• Winners: oncology (ADCs, bispecifics, radiopharmaceuticals); obesity (oral GLP-1s, combinations — Pfizer's Bourla compared the cash-pay obesity opportunity to Viagra during the week); rare disease; neuroscience; immunology.
  • Headwinds: FDA dysfunction was a recurring complaint — Sanofi singled out the Dec 24, 2025 Complete Response Letter on tolebrutinib, citing the FDA's skipped advisory committee step.

docs.title: Surprises / what was notably absent
docs.text:
• Notably absent: a JPM-week pharma megamerger. Fierce Biotech's "All the meetings, none of the megadeals" was the canonical framing.
  • Notably present: China dominance (the "Sputnik moment" framing from BioPharma Dive on Day 1 carried through to Day 4 with Hengrui/Kelun).
